docs.title: About
docs.text:
LinkedIn | GitHub | Podcast | Email

Andrea Dainese works alongside organizations as a cybersecurity advisor with over 20 years of experience protecting critical infrastructure and industrial control systems (ICS/OT). He helps organizations define a concrete and effective security strategy, aligned with international standards, leveraging automation to scale compliance, defenses, and optimize operational processes.

Known in the technical community as the father of UNetLab (now EVE-NG), he is an author, podcast host, and active mentor for professionals looking to grow into CISO-level roles.

He also brings digital security awareness into schools, educating students and adults on how to recognize and defend against cyber threats.

For Andrea, hacking means understanding something deeply and making it better, and that includes oneself. After years of growing more sensitive to the cold, he decided to stop avoiding it and train for it instead. Cold-water immersion and daily cold showers became a practice in consistency and self-discipline, and a reminder that discomfort fades if you stay with it. He brings the same mindset to his work: understand the system, respect the process, and keep going.

docs.title: Introduction to network automation with Ansible
Introduction to network automation with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Welcome to our series focused on Network Automation with Ansible! This series is designed to help you streamline operations, standardize workflows, and manage multiple devices in significantly less time. Network automation is no longer just the domain of network engineers; it is now expanding to include Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) teams.

While there are various frameworks available for automation, Ansible stands out as an excellent choice. It does not require programming skills, making it accessible with a relatively easy learning curve.

Our Ansible Workbook for DevNetOps is a comprehensive guide for students in my network automation courses. It provides useful "recipes" to help you develop your own automations using Ansible. By the end of this series, you'll be able to design and write Ansible playbooks to automate tasks across numerous network devices.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Become familiar with Ansible terminology.
  • Learn how to approach an automation project with Ansible.
  • Understand the pros and cons of Ansible.
  • Develop skills to write Ansible playbooks and roles.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Some prerequisites are covered in other courses:

  • Automation fundamentals: Approaching automation projects.
  • DevOps fundamentals: Understanding DevOps methodology and tools.
  • Infrastructure as Code: Managing infrastructure with coding practices.
  • Automation frameworks: We will focus on Ansible, but also discuss its pros and cons compared to other frameworks. The choice of framework should be a result of the project needs, not a prerequisite.
  • Modeling: Abstracting infrastructure into data structures for automation.
  • Golden configurations: Approaches, pros, and cons.
  • Templating: Tools for writing parameterized templates.
  • Text scraping: Converting human-readable text into data structures.
  • Parsers: Writing and modifying parsers for text scraping.

docs.title: Required Tools
docs.text:
You'll need the following tools, described in a specific course:

  • A development server (Ubuntu Linux 22.04)
  • A programming language (Python 3.9)
  • A distributed version control system (Git)
  • A testing environment (EVE-NG)
  • An IDE (Visual Studio Code)

docs.title: Required Skill Sets
docs.text:
• Linux: Ability to install and configure.
  • Python: Ability to read and write simple scripts.
  • Git: Ability to manage repositories.
  • Vi/Vim: Ability to edit and exit.
  • RegEx: Ability to read and write simple regex.
  • Jinja2: Ability to write simple templates.
  • Parsers: Ability to write and modify templates.

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
Keep these essential points in mind:

  • Network automation engineers must often find documentation through research (e.g., Googling and/or reverse engineering).
  • Network automation engineers need to write code and prototypes (sometimes referred to as "spaghetti-code").
  • Developers can turn prototypes into robust software, but this is not the task of network automation engineers.
  • Developers often lack the specific networking skills and vendor knowledge to write network automation software but are better at writing code.

docs.title: Preparing your Ansible environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Ansible, based on Python, can be easily installed using the package manager PIP. The functionalities of Ansible available obviously depend on its version, which is closely tied to the version of Python in use. The examples we will see later presume having Ansible core 2.15.9, and Python 3.10.

In this regard, reference should be made to the EVE-NG for DevNetOps, which describes in detail how to obtain your own development laboratory. In particular, we will refer to the GitHub repository for DevNetOps courses available in /opt.

Let's prepare a dedicated Python environment and install Ansible:

python3.10 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r /opt/courses/requirements.txt

We can verify the installed version by running:

$ ansible --version
ansible [core 2.15.10]
  config file = None
  configured module search path = ['/home/dev/.ansible/plugins/modules', '/usr/share/ansible/plugins/modules']
  ansible python module location = /home/dev/venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/ansible
  ansible collection location = /home/dev/.ansible/collections:/usr/share/ansible/collections
  executable location = /home/dev/venv/bin/ansible
  python version = 3.10.13 (main, Oct 29 2023, 09:51:31) [GCC 9.4.0] (/home/dev/venv/bin/python3.10)
  jinja version = 3.1.3
  libyaml = True

docs.title: Introduction to Ansible Automation
docs.text: 01 August 2024

docs.title: Introduction to Ansible Automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Ansible is often described as an agentless automation framework. However, it relies on Python, which must be installed along with certain modules on the hosts where playbooks are executed. In this sense, Python acts as the necessary "agent" on the remote system.

Originally designed to automate Linux hosts, Ansible has expanded to support various systems, including Windows, networking devices, and security appliances.

In this series, we'll focus on using Ansible for automating network devices. For these purposes, Ansible truly functions in an agentless manner.

docs.title: Declarative vs. Procedural
docs.text:
There are two main approaches to automation: declarative and procedural.

  • Declarative Approach: You define the desired state of a system. The automation system figures out the steps to transition the current state to the desired state. Terraform is a popular example of this approach.
  • Procedural Approach: You specify the exact steps the automation system must take to achieve the desired state. This method is generally more intuitive as it follows the human thought process of breaking tasks into smaller sub-tasks. Troubleshooting is also simpler due to the absence of underlying "magic." Ansible is a prime example of this approach.

Ansible is often considered a hybrid system because some modules allow for declaring a desired state, which Ansible then translates into multiple sub-tasks. For instance, the community.vmware.vmware_guest module can create a virtual machine in a single task (declarative), but the VM depends on a pre-existing vSwitch (procedural).

There's also a third concept to consider: immutability. An immutable approach involves defining instances that cannot be modified. Any change requires redefining the instance from scratch. This approach is common in container management and can be applied to network automation through golden configurations.

docs.title: Pros and Cons of Ansible
docs.text:
Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of Ansible will help determine if it's the right framework for your project.

Pros:

  • No Programming Skills Required: Ansible uses YAML for its playbooks, which is human-readable and does not require complex programming knowledge. This lowers the entry barrier, allowing network engineers and administrators to automate tasks without needing to learn a programming language.
  • Idempotency: Ansible ensures that running a playbook multiple times will result in the same state on the managed hosts. This feature reduces the risk of errors and ensures consistency across deployments, making it reliable for continuous integration and delivery pipelines.
  • Procedural Approach: Ansible playbooks follow a step-by-step approach, which aligns with the way humans naturally think about task execution. This makes playbooks easier to write, understand, and debug. It allows for clear and organized automation workflows.
  • Integrated Documentation: Tasks within Ansible playbooks can include descriptions and comments. This serves as in-line documentation, making it easier to understand the purpose and function of each task without needing separate documentation files.
  • Compliance Checks: Ansible playbooks can be used to verify if network devices or systems comply with predefined configurations. This ensures that configurations adhere to company policies and standards, enhancing security and governance.
  • Standardization: Playbooks provide a standardized method to execute tasks and manage configurations. This promotes consistency across different environments and reduces the variability and errors caused by manual processes.
  • Reusable Code: Ansible allows for the reuse of roles and collections across multiple playbooks. This encourages modular design and reduces duplication of code, saving time and effort in maintaining automation scripts.
  • Sensitive Data Protection: Ansible Vault can encrypt sensitive data like passwords and API keys. This enhances security by ensuring that sensitive information is not exposed in plain text within playbooks.
  • Troubleshooting: Ansible allows isolating and running individual steps to identify and fix errors. This makes the debugging process more straightforward, as you can focus on specific tasks that may be causing issues.
  • Multiple Connection Methods: Ansible can connect to managed nodes using various methods like SSH, local connections, WinRM, and network connections. This flexibility allows Ansible to manage a wide range of devices and platforms, increasing its applicability in diverse environments.
  • User Interfaces: Tools like Ansible Tower and AWX provide graphical interfaces for managing Ansible automation. These interfaces simplify the execution and monitoring of playbooks, making it easier to manage large-scale automation.

Cons:

  • Performance: Ansible's performance can be slower compared to other automation tools, especially in large-scale environments. Optimizing playbooks for speed requires specific strategies.
  • Complexity in Statements: Writing complex logic in playbooks, such as conditional statements (if-then-else) and loops, can be non-intuitive. This can make playbooks harder to read and maintain, requiring a deeper understanding of Ansible’s syntax and capabilities.
  • Troubleshooting: Debugging playbooks can be complex and time-consuming. Errors can be hard to trace, especially when dealing with large playbooks or complex workflows. Effective troubleshooting often requires experience and familiarity with Ansible.
  • Limited Callback Plugins: The options for customizing output and logging via callback plugins are limited. Ansible tends to operate as a stand-alone system, making it harder to integrate with some external monitoring and logging tools.
  • Breaking Changes: Major Ansible versions can introduce changes that break existing playbooks. This requires continuous updates and testing of playbooks to ensure compatibility, adding maintenance overhead.
  • Module Limitations: While Ansible supports a wide range of platforms, not all platforms are equally supported. Some platforms might lack comprehensive module support, necessitating custom module development or workarounds.

By understanding these pros and cons, you can better determine whether Ansible is the right automation tool for your specific needs and projects.

docs.title: Ansible Components
docs.text:
Understanding the core components of Ansible is essential to effectively using this powerful automation tool. Each component plays a crucial role in how Ansible functions and interacts with managed hosts. Here's a detailed look at the key components:

  • Data Format: YAML. YAML (Yet Another Markup Language) is a human-readable data serialization standard that Ansible uses to define playbooks and variable files. YAML’s readability makes it easy for users to write and understand Ansible playbooks without requiring extensive programming knowledge. Its structure is straightforward and intuitive, reducing the likelihood of syntax errors.
  • Templating: Jinja. Jinja is a templating engine for Python, which Ansible uses to render dynamic content in playbooks. Jinja2 allows for the creation of flexible and dynamic configurations. With Jinja, users can use variables, control structures (like loops and conditionals), and filters to generate configuration files or scripts dynamically based on the specific needs of each host.
  • Parsers: TextFSM, NTC-Templates, PyATS, TTP... Parsers are tools that Ansible uses to process and convert raw text data into structured data.
  • Plugins: Python. Plugins extend Ansible’s core functionality. They are small pieces of code written in Python that can be used to add new capabilities to Ansible.

Several interfaces can simplify playbook execution, such as:

  • Ansible Navigator: A command-line tool that provides an enhanced user experience for running and troubleshooting playbooks.
  • Ansible Tower: A web-based interface that provides enterprise-level features like role-based access control, job scheduling, and logging.
  • Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform: A complete enterprise framework for automating across IT operations, including security, network, and infrastructure.
  • AWX: The open-source version of Ansible Tower, providing a web-based interface and API for managing Ansible playbooks.
  • ARA Records Ansible: A tool that records Ansible playbook runs and provides reporting and analysis.
  • eNMS: An open-source network management system that integrates with Ansible to provide automation and orchestration capabilities.

docs.title: Learning Approach
docs.text: We'll adopt a learn-by-doing approach, starting with simple cases and gradually expanding them. Documenting your work and maintaining an updated set of recipes will be invaluable for implementing specific scenarios in the future.

docs.title: Ansible inventory
docs.text: 02 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible inventory
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

The inventory is the source of truth containing the information that Ansible will use to connect to devices. The inventory also allows defining variables at the host or group level. Particularly, variables can be used, in advanced scenarios, to define all infrastructure parameters, such as interfaces, IP addresses, router ID, etc.

Ansible supports both static and dynamic inventories. The static inventory is defined by a file in INI or YAML format, while the dynamic inventory is an executable that prints JSON to standard output.

We must also pay attention to selecting the correct protocol for communication with remote devices and the correct platform based on the device. In the upcoming examples, we will connect to Cisco IOS devices, which require executing commands via an SSH connection. In this regard, we need to set:

  • ansible_connection: network_cli, indicating that we will use CLI over an SSH channel;
  • ansible_network_os: ios, indicating that we will use the module written for Cisco IOS devices.

Initially, we assume that we can log in with a privileged user. We will address how to manage non-privileged users later.

docs.title: Static Inventory in INI Format
docs.text:
The static inventory in INI format has the following structure:

[all]
r1.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.21

[routers]
r[1:9].example.com

[routers:vars]
ansible_user=admin
ansible_ssh_pass=cisco
ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios

All devices should be part of group all then he can be inserted into additional groups. We can also define host level or group level vars.

We can verify the correctness of our inventory with the following command:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --list

docs.title: Static Inventory in YAML Format
docs.text:
The static inventory in YAML format has the following structure:

all:
  hosts:
    r1.example.com:
      ansible_host: 169.254.1.21

routers:
  hosts:
    r[1:9].example.com:
  vars:
    ansible_user: admin
    ansible_ssh_pass: cisco
    ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
    ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios

We can verify the correctness of our inventory with the following command:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list

docs.title: Dynamic Inventory in JSON Format
docs.text:
As described earlier, the dynamic inventory must write in the standard output the inventory in JSON format according to the following structure:

{
    "_meta": {
        "hostvars": {
            "r1.example.com": {
                "ansible_host": "169.254.1.21"
            }
        }
    },
    "routers": {
        "hosts": [
            "r1.example.com"
        ],
        "vars": {
            "ansible_connection": "ansible.netcommon.network_cli",
            "ansible_network_os": "cisco.ios.ios",
            "ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco",
            "ansible_user": "admin"
        }
    }
}

Now, suppose the following CSV contains our inventory:

FQDN;IP Address;Groups
r1.example.com;169.254.1.21;routers
r2.example.com;169.254.1.22;routers
sw1.example.com;169.254.1.101;switches,core
sw2.example.com;169.254.1.102;switches,core
sw3.example.com;169.254.1.103;switches,access
sw4.example.com;169.254.1.104;switches,access
sw5.example.com;169.254.1.105;switches,access
sw6.example.com;169.254.1.106;switches,access

We can create a simple script using Python that dynamically creates an inventory. First, let's create the inventory structure:

inventory = {
    "_meta": {
        "hostvars": {},
        "vars": {
            "ansible_connection": "ansible.netcommon.network_cli",
            "ansible_network_os": "cisco.ios.ios",
        },
    },
    "routers": {
        "hosts": [],
        "vars": {"ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco", "ansible_user": "admin"},
    },
    "switches": {
        "hosts": [],
        "vars": {"ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco", "ansible_user": "admin"},
    },
    "core": {
        "hosts": [],
    },
    "access": {
        "hosts": [],
    },
}

At this point, we are not concerned with security and defer handling passwords to a subsequent lesson.

Next, we read the CSV file, line by line:

with open(INVENTORY_CSV, "r") as fh:
    csv_reader = csv.reader(fh, delimiter=";", dialect="excel")
    next(csv_reader, None)  # skip first row (header)

    for row in csv_reader:
        # Parse each row

For each row, we populate the template described earlier:

fqdn = row[0]
ip_address = row[1]
groups = row[2].split(",")

# Add device to group "all"
inventory["_meta"]["hostvars"][fqdn] = {"ansible_host": ip_address}

for group in groups:
    # Add device to group
    inventory[group]["hosts"].append(fqdn)

Finally, we print the inventory in a readable format to standard output:

# Print inventory
print(json.dumps(inventory, sort_keys=True, indent=2))

We can verify the correctness of our inventory with the following command:

python3 inventory.py
ansible-inventory -i inventory.py --list

This setup provides a flexible and scalable approach to managing inventories for network automation using Ansible.

The Ansible inventories can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: Ansible configuration
docs.text: 05 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible configuration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Ansible typically works out-of-the-box without requiring additional configuration. However, advanced usage might necessitate some customization. Ansible can be configured through files or variables.

For example, the DEFAULT_HOST_LIST parameter defines the inventory file. The official documentation specifies:

  • Default: The default value if not specified otherwise (/etc/ansible/hosts).
  • INI* How to specify the parameter in an INI configuration file (in this case, the section is [defaults] and the parameter is inventory).
  • Environment: The environment variable name to specify this parameter (ANSIBLE_INVENTORY).

If you choose to configure Ansible via INI files, you have four options:

  • Use the file at /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg
  • Use the file ~/.ansible.cfg in the home directory
  • Use the file ./ansible.cfg in the current directory
  • Use the file defined by the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable

The DEFAULT_HOST_LIST parameter can also be specified on the command line with -i. Additionally, some parameters can be defined within a playbook.

Ansible uses a precedence to determine which parameter value to use if it is specified multiple times. The order is:

  • Configuration settings
  • Command-line options
  • Playbook keywords
  • Variables

Lower items in the list override higher ones.

There are handy utilities to get general and specific information about your environment:

  • ansible-config list: Lists all possible variables and how to configure them.
  • ansible-config dump: Prints current values for each variable.
  • ansible-config init > ansible.cfg: Creates a sample configuration file, comprehensive but complex.
  • ansible-config view: Verifies and prints the current configuration.
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST:
  default: /etc/ansible/hosts
  description: Comma separated list of Ansible inventory sources
  env:
  - name: ANSIBLE_INVENTORY
  expand_relative_paths: true
  ini:
  - key: inventory
    section: defaults
  name: Inventory Source
  type: pathlist
  yaml:
    key: defaults.inventory

Let’s check the current configuration of the DEFAULT_HOST_LIST variable:

$ ansible-config dump | grep DEFAULT_HOST_LIST
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST(default) = ['/etc/ansible/hosts']

Now, modify it using an environment variable and verify the change:

$ export ANSIBLE_INVENTORY=inventory.yml
$ ansible-config dump | grep DEFAULT_HOST_LIST
DEFAULT_HOST_LIST(env: ANSIBLE_INVENTORY) = ['/Users/dainese/inventory.yml']

As we'll see later, there is a useful tool called ansible-navigator. It allows you to view the configuration, highlighting variables that alter the default behavior:

docs.title: Configuring SSH
docs.text:
There is a particular case that needs careful handling, especially when automating obsolete devices via SSH. Through SSH, we have two important parameters:

  • ANSIBLE_HOST_KEY_CHECKING: Set this to False to avoid host key checking by the underlying tools Ansible uses to connect to the host. In other words, it disables host verification. This variable can be configured in both the [defaults] and [paramiko_connection] sections.
  • PARAMIKO_LOOK_FOR_KEYS: Set this to False to disable searching for private key files. In other words, it disables private key authentication. This variable can be configured in the [paramiko_connection] section.

Ansible can use either Paramiko or LibSSH to connect to remote devices via SSH. By default, LibSSH is used if found; otherwise, Paramiko is used.

To force the use of Paramiko, you can use the following configuration:

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = paramiko

[paramiko_connection]
host_key_checking = true
look_for_keys = true

To increase performance or meet specific constraints, you can force LibSSH:

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = libssh

[libssh_connection]
host_key_checking = False
look_for_keys = False

docs.title: SSH Access to Obsolete Devices
docs.text:
When accessing very old devices, such as those in a lab, you might encounter the following error:

Unable to negotiate with 169.254.1.21 port 22: no matching key exchange method found. Their offer: diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

This occurs because the device does not support secure ciphers, while the system you are connecting from no longer supports weak ciphers. You need to modify the ~/.ssh/config file to re-enable the necessary ciphers, knowing this negatively impacts your environment's security:

KexAlgorithms +diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

On macOS systems, the + symbol is not recognized, so you must define the entire list of ciphers:

KexAlgorithms diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1,diffie-hellman-group1-sha1

docs.title: pylibssh on macOS
docs.text:
The pylibssh library is generally installed with the following command:

pip install ansible-pylibssh

On macOS, you might encounter the following error:

Failed to import the required Python library (ansible-pylibssh)

This happens because the ansible-pylibssh library, though seemingly installed correctly (pip freeze | grep pylibssh), does not function. You need to install it from source:

sudo xcode-select --install
brew install libssh libssh2
export CFLAGS="-I $(brew --prefix)/include -I ext -L $(brew --prefix)/lib -lssh"
git clone https://github.com/ansible/pylibssh.git ~/src/pylibssh
pip install ~/src/pylibssh/

docs.title: Ansible ad hoc commands
docs.text: 03 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible ad hoc commands
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Ansible provides a way to execute single commands without the need to build playbooks. This mode is called ad hoc and can be useful for executing one-time commands in very specific scenarios.

Let's open the Simple Network Lab and start R1. Ensure that the router is active and reachable:

$ ping -c3 169.254.1.21
PING 169.254.1.21 (169.254.1.21) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 169.254.1.21: icmp_seq=1 ttl=255 time=0.515 ms
64 bytes from 169.254.1.21: icmp_seq=2 ttl=255 time=0.539 ms
64 bytes from 169.254.1.21: icmp_seq=3 ttl=255 time=0.522 ms

--- 169.254.1.21 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss, time 2051ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.515/0.525/0.539/0.010 ms

If it is not, connect to the console and ensure that it is powered on, configured, and has the correct IP address.

Now, let's try to execute a ping using the Ad hoc mode:

$ ansible all -m ping
r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}
r2.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}

We immediately notice that R2, even though it's not powered on, appears to be active. This happens because the command we used is not a real ping but a connectivity test performed via SSH, which checks the access and remote existence of a usable Python interpreter. This is the classic mode used for managing Linux systems, but as we have seen previously, we are working with network devices, and in this case, the behavior changes significantly. In particular, Ansible uses a local Python interpreter, and for this reason, the ping module does not work correctly.

The correct module to use is net_ping, which requires specifying the destination IP address. In our case, the destination IP address is the IP address of the node itself, defined in the ansible_host variable:

$ ansible all -m net_ping -a "dest='{{ ansible_host }}'"
r2.example.com | FAILED! => {
    "changed": false,
    "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: Failed to resolve hostname r2.example.com (Name or service not known)"
}
r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "commands": "ping ip 169.254.1.21",
    "packet_loss": "0%",
    "packets_rx": 5,
    "packets_tx": 5,
    "rtt": {
        "avg": 1,
        "max": 1,
        "min": 1
    }
}

In the example, dest has been set to the value of ansible_host using Jinja syntax. We also see that an IOS command has been executed, not Linux. We are not initiating a ping from the Ansible host to R1. Instead, we are running a ping command on R1 itself, where R1 pings its own interface.

The problem is not easily solved, but the reason is that we are making a mistake. Ansible is not a monitoring system but a task execution system: tasks fail if the system is unreachable, and that is sufficient for our needs.

In the last example, we want to execute the show version command:

$ ansible r1.example.com -m ios_command -a "commands='show version'"
r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "stdout": [
        "Cisco IOS Software, Linux Software (I86BI_LINUX-ADVENTERPRISEK9-M), Version 15.7(3)M2, DEVELOPMENT TEST SOFTWARE\nTechnical Support: http://www.cisco.com/techsupport\nCopyright (c) 1986-2018 by Cisco Systems, Inc.\nCompiled Wed 28-Mar-18 11:18 by prod_rel_team\n\nROM: Bootstrap program is Linux\n\nR1 uptime is 5 minutes\nSystem returned to ROM by reload at 0\nSystem image file is \"unix:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/i86bi_LinuxL3-AdvEnterpriseK9-M2_15\"\nLast reload reason: Unknown reason\n\n\n\nThis product contains cryptographic features and is subject to United\nStates and local country laws governing import, export, transfer and\nuse. Delivery of Cisco cryptographic products does not imply\nthird-party authority to import, export, distribute or use encryption.\nImporters, exporters, distributors and users are responsible for\ncompliance with U.S. and local country laws. By using this product you\nagree to comply with applicable laws and regulations. If you are unable\nto comply with U.S. and local laws, return this product immediately.\n\nA summary of U.S. laws governing Cisco cryptographic products may be found at:\nhttp://www.cisco.com/wwl/export/crypto/tool/stqrg.html\n\nIf you require further assistance please contact us by sending email to\nexport@cisco.com.\n\nLinux Unix (Intel-x86) processor with 863257K bytes of memory.\nProcessor board ID 73402369\n4 Ethernet interfaces\n1024K bytes of NVRAM.\n\n\n\nConfiguration register is 0x0"
    ],
    "stdout_lines": [
        [
            "Cisco IOS Software, Linux Software (I86BI_LINUX-ADVENTERPRISEK9-M), Version 1

The output will show us the result of the command for R1.

docs.title: Ansible Playbooks and variables
docs.text: 15 August 2024

docs.title: Ansible Playbooks and variables
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

A playbook is a YAML file that sequentially outlines the operations to be performed on devices or groups of devices. Each playbook is composed of one or more plays, which can include pre_tasks, tasks, and post_tasks.

When planning and writing playbooks, variables play a crucial role. These variables can be defined at different levels, such as configuration, playbook, inventory, environment, files, or facts. It's helpful to have a method for printing the value of all defined variables.

Let's start by opening the Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology lab and ensuring all devices are active and reachable.

docs.title: Printing All Variables
docs.text:
As we know, a playbook is a YAML file containing a list of plays. Each play defines the operations to be performed and where they should be executed:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: PRINT DEBUG VARIABLES
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: true
  pre_tasks:
    - ...
  tasks:
    - ...
  post_tasks:
    - ...

The example above defines a play with a general list of pre_tasks, tasks, and post_tasks. This play runs on all inventory objects (all) and collects facts before executing any tasks. Although gathering facts can slow down the play, it's essential for our purpose.

The first line, known as the "shebang", allows the playbook file to be executed directly without specifying the ansible-playbook interpreter manually. As the name suggests, pre_tasks and post_tasks group tasks that need to be executed before any other tasks or just before finishing the play, respectively. In this example, we'll focus only on the tasks.

The playbook's goal is defined by the hosts key, which can select all hosts in the inventory (all), specific groups, or individual hosts. Here are some examples:

  • all: selects all hosts in the inventory;
  • r1.example.com: selects only R1;
  • routers,switches: selects hosts in the routers or switches groups;
  • routers,!switches: selects hosts in the routers group but not in the switches group.

Now, let's write a playbook to print all environment variables. The variables we want to print are grouped into:

  • Module variables (vars)
  • Environment variables (environment)
  • Group names variables (group_names)
  • Groups variables (groups)
  • Host variables (hostvars)

We'll define five tasks to print these variables:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: PRINT DEBUG VARIABLES
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: true
  tasks:
    - name: PRINT MODULE VARIABLES (vars)
      tags: modules
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ vars }}"
    - name: PRINT ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES (environment)
      tags: environment
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ environment }}"
    - name: PRINT GROUP NAMES VARIABLES (group_names)
      tags: group_names
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ group_names }}"
    - name: PRINT GROUPS VARIABLES (groups)
      tags: groups
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ groups }}"
    - name: PRINT HOST VARIABLES (hostvars)
      tags: hosts
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ hostvars }}"

Each task uses the ansible.builtin.debug module to define the msg variable, which is set to the contents of vars, environment, group_names, groups, and hostvars.

If Ansible is correctly configured and the playbook is executable, running it is straightforward:

$ ./playbook-print_all_vars.yml
TASK [PRINT HOST VARIABLES (hostvars)] *****************************************
ok: [sw1.example.com] => {
    "msg": {
        "r1.example.com": {
            "ansible_check_mode": false,
            "ansible_config_file": "/home/dev/courses/Ansible/07. Playbooks/ansible.cfg",
            "ansible_connection": "ansible.netcommon.network_cli",
            "ansible_diff_mode": false,
            "ansible_facts": {},
            "ansible_forks": 5,
            "ansible_host": "169.254.1.21",
            "ansible_inventory_sources": [
                "/home/dev/courses/Ansible/07. Playbooks/inventory.ini"
            ],
            "ansible_network_os": "cisco.ios.ios",
            "ansible_playbook_python": "/home/dev/venv/bin/python3.10",
            "ansible_run_tags": [
                "all"
            ],
            "ansible_skip_tags": [],
            "ansible_ssh_pass": "cisco",
            "ansible_user": "admin",
            "ansible_verbosity": 0,
            "ansible_version": {
                "full": "2.15.10",

Analyzing the output, we see many available variables, but, for example, there is no variable containing the domain of the devices (example.com).

We also notice that the facts include, for instance:

            "ansible_net_hostname": "SW6",
            "ansible_net_image": "unix:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/i86bi_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.SS",
            "ansible_net_iostype": "IOS",
            "ansible_net_operatingmode": "autonomous",
            "ansible_net_python_version": "3.10.13",
            "ansible_net_serialnum": "73412614",
            "ansible_net_system": "ios",
            "ansible_net_version": "15.2(CML_NIGHTLY_20190423)FLO_DSGS7",

As we observed earlier, Ansible works differently when managing network devices (network_cli). In this case, the facts are gathered using the cisco.ios.ios_facts module, specific to the ansible_network_os we are using. This means that if we switch to another device and module, the behavior might differ.

docs.title: Limiting Execution
docs.text:
During playbook development and in general use, limiting execution to specific hosts or groups and particular parts of the playbook is helpful. Here are some examples:

./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --limit sw1.example.com
./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --limit switches
./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --limit 'switches,!sw1.example.com'

The three examples above run the playbook only on:

  • The host sw1.example.com
  • Hosts in the switches group
  • Hosts in the switches group, except sw1.example.com

To limit execution to parts of the playbook, we use the concept of tags. Tasks and roles can be associated with tags. If we modify the playbook by assigning a specific tag to each task, we can limit playbook execution to a single task:

./playbook-print_all_vars.yml --tags groups

There are also special tags:

  • always: tasks with this tag are always executed unless the --skip-tags always parameter is specified.
  • never: tasks with this tag are never executed unless the tag is explicitly specified (--tags never).

docs.title: Configuring NTP with ios_ntp_global
docs.text:
Now that we've seen how to create a playbook let's take it further and create our first role. A role is a reusable set of tasks that can be shared across playbooks. A role has a specific structure and is typically stored within the roles directory. Roles are executed after pre_tasks but before tasks.

Let's create the skeleton for our first role, which will configure NTP on Cisco IOS devices:

ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_ntp

The structure includes several directories that we will explore in future lessons. Initially, we are interested in the tasks directory, which contains the list of operations to be performed.

In this role, we want to use ios_ntp_global, and before starting, we always refer to the official documentation. In the examples, we see that the module configuration can become quite complex. We'll keep it simple and focus on configuring two NTP peers.

Before starting development, we need to consider how to model the variables used in the role to configure the NTP peers. Let's assume, for simplicity, that the configuration involves two variables with the IP addresses of the two NTP peers: ntp_server_1and ntp_server_2.

- name: CONFIGURE NTP PEERS
  cisco.ios.ios_ntp_global:
    config:
      peers:
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_1 }}"
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_2 }}"
    state: replaced

Next, we'll create a playbook that calls the role we just wrote:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10
  roles:
    - role: cisco_ios_ntp

We run the playbook and check that the idempotence property is satisfied:

  • The first run should configure (status changed) the two IP addresses (verify with show running-config | include ntp);
  • The second run should confirm what was done (status ok);
  • If we change an IP address, the run should add the missing IP address and remove the one that is no longer needed (verify with show running-config | include ntp).

We find that the third point is not met. This happens because the merged mode is used, meaning the current and intended configurations are combined. What we want requires the replaced or overridden state.

We modify the role and retest to find that the role now behaves as expected.

docs.title: Saving the Configuration
docs.text:
By default, Ansible modules for Cisco IOS do not save the configuration. Let's see how to save the configuration easily and only when necessary. We refer again to the ios_config module and the official documentation. We see that the save_when option is available, and it can be used even without performing any configuration. We can either create a specific role or a post_tasks. We'll choose the latter, as saving the configuration is one of those tasks that is ideally executed before finishing the play.

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10
  roles:
    - role: cisco_ios_ntp
  post_tasks:
    - name: SAVING CONFIG
      tags: always
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: modified

We also used the always tag because we want the configuration always to be saved.

Performing the tests again, we find that now everything works as expected.

docs.title: Ansible Galaxy and Collections
docs.text:
While using Ansible, you might need specific modules managed by external collections. These collections can be managed via ansible-galaxy. For example, to list all installed collections:

ansible-galaxy collection list

To update a specific collection:

ansible-galaxy collection install -U cisco.ios

It's good practice to keep track of the collections you use and their versions through a collections/requirements.yml file:

collections:
  - name: cisco.ios
    version: 8.0.0
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com

You can install all the collections specified in the file with a single command:

ansible-galaxy collection install -U -r collections/requirements.yml

Later, we will see how to create and publish your own collection on Ansible Galaxy.

The Ansible playbooks can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: Defining and using variables in Ansible
docs.text: 01 September 2024

docs.title: Defining and using variables in Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

Variables in Ansible can be defined in various ways, offering flexibility in managing configuration and customizing playbooks.

Defining Variables in the Playbook: one simple and direct way to define variables is to include them directly in the playbook:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  vars:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

In this example, the variables ntp_server_1 and ntp_server_2 are defined within the playbook itself.

Defining Variables in a Configuration File: to keep playbooks cleaner and manage configuration separately, variables can be defined in an external file:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: NTP PEERS
  vars:
    - config.yml

The config.yml file will contain the variable definitions:

ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

Defining Variables in the Inventory: variables can also be defined directly in the inventory, applying them to all hosts or specific groups:

[all:vars]
ntp_server_1=194.239.208.213
ntp_server_2=130.60.204.10

This option is useful when you want to apply the same configurations to multiple hosts.

Defining Variables at the Role Level: variables can also be defined within roles, making them available only when the role is used:

# roles/cisco_ios_ntp/vars/main.yml
ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

Defining Variables at the Host or Group Level: you can define variables specific to a single host or a group of hosts using host_vars and group_vars files, respectively:

  • host_vars/sw1.example.com
  • group_vars/all.yml

Using the set_fact Module: variables can also be dynamically created during the execution of a playbook using the set_fact module:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_server_1: 194.239.208.213
    ntp_server_2: 130.60.204.10

docs.title: Accessing Variables from Other Hosts
docs.text:
In some cases, it may be necessary to access variables from another host during the execution of a playbook. This can be done using the hostvars syntax:

hostvars['sw2.example.com']['ansible_host']

docs.title: Storing the Output of a Task
docs.text:
To store the output of a task in a specific variable, you don't use set_fact but instead use the register parameter within the task you want to capture the output from:

- name: GETTING NTP CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "show running-config | include ntp peer"
  register: show_run_ntp_peer

docs.title: Ansible statements
docs.text: 16 September 2024

docs.title: Ansible statements
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

If you’ve got some experience with programming languages, you might find Ansible's constructs a bit clunky. But no worries, let's break them down with some practical examples to make things clearer.

docs.title: Conditionals (if, then, else)
docs.text:
In Ansible, the if-then-else construct is simplified to a single word: when.

- ansible.builtin.command: /sbin/shutdown -t now
  when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == "Debian"

Unlike traditional languages, there’s no direct else or elif. You’ll handle them all with separate when statements and the right expressions.

If you’ve got a bunch of conditions that all need to be true at the same time (logical AND), you can list them out:

- ansible.builtin.command: /sbin/shutdown -t now
  when:
    - ansible_facts['distribution'] == "CentOS"
    - ansible_facts['distribution_major_version'] == "6"

Each variable in Ansible can be one of the following types:

  • List
  • Dictionary
  • Boolean (True/true/yes/on or False/false/no/off)
  • Integer
  • Float
  • String (if it’s wrapped in quotes or doesn’t fit the above types)

Ansible heavily relies on Jinja, which adds a bit more complexity to the mix. Any variable created using Jinja is treated as a string, and you'll often need to convert it before use. But sometimes Ansible takes care of this for you, like when it automatically converts a string containing JSON into a list or dictionary when used in a loop.

Here’s a quick breakdown to help you navigate this:

  • Variables can be either defined or undefined.
  • A defined variable might be empty (None) or have some data.
  • The variable’s type depends on the data it holds (Ansible uses weak typing).
  • Ansible often creates strings using Jinja, which may require conversion.
  • Ansible will automatically convert strings into lists or dictionaries when needed.
  • Before performing mathematical operations, it’s a good habit to explicitly convert variables using Jinja filters like | int or | float.

The best approach? Always double-check how Ansible handles different cases. You can use debug tools to inspect the type and value of your variables:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "Type of var is {{ var | type_debug }}"
- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "Content of var is {{ var }}"

For more details and examples, check out the official Ansible documentation.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
A block is a group of tasks. Blocks can be used to:

  • Group tasks that share the same when condition.
  • Handle errors using the rescue and always directives.
- block:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ value | int }}"
  rescue:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Value is not defined"

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
A loop can be applied to lists or dictionaries to iterate over elements and perform one or more actions. There are two important considerations:

  • Using loops impacts performance directly.
  • A loop can only be applied to a single action, not a group of actions.

For simplicity, let’s look at three common approaches and leave deeper insights for the official documentation.

With with_items, you can iterate over a list of elements. In each iteration, by default, the item variable takes on the value of each list element:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ item }}"
  with_items:
    - red
    - green
    - blue

With with_dict, you can iterate over a dictionary. In each iteration, item.key and item.value will hold the key and value of each key-value pair in the dictionary:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ item.value }} is {{ item.key }}"
  with_dict:
    red: tomato
    green: grass
    blue: sky

Ansible later standardized loops with the loop construct. However, out of habit and convenience, I still tend to use with_items and with_dict, which feel more straightforward to me. That said, loop can be more useful for more complex scenarios.

docs.title: Nested Loops
docs.text:
We've already seen how to implement loops in Ansible. Sometimes, however, you might need to implement loops within loops (nested loops) or loops over groups of tasks. In both cases, the solution is similar and involves using external files:

- ansible.builtin.include_tasks: sub_task1.yml
  with_items:
    - macos
    - windows
    - linux
  loop_control:
    loop_var: os_item

In this example, we iterate over a list and call an external task file sub_task1.yml. All the tasks in this file can use the variable os_item, which takes on each value from the os list.

When I need to call an external task file, I always prefer to explicitly specify the variable value. This avoids confusion and prevents the variable from being overwritten by any loops inside the external file.

docs.title: Until
docs.text:
Finally, let's look at how to execute a task until the desired result is achieved:

- ansible.builtin.shell: /usr/bin/foo
  register: result
  until: result.stdout.find("ready") != -1
  retries: 5
  delay: 10

In this example, we run a (fictional) command until the output contains the word ready. The execution stops with an error after 5 failed attempts, with a 10-second interval between each try.

docs.title: Configuring NTP with ios_config
docs.text:
Let's explore how to configure NTP peers using the ios_config module. Before writing the playbook, we should review the official documentation and consider how we would configure NTP peers manually. Here’s the typical process:

  • Configure the NTP servers.
  • Verify the NTP servers configured on the device.
  • Remove any NTP servers configured on the device that are not in the desired NTP server list.

Now, we need to write a role that performs these three tasks exactly as described.

First, we’ll refer to the official documentation and add the missing NTP peers:

- cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - "ntp peer {{ ntp_server_1 }}"
      - "ntp peer {{ ntp_server_2 }}"

Next, we need to remove any unnecessary NTP peers. When working manually, we would retrieve the running-config to check for any unknown addresses. In Ansible, we do something similar:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "show running-config | include ntp peer"
  register: show_run_ntp_peer

The register option saves the output into a variable that we define. If we print this variable using debug, we can analyze its structure.

The output is in JSON format and contains the raw output (stdout) and the output split into lines (stdout_lines). Both are arrays because multiple commands can return output simultaneously.

For convenience, we'll extract only the NTP peer IP addresses into specific variables:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    current_ntp_peers: "{{ show_run_ntp_peer['stdout'][0] | regex_findall('^ntp peer .*$', multiline=True) | regex_replace('ntp peer ', '') }}"
    expected_ntp_peers:
      - "{{ ntp_server_1 }}"
      - "{{ ntp_server_2 }}"

The current_ntp_peers variable stores all lines starting with ntp peer. Before saving, the prefix ntp peer is removed, leaving us with a list of only the NTP peer IP addresses.

Note: If any of our IPs are configured as preferred, the configuration would become more complex.

At this point, we need to compare the current configuration and remove any unnecessary peers. Specifically, we compare each element of the configuration, and if it is not part of the expected NTP peer list, we remove it:

- name: REMOVING NTP PEERS
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - "no ntp peer {{ item }}"
  with_items: "{{ current_ntp_peers }}"
  when: item not in expected_ntp_peers

The code above loops (with_items) through the current_ntp_peers list, and each item is compared with the expected_ntp_peers list. If (when) the address is not found, it is removed using the ios_config module.

This playbook could be optimized for efficiency, but it’s designed to be more readable and understandable.

docs.title: Strategies for troubleshooting Ansible errors
docs.text: 02 October 2024

docs.title: Strategies for troubleshooting Ansible errors
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

One of the biggest challenges when using Ansible, especially at the beginning, is troubleshooting. You often run into errors that are unclear, poorly described, or misleading.

Let's look at some strategies to help resolve otherwise incomprehensible errors.

dos2unix: In rare cases, issues arise from how different operating systems handle text files. When working in Linux environments, ensure that your files are in the correct format.

yamllint and yamlfmt: Ansible playbooks are written in YAML. Before troubleshooting further, make sure your files are correctly formatted as valid YAML.

ansible-lint: Ansible playbooks follow a specific structure, which can be validated with the built-in linter included in the Ansible package.

Verbosity: You can make the execution of playbooks more verbose by adding one or more -v flags. Usually, -vvv is enough to reveal hidden errors.

Simplify: If the cause of the error is still unclear, simplify the playbook until you can isolate the task that is causing the issue.

ansible.builtin.debug: The debug feature lets you print variable contents, helping identify any anomalies.

type_debug: In addition to checking variable contents, make sure the variable type is correct, especially if you are performing mathematical operations.

fail...when: Using fail-when allows you to check if conditional tests return the expected result.

Facts: Before using facts, always check for availability and correct values. The to_nice_json filter helps print them in a readable format.

Debugger: Once you’ve identified the task causing the issue, you can enable the debugger:

- ansible.builtin.command: "false"
  debugger: on_failed

Timeout: If tasks are taking too long, you can increase the timeout for SSH connections:

- ansible.builtin.command: "false"
  debugger: on_failed

Async: For long-running tasks, it’s good practice to configure them as asynchronous:

- ansible.builtin.command: /bin/sleep 15
  async: 45
  poll: 5

SSH no match: If you need to manage outdated devices, you might run into issues where a common set of encryption ciphers can’t be established between the Ansible host and the device:

fatal: [pe.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: kex error : no match for method encryption client->server: server [aes128-cbc,3des-cbc,aes192-cbc,aes256-cbc], client [aes192-ctr,aes256-ctr]"}

This example shows a failed connection because there’s no matching key exchange protocol. If you’re using libssh, the ~/.ssh/config file is loaded by default. You can specify a new configuration file in the ansible.cfg file:

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = libssh

[libssh_connection]
config_file = ansible_ssh.conf

docs.title: Handling errors in Ansible playbooks
docs.text: 09 October 2024

docs.title: Handling errors in Ansible playbooks
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

When developing playbooks, it’s often necessary to modify Ansible’s default behavior in case of errors.

Here are three common scenarios:

  • When a task should only run in a specific mode
  • When a task should never report changes
  • When a task should fail under certain conditions

Additionally, we'll explore three scenarios that are useful to know but rarely encountered in practice.

docs.title: Running Tasks in a specific mode
docs.text:
You can enforce a task to run only in a specific mode. For instance, the following task runs only in check mode (-C):

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "show running-config | include ntp peer"
  when: ansible_check_mode

However, this doesn’t change the task’s behavior, only when it is executed. In check mode, commands that can alter the system are not executed. Each module handles check mode differently.

For example, the ios_command module won't work in check mode unless commands start with show. A command like dir won’t run in this mode.

You can force the ios_command module to behave normally, even in check mode:

- name: Forced in check mode
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - "dir"
  check_mode: false

docs.title: Force Change and Failed codes
docs.text:
Task execution returns a change and failed code to indicate whether something in the system has changed and whether the task completed successfully.

You can force the behavior as follows:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  register: output
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: '"I86BI_LINUX" in output.stdout[0]'

docs.title: Custom failure messages
docs.text:
To print a more informative error message when forcing a failed state, split the task into two parts as shown:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  register: output
- ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: “Router is IOL”
  when: '"I86BI_LINUX" in output.stdout[0]'

docs.title: Try-Catch with Blocks
docs.text:
In Ansible, you can implement a try-catch block to handle errors across multiple tasks:

- block:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "{{ value | int }}"
  rescue:
    - ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Value is not defined"

docs.title: Running Playbooks on Failed Hosts
docs.text:
Ansible can track hosts where a playbook has failed. To enable this, set the retry parameter in the configuration:

[defaults]
retry_files_enabled: True

Then, you can rerun the playbook, limiting it to failed hosts only:

./playbook.yml -i inventory.ini --limit @playbook.retry

docs.title: Ignoring unreachable hosts
docs.text:
A task can be configured to avoid interrupting the playbook if a host becomes unreachable:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  ignore_unreachable: true

If this task fails, the playbook will continue executing subsequent tasks, even for unreachable hosts.

docs.title: Using Ansible handlers for optimized task execution
docs.text: 16 October 2024

docs.title: Using Ansible handlers for optimized task execution
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Handlers allow you to associate actions with tasks that make changes to devices. The key feature of handlers is that they are executed once, right before the end of the playbook.

A good example is saving a configuration. Throughout a playbook, configurations may be modified multiple times, but saving can happen only once at the end of the playbook.

Here’s a task that configures NTP servers:

- cisco.ios.ios_ntp_global:
    config:
      peers:
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_1 }}"
        - peer: "{{ ntp_server_2 }}"
    state: replaced
  notify: SAVE CONFIG

The task calls (notify) the SAVE CONFIG handler. At the end of the playbook, the handler will be triggered once, even if it's notified by multiple tasks.

- name: SAVE CONFIG
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    save_when: always

The handler is simply a task stored in the handlers directory. The only thing to keep in mind is to provide a name that will be used to invoke it.

However, handlers come with a significant issue. Let's look at an example:

  • A series of tasks modify the configuration of a device, and the handler execution is deferred.
  • Due to an error, the playbook stops before the handler is executed.
  • The next time the playbook is run, no changes are made to the device configuration, so no handler is triggered.

In this scenario, we end up in an undesirable state: the device has been reconfigured, but the changes haven't been saved.

For this reason, I tend to avoid using handlers.

docs.title: Ansible parsers and filters
docs.text: 06 November 2024

docs.title: Ansible parsers and filters
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

The method we are using with Ansible is called "screen-scraper", meaning the interaction with the device is not done through APIs but via CLI, emulating human activity. While this approach might be straightforward when typing commands, reading the outputs can be particularly challenging.

Consider the following output:

R1#show ip int brie
Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up
Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

The above output is readable by humans but requires some work to be usable in a program. For instance, if we wanted to read the IP address of the Ethernet0/0 interface, we would need to search for the line where the interface name appears and then move a certain number of characters until we encounter the IP address. However, this is the format used by the Cisco IOS device in this example. If we change vendors or, in some cases, versions, the format of the table might change.

Parsers in Ansible handle this task: they read a text and convert it into a data structure. Parsers, essential unless working with APIs, are available for various types of text.

Regarding the topic we are addressing, we will look at four of them:

  • TextFSM
  • NTC Templates
  • PyATS / Genie
  • TTP

For our tests, we will use the Simple Network Lab environment, with R1 already running and reachable.

docs.title: TextFSM
docs.text:
TextFSM, explored in a module of the basic course, is a module that reads a text and transforms it into a list of dictionaries. For example, the following text:

R1#show ip int brie
Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up
Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

Can be transformed into:

[
    {
        "interface": "Ethernet0/0",
        "ip_address": "169.254.1.118",
        "proto": "up",
        "status": "up"
    },
    {
        "interface": "Ethernet0/1",
        "ip_address": "unassigned",
        "proto": "down",
        "status": "administratively down"
    }
]

Writing a template for TextFSM, at first glance, may not be simple, but once understood, it is not so complex. In this course, we limit ourselves to using existing templates, and in particular, we will refer to the NTC Templates repository. Let's retrieve the template for the show ip interface brief command on Cisco IOS devices.

Now, we need to write a short playbook to connect to the device, issue the show ip interface brief command, and save it in a variable. The task is as follows:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show ip interface brief
  register: output

We now need to transform the output using the TextFSM parser and its corresponding template:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.utils.textfsm
      template_path: templates/cisco_ios_show_ip_interface_brief.textfsm
    set_fact: output_parsed

If we print the contents of output_parsed using debug, we see that it is structured in JSON format.

docs.title: NTC Templates
docs.text:
NTC Templates, as previously mentioned, is a public repository maintained by network.toCode(), containing TextFSM templates for various vendors and devices. Anyone can contribute to the repository by publishing their own templates.

NTC Templates is also available as a Python module and is a simpler way than the previous one, but it offers less flexibility. The Python module is not released frequently, and if you need updated templates, the previous method is preferable.

Once the ntc_templates module is installed, we can use the repository within our playbook:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    command: "show ip interface brief"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.ntc_templates
      os: "cisco_ios"
    set_fact: output_parsed

We see that using this parser requires us to specify the device type (cisco_ios) and the command. If we print the contents of output_parsed using debug, we see that it is structured in JSON format and has some differences from what we saw previously, although the template used is the same.

In the above task, the module directly executes the command on the device, retrieves the output, and applies the parser. For performance reasons, which we will see later, it is possible to use the output from a variable. In this case, the syntax is slightly different:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.ntc_templates
      os: "cisco_ios"
      command: "show ip interface brief"
    set_fact: output_parsed

docs.title: TTP
docs.text:
TTP or Template Text Parser Templates is a more elaborate parser than TextFSM, but, on the flip side, there are very few available templates and the effort to create them is often not worth it. TTP, however, can be used to parse entire configurations, and this is its main strength compared to TextFSM. Like TextFSM, TTP is also covered in the basic module.

Once the ttp_templates module is installed, for example, let's download the template for the show ip arp command on Cisco IOS devices into the templates directory with a .ttp extension.

We can now use the repository within our playbook:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    command: show ip arp
    parser:
      name: ansible.utils.ttp
      os: "cisco_ios"
    set_fact: output_parsed

Here too, there is the possibility of passing the output as a variable:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.utils.ttp
      os: "cisco_ios"
      command: "show ip arp"
    set_fact: output_parsed

docs.title: PyATS / Genie
docs.text:
Parallel to TextFSM and TTP, we find the PyATS / Genie suite developed by Cisco. Although it is an open solution, it is clearly designed for Cisco devices and therefore generally limited to these.

Consulting the list of parsers verifies that there is a parser for show ip interface brief.

Once the pyats and genie modules are installed, we can then write a task to use this parser within our playbook:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    command: "show ip interface brief"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.pyats
    set_fact: output_parsed

Notice some things:

  • Unlike the previous parsers, we did not have to specify the type of device. This is because the parser automatically reads information from the ansible_network_os variable.
  • The output is not a list but a dictionary, with the interface name as the key. This can be very useful for more easily selecting the desired line.

Here too, there is the possibility of passing the output as a variable:

- ansible.utils.cli_parse:
    text: "{{ output['stdout'][0] }}"
    parser:
      name: ansible.netcommon.pyats
      command: show ip interface brief
    set_fact: output_parsed

docs.title: Custom Filters
docs.text:
Ansible provides several filters that allow altering the content of a variable. For example:

  • var | int converts the variable to an integer;
  • var | to_nice_json formats a JSON to be human-readable;
  • var | upper transforms a string using only uppercase letters.

If the previously seen parsers are insufficient or if there is no filter that meets our needs, we can easily add a custom filter by writing Python code.

We can divide filters into two groups: those that do not accept additional parameters, meaning their only input value is the variable to which they are applied, and those that accept additional parameters. Let's see two examples.

In the first example (without additional parameters), the filter:

  • takes as input the output of show ip interface brief manipulated with the NTC Templates parser;
  • removes inactive interfaces.

The first consideration we need to make is regarding typing. If Python has weak typing, we can say that Ansible is even darker. Later, we will delve into the use of the type_debug filter, which can help us in case of doubts.

Custom filters must be saved inside the same file filter_plugins/filters.py. Filters are, in fact, functions of the FilterModule class. The reserved function filters associates a name with which to call the filters, to the functions that define each filter.

Let's see an example:

class FilterModule(object):
    """Ansible filter."""

    def drop_down_interfaces(self, interfaces: list) -> list:
        """Return a list of active interfaces."""
        result = []
        for interface in interfaces:
            if interface["status"] == "up":
                result.append(interface)
        return result

    def filters(self):
        """Invoked function. Keys define how filters are called."""
        return {
            "drop_down_interfaces": self.drop_down_interfaces,
        }

In the example class:

  • The drop_down_interfaces function takes as input and returns a list of interfaces. The output includes only interfaces that are in the up state.
  • The filters function associates the name drop_down_interfaces with the anonymous function.

In a playbook, the filter can be used as follows:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ output_parsed | drop_down_interfaces }}"

Now, let's enrich our class with a second filter that transforms a list of dictionaries into a dictionary of dictionaries. The key to use is read as an additional parameter. So, let's add this function to the previously seen class:

class FilterModule(object):
    """Ansible filter."""

    def get_to_dict(self, items: list, key: str = None) -> dict:
        """Convert a list of dict into a dict of dict."""
        return {item[key]: item for item in items}

    def filters(self):
        """Invoked function. Keys define how filters are called."""
        return {
            "to_dict": self.get_to_dict,
        }

The to_dict function transforms the list of dictionaries items into a dictionary of dictionaries, using the specified key value as the key.

We can use this second filter as follows:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ output_parsed | to_dict(key='interface') }}"

All the scripts and playbooks described in this post are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Password Management with Ansible
docs.text: 25 December 2024

docs.title: Password Management with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Password management is one of the topics that should be analyzed during the design phase, i.e., before starting to write code. However, from a learning perspective, I prefer to postpone the topic in order to have some basic knowledge.

In general, I feel inclined to discourage any approach that involves having credentials saved in clear text in files or playbooks. Where possible, I recommend using named credentials that are manually entered during playbook execution.

The use of orchestrators like Ansible Tower or AWX might make it preferable to choose a particular vault, i.e., an encrypted password database accessible via API. The use of a vault in manually executing playbooks, in my opinion, makes little sense because it simply shifts the problem: the credentials are contained in the vault, but somewhere the token must be saved so that the playbook can access the vault.

Finally, as seen previously, the use of dynamic inventories might make it preferable to save credentials within the inventory itself, which, being generated dynamically, leaves no trace except in RAM. However, once again, we are shifting the problem: somehow the script that generates the inventory must be able to authenticate itself.

Let's see two examples, knowing that each environment will require specific considerations regarding the security and confidentiality of credentials. So, let's open the Simple Network Lab and start R1.

docs.title: Named Credentials
docs.text:
The simplest and safest way to manage credentials is to pass them directly on the command line during each execution:

./playbook-auth.yml -u admin -k

Before execution, we will be asked for the password of the admin user. If the user needs to perform privilege escalation, it is possible to use the -K parameter, which would prompt us for the enable password.

docs.title: Ansible Vault
docs.text:
Especially if we use an orchestrator, it becomes difficult to use named credentials to access devices. In this scenario, it is easier to have one or more service accounts saved inside the vault.

Let's see how to create a native Ansible vault:

ansible-vault create secrets.vault

The file is nothing but an encrypted key-value dictionary with the password requested during creation. For example, we can save the password of the admin user:

cisco_admin_password: cisco

If necessary, the vault can be edited:

ansible-vault edit secrets.vault

As we said, we are shifting the problem: the playbook must know the vault password in order to read it and access the device. There are several options:

  • insert the vault password on the command line --ask-vault-pass;
  • read the password from a specific file or script --vault-password-file;
  • read the password from the environment variable through a script (see previous point).

As mentioned, the use of vaults should be preferred in case the playbooks are managed by an orchestrator. In this case, the best choice depends on the orchestrator itself. Whatever system we choose, the vault file is loaded as a variable file and then used:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: ANSIBLE VAULT
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars_files:
    - secrets.vault

This is why we used the key ansible_ssh_pass in the vault.

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
As we have seen, the integrated vault of Ansible is quite simple. In corporate environments, more advanced vaults are generally present, and very often I come across HashiCorp Vault. Let's refer to the official documentation and see how to use it.

Let's add the hvac environment and assume that HashiCorp Vault is configured with two keys to be used as username and password:

$ vault read -tls-skip-verify kv/ansible
Key Value
--- -----
refresh_interval 768h
password cisco
username admin

We set environment variables for the vault access parameters:

export VAULT_TOKEN=hvs.R3R5z2SmlSFGi9aR1VJlBZJH
export VAULT_ADDR=https://localhost:8200

In particular, we will use the lookup feature that allows us to define variables dynamically:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: HASHICORP VAULT
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    ansible_user: "{{ lookup('hashi_vault', 'secret=kv/ansible:username validate_certs=no') }}"
    ansible_ssh_pass: "{{ lookup('hashi_vault', 'secret=kv/ansible:password validate_certs=no') }}"

By inserting the variables at the play level, we ensure the ability to use gather_facts.

All sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Enhancing Ansible output
docs.text: 01 January 2025

docs.title: Enhancing Ansible output
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

By default, the output of Ansible shows us the tasks executed, for each device, with a brief summary at the end of what has been done. The color determines the outcome of the task: green if no changes were made, yellow if the configuration was modified, red in case of an error, and blue if the task was skipped.

The output can be customized using callbacks by acting on the ansible.cfg configuration file:

  • stdout_callback allows setting the main plugin that generates the output, by default it is ansible.builtin.default;
  • callbacks_enabled allows specifying which plugins are enabled, by default the list is empty.

The official documentation lists numerous plugins that can also be viewed with:

ansible-doc -t callback -l

Let's see the ones, in my opinion, most interesting.

docs.title: ansible.builtin.default
docs.text:
We already know the default plugin, it is sufficiently explanatory and allows to increase details with -v.

PLAY [TEST OUTPUT] *************************************************************

TASK [READING OUTPUT] **********************************************************
ok: [r1.example.com]

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
r1.example.com             : ok=1    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0
   rescued=0    ignored=0

The default plugin is indeed the best option to choose for normal operation.

docs.title: ansible.builtin.minimal
docs.text:
The minimal plugin provides a summary of the entire playbook execution:

r1.example.com | SUCCESS => {
    "changed": false,
    "stdout": [
        "Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol\nEthernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      \nEthernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    \nEthernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    \nEthernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"
    ],
    "stdout_lines": [
        [
            "Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol",
            "Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      ",
            "Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ",
            "Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ",
            "Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"
        ]
    ]
}

The minimal plugin can be helpful on very complex playbooks.

docs.title: ansible.posix.json
docs.text:
The JSON plugin returns execution information in JSON format.

{
    "custom_stats": {},
    "global_custom_stats": {},
    "plays": [
        {
            "play": {
                "duration": {
                    "end": "2024-10-26T06:58:57.910802Z",
                    "start": "2024-10-26T06:58:54.813940Z"
                },
                "id": "72edea89-cc55-4261-0c41-000000000002",
                "name": "TEST OUTPUT",
                "path": "/Users/dainese/src/courses/Ansible/15. Output/playbook-output.yml:2"
            },
            "tasks": [
                {
                    "hosts": {
                        "r1.example.com": {
                            "_ansible_no_log": false,
                            "action": "cisco.ios.ios_command",
                            "changed": false,

The JSON plugin is particularly useful if the playbook output needs to be used as input for other processes.

docs.title: community.general.log_plays
docs.text:
The log_plays plugin allows saving logs to a file for each device. The plugin must be configured by specifying the directory where the logs will be saved:

[callback_log_plays]
log_folder = /var/log/ansible/hosts

The plugin is suitable for use with a plugin that manages screen output.

Oct 26 2024 09:00:03 - ./playbook-output.yml - READING OUTPUT - cisco.ios.ios_command - OK - {"module_args": {"commands": ["show ip interface brief"], "match": "all", "retries": 9, "interval": 1, "wait_for": null}} => {"changed": false, "stdout": ["Interface                  IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      
Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    
Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    
Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"], "stdout_lines": [["Interface                  IP-Address      OK?
