Method Status                Protocol", "Ethernet0/0                169.254.1.118   YES DHCP   up                    up      ", "Ethernet0/1                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ", "Ethernet0/2                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down    ", "Ethernet0/3                unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down"]], "_ansible_no_log": false}

All sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Boosting Ansible performance
docs.text: 13 November 2024

docs.title: Boosting Ansible performance
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

While Ansible is an ideal choice in terms of accessibility, it's certainly not the best choice for those seeking performance.

Let's look at some specific configurations that allow us to improve performance in a simple way.

docs.title: Parallelism (fork)
docs.text:
The first configuration concerns the number of forks, which are the parallel processes that interact with devices. In general, it should be a number proportional to the number of processors, however, it's important to consider that much of the playbook time is actually spent waiting for the device to execute a specific command. The optimal value for forks could therefore be double the number of available processors, but it can be further increased. Obviously, the value of forks improves performance only if the playbook is executed in parallel on multiple nodes. Otherwise, it has no influence.

[defaults]
forks = 8

docs.title: Dependency (strategy)
docs.text:
The second value concerns the execution strategy (strategy). There are two types of strategies: linear and free.

With the linear strategy, a task is executed only if the previous one has been completed on all nodes. In fact, in the output, we notice this because we see the results of a specific task grouped together. With the free strategy, each node executes its own tasks without any waiting time. The free strategy can and should be used if each task depends only on the past of the node itself. In other words, free can be used if the execution of a play on R2 never depends in any way on the execution of the same play on R1. Obviously, the choice of strategy improves performance only if the playbook is executed in parallel on multiple nodes. Otherwise, it has no influence.

[defaults]
strategy = free

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text:
The next step to improve the performance of a playbook is to profile it, that is, to understand how time is spent, globally, by role, and by task.

There are three callbacks that allow adding time-related information to the standard output.

[defaults]
stdout_callback = ansible.builtin.default
callbacks_enabled = ansible.posix.profile_roles,ansible.posix.profile_tasks,ansible.posix.timer

These three plugins are essential for understanding which tasks require more time and therefore, following the Pareto Principle, where to focus.

docs.title: Reduce "show running-config"
docs.text:
Working in screen-scraping mode, the show running-config command is widely used. If specific modules cannot be optimized, when we use ios_config we can read the configuration from a previously populated variable:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    command: show running-config
  register: output
- cisco.ios.ios_config:
    running_config: output.stdout_lines[0]

docs.title: Disable "gather_facts"
docs.text:
As we have seen, Ansible allows reading some information from the nodes, information that is available before the execution of tasks. If this information is not necessary, disabling gather_facts can significantly improve performance.

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- hosts: all
  gather_facts: false

docs.title: Save configuration only once
docs.text:
Previously, we have already chosen to save the configuration only once at the end of the play using post_tasks. Saving the configuration is an activity that, depending on the platform, may take different amounts of time and significantly reduce execution times.

Therefore, we confirm the choice we have already made:

post_tasks:
  - cisco.ios.ios_config:
      save_when: modified

docs.title: Eliminate loops
docs.text:
In general, loop management in Ansible significantly impacts performance. Where possible, loops should be avoided or converted. Let's see some examples.

Suppose we have a list of NTP peers:

ntp_servers:
  - 194.239.208.213
  - 130.60.204.10

We can create a list to be used with the ios_ntp_global module:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_peers_config_list: "{{ ntp_peers_config_list|default([]) + [{'peer': item}] }}"
  with_items: "{{ ntp_peers }}"

However, this approach is rather slow. We can move the loop into a Jinja template:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_peers_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for host in ntp_servers %}
          {"peer": "{{ host }}"},
        {% endfor %}
      ]

Since Ansible is not typed, the result is the same but much more performant.

docs.title: Running Ansible playbooks through a Bastion host
docs.text: 20 November 2024

docs.title: Running Ansible playbooks through a Bastion host
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

In many environments, there exists a particularly secure host that must handle all management operations performed by operators on production environments. This host is usually subject to audits and continuous verification.

Ansible can be configured to be used through a bastion host, but the configuration depends closely on the protocol used. For our purposes, we will limit ourselves to SSH.

In our environment, our computer, Linux or MacOS, acts as the Ansible Controller, while the server EVE-NG acts as the bastion host: the devices are only reachable from the EVE-NG server.

It is important to note that in this way, the local Python environment will be used, not that of the bastion host. Any library or module errors, therefore, refer to the local system. The bastion host is simply used as a bridge, and for this reason, it does not require any particular configuration, except for authentication via public key.

docs.title: SSH via Bastion Host
docs.text:
Referring to the diagram above, we need to be able to connect via SSH to the server EVE-NG, using public key authentication. We therefore exchange keys manually or through a specific command in order to connect automatically to the bastion host with the user dev:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub dev@172.25.82.110

At this point, we need to act on the parameter ansible_ssh_common_args to force the execution of the playbook through the bastion host.

We can act at the playbook level by setting the variable ansible_ssh_common_args:

- ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ansible_ssh_common_args: >-
      -o ProxyCommand="ssh
      -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa
      -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no
      -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
      -W %h:%p
      -q dev@172.25.82.110"

The syntax >- allows us to specify the content of a variable on multiple lines without having EOL characters within the value.

We can act at the environment variable level, and this is probably the most convenient choice in a mixed development environment:

export ANSIBLE_SSH_COMMON_ARGS='-o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110"'

Or we can act at the command line level:

./playbook-ntp-via-bastion.yml -i inventory.ini --ssh-common-args '-o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110"'

If we encounter problems, let's try to connect to R1 via the bastion host:

ssh -o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=~/.ssh/id_rsa -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110" admin@169.254.1.21

And let's analyze any errors.

docs.title: Ansible orchestrators and integration tools
docs.text: 13 January 2025

docs.title: Ansible orchestrators and integration tools
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner

In this course, we used Ansible manually. To take the next step, we need an orchestrator that can help organize playbooks, manage execution, and generate reports.

There are several solutions available, and in this post, we will describe the most popular ones.

docs.title: Ansible Navigator
docs.text:
Ansible Navigator is a command-line tool and a text-based user interface (TUI) for creating, reviewing, running and troubleshooting Ansible content, including inventories, playbooks, collections, documentation and container images (execution environments).

Ansible Navigator is designed to run from within containers. Personally, I prefer to disable this behavior:

ansible-navigator --ee=false run playbook-output.yml

As we've seen, Ansible Navigator isn't exactly an orchestrator; it's a utility that allows you to run playbooks, analyze configurations, inventories, and collections, as well as perform linting.

docs.title: ARA Records Ansible
docs.text:
ARA provides Ansible reporting by recording ansible and ansible-playbook commands regardless of how and where they run.

The recorded results are available via an included CLI, a REST API as well as a self-hosted, local-first web reporting interface.

ARA is not an orchestrator, but it provides a simple way to have a dashboard that displays playbook execution progress. However, the playbooks must be run manually or from an external system.

docs.title: Ansible Tower
docs.text:
Ansible Tower represents a refined layer of the Ansible automation ecosystem, providing a web-based User Interface (UI) and RESTful API access. As a commercial offering, it introduces a more intuitive and visually engaging method to administer Ansible projects, inventories, and schedules.

Ansible Tower is Red Hat's official orchestrator for Ansible, designed to centralize the Ansible ecosystem and provide users with a single pane of glass for managing automation tasks.

docs.title: Ansible AWX
docs.text:
AWX provides a web-based user interface, REST API, and task engine built on top of Ansible. It is one of the upstream projects for Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform.

AWX is the open-source version of Ansible Tower, and it is often subject to significant changes, including major refactoring and updates.

docs.title: Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform
docs.text:
The Ansible Automation Platform stands as an expansive solution that encapsulates Ansible Tower as one of its vital components. It goes beyond the capabilities of Tower, forging a comprehensive ecosystem replete with additional tools, integrations, and features, thereby extending the horizons of automation possibilities.

The Ansible Automation Platform also includes Event-Driven Ansible, enabling automated responses to events or triggers within your infrastructure. EDA recognizes the specified event, matches it with the appropriate action, and automatically executes it. Actions can include executing existing Ansible Playbooks, templates, or modules to extend value from your trusted automation, as a user you have the option to decide.

docs.title: eNMS
docs.text:
eNMS is a vendor-agnostic Network Management System (NMS) designed for building workflow-based network automation solutions.

An Ansible Playbook service runs an ansible playbook on a set of target devices and returns a JSON formatted result. The output can be validated with a command / pattern mechanism, like the Data Validation Service.

eNMS centralize Ansible ecosystems giving a single pane of glass to users.

docs.title: Other orchestrators
docs.text:
Ansible can be integrated with numerous other tools, for example:

  • Spacelift: a sophisticated CI/CD platform for OpenTofu, Terraform, Terragrunt, CloudFormation, Pulumi, Kubernetes, and Ansible.
  • Netbox / [Nautobot: the network Source of Truth.
  • Semaphore UI: a modern UI for Ansible
  • Uyuni: the open-source configuration and infrastructure management solution for software-defined infrastructure.
  • InfraHub: unifies and syncs your infrastructure data foundation while preserving its context and intent, so teams can store and manage their automation blueprints in one place and integrate natively with the deployment tools they already use.

docs.title: Key takeaways from the Ansible course
docs.text: 18 December 2024

docs.title: Key takeaways from the Ansible course
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner

We have seen that Ansible is an excellent tool for enhancing operations by automating tasks and orchestrating processes. Ansible's procedural structure makes it easy to transform manual tasks into automated ones: if we can describe a task, we can build a playbook to implement it.

When properly structured, a playbook not only becomes the official way of operating but also serves as documentation of the process itself.

However, Ansible is not the only framework available, and it’s important to understand its strengths and limitations.

Ansible is well-suited for those without a programming background, which is why it’s often my first choice when approaching automation projects.

Organizations rarely have the capacity to develop and maintain new modules, so in that sense, Ansible’s scope is limited to the existing modules available.

From a performance perspective, there are frameworks more efficient than Ansible. Initially, this is rarely a concern, but as projects grow, different needs may emerge.

docs.title: Comprehensive Ansible Lab
docs.text: 11 December 2024

docs.title: Comprehensive Ansible Lab
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

In the final exercise, we'll see how to put together what we've learned to configure and manage a legacy fabric (based on STP).

So let's open the Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology lab, start all the devices, and make sure they're reachable.

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
Before even thinking about writing playbooks, we need to create a model of our environment, which means creating a data structure that can represent our fabric and serve as a working tool. There are many possibilities:

  • NetBox / Nautobot: I've seen integration between these applications, Ansible, and devices. People would make a change on NetBox / Nautobot regarding a device's interface. The change would trigger an Ansible playbook that would modify the configuration on the physical device.
  • GitLab / GitHub: This approach leans more towards Infrastructure as Code. An operator makes a change on the data structure, typically based on CSV / YAML / JSON, and the CI / CD pipeline runs various tests. If everything works, it adjusts the configuration of the devices in production.
  • CSV / XLS / YAML: This is the simplest case, where a simple file contains the parameters of the structure, and the manual execution of a playbook adjusts the configuration of the devices. Any tests are done manually by the operator.

For simplicity, let's choose the third approach. The first two would require significant development beyond the scope of this specific course.

In particular, for its readability and flexibility, we choose to use a YAML file. The YAML file should contain all the parameters that define our fabric. In particular, we definitely need to include information about:

  • DNS
  • hostname and domain
  • NTP
  • SNMP

Operationally, we definitely need to apply the following as well:

  • hardening of devices
  • configure interfaces

In particular, we can imagine that the interfaces have a template based on their function. We will definitely need templates for:

  • inter-switch-link (ISL) interfaces
  • interfaces to endpoints

Furthermore, the interfaces to endpoints will have a profile based on the connected device, for example:

  • virtualization server
  • firewall
  • client access with VoIP phone
  • management access
  • office devices access

We have made this analysis based on our experience, but in a real case, the analysis must be done on the environment we are willing to automate. We must understand how a particular environment is structured and the way people work. Our goal is to formalize a structure (modeling) and standardize the way of working. Only then can we start developing the working tools, which in our case will be based on Ansible.

Practically speaking, we can create a first draft of a data structure that will define our environment:

dns_domain: example.com
dns_lookup: false
dns_servers:
  - 8.8.4.4
  - 8.8.8.8
ntp_servers:
  - 195.201.19.162
  - 141.98.136.83
snmp_community: 494174af4b08f87467a138584f4edb33

We also need to define the VLANs that need to be configured in the fabric:

vlans:
  - id: 50
    name: SERVER
  - id: 51
    name: DMZ
  - id: 52
    name: MGMT
  - id: 53
    name: OFFICE
  - id: 54
    name: VOIP
  - id: 55
    name: INTERNET
  - id: 999
    name: NATIVE

Finally, we need to define the profile associated with each interface:

interfaces:
  Ethernet0/1:
    profile: unused
  Ethernet0/2:
    description: to Hypervisor
    profile: hypervisor
  Ethernet0/3:
    description: to Firewall
    profile: firewall
  Ethernet1/0:
    description: to SW3
    profile: isl
  Ethernet1/1:
    description: to SW4
    profile: isl
  Ethernet1/2:
    description: to SW5
    profile: isl
  Ethernet1/3:
    description: to SW6
    profile: isl

The decision on how to formalize the interface-profile association is crucial because it has a huge impact on the way of operating but at the same time must ensure the integrity of the infrastructure. The format chosen in the example above appears cumbersome but ensures that interfaces are not associated with multiple profiles.

Let's see a second example:

profiles:
  isl:
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/0
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/1
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/2
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet1/3
  firewall:
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet0/3
  unused:
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet0/1
    - switch: SW1
      interface: Ethernet0/2

If we had chosen the second format, apparently more convenient, the operator would have had to ensure that an interface is not associated with multiple profiles.

Therefore, we decide to use the first format, where the interface is defined as a unique key within the file.

docs.title: Define the Inventory
docs.text:
Next, let's define the inventory file, which for convenience we'll implement as an INI file:

[all]
sw1.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.101
sw2.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.102
sw3.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.103
sw4.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.104
sw5.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.105
sw6.example.com ansible_host=169.254.1.106

[access]
sw[3:6].example.com

[core]
sw[1:2].example.com

[cisco_ios]
sw[1:6].example.com

[cisco_ios:vars]
ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios

We'll place the host- and group-associated variables respectively in the host_vars and group_vars directories. In particular:

  • host_vars/sw1.examle.com.yml: will contain the interface-profile association for SW1;
  • host_vars/sw2.examle.com.yml: will contain the interface-profile association for SW2;
  • host_vars/sw3.examle.com.yml: will contain the interface-profile association for SW3;
  • host_vars/sw4.examle.com.yml: will contain the interface-profile association for SW4;
  • host_vars/sw5.examle.com.yml: will contain the interface-profile association for SW5;
  • host_vars/sw6.examle.com.yml: will contain the interface-profile association for SW6;
  • group_vars/all.yml: will contain all the fabric variables;

docs.title: Credential Management
docs.text:
In planning our automation, we need to consider how credentials will be managed. This choice is tied to the use of any orchestrators and directly impacts the security of our environment.

In general, two choices are possible:

  • the playbook is manually invoked by an operator, and in this case, the best choice is for the operator to interactively enter the credentials to be used;
  • the playbook is invoked by an orchestrator, and in this case, the credentials will probably be passed as environment variables. The use of a vault is strongly recommended.

For simplicity, we decide to use the first option: credentials will be interactively entered during playbook execution.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Given the purpose we've set, we can easily identify four roles:

  • system, which will handle the configuration of the hostname, domain, and DNS servers;
  • ntp, which will handle the configuration of NTP servers;
  • snmpv2, which will handle the configuration of SNMP v2 community;
  • interface_profile, which will handle configuring interfaces by applying the correct profile;
  • vlan, which will handle creating the necessary VLANs.

So let's create the skeleton for the four roles:

ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_ntp
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_interface_profile
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_snmpv2
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_system
ansible-galaxy role init roles/cisco_ios_vlan

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_system
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_system role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_system/tasks/main.yml file, which will contain the tasks to configure hostname, domain, DNS lookup, and DNS server.

We split the task into two parts, as it will be more convenient for compliance to know which configuration needs modification. In the first part, we configure the hostname and domain. In particular, as a standard, we want to configure the hostname in uppercase and the domain in lowercase:

# Set and normalize hostname and domain
- name: SETTING FACTS
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    device_hostname: "{{ inventory_hostname_short | upper }}"
    device_domain: "{{ inventory_hostname.split('.', 1)[1] | lower }}"
# Configure hostname
- name: CONFIGURING HOSTNAME AND DOMAIN NAME
  cisco.ios.ios_system:
    hostname: "{{ device_hostname }}"
    domain_name: "{{ device_domain }}"

In the second part, we configure the DNS servers:

# Configure DNS lookup
- name: CONFIGURING DNS LOOKUP
  cisco.ios.ios_system:
    lookup_enabled: "{{ dns_lookup }}"
    name_servers: "{{ dns_servers }}"

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_ntp
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_ntp role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_ntp/tasks/main.yml file, which will contain the tasks to configure NTP peers.

Before configuring NTP peers, we need to transform the list of IP addresses into the data structure required by the module:

# Convert a list of IP into a list of peers
- name: SETTING NTP PEER LIST
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    ntp_peers_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for peer in ntp_servers %}
          {"peer": "{{ peer }}"},
        {% endfor %}
      ]

Now we can apply the configuration:

# Configure NTP peers
- name: CONFIGURING NTP PEERS
  cisco.ios.ios_ntp_global:
    config:
      logging: true
      peers: "{{ ntp_peers_config_list }}"
    state: replaced

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_snmpv2
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_snmpv2 role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_snmpv2/tasks/main.yml file, which will contain the task to configure a single SNMPv2 read-only community.

# Configure the SNMPv2 read-only community
- name: CONFIGURING SNMPv2 COMMUNITY
  cisco.ios.ios_snmp_server:
    config:
      communities:
        - name: "{{ snmp_community }}"
          ro: true
    state: replaced

docs.title: Role cisco_ios_vlan
docs.text:
The cisco_ios_vlan role requires only the roles/cisco_ios_vlan/tasks/main.yml file, which will contain the tasks to configure VLANs.

Before configuring VLANs, we need to transform the list defined in the design phase into the data structure required by the module:

# Convert a list of VLAN to be used with ios_vlans module
- name: SETTING VLAN LIST
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    vlans_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for vlan in vlans %}
          {
            "vlan_id": "{{ vlan.id }}",
            "name": "{{ vlan.name }}",
            "mtu": 1500,
            "state": "active",
            "shutdown": "disabled",
          },
        {% endfor %}
      ]

Now we can apply the configuration:

# Configuring VLANs
- name: ADDING VLANS
  cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
    config: "{{ vlans_config_list }}"
    state: replaced

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
In the initial phase, we identified seven types of interfaces:

  • isl: used for interfaces connecting to other switches (inter-switch-link);
  • hypervisor: used for hypervisor interfaces, configured as trunks with all passing VLANs;
  • firewall: used for firewall interfaces, configured as trunks with all passing VLANs;
  • client: used for user computer interfaces, configured in access with passing VoIP VLAN;
  • management: used for device management interfaces, configured in access;
  • office: used for office devices like printers and fax machines, configured in access;
  • unused: used for unused interfaces.

We have two options for approaching profile development:

  • we can parameterize the profiles, creating a single set of tasks that configures the interfaces;
  • we can create multiple sets of tasks, one per profile.

The first choice would be more correct from a software design perspective, but the second is simpler, more readable, and more maintainable for the network automation we are creating. Once again, there is no correct choice, but a balance between different possibilities that determines the best choice given the specific context.

The cisco_ios_interface_profile role, for each device, will read the interface definitions and apply the correct profile. It requires the roles/cisco_ios_interface_profile/tasks/main.yml file and a file for each profile, placed within the same directory.

The main file, to optimize performance, will read the configuration that will then be used during the configuration of individual interfaces. Then, the task file will be invoked based on the associated profile:

# Get running-config
- name: GETTING RUNNING CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - show running-config
  register: show_running_config
# Attach profile to interface
- name: ATTACHING PROFILE TO INTERFACE
  ansible.builtin.include_tasks: "profile_{{ interface.value.profile }}.yml"
  with_dict: "{{ interfaces }}"
  loop_control:
    loop_var: interface

The main file will also handle configuring the interface state and description. However, we first need to create a data structure usable with the ios_interface module:

# Generate interface status/description data to ve used with ios_interface
- name: SETTING INTERFACE LIST
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    interface_config_list: >-
      [
        {% for interface, interface_data in interfaces.items() %}
          {
            "name": "{{ interface }}",
            {% if interface_data.profile == 'unused' %}
              "enabled": false,
            {% else %}
              "description": "{{ interface_data.description }} ({{ interface_data.profile }})",
              "enabled": true,
            {% endif %}
          },
        {% endfor %}
      ]
# Set description and activate interface if used
- name: "SETTING INTERFACE STATUS"
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config: "{{ interface_config_list }}"

Finally, let's implement the files that define the profiles. Although the ios_interface module allows for various configurations, it does not provide enough freedom of action. Therefore, we decide to use the ios_config module to configure the interfaces as desired.

# Configure profile isl
- name: "APPLYING PROFILE ISL TO INTERFACE {{ interface.key }}"
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    config: "{{ show_running_config.stdout.0 }}"
    lines:
      - switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
      - switchport mode trunk
      - switchport nonegotiate
      - udld port aggressive
    parents: "interface {{ interface.key }}"
    before: "default interface {{ interface.key }}"

Above, we see the configuration of the isl profile in detail. In particular, if the module detects any differences, it first deletes the interface configuration (default interface) and then configures it. This is why we decided to separate the description.

docs.title: Playbook
docs.text:
All that's left is to put together what we've created previously, creating the playbook that calls the roles in order and saves the configuration:

#!/usr/bin/env ansible-playbook
- name: CONFIGURE FABRIC
  hosts: core,access
  gather_facts: false
  roles:
    - role: cisco_ios_system
      tags: dns,hostname
    - role: cisco_ios_ntp
      tags: ntp
    - role: cisco_ios_snmpv2
      tags: snmp
    - role: cisco_ios_vlan
      tags: vlan
    - role: cisco_ios_interface_profile
      tags: interface
  post_tasks:
    - name: SAVING CONFIG
      tags: always
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: modified

We are aware that we have omitted some important configurations, such as those related to spanning tree and logging.

docs.title: Ansible Configuration
docs.text:
Before running the playbook, let's focus on configuring Ansible through the ansible.cfg file and optimize performance by adjusting the fork and strategy parameters:

[defaults]
inventory = inventory.ini
stdout_callback = ansible.builtin.default
strategy = free
forks = 8

[persistent_connection]
ssh_type = libssh

[libssh_connection]
host_key_checking = false
look_for_keys = false

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Now let's move on to the testing phase. For each role, we need to verify:

  • that the configuration performed by the role is as expected;
  • that a new execution confirms the state of the devices without further changes (idempotence);
  • that changing the configuration is correctly reflected on the devices.

So we execute the playbook and wait for it to finish without errors:

./playbook-fabric-setup.yml -i inventorydev.ini -u admin -k

Now we need to check on the devices if the configuration is as expected.

Then we run the playbook again to verify that there are no further changes.

Now we need to vary the configuration, for example:

  • by replacing a DNS server;
  • by replacing an NTP peer;
  • by changing the SNMP community;
  • by changing the profiles of two interfaces.

We run the playbook again and verify the configuration on the devices upon completion.

We run the playbook one last time and verify that there are no further changes.

All sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Managing CLI prompts with Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Some commands, before becoming operational, ask for confirmation from the operator. Ansible has a basic capability to handle these situations thanks to the cli_command and ios_command modules. The first one is generic, the second one is specific to Cisco IOS systems, but both essentially perform the same function with some peculiarities and limitations. In general, vendor-specific modules should handle syntax errors correctly, but as we will see later, this is not always true.

Let's see some examples based on the Simple Network Lab laboratory.

docs.title: Resetting Interface Counters
docs.text:
The first example we see concerns resetting interface counters. The command requires a simple confirmation:

R1#clear counters
Clear "show interface" counters on all interfaces [confirm]

We can use cli_command to execute the command and respond to the confirmation. We refer to the official documentation:

- name: CLEARING INTERFACE COUNTERS WITH cli_command
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: clear counters
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Clear "show interface" counters on all interfaces
    answer:
      - y

Technically, the check_all parameter should check all listed prompts. However, if we change the command to show interfaces, we can verify that the task does not generate any errors. In other words, it is not always possible to distinguish whether the operation was successful.

Alternatively, we can use ios_command. We refer to the official documentation:

- name: CLEARING INTERFACE COUNTERS WITH ios_command
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - command: clear counters
        prompt: Clear "show interface" counters on all interfaces
        answer: y

We can verify that this option also presents the same problem.

docs.title: Saving Configuration
docs.text:
The first example we see concerns saving the configuration. Previously, we used write memory, which does not require any confirmation. Now, let's implement a task that handles the command:

R1#copy running-config startup-config
Destination filename [startup-config]?
Building configuration...

  [OK]

The implementation with cli_command is similar to what we saw earlier:

- name: SAVING CONFIGURATION WITH cli_command
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: copy running-config startup-config
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Destination filename
    answer:
      - startup-config

Here is the implementation with ios_command:

- name: SAVING CONFIGURATION WITH ios_command
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - command: copy running-config startup-config
        prompt: Destination filename
        answer: startup-config

docs.title: Multiple Prompts
docs.text:
Some commands require handling multiple prompts, for example:

R1#ping
Protocol [ip]: ip
Target IP address: 8.8.8.8
Repeat count [5]: 3
Datagram size [100]: 40
Timeout in seconds [2]: 1
Extended commands [n]: n
Sweep range of sizes [n]: n
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 3, 40-byte ICMP Echos to 8.8.8.8, timeout is 1 seconds:
!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (3/3), round-trip min/avg/max = 13/13/13 ms

We can handle multiple prompts with cli_command as follows:

- name: PING WITH cli_command
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: ping
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Protocol
      - Target IP address
      - Repeat count
      - Datagram size
      - Timeout in seconds
      - Extended commands
      - Sweep range of sizes
    answer:
      - ip
      - 8.8.8.8
      - 3
      - 40
      - 1
      - n
      - n

All sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Reboot a device with Ansible and wait for it to come online
Reboot a device with Ansible and wait for it to come online
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible

A more complex interactive task than those seen before is rebooting the device and waiting for it to be available again. Although Ansible is not designed specifically for this purpose, it can be useful, for example, in a procedure that updates device firmware.

Let's analyze the manual procedure:

  • The device must obviously be reachable.
  • The configuration register should be set to 0x2101.
  • The configuration must be saved.

At this point, the reload command can be issued, followed by waiting for it to be reachable again before issuing further commands.

The preliminary tasks, which have already been analyzed before, can be implemented very simply:

- name: READING SHOW VERSION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  register: output
- name: CHECKING CONFIGURATION REGISTER
  ansible.builtin.fail:
    msg: The configuration register must be 0x2101
  when: "'0x2101' not in output['stdout'][0]"
- name: SAVING CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    save_when: modified

The check of the register could have been done with a single task, but with significantly lower usability:

- cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands: show version
  failed_when: "'Configuration register is 0x2101' not in output['stdout'][0]"

In case of error, the output would have been as follows:

fatal: [r1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "failed_when_result": true, "stdout": "Cisco IOS Software, Linux Software (I86BI_LINUX-ADVENTERPRISEK9-M), Version 15.7(3)M2, DEVELOPMENT TEST SOFTWARE\nTechnical Support: [http://www.cisco.com/techsupport\nCopyright (c) 1986-2018 by Cisco Systems, Inc.\nCompiled Wed 28-Mar-18 11:18 by prod_rel_team\n\nROM: Bootstrap program is Linux\n\nR1 uptime is 10 minutes\nSystem returned to ROM by reload at 0\nSystem restarted at 10:01:15 UTC Sun Apr 7 2024\nSystem image file is \"unix:/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/i86bi_LinuxL3-AdvEnterpriseK9-M2_15\"\nLast reload reason: Unknown reason\n\n\n\nThis product contains cryptographic features and is subject to United\nStates and local country laws governing import, export, transfer and\nuse...

The approach with fail instead of failed_when provides the ability to specify the error message, resulting in much better usability:

fatal: [r1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "The configuration register must be 0x2101"}

The task to reboot the device is similar to what we have seen before:

- name: RELOADING DEVICE
  ansible.netcommon.cli_command:
    command: reload
    check_all: true
    prompt:
      - Proceed with reload
    answer:
      - y
  async: 1
  poll: 0

The difference from what was seen previously relates to the async and poll parameters. The reboot will surely cause the SSH connection to close. The async mode allows us to disconnect from the SSH connection and immediately move on to the next task (poll: 0).

The version with ios_command is very similar:

- name: RELOADING DEVICE
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - command: reload
        prompt: Proceed with reload
        answer: "y"
  async: 1
  poll: 0

Finally, we need to wait for the device to be available again. Technically, we are waiting for port 22 (SSH) to be listening again. This operation is done locally by the Ansible controller (connection: local):

- name: WAITING FOR REBOOT
  ansible.builtin.wait_for:
    delay: 30
    connect_timeout: 3
    sleep: 10
    port: 22
    host: "{{ ansible_host }}"
    timeout: 600
  connection: local

The wait_for module is used to wait for an event, such as a particular line in a log file, or, as in our case, the availability of a port:

  • port: specifies the TCP port number to check.
  • host: specifies the IP address of the device on which to check the port.
  • delay: specifies the time to wait before starting the test.
  • connect_timeout: specifies the time to wait before declaring the port inactive.
  • sleep: specifies the time between two tests.
  • timeout: specifies the maximum waiting time (task duration).

This system cannot be used in the presence of bastion hosts because it requires direct connectivity between the Ansible controller and the device.

After this task, all post-reboot verification operations can be performed.

All sources are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Event-Driven Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced

Event-Driven Ansible (EDA) allows the execution of an Ansible playbook to be triggered by a specific event.

This capability exponentially increases Ansible's potential, transforming it into a tool for automating processes based on specific events, such as troubleshooting, threat intelligence, IoCs, data collection, and general analysis. These activities can be partially or fully automated.

Many security vendors have released specific modules. For instance, Palo Alto Networks has developed a plugin for analyzing firewall logs and triggering initial automated diagnostics in case of SSL decryption errors.

docs.title: Rulebook
docs.text:
An Ansible Rulebook is a set of rules that EDA uses to execute specific actions. A rulebook can:

  • Monitor one or multiple sources.
  • Contain one or multiple rules.
  • Trigger one or multiple actions.

The first part of a rulebook defines one or more event sources to be monitored. EDA uses Event Source Plugins to monitor these sources.

docs.title: Event Source Plugins
docs.text:
Event Source Plugins can be classified into three types:

  • Event Bus Plugins: Listens to a stream of events from a source where the connection is established by the plugin itself (e.g., Kafka and AWS SQS Queue plugins).
  • Scraper Plugins: Connects to a source and scrapes data from it, usually at predefined intervals (e.g., URL Check and Watchdog plugins).
  • Callback Plugins: Provides a callback endpoint that the event source can call when data is available (e.g., Webhook and Alertmanager plugins). Callback plugins are the least reliable as they depend on the event source to call the endpoint and are highly susceptible to data loss.

When an Event Source Plugin detects an event, EDA uses rules to determine which action to take. If an event matches a rule, EDA executes the specified actions. Actions can include:

  • run_playbook: Executes an existing Ansible Playbook.
  • run_job_template: Runs a job template via the Ansible Automation Platform.
  • run_module: Runs a specific Ansible module for targeted execution without running an entire playbook.
  • post_event: Posts an event to a running ruleset, allowing action results to feed back into EDA.
  • set_fact: Stores specific event data to be reused within EDA.
  • debug: Outputs debug information, similar to the debug module in Ansible Playbooks.

docs.title: Installing Event-Driven Ansible
docs.text:
First, we need a JRE. We will use OpenJDK 21.0.1:

tar xzvf openjdk-21.0.1_linux-x64_bin.tar.gz
export PATH=~/jdk-21.0.1/bin:$PATH
which java

Then, we install EDA:

pip install ansible ansible-rulebook ansible-runner
ansible-galaxy collection install ansible.eda

docs.title: Example: monitoring router configuration changes
docs.text: In this example, we configure a Cisco router to send syslog messages, set up EDA to read those logs, and trigger a playbook when the router configuration is modified. The activated playbook will export the router configuration to a local directory.

docs.title: Action Playbook
docs.text:
First, we create a simple playbook to handle the backup action:

- hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: "BACKUP RUNNING CONFIG"
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        backup: true
        backup_options:
          filename: "/tmp/{{ ansible_host }}-backup.cfg"
          dir_path: backup

The playbook, using the cisco.ios.ios_config module, performs a backup of the configuration to a local directory, using the ansible_host variable as the base for the filename.

docs.title: Rulebook example
docs.text:
Now, we define a rulebook that triggers the playbook when a relevant syslog message is received:

- name: "LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG"
  hosts: all
  sources:
    - dainok.courses.syslog:
        host: 0.0.0.0
        port: 1514
  rules:
    - name: "RUN PLAYBOOK WHEN ROUTER IS CONFIGURED"
      condition: event.message is match("Configured from.*", ignorecase=true)
      actions:
        - run_playbook:
            name: playbook-backup.yml
        - print_event:
            pretty: true

The rulebook monitors all hosts, uses the dainok.courses.syslog plugin as the event source, and includes a single rule: if the event.message contains Configured from, it runs the backup playbook and logs the event.

docs.title: Syslog Callback plugin
docs.text:
The most complex part is handled by the dainok.courses.syslog plugin. This plugin is responsible for receiving messages from devices via syslog, formatting them, and making them available to the rulebook.

async def main(queue: asyncio.Queue, args: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Receive events via syslog."""
    # Load or set default variables
    host = args.get("host") or "0.0.0.0"
    port = args.get("port") or 1514

    # Listening
    transport, protocol = await asyncio.get_running_loop().create_datagram_endpoint(
        lambda: SyslogUDPProtocol(queue), local_addr=((host, port))
    )

    # Listening
    logging.info(f"Starting daemon on {host}:{port}")
    try:
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(300)
    finally:
        transport.close

The main class initializes the syslog server on the specified host and port. The SyslogUDPProtocol class is responsible for receiving messages, formatting them, and returning them to the rulebook:

output = {
    "prival": prival,
    "version": version,
    "host": host,
    "seq": seq,
    "timestamp": timestamp,
    "facility": facility,
    "severity": severity,
    "mnemonic": mnemonic,
    "message": message,
    "raw": raw,
}
if host:
    # Limit the inventory for the action
    output["meta"] = {"hosts": host}

# Send data to Ansible
logging.info(f"Sending to EDA {output}")
queue = self.edaQueue
await queue.put(output)

Specifically, the hosts key must be present to restrict the execution of the playbook to the host that generated the event. This information is transmitted by the configured router via syslog.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
We can now activate our rulebook:

ansible-rulebook -r playbook-rulebook.yml -i inventory.ini -v

The output informs us that the rulebook has been started and that the syslog server is ready to receive events.

2025-03-09 17:28:38,987 - ansible_rulebook.engine - INFO - Waiting for all ruleset tasks to end
2025-03-09 17:28:38,987 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - Waiting for actions on events from LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG
2025-03-09 17:28:38,987 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - Waiting for events, ruleset: LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG
2025-03-09 17:28:38 987 [drools-async-evaluator-thread] INFO org.drools.ansible.rulebook.integration.api.io.RuleExecutorChannel - Async channel connected

To ensure that the parser within syslog correctly formats the events, we configure the devices with the following commands:

service timestamps debug datetime msec localtime year
service timestamps log datetime msec localtime year
service sequence-numbers
logging host 169.254.1.1 transport udp port 1514
logging origin-id hostname

If we configure a router, as soon as we return to exec mode, the router will send a message to the syslog server, which will then process it:

2025-03-09 17:32:18,965 - root - INFO - Received Syslog message: <189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)
2025-03-09 17:32:18,967 - root - INFO - Sending to EDA {'prival': 189, 'version': 85, 'host': 'sw1.example.com', 'seq': 97, 'timestamp': 'Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933', 'facility': 'SYS', 'severity': '5', 'mnemonic': 'CONFIG_I', 'message': 'Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'raw': '<189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'meta': {'hosts': 'sw1.example.com'}}
2025-03-09 17:32:19 006 [main] INFO org.drools.ansible.rulebook.integration.api.rulesengine.RegisterOnlyAgendaFilter - Activation of effective rule "RUN PLAYBOOK WHEN ROUTER IS CONFIGURED" with facts: {m={prival=189, version=85, host=sw1.example.com, seq=97, timestamp=Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933, facility=SYS, severity=5, mnemonic=CONFIG_I, message=Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1), raw=<189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1), meta={hosts=sw1.example.com, source={name=dainok.courses.syslog, type=dainok.courses.syslog}, received_at=2025-03-09T16:32:18.967429Z, uuid=978910b9-6589-47e5-bdf1-b6784eb39b39}}}

The playbook will then be executed only on the necessary host:

2025-03-09 17:32:19,015 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - call_action run_playbook
2025-03-09 17:32:19,015 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - substitute_variables [{'name': 'playbook-backup.yml'}] [{'event': {'prival': 189, 'version': 85, 'host': 'sw1.example.com', 'seq': 97, 'timestamp': 'Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933', 'facility': 'SYS', 'severity': '5', 'mnemonic': 'CONFIG_I', 'message': 'Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'raw': '<189>85: SW1: 000097: Mar 9 2025 17:32:17.933: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)', 'meta': {'hosts': 'sw1.example.com', 'source': {'name': 'dainok.courses.syslog', 'type': 'dainok.courses.syslog'}, 'received_at': '2025-03-09T16:32:18.967429Z', 'uuid': '978910b9-6589-47e5-bdf1-b6784eb39b39'}}}]
2025-03-09 17:32:19,015 - ansible_rulebook.rule_set_runner - INFO - action args: {'name': 'playbook-backup.yml'}

If needed, the event data is sent from EDA to the playbook through the ansible_eda variable.

TASK [debug] *******************************************************************
ok: [sw1.example.com] => {
    "msg": {
        "event": {
            "facility": "SYS",
            "host": "sw1.example.com",
            "message": "Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)",
            "meta": {
                "hosts": "sw1.example.com",
                "received_at": "2025-03-09T16:35:14.521860Z",
                "source": {
                    "name": "dainok.common.syslog",
                    "type": "dainok.common.syslog"
                },
                "uuid": "4a1a9a8c-e386-4f48-b666-0c80be4cc558"
            },
            "mnemonic": "CONFIG_I",
            "prival": 189,
            "raw": "<189>86: SW1: 000098: Mar  9 2025 17:35:13.514: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by admin on vty0 (169.254.1.1)",
            "seq": 98,
            "severity": "5",
            "timestamp": "Mar  9 2025 17:35:13.514",
            "version": 86
        },
        "rule": "RUN PLAYBOOK WHEN ROUTER IS CONFIGURED",
        "ruleset": "LISTEN FOR EVENTS VIA SYSLOG"
    }
}

The use of EDA:

  • requires authentication to be automatic (non-interactive)
  • requires the use of collections (theoretically, local plugins can be used, but I couldn't find the correct syntax in practice)

The collection containing the plugin used is available on the Ansible GitHub repository and can be installed via Galaxy. The playbook is available in the course GitHub repository.

docs.title: Ansible reporting with ARA
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

ARA Records Ansible provides a simple dashboard to visualize the execution of Ansible playbooks. It is not an orchestration tool but rather a reporting tool that facilitates visualization and troubleshooting.

ARA works with any Ansible playbook, regardless of how it is executed. Therefore, ARA can be integrated with other tools. However, the information stored by ARA can be enhanced by integrating playbooks with specific parameters.

To better understand ARA, we can explore the demo.

By configuring ARA as a callback, playbook execution results are stored in a database:

docs.title: Installing and Configuring ARA
docs.text:
ARA is installed as a Python module:

pip install ara[server]

We then need to configure ARA as a callback. To do this, we run the following command:

python -m ara.setup.ansible

We integrate the output of the above command into the ansible.cfg file:

[defaults]
inventory = inventory.ini
stdout_callback = ansible.builtin.default
callback_plugins = ../../venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ara/plugins/callback
action_plugins = ../../venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ara/plugins/action
lookup_plugins = ../../venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/ara/plugins/lookup
strategy = free
forks = 8

ARA can be customized with specific parameters configured in the ansible.cfg file. Initially, the default parameters can be used.

We start the ARA server with the following command:

ara-manage runserver

docs.title: Executing a Playbook
docs.text:
ARA does not require any modifications to the execution of Ansible playbooks. For example, we can execute a previously created playbook to configure a small sample fabric.

On the first execution, ARA creates default settings and an SQLite database:

[ara] No setting found for SECRET_KEY. Generating a random key...
[ara] Creating data & configuration directory: /Users/dainese/.ara/server
[ara] Writing default settings to /Users/dainese/.ara/server/settings.yaml
Operations to perform:
  Apply all migrations: admin, api, auth, contenttypes, db, sessions
Running migrations:
  Applying contenttypes.0001_initial... OK
  Applying auth.0001_initial... OK
  Applying admin.0001_initial... OK
  Applying admin.0002_logentry_remove_auto_add... OK
  Applying admin.0003_logentry_add_action_flag_choices... OK
  Applying api.0001_initial... OK
  Applying api.0002_remove_host_alias... OK
  Applying api.0003_add_missing_result_properties... OK
  Applying api.0004_duration_in_database... OK

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
After the first execution, we can connect to the ARA server and verify that the playbook execution has been correctly recorded:

By examining the details in the hosts tab, we can analyze the playbook duration on each host:

We can view the details of the tasks executed on a specific host:

Finally, we can review the execution details of each task:

docs.title: Recording Additional Values
docs.text:
ARA can be configured to record additional parameters. This configuration requires adding specific tasks:

- name: "ARA: INTERFACE CONFIG"
  delegate_to: localhost
  throttle: 1
  ara_record:
    key: interface_config
    value: "{{ interface_config_list }}"

There are some important caveats:

  • Adding ara_record tasks breaks compatibility with normal execution.
  • Running ARA with ara_record tasks often results in errors:
An exception occurred during task execution. To see the full traceback, use -vvv. The error was: requests.exceptions.ConnectionError: HTTPConnectionPool(host='localhost', port=60417): Read timed out.
An exception occurred during task execution. To see the full traceback, use -vvv. The error was: requests.exceptions.ConnectionError: ('Connection aborted.', BadStatusLine('Date: Sun, 09 Mar 2025 10:18:10 GMT\r\n'))

These errors can be mitigated using the delegate_to and throttle parameters; however, my tests have shown that ARA becomes unusable.

When it works, the output is similar to the following:

The playbook is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Orchestrating playbooks with Ansible AWX
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible awx

Ansible AWX is the open-source version from which Ansible Tower draws inspiration. Both AWX and Tower are orchestrators for Ansible playbooks, allowing management of playbooks in the form of projects, credentials, schedules, and reports.

The installation of Ansible AWX is particularly complex and has changed multiple times over time. Currently, it requires a Kubernetes environment which we will install on an Ubuntu Linux Server system.

Therefore, we need a system with the following specifications:

  • Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04
  • 8 cores
  • 8 GB of RAM
  • 50 GB of disk space

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
First, we install Docker  by following the official documentation.

Remove any packages related to previous versions:

apt-get purge docker.io docker-doc docker-compose docker-compose-v2 podman-docker containerd runc

Add the official Docker repository:

wget -qO- https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | apt-key add -
add-apt-repository "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture)] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable"

Finally, install Docker:

apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

docs.title: Minikube
docs.text:
Minikube allows us to have a complete instance of Kubernetes within a single virtual machine.

So, let's install Minikube:

curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube && rm minikube-linux-amd64

Then, with an unprivileged user but belonging to the docker group, we create the Kubernetes instance:

minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=6g --addons=ingress
minikube kubectl -- get nodes

For simplicity, let's add an alias that allows us to use the kubectl command:

alias kubectl="minikube kubectl --"

docs.title: Installing AWX
docs.text:
Check the AWX Operator repository to see which tag we can use (2.16.1) and create the necessary files for the environment setup:

# awx/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: awx
images:
  - name: quay.io/ansible/awx-operator
    newTag: 2.16.1
resources:
  - github.com/ansible/awx-operator/config/default?ref=2.16.1

Then apply the changes:

kubectl apply -k awx/

Monitor the pod creation with the following command and wait for it to finish:

kubectl get pods -n awx -w

Then create the resource file:

# awx/awx.yaml
apiVersion: awx.ansible.com/v1beta1
kind: AWX
metadata:
  name: awx
spec:
  service_type: nodeport

And associate it with the previously created file:

# awx/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: awx
images:
  - name: quay.io/ansible/awx-operator
    newTag: 2.16.1
resources:
  - github.com/ansible/awx-operator/config/default?ref=2.16.1
  - awx.yaml

Then apply the changes:

kubectl apply -k awx/

And monitor the logs related to the creation of the AWX service:

kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-operator-controller-manager -c awx-manager

We can also monitor the pod status:

kubectl get pods -A

At the end of the process, the AWX service should be available:

minikube service awx-service --url -n awx

Now we need to make the AWX service reachable from the outside:

kubectl port-forward svc/awx-service -n awx --address 0.0.0.0 8080:80 &> /dev/null &

The AWX web interface should now be available on port 8080. Login is possible with the user admin and the password can be retrieved using the following command:

kubectl get secret awx-admin-password -n awx -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 --decode; echo

In case of issues, we need to check the status of the entire environment using the following commands:

minikube status
minikube service list
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl get services -n awx
kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-operator-controller-manager
kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-task
kubectl logs -n awx -f deployments/awx-web

In case of extreme necessity, it is possible to get a shell inside the various containers:

kubectl exec --stdin --tty --namespace awx awx-task-5f88767b44-87m9p -- /bin/bash

docs.title: ansible-pylibssh
docs.text:
If we need the ansible-pylibssh library, we need to make an additional modification. AWX, like Ansible, by default, uses the paramiko library. Playbook execution is performed by a container created at runtime from the awx-ee image:

minikube ssh docker images

If we run a playbook using the default environment, we get the following error:

[WARNING]: ansible-pylibssh not installed, falling back to paramiko
fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "No existing session"}

We can force the use of pylibssh by setting the following variable:

ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: libssh

In this case, we would get a more explicit error:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "Failed to import the required Python library (ansible-pylibssh) on automation-job-11-m85n8's Python /usr/bin/python3. Please read the module documentation and install it in the appropriate location. If the required library is installed, but Ansible is using the wrong Python interpreter, please consult the documentation on ansible_python_interpreter"}

There is a third-party EE image (Execution Environment) containing ansible-pylibssh: however, it is a year old and without any guarantee.

The GitHub repository contains the structure contributing to the creation of the dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh image. In particular, there are four files:

  • dependencies/bindep.txt: contains the list of RPM packages to install in the image.
  • dependencies/requirements.txt: contains the list of Python packages to install in the image.
  • dependencies/requirements.yml: contains the Ansible Galaxy modules to install in the image.
  • execution-environment.yml: defines how to create the image from a specific version of awx-ee based on the dependencies defined above.

So, let's create the environment to build the image:

cd "/opt/courses/Ansible/A5. AWX"
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install ansible==9.5.1 ansible-builder==3.0.1
ansible-builder build --tag dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1 --container-runtime docker --verbosity 3

Once the creation is complete, we can publish the image on Docker Hub:

docker login
docker tag dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1 dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:latest
docker push dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1
docker push dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:latest

docs.title: Bastion host
docs.text:
The architecture of the bastion host has already been described in a previous lesson and we will refer to the same architecture.

First, we need to copy the contents of the id_rsa.pub file into the authorized_keys file of the bastion host. Then, we make the private key id_rsa available to AWX:

kubectl create secret generic bastion-host-key -n awx --from-file=ssh-privatekey=.ssh/id_rsa

In AWX, go to Instance Groups → default → Edit → Customize pod specification. The content should be similar to the following:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: awx
spec:
  serviceAccountName: default
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - image: quay.io/ansible/awx-ee:latest
      name: worker
      args:
        - ansible-runner
        - worker
        - '--private-data-dir=/runner'
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 250m
          memory: 100Mi

Customize the configuration so that the key referenced as Secret is available as a local file:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: awx
spec:
  serviceAccountName: default
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - image: quay.io/ansible/awx-ee:latest
      name: worker
      args:
        - ansible-runner
        - worker
        - '--private-data-dir=/runner'
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 250m
          memory: 100Mi
      # Custom config starts here
      volumeMounts:
        - name: ssh-keys
          mountPath: /opt/bastionhost_id_rsa
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: ssh-keys
      secret:
        secretName: bastion-host-key
        defaultMode: 0400
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000 # The AWX user
    fsGroup: 1000 # The AWX user

Finally, in the inventory Resources → Inventories → Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology, add the variable that forces the use of the bastion host:

ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios
ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: paramiko
ansible_ssh_common_args: -o ProxyCommand="ssh -o IdentityFile=/opt/bastionhost_id_rsa/ssh-privatekey -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -W %h:%p -q dev@172.25.82.110"

Now, all playbooks associated with the inventory Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology will be executed via the bastion host.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
The playbook repositories we will use in AWX must contain the list of Ansible Galaxy modules needed within the collections/requirements.yml file:

collections:
- name: cisco.ios
  version: 8.0.0
  source: https://galaxy.ansible.com

The same file can be used to install dependencies in the local environment:

ansible-galaxy collection install -r src/courses/collections/requirements.yml

docs.title: Configuring AWX
docs.text:
First, let's create the execution environment (EE) using the Docker image created earlier. In Administration → Execution Environments, add a new image:

  • Name: awx-ee-pylibssh
  • Image: dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh:1
  • Pull: Only pull the image if not present before running

Now, go to Resources → Projects and add a project using the course's GitHub repository:

  • Name: Courses
  • Execution Environment: awx-ee-pylibssh
  • Source Control Type: Git
  • Source Control URL: https://github.com/dainok/courses

Next, go to Resources → Inventories to create a new inventory of type inventory:

  • Name: Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology

The inventory will have the following variables defined in YAML format:

ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios
ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: libssh

Then, create the two groups used in the playbooks: core and access.

Add the credentials by going to Resources → Credentials:

  • Name: Cisco Lab
  • Credential Type: Machine
  • Username: admin
  • Password: cisco

Finally, add the six devices associating them with the correct group:

  • sw1.example.com: associated with the core group with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.101
  • sw2.example.com: associated with the core group with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.102
  • sw3.example.com:associated with the access group with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.103
  • sw4.example.com: associated with the access group with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.104
  • sw5.example.com: associated with the access group with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.105
  • sw6.example.com: associated with the access group with variable ansible_host: 169.254.1.106

Finally, create the template for playbook execution. Go to Resources → Templates and add a new template:

  • Name: Fabric provisioning
  • Job Type: Run
  • Inventory: Cisco Legacy Core-Access topology
  • Project: Courses
  • Playbook: Ansible/17. Final lab/playbook-fabric-setup.yml
  • Credentials: Cisco Lab

Save the template and run it. Under Jobs, you can see the task result and its logs.

The first execution may take longer as it needs to create the container used to run the playbook:

$ kubectl get pods -A
NAMESPACE   NAME                                               READY   STATUS              RESTARTS        AGE
awx         automation-job-5-plmtj                             0/1     ContainerCreating   0               6m56s
awx         awx-migration-24.3.1-qmncx                         0/1     Completed           0               42h
awx         awx-operator-controller-manager-5b795f7bb-597fv    2/2     Running             17 (22h ago)    42h
awx         awx-postgres-15-0                                  1/1     Running             0               42h
awx         awx-task-77b9bcbc8d-txjl8                          4/4     Running             0               42h
awx         awx-web-7569c8f4f9-dxmvk                           3/3     Running             0               42h

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
There are a large number of moving parts that can malfunction. Let's summarize potential errors we may encounter.

The task execution should trigger the download of the Docker image we created. Let's verify this with:

$ minikube ssh docker images
REPOSITORY                  TAG   IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
dainok/awx-ee-pylibssh      1     f2bee65d1f1c   18 hours ago   3.36GB

If the container creation takes longer than expected and particularly if it stops at ContainerCreating, we can analyze the problem with:

kubectl describe pods -n awx automation-job-12-gqzxr

If the image is not downloaded correctly, check the URL including the tag. The error associated with the inability to retrieve the image is:

Receptor detail:
Error creating pod: container failed to start, ImagePullBackOff

If the logs indicate a timeout when connecting to devices, it's possible the bastion host configuration is incorrect:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: Timeout connecting to 169.254.1.111"}

A similar error indicates probably the inability to access the bastion host, if used:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: Socket error: Connection reset by peer"}

In this case, we should see similar logs on the bastion host:

May 11 06:14:50 eve-ng sshd[1885336]: Failed password for dev from 172.25.82.1 port 49826 ssh2

If you encounter errors related to the pylibssh library, it's crucial to ensure that you are using the correct EE image referenced at the inventory and/or template level. For instance, if you receive a warning about ansible-pylibssh not being installed and a failure message indicating no existing session, you might encounter the following:

[WARNING]: ansible-pylibssh not installed, falling back to paramiko
ok: [sw1.example.com]
TASK [cisco_ios_system : CONFIGURING HOSTNAME AND DOMAIN NAME] *****************
fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "No existing session"}

To avoid ambiguity, if you are not using a bastion host, ensure that the use of pylibssh is enforced by the configuration; otherwise, you might encounter an error similar to this:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "Failed to import the required Python library (ansible-pylibssh) on automation-job-11-m85n8's Python /usr/bin/python3. Please read the module documentation and install it in the appropriate location. If the required library is installed, but Ansible is using the wrong Python interpreter, please consult the documentation on ansible_python_interpreter"}

If you are experiencing connection issues with outdated devices, you might see an error message like this:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: ssh connect failed: kex error : no match for method kex algos: server [diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1,diffie-hellman-group1-sha1], client [curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,ecdh-sha2-nistp256,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256,diffie-hellman-group14-sha256,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18-sha512]"}

In this case, you may need to use paramiko instead of ansible-pylibssh by setting the following configuration variable:

ansible_network_cli_ssh_type: libssh

Finally, if you receive an error related to credentials or credential type, you might see a message like this:

fatal: [sw1.example.com]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "ssh connection failed: Failed to authenticate public key: Access denied for 'none'. Authentication that can continue: publickey,keyboard-interactive,password"}

docs.title: Ansible Galaxy
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

Ansible provides Galaxy, which allows managing packages containing roles and collections. Roles and collections can be directly referenced by Ansible playbooks. Galaxy enables the use of packages published directly on the public portal but also allows managing private repositories.

In this post, we will focus on the official Galaxy portal. The Galaxy portal is fully integrated with GitHub, where various repositories available as collections in Galaxy are stored.

The structure of a collection is quite rigid, and to create one, it is best to rely on ansible-creator, which we can install using pip:

pip install ansible-creator

We then create a collection using the format github_nickname.collection_name. In my case, I used dainok.courses:

ansible-creator init collection dainok.courses

This command creates a complete but rather complex structure:

Let's examine the essential parts.

docs.title: galaxy.yml
docs.text:
The galaxy.yml file contains the collection metadata and the instructions to generate it. For further details, refer to the official documentation and the example repository.

namespace: "dainok"
name: "common"
version: 1.0.0
readme: README.md
authors:
  - your name <example@domain.com>
description: your collection description
license_file: LICENSE
tags: ["linux", "tools"]
dependencies:
  "ansible.utils": "*"
repository: http://example.com/repository
documentation: http://docs.example.com
homepage: http://example.com
issues: http://example.com/issue/tracker
build_ignore:
  - .gitignore
  - changelogs/.plugin-cache.yaml

docs.title: Extensions, plugins, roles, playbooks
docs.text:
Extensions, plugins, roles, and playbooks should be stored in their respective directories. Each role must be described by a README.md file and the meta/main.yml file.

galaxy_info:
  author: foo
  description: Dainok.Common Run Role
  company: Dainok
  license: GPL-2.0-or-later
  min_ansible_version: "2.14"
  galaxy_tags:
    []
dependencies:
  []

We can note that some information is duplicated: for example, the description is present in both the meta file and the README, and dependencies exist at both the role level and the overall collection level.

Filters are stored inside the plugins directory and are described in Python files:

DOCUMENTATION = """
    name: hello_world
    author: Your Name
    version_added: "1.0.0"
    short_description: A custom filter plugin for Ansible.
    description:
      - This is a demo filter plugin designed to return Hello message.
    options:
      name:
        description: Value specified here is appended to the Hello message.
        type: str
"""

EXAMPLES = """
# hello_world filter example

- name: Display a hello message
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ 'ansible-creator' | hello_world }}"
"""

docs.title: Ansible Galaxy token
docs.text:
Before proceeding, we need to register on the Galaxy portal and obtain a token. Since Galaxy is integrated with GitHub, we need a valid GitHub account and must authenticate on Galaxy via GitHub:

A token can be obtained by navigating to Collections → API token.

docs.title: Building and publishing
docs.text:
Once the repository is ready, we can create the package and publish it as a collection:

ansible-galaxy collection build
ansible-galaxy collection publish --token <token> dainok-courses-0.0.17.tar.gz

The courses collection will be available under the dainok namespace. We can manage our collections on the Galaxy portal by navigating to Collections → Namespaces → My namespaces.

We can also view the logs related to the collection publication:

docs.title: Using a collection
docs.text:
The simplest way to install a collection is via the command line:

ansible-galaxy collection install --force dainok.courses

However, it is more practical, as we do with Python, to define a collections/requirements.yml file that describes dependencies:

collections:
  - name: cisco.ios
    version: 8.0.0
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com
  - name: paloaltonetworks.panos
    version: 2.20.0
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com
  - name: networktocode.nautobot
    version: 5.2.1
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com
  - name: dainok.courses
    version: 0.0.17
    source: https://galaxy.ansible.com

We can install collections defined as dependencies:

ansible-galaxy collection install -r collections/requirements.yml

Finally we can list installed collection:

ansible-galaxy collection list

The sample collection is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Delegate Ansible tasks to a different host
Delegate Ansible tasks to a different host
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate

By default, Ansible executes playbooks on a single host. However, in various scenarios, tasks need to be executed across multiple hosts in a specific sequence. A common example is a web server that must be taken offline from the load balancer before being modified. A typical playbook for this scenario would:

  • Reconfigure the load balancer to take the web server offline
  • Reconfigure the web server
  • Reconfigure the load balancer to bring the web server back online

If we refer to our previously mentioned network fabric, we can adapt this approach:

We can write a playbook to configure access switches while enabling the corresponding core switch interfaces step by step.

In other words, once an access switch is configured, a specific task will connect to the core switches to configure the interfaces associated with that switch.

To achieve this, we need to use the delegate_to functionality.

docs.title: Using delegate_to in Ansible
docs.text:
The syntax is straightforward: within a task, we must specify which host is delegated to execute it. In many cases, we can use localhost for local task execution. In our scenario, we delegate the configuration tasks to the core switches:

- name: "CONFIGURING UPSTREAM SW1"
  delegate_to: sw1.example.com
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    lines:
      - switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
      - switchport mode trunk
      - switchport nonegotiate
      - udld port aggressive
    parents: "interface {{ upstream_interface }}"
    before: "default interface {{ upstream_interface }}"
- name: "ENABLING UPSTREAM SW1 INTERFACE"
  delegate_to: sw1.example.com
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config:
      - name: "{{ upstream_interface }}"
        enabled: true
        description: "to {{ inventory_hostname }}"

docs.title: Key Considerations
docs.text:
There are some important aspects to keep in mind when using delegate_to:

  • delegate_to cannot be used with loops (with_items). However, we can work around this limitation by including a separate task, as shown previously.
  • delegate_to does not function correctly when using a bastion host. If misconfigured, we might encounter the following error:
fatal: [sw6.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]: FAILED! => {"changed": false, "msg": "unable to connect to socket /Users/dainese/.ansible/pc/ff42547828. See the socket path issue category in Network Debug and Troubleshooting Guide"}

The official documentation provides a detailed explanation of this functionality, including specific cases related to variable handling.

When running the playbook, Ansible's output will indicate that a task for a specific switch has been delegated to another host, such as sw1.example.com:

TASK [cisco_ios_uplink_interface : CONFIGURING UPSTREAM SW1] *******************
ok: [sw3.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]
ok: [sw5.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]
ok: [sw6.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]
ok: [sw4.example.com -> sw1.example.com(169.254.1.101)]

The playbook is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Network Provisioning with ServiceNow and Ansible
Automating Network Provisioning with ServiceNow and Ansible
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

ServiceNow is a cloud-based SaaS platform that digitalizes, automates, and optimizes enterprise workflows, improving operational efficiency.

One of its core capabilities is the definition of services offered to users through a service catalog, along with full lifecycle management of those requests. The goal here is to extend that catalog to include all relevant IT services, automating their provisioning end-to-end.

We will walk through a practical example by creating a network provisioning entry in the service catalog — parameterizable and orderable by end users.

Incoming requests will be handled automatically by a Python script responsible for applying changes in the production environment.

The architecture supports two integration modes:

  • Pull: the script polls ServiceNow periodically to retrieve unfulfilled requests
  • Push: a webhook notifies the script of new requests in real time

While polling is generally discouraged, it is worth noting that many organizations apply infrastructure changes only within specific maintenance windows. In that context, it is entirely natural to pull all pending requests at the start of each window and process them serially until it closes.

This experiment requires a ServiceNow instance. I used a personal developer instance, available free of charge through the ServiceNow Developer Program.

docs.title: ServiceNow Catalog Configuration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible servicenow

In this post we look at how to extend the ServiceNow service catalog to include a new item for managing network creation. The example is intentionally straightforward, but in real-world environments it is essential to first conduct a thorough analysis of the architecture, the services offered, and the organization's existing processes. Automation improves processes — if those processes do not yet exist, that is where the work needs to start.
