docs.title: Filtering Cisco API Output
docs.text: 11 January 2026

docs.title: Filtering Cisco API Output
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci cisco intermediate

Previously, we created a simple script to print a table of CDP neighbors for all interfaces in the fabric. While writing it, we realized it could be optimized.

To optimize the script, we need to change the way we retrieve data.

The class used to get the fabric nodes is fabricNode. Open the Viewer and perform a query with role == leaf:

In the address bar, we can see that parameters have been added to filter the query. To achieve the same effect using the APIs, we need to call this URL:

https://172.25.82.1/api/class/fabricNode.json?query-target-filter=and(eq(fabricNode.role,"leaf"))

We queried the objects belonging to the fabricNode class, filtering for nodes where role == leaf.

We can build our filters using different functions. The most common are:

  • eq(attr, val) → equals
  • ne(attr, val) → not equal
  • like(attr, "pattern") → pattern matching

These functions can be combined with:

  • and(...)
  • or(...)

At this point, we can improve our script to show CDP neighbors by querying just two classes: fabricNode and cdpAdjEp. The two results can then be combined like this:

# Print output

for neighbor in neighbor_list:
    m = re.search(r"topology/pod-(\d+)/node-(\d+)/.*?/if-\[([^\]]+)\]", neighbor["dn"])
    pod_id, leaf_id, interface_id = m.groups()
    leaf_id = int(leaf_id)
    leaf_name = None
    for leaf in leaf_list:
        if leaf["id"] == leaf_id:
            leaf_name = leaf["name"]

    data.append([
        pod_id, # PodID
        leaf_id, # LeafID
        leaf_name, # LeafName
        interface_id, # Interface
        neighbor["devId"], # RemoteName
        neighbor["portId"], # RemoteInterface
    ])

print(tabulate(data, headers=headers))

The second version of the script is 13× faster.

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Pagination with Cisco ACI
docs.text: 18 January 2026

docs.title: Pagination with Cisco ACI
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci cisco intermediate

When dealing with a large number of records, pagination becomes necessary. By default, Cisco ACI pagination allows you to retrieve up to 500 objects. A maximum value is not explicitly documented; however, it is not recommended to go beyond this limit in order to avoid overloading the APIC.

Pagination can be controlled using the following parameters:

  • page-size, which defines the size of each page
  • page, which defines which page to retrieve, starting from 0

The response includes the totalCount attribute, which indicates the total number of objects available for the specific query.

To use pagination correctly, each page should be requested only when it is actually needed. To achieve this, we can use yield. Yield allows us to return one object at a time, suspending iteration until the next request.

def fetch_objects(class_name, page_size=10):
    page = 0
    while True:
        url = f"https://{apic_address}/api/class/{class_name}.json?page-size={page_size}&page={page}"
        res = session.get(url, verify=False)
        res.raise_for_status()
        items = res.json().get("imdata", [])
        if not items:
            # No more data
            break
        for item in items:
            # Return one object
            yield item
        # Next page
        page += 1

We can retrieve the list of interfaces with:

interface_list = fetch_objects("l1PhysIf")

However, no API calls are made until we actually start using interface_list. The API calls are performed progressively as we iterate over the list. This allows us to spread out API calls and execute them only when necessary.

We must keep in mind that interface_list can only be used once. If we want to reuse it multiple times, we need to convert the object from a generator to a list:

leaf_list = list(fetch_objects("fabricNode"))

We can now use what we’ve built to create a simple script that prints all interfaces:

# Get leaves

leaf_list = list(fetch_objects("fabricNode"))

# Get interfaces

interface_list = fetch_objects("l1PhysIf")

for interface in interface_list:
    interface_attrs = interface["l1PhysIf"]["attributes"]
    m = re.search(r"topology/pod-(\d+)/node-(\d+)/.*?/.*", interface_attrs["dn"])
    pod_id, leaf_id = m.groups()
    leaf_name = None
    for leaf in leaf_list:
        leaf_attribute = leaf["fabricNode"]["attributes"]
        if leaf_id == leaf_attribute["id"]:
            leaf_name = leaf_attribute["name"]
    data.append([
        pod_id, # PodID
        leaf_id, # LeafID
        leaf_name, # LeafName
        interface_attrs["id"], # Interface
        interface_attrs["adminSt"], # Admin
        interface_attrs["autoNeg"], # AutoNeg
        interface_attrs["descr"], # Description
    ])

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: From Single-Site to Multi-Site with NDO
docs.text: 24 September 2025

docs.title: From Single-Site to Multi-Site with NDO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cisco ndo

As infrastructures expand across different geographic locations and distances grow larger, moving from a single-site setup to a multi-site architecture becomes a natural step.

In an ideal world, each site in a multi-site deployment should operate independently. In practice, though, applications often have specific requirements that call for stretched L2 networks between sites. Since this is driven by the applications themselves, my advice is to design self-sufficient and independent silos that can continue running even if another site goes down.

When the real need is to connect applications across multiple sites in a native and consistent way, the tool of choice is Cisco Nexus Dashboard Orchestrator (NDO).

NDO is a powerful platform, but also a complex one with some limitations. Like any automation project, it requires the involvement of multiple roles and skill sets. Here we’ll focus only on the aspects that matter most for our use case, without going too deep into the overall design and configuration architecture of NDO.

docs.title: Object Structure
docs.text:
NDO organizes its configuration using schemas and templates, which are then applied to tenants and sites:

  • Schemas: collections of templates that share a common use case.
  • Templates: define the objects that will be deployed to one or more sites. These objects can include Applications, EPGs, Contracts, VRFs, Bridge Domains, Filters, External EPGs, and L3Outs. At the template level, you can choose which sites the objects will be applied to.
  • Tenants: logical containers for objects, mapped one-to-one with the tenants defined in the APIC.

docs.title: Key Considerations
docs.text:
There are a few important points to keep in mind when working with NDO:

  • NDO doesn’t cover everything. You can’t configure the entire fabric exclusively through NDO. Some operations will still need to be performed directly on the APIC.
  • Avoid circular dependencies. Objects defined in different templates should not create circular relationships between each other (we’ll dive deeper into this later).

docs.title: Circular Dependencies with NDO
docs.text: 01 October 2025

docs.title: Circular Dependencies with NDO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese cisco intermediate ndo

We already highlighted how critical the design phase is in any automation project. This is even more true when working with NDO, since a design mistake could easily compromise the entire project.

When designing templates, you must carefully plan the deployment order to ensure no circular dependencies are created. Dependency checks are performed at the template level, not at the level of the individual objects inside them. Let’s look at an example:

In this example (courtesy of Mario Rosi), we have a single schema containing six templates. Each template includes the objects listed below:

  • The first two templates are site-specific and contain objects that are meaningful only within their respective site. These objects do not need to communicate with objects in other sites.
  • The third template is shared across all sites and includes objects that must communicate with those in other sites.
  • The remaining templates contain reusable objects that are also shared across all sites.
  • The arrows in the diagram represent dependencies: they start from the dependent object and point to the object they rely on. For example, a Bridge Domain requires a VRF to be created first.

In this case, the deployment order of the templates would be:

  1. Template #6 – containing Contracts and Filters
  2. Template #4 – containing VRFs
  3. Templates #1, #2, #3 – containing objects specific to each site or shared across all sites (no dependencies between them)
  4. Template #5 – containing External EPGs

A circular dependency occurs when an object in one template depends on an object in another template, and the reverse is also true. For instance, if you place both External EPGs and VRFs in the same template, that template would need to be deployed both before and after others, because:

  • External EPGs depend on L3Outs
  • Bridge Domains depend on VRFs

docs.title: Key Factors for Approaching Automation
docs.text:
From an automation perspective, there are several important consequences:

  • If NDO has limitations, using NaC (Network as Code) on NDO introduces even more. You must always validate how your specific use case will be handled.
  • Since some objects are configured through NDO while others are managed directly on the APIC, it’s essential to validate the final outcome.
  • Regarding Cisco NaC, the deployment sequence of templates should not exceed three steps.

In the example above, we need to reduce the deployment sequence from four steps down to three. Since the template with Contracts and Filters and the template with VRFs are independent from each other, they can either be merged or deployed simultaneously.

From the customer’s perspective, there is often an additional requirement: stretching networks across multiple sites without service disruption. This expectation needs to be factored into both the design and the automation workflow.

docs.title: Frameworks for Projects with Cisco ACI and NDO
docs.text: 12 October 2025

docs.title: Frameworks for Projects with Cisco ACI and NDO
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci beginner cisco ndo

When developing an automation system for Cisco ACI and NDO, we have several frameworks to choose from:

  • APIs: maximum flexibility, but requiring significant effort and strong programming skills.* APIC: API-first approach, with documentation available directly through the Web UI.
  • NDO: APIs are available, but beware of potential breaking changes. The documentation is online (via OpenAPI/Swagger), along with a changelog of breaking changes.
  • Ansible: simplified framework, does not require programming experience.* APIC: a fairly complete Ansible collection is available.
  • NDO: a fairly complete Ansible collection is also available.
  • Terraform: more complex, requiring prior expertise; best suited for greenfield environments.* APIC: a fairly complete Terraform provider is available.
  • NDO: a Terraform provider exists, but with several limitations.
  • NaC (Network as Code): a framework that abstracts Terraform’s complexity.* APIC: a specific module is available, with some limitations.
  • NDO: a specific module exists, but with more significant limitations.

For NDO specifically, I recommend using NaC whenever possible, because it greatly simplifies automation. Object creation and deletion in NDO must follow a specific sequence. Terraform (and therefore NaC) implements the correct sequence out of the box, allowing projects to move much faster.

We will dive deeper into NaC in a dedicated article.

And no, we are not even considering the Web UI, trying to manage this level of complexity manually is simply not practical.

docs.title: Managing Limitations
docs.text:
Unless you are working directly with APIs on both APIC and NDO, you will inevitably run into framework limitations. And even then, we know NDO has inherent restrictions compared to APIC.

A practical example is IGMP Snooping: due to certain products implementing multicast in a somewhat “loose” way, I often find myself needing to disable IGMP Snooping.

If we manage Cisco ACI fabrics through NDO, we must always check how (and if) this can be done. Here are some examples:

From this, we can conclude:

  • We will almost always need a hybrid approach, working on both NDO and APIC.
  • APIs provide maximum flexibility, but they are also the most complex and expensive to implement.
  • NaC covers most scenarios, but sometimes must be complemented with a custom Terraform module.

NaC is heavily used by hundreds of customers to manage entire ACI infrastructures. In theory, you could find something supported by Terraform but not directly by NaC, although the probability is very low. As an example, we are configuring a vPC Explicit Protection Group outside of NaC.

This mindset should be applied to every configuration in your environment. As we’ve said before, planning is the most important phase of any automation project.

docs.title: Managing Cisco NDO Limitations from the APIC
docs.text: 26 October 2025

docs.title: Managing Cisco NDO Limitations from the APIC
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco ndo netascode

We have observed that NDO currently has some important limitations that must be kept in mind:

  • NDO frameworks have limitations, particularly NaC
  • NDO itself has limitations
  • certain configurations must necessarily be managed directly on the APIC

This consideration is far from trivial, and to fully understand it, we need to analyze how objects are created by NDO on the APIC.

docs.title: Objects Created by APIC vs. NDO
docs.text:
When I manually create an object on the APIC, the annotation field is empty. If I create it through Terraform or Ansible, the field is populated with the name of the framework used.

However, when the object is created by NDO, it results in:

annotation: orchestrator:msc-shadow:no
children -> fvSiteAssociated -> children -> fvRemoteId

See files BD-MANUAL-ON-APIC.json and BD-94-FROM-NDO.json in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Modifying an Object Created by NDO
docs.text:
Let’s now look at a practical example: we need to add the IGMP Snooping policy since it is not supported by NDO with NaC. The Bridge Domain has unicastRoute disabled.

We modify the Bridge Domain using Terraform/NaC. The final result shows the following differences:

annotation: orchestrator:terraform
unicastRoute: no -> yes

See files BD-94-SHADOW-FROM-NDO.json and BD-94-FROM-NDO-MODIFIED.json in the GitHub repository.

If I redeploy from NDO, I get:

annotation: orchestrator:terraform -> orchestrator:msc-shadow:no
unicastRoute: yes -> no
children -> fvSiteAssociated -> name: -> msc-local

This happens even if I manually modify an object on the APIC that was originally created by NDO.

See files BD-94-FROM-NDO-REDEPLOYED.json and BD-94-FROM-NDO-MODIFIED.json in the GitHub repository.

We can therefore conclude that if we modify on the APIC an object created by NDO:

  • it will then be interpreted as locally managed by NDO (msc-local)
  • if we use a framework, the annotation field will be overwritten
  • if we use a framework, parameters will be reset to default

We must therefore remember to:

  • use the ndo_managed parameter to preserve the annotation field
  • when using a framework, specify the same parameters used to create the object in NDO

docs.title: Shadow Objects
docs.text:
When using NDO, even if templates are tied to different sites, NDO creates all objects on all APICs. This is why identical objects, belonging to different templates, must have different names.

Objects on an APIC belonging to a different fabric are marked as shadow objects, and this information is always stored in the annotation field:

annotation: orchestrator:msc-shadow:yes
annotation: orchestrator:msc-shadow:no

See files BD-94-FROM-NDO.json and BD-94-SHADOW-FROM-NDO.json in the GitHub repository.

From the Web UI, we can enable visibility of shadow objects by navigating to Manage my profile → Settings → Show Hidden Policies:

At this point, shadow objects become visible:

docs.title: Stretching a Stretched Network
docs.text:
A critical point during the design phase is how to extend networks without causing service disruption.

We have seen that during design we must configure our networks (Bridge Domains) within a template, which can be either local to a site or shared across multiple sites. The consequence of this design is that if we need to extend a network that was previously configured in a site-local template, we must move it to the appropriate shared template.

NDO provides a dedicated function for this:

However, our Infrastructure as Code approach does not rely on the Web UI.

It is also likely that object names depend on the associated template: changing the template means changing the name, and changing the name means deleting the object on the APIC and recreating it from scratch, with all its dependencies.

My approach is therefore to define networks as shared unless we are certain that they will always remain strictly local. Of course, architectural limits must be considered to ensure we do not exceed the allowed number of objects per type.

docs.title: Safeguarding the Critical Tenant
docs.text:
Each ACI fabric is composed of an infrastructure tenant, which defines its basic functionality and connectivity. On top of that, production workload tenants are added.

In my view, we must consider managing the infrastructure tenant separately from production tenants: both can be handled through Infrastructure as Code, but they have different characteristics and requirements.

The Infra tenant is prepared initially, with very rare changes. An error on the Infra tenant can compromise the entire fabric.

Production tenants undergo constant modifications. An error impacts only the specific tenant.

My approach is therefore to separate the two implementations, minimizing changes and limiting access to the Infra tenant.

With respect to NDO, dividing management into multiple workspaces also improves automation system performance (especially with Terraform and NaC).

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case modelling
docs.text: 02 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case modelling
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo

The example presented here covers the deployment of a multi-site fabric managed through NDO. The current setup, based on a legacy environment, must be migrated to a newly implemented multi-site environment. Although this is not a greenfield project, we can treat it as such since the entire configuration will be generated from scratch.

The automation project requirements are to:

  • Distribute the production workload across all sites
  • Ensure fast deployment
  • Provide simple tools for the operations team

In the current infrastructure, most of the L3 routing is handled by firewalls. Some basic L3 routing scenarios within the fabric may be implemented in the future.

Unfortunately, there is no single “correct” approach that guarantees results. Furthermore, what works today may require changes tomorrow, as NDO, the Terraform NDO provider, and NaC are constantly evolving.

In this case, I chose to:

  • Focus on the production tenant, managing fabric setup and inter-site communication manually
  • Prefer tools in the order: NaC, Terraform, Python
  • Store automation code and data structures in Git
  • Manage configuration on NDO, configuring only unsupported features directly on APIC
  • Use NaC data structures for objects that rarely require modification
  • Use a simple CSV-based structure for operations requiring frequent updates (networks, L3Outs)
  • Create a parser to convert CSV files into NaC and Terraform data structures

docs.title: NDO
docs.text:
All logical configuration, i.e., related to templates, is managed by NDO, with a few exceptions described later. The physical configuration, however, is managed directly on the APIC for two reasons:

  • There is currently no complete NaC or Terraform module for managing the physical layer.
  • The Terraform provider for NDO has poor performance, so it’s more efficient to perform non-critical tasks directly on the APIC.

NDO therefore contains:

  • The production tenant, applied across all sites
  • A schema template

The schema contains six tenant templates:

  • One template per site containing BDs, subnets, Applications, and EPGs (deploy order 2)
  • One shared template for all sites containing BDs, Applications, and EPGs (deploy order 2)
  • One shared template for all sites containing VRFs (deploy order 1)
  • One shared template for all sites containing Contracts (deploy order 1)
  • One shared template for all sites containing External EPGs (deploy order 3)

Operational activity will typically be limited to templates containing BDs, Applications, and EPGs. The others will remain mostly static.

The Terraform provider for NDO does not support tenant-level policies (e.g., IGMP snooping policies). If such policies are required, they must be configured directly on the APIC.

docs.title: APIC
docs.text:
All configuration not managed by NDO, particularly physical configuration is managed directly on the APIC. Specifically, the APIC manages:

  • Access policies (AAEPs, interface policies, leaf interface policy groups, physical domains, VLAN pools)
  • Physical topology (interfaces, vPCs)
  • Physical association with EPGs

Each site will also have its own dedicated Terraform environment, ensuring visibility into changes and their impact on the infrastructure.

docs.title: NaC and Terraform
docs.text:
In this project, NaC manages nearly the entire configuration. The only exception is for vPC explicit protection groups, which are handled via Terraform.

While Terraform may initially seem complex, it provides significant advantages when used with Cisco ACI: object creation and deletion are performed safely and automatically.

docs.title: Modelling
docs.text:
Infrastructure construction occurs at multiple levels, NDO, APIC, NaC, and Terraform. Practically, this requires building a relatively complex data structure that includes some duplicated information.

For example, when creating an EPG, it must be associated with both a BD and the relevant physical interfaces. On NDO, we define BDs, Applications, and EPGs; on APIC, we associate the EPG with physical interfaces.

Validating the data structure to prevent human errors can be challenging.

Modelling should never be influenced by the technical solution, it must be defined according to the architecture and operational requirements.

In this case, I chose to work with:

  • CSV files containing networks and interfaces
  • YAML files for NaC containing static, non-duplicated information

I developed a parser that:

  • Validates the CSV data structure
  • Performs integrity checks (e.g., VLAN usage depends on the definition of its associated network)
  • Safely generates NaC and Terraform structures for NDO and APIC

Adding or removing objects simply requires editing CSV files, which are designed to be human-readable. The rest is handled safely by Terraform.

docs.title: Parser
docs.text:
The core of the automation is a custom parser that converts CSV-based data structures into NaC and Terraform formats.

The parser enables a user interface that transforms input files (CSV) into the structures required by NaC and Terraform.

It also validates and normalizes CSV input, performing multiple integrity checks.

The parser can be easily integrated into a CI/CD pipeline: the user only needs to update a CSV file. After committing, the configuration deployment is automatically managed during a maintenance window.

This approach also allows parser modifications with full safety: if the generated data structure remains unchanged, no errors were introduced. Similarly, the CSV structure can evolve, for example, integrating with an IPAM.

docs.title: CSV
docs.text:
In this scenario, input data is managed using two main CSV files.

Network CSV:

IT teams are typically accustomed to thinking of networks in terms of VLANs. VLAN tags are also critical when connecting ACI with environments that don’t natively support VXLAN. Furthermore, all objects must have unique names to avoid overlap with shadow objects created on other sites.

Each network can include a subnet and may be L2 stretched. If the VRF is not defined, a default one is used. The application name is derived from the site and VRF name, since this migration project follows a network-centric model from legacy to ACI.

This CSV file generates:

  • VRFs (e.g., replica_VRF or default_VRF)
  • Applications (e.g., MI-storage_replica_App or MI-default_App)
  • Bridge Domains (e.g., MI-0011-INFRA-DMZ_BD)
  • EPGs (e.g., MI-0011-INFRA-DMZ_EPG)

Objects are created on NDO (VRF, Application, Bridge Domain, Subnets, Endpoint Groups). They are deployed on the shared template if SITE=SHARED, or on the site-specific template otherwise.

Using this model, we immediately identify a critical issue: if a site-local network (non-L2 stretched) later needs to become L2 stretched, we must set SITE=SHARED. In practice, this destroys and recreates the object with a new name, requiring all associated interfaces to be re-bound, significantly impacting the infrastructure.

However, the client requirement is to make a network L2 stretched without disruption. To achieve this, only objects that will never need to be stretched should be defined as site-local. All others that may potentially be stretched should be defined with SITE=SHARED.

Interface CSV:

Each interface group specifies the site, the corresponding leaf, policy group, configured interfaces, tagged VLANs, and native VLAN.

A unique GROUP_NAME must be defined, it is used to build related objects and cannot be changed later. PORT_DESCRIPTION can be modified freely and defaults to the same value as GROUP_NAME.

For individual interfaces, POLICY_GROUP references one of the predefined policy groups, created via a dedicated NaC file.

This CSV file generates:

  • Selectors (e.g., MI-SERVER-1A_Sel) associated with leaf interface profiles (e.g., TrustedPort_PolGrp)
  • Port blocks (e.g., Block3) associated with selectors and their descriptions (e.g., to Server 1)

For vPC-configured interfaces, POLICY_GROUP references a policy template used during vPC policy group creation.

For vPCs, this CSV file generates:

  • vPC-type policy groups (e.g., MI-BLADE-1_PolGrp)
  • Selectors (e.g., MI-BLADE-1_Sel) associated with policy groups and leaf interface profiles
  • Port blocks (e.g., Block1) linked to selectors with descriptions (e.g., vPC to Blade Servers Chassis 1)

Finally, the file creates static EPG-to-port/vPC associations for each VLAN.

CSV files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case additional configuration
docs.text: 09 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case additional configuration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo netascode

In the previous article, we built the data structure that defines our infrastructure and most of its operational logic. However, there are some elements that require a different handling approach.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
I usually work with two main files to store the required variables: config.yml and secrets.yml.

Specifically, the config.yaml file includes:

  • The access references for APIC and NDO
apics:
  mi:
    name: MI-FABRIC
    url: https://192.168.1.1
    url_insecure: true
  rm:
    name: RM-FABRIC
    url: https://192.168.2.1
    url_insecure: true
ndo:
  url: https://192.168.0.1
  url_insecure: true
  • Template names and deployment order
ndo:
  templates:
    contracts:
      name: Template-Contracts
      deploy_order: 1
    stretched_extepg:
      name: Template-Stretched-ExtEPG
      deploy_order: 3
    stretched_vrf:
      name: Template-Stretched-VRF
      deploy_order: 1
    site_mi:
      name: Template-MI
      deploy_order: 2
    site_rm:
      name: Template-RM
      deploy_order: 2
  • Parameters for optional filters
ndo:
  templates:
    site_stretched:
      filters:
        - name: ANY_Filter
          entries:
            - name: Any
              ethertype: unspecified
  • The name of the physical domain

The secrets.yaml file, on the other hand, stores the credentials required to access NDO and APIC:

ndo:
  username: admin
  password: "password"
mi:
  username: admin
  password: "password"
rm:
  username: admin
  password: "password"

Both files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: NaC Static Files
docs.text:
Some NaC-related configurations are rarely modified. Before making changes to these, it’s essential to evaluate their potential impact on the fabric, since they represent the foundational building blocks of the entire infrastructure.

My approach is to use the NaC data structure for components that are statically defined, do not interact with other systems (e.g., NDO, APIC), and seldom require modification. These configurations are defined in the file custom-apic-fabric.nac.yaml.

In particular, I’ve chosen to statically define the fabric access policies for:

  • AAEPs
apic:
  access_policies:
    aaeps:
      - name: Phy_AAEP
        routed_domains:
          - PhyL3Out_RoutedDomain
        physical_domains:
          - Phy_Domain
  • Interface policies (e.g., CDP, LLDP, port channel)
apic:
  access_policies:
    interface_policies:
      cdp_policies:
        - name: ENABLE_CDP_IntPol
          admin_state: true
        - name: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
          admin_state: true
      lldp_policies:
        - name: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
          admin_rx_state: true
          admin_tx_state: true
        - name: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
          admin_rx_state: false
          admin_tx_state: false
      port_channel_policies:
        - name: ENABLE_LACP_PO_IntPol
          mode: active
          suspend_individual: true
          graceful_convergence: true
        - name: ENABLE_STATIC_PO_IntPol
          mode: off
          suspend_individual: true
          graceful_convergence: true
  • Leaf interface policy groups (e.g., TrustedPort_PolGrp, UntrustedPort_PolGrp)
apic:
  access_policies:
    leaf_interface_policy_groups:
      - name: TrustedPort_PolGrp
        type: access
        cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
        lldp_policy: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
        aaep: Phy_AAEP
      - name: UntrustedPort_PolGrp
        type: access
        cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
        lldp_policy: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
        aaep: Phy_AAEP
  • Physical and routed domains
apic:
  access_policies:
    vlan_pools:
      - name: Phy_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 1
            to: 1001
            role: external
          - from: 1006
            to: 3499
            role: external
      - name: PhyL3Out_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 3500
            to: 3999
            role: external
  • VLAN pools
apic:
  access_policies:
    vlan_pools:
      - name: Phy_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 1
            to: 1001
            role: external
          - from: 1006
            to: 3499
            role: external
      - name: PhyL3Out_VlanPool
        allocation: static
        ranges:
          - from: 3500
            to: 3999
            role: external

These files are also available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Single Ports and vPC Profiles
docs.text:
We’ve seen that when defining a static port, we can associate a policy group that acts as a template:

In our CSV file, port 3 of leaf 101 is associated with the TrustedPort policy group. Therefore, the port will be configured with LLDP enabled and CDP disabled. As previously mentioned, the TrustedPort policy group is statically defined in custom-apic-fabric.nac.yaml.

When configuring a vPC, however, we can’t use the same approach because each vPC requires a unique policy group, effectively missing an abstraction layer.

During the modelling phase, we decided to configure vPCs using a template-based approach, similar to how we handle single interfaces.

The templates are defined in config.yaml:

fabric:
  port_channel_policies:
    TrustedLACPVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: ENABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_LACP_PO_IntPol
    TrustedStaticVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: ENABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: ENABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_STATIC_PO_IntPol
    UntrustedLACPVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_LACP_PO_IntPol
    UntrustedStaticVPC:
      type: vpc
      cdp_policy: DISABLE_CDP_IntPol
      lldp_policy: DISABLE_LLDP_IntPol
      aaep: Phy_AAEP
      port_channel_policy: ENABLE_STATIC_PO_IntPol

Each template contains the configuration that will be applied when creating the policy group associated with each vPC.

For example, if a vPC is defined as TrustedLACPVPC in the fabric-interfaces.csv file, the automation process creates a policy group by copying the configuration from the corresponding template.

This allows us to manage both single interfaces and vPCs with a unified, centralized approach to defining configuration profiles.

The files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case data validation
docs.text: 16 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case data validation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo netascode

As we’ve seen, CSV files are used to generate the NaC configuration. However, it’s necessary to perform validation tests to ensure correctness.

Starting with the CSV file defining networks:

  • VLAN_ID must contain an integer within a defined VLAN pool.
  • VLAN_NAME must contain an alphanumeric string without spaces (hyphens and underscores are allowed). Uppercase or lowercase can be enforced if needed.
  • SITE must contain one of the following values: RM, MI, or SHARED. This field defines the object name and the associated tenant template in NDO.

The fields VLAN_ID, VLAN_NAME, and SITE together define the object name, e.g. MI-0011-INFRA-DMZ.

  • L2_STRETCHED specifies whether the network is stretched between MI and RM. Only networks in the SHARED template can be L2 stretched.
  • ANYCAST_ADDRESS defines the subnet associated with the Bridge Domain. If a network has an Anycast address and is associated with the SHARED template, it must be L2 stretched.
  • VRF defines the associated VRF name. If empty, a default VRF is created.
  • ADVERTISED specifies whether the subnet is advertised via dynamic routing protocols.

An additional (yet unimplemented) check could verify whether a VLAN is already in use within the fabric-interfaces.csv file.

Now let’s move on to the CSV file defining interfaces:

  • SITE must contain RM or MI.
  • LEAF_ID contains the ID of a single leaf or a pair of leaves. Each ID must be present in fabric-leaves.csv.
  • POLICY_GROUP contains the associated policy group. If the LEAF_ID is a single value, the policy group must exist in custom-apic-fabric.nac.yaml. If it’s a pair, it must exist in config.yaml.
  • INTERFACES lists the interfaces to configure, separated by commas. Each interface can only be used once per leaf.
  • TAGGED_VLANS can include a VLAN range; each VLAN must exist in l2-networks.csv.
  • NATIVE_VLAN can include a VLAN defined in l2-networks.csv.
  • GROUP_NAME defines object names on the APIC (selectors, policy groups), these values must remain unchanged.
  • PORT_DESCRIPTION defines the interface description. If empty, the value of GROUP_NAME is used.

CSV files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case building the parser
docs.text: 23 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case building the parser
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco ndo netascode

The parser is a custom script that converts user input (via CSV files) into NaC configuration. It also performs data validation, as described in the previous post. If successful, the parser generates NaC files within the nac-data directory, these are then consumed by Terraform to configure NDO and APIC.

The parser consists of two main files:

  • infra.py: reads CSV files, validates data, and builds the NaC data structure.
  • build-nac-data.py: uses infra.py to generate the Terraform files, organized by environment (NDO, APIC) and site (MI, RM, SHARED).

It’s nearly impossible to describe both Python files in full detail here, so we’ll provide a high-level overview.

docs.title: infra.py
docs.text:
The infra.py file defines the object classes for APIC, VRF, Leaf, Network, and InterfaceGroup. Objects are defined using Pydantic, enabling data normalization and first-level validation.

The VRF class:

class VRF(BaseModel):
    name: str

    def __str__(self):
        return self.name

    @field_validator("name", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def parse_name(cls, raw=str | None):
        if raw:
            return raw.strip()
        return "default"

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def validate_rules(self):
        if not self.name.replace("_", "").replace("-", "").isalnum():
            raise ValueError(f"With VRF {self.name}, name is not valid")

        return self

The class defines a name attribute (string type). A before validator assigns name=default if the field is empty, while an after validator ensures the name is alphanumeric (allowing - and _).

The Infra class loads all infrastructure-defining files (l2-networks.csv, fabric-interfaces.csv, fabric-leaves.csv, config.yaml, secrets.yaml) and builds a complete data structure:

class Infra:
    def __init__(self):
        # Reading config file
        with open(self._config_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)

        # Reading secret file
        with open(self._secrets_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.secrets = yaml.safe_load(f)

        # Read APIC customization
        with open(self._apic_customization_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            self.apic_customization = yaml.safe_load(f)

        # Reading input data
        self.__load_apics__()
        self.__load_l2_networks__()
        self.__load_fabric_leaves__()
        self.__load_fabric_interfaces__()

Each __load function performs global validation. For example, __load_l2_networks__ ensures that VLANs are unique and belong to a defined VLAN pool.

Getter functions allow reading the data structure and applying optional filters. For example, we can retrieve interface groups based on site, leaf ID, and interface:

# ***************************************************************************
# Getters: Interface
# ***************************************************************************

def get_interface_group_by_interface_leaf_site(
    self, leaf: Leaf, site: Site, iface: int
) -> InterfaceGroup | None:
    for item in self.interface_groups:
        if (
            item.leaf.name == leaf.name
            and item.site.name == site.name
            and iface in item.ifaces
        ):
            return item
    return None

This helps determine whether an interface is already in use.

NaC getters generate the NaC-formatted data structures:

# ***************************************************************************
# NaC getters: Fabric
# ***************************************************************************

def get_fabric_access_leaf_interface_vpc_policy_groups(
    self, site: Site, apic: bool = False
) -> List[dict]:
    """Return Fabric -> Access Policies -> Interfaces -> Leaf Interfaces -> Policy Groups."""
    if not apic:
        raise ValueError(
            "With get_fabric_access_leaf_interface_vpc_policy_groups, apic=False is not supported"
        )

    policy_groups_data = []
    for interface_group in self.get_interfaces_group_by_site(site=site):
        # Building vPC policy groups
        if "-" not in interface_group.leaf.name:
            # Skip non vPC
            continue

        policy_group_data = dict(
            self.config["fabric"]["port_channel_policies"][interface_group.profile]
        )
        policy_group_data["name"] = f"{interface_group.selector}_PolGrp"
        policy_groups_data.append(policy_group_data)

    return policy_groups_data

For example, get_fabric_access_leaf_interface_vpc_policy_groups is used by build-nac-data.py to create the file nac-data/apic-fabric-mi.nac.yaml.

NaC getters are particularly important when data requires customization or is shared between NDO and APIC.

For instance, subnets defined at the Bridge Domain level are managed in NDO. However, if a subnet is site-specific, it must be configured at the site level, not the template level:

# NDO specific attributes
if site.name == "SHARED":
    bridge_domain["subnets"] = subnets
else:
    bridge_domain["sites"] = [
        {
            "name": self.get_apic_name_by_site(Site(site.name)),
            "subnets": subnets,
        }
    ]

Another example involves EPGs: while EPGs are configured in NDO, their interface associations are applied at the APIC level. Since Terraform executed on APIC overrides NDO-managed configurations, the get_tenant_application_profiles function ensures consistent object definitions across both domains by setting the ndo_managed flag.

docs.title: build-nac-data.py
docs.text:
The build-nac-data.py script uses infra.py to process input data and generate the Terraform configuration files.

Files created for NDO:

  • ndo.nac.yaml: defines sites, schema, and templates.
  • ndo-*.nac.yaml: defines Bridge Domains, Subnets, Applications, and EPGs per site.

Files created for APIC:

  • apic-fabric-*.nac.yaml: defines access policies (Leaf Interface Policy Groups, Leaf Interface Profiles, and Leaf Switch Profiles) per site, mapping physical interfaces to policy groups.
  • apic-*.terraform.yaml: defines switch access policies per site.
  • apic-tenant-*.nac.yaml: redefines Applications and EPGs per site, mapping interfaces and VLANs to each EPG.

Terraform files generated from Jinja2 templates:

  • site-*/main.tf: defines parameters for NaC integration.
  • site-*/versions.tf: defines module versions.
  • site-*/terraform.tfvars includes credentials for NDO and APIC access.
  • site-*/providers.tf: defines the Terraform provider.
  • site-*/variables.tf: defines variables referenced in terraform.tfvars.
  • site-*/custom.tf: includes the Terraform module for configuring resources not supported by NaC.

Parser files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case config deploy
docs.text: 30 November 2025

docs.title: A practical Cisco NDO multi-site use case config deploy
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci beginner cisco ndo netascode

At this stage, we can build the configuration:

./build-nac-data.py

If everything runs successfully, the script completes silently (“no news is good news”), creating or updating files under nac-data and site-* directories.

We can now apply the configuration to NDO using Terraform:

cd site-shared
terraform apply -parallelism=1

Then, proceed with the APIC configurations:

cd site-mi
terraform apply
cd ../site-rm
terraform apply

During testing, this workflow has consistently performed correctly, except in one specific case: when renaming or reusing an object (e.g., reassigning an interface).

In such cases, it’s best to delete the old entry from the CSV, run Terraform to remove the previous object, and then recreate it. Otherwise, resource conflicts may occur if the same object is recreated before the previous one is fully deleted.

For example, creating approximately 600 networks on NDO (including Bridge Domains, Applications, and EPGs, for a total of about 1,100 objects) took roughly 35 minutes.
