docs.title: Managing a brownfield Cisco ACI fabric with NaC and Terraform
Managing a brownfield Cisco ACI fabric with NaC and Terraform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco netascode terraform

After using NaC in recent projects, I started wondering whether it would be possible to manage an existing (brownfield) infrastructure with NaC. Within the NaC suite, this capability is provided directly by Cisco.

Ideally, after using NaC in recent projects, I asked myself whether it would be possible to manage an existing (brownfield) infrastructure with NaC. Within the NaC suite, this capability is provided directly by Cisco.

In theory, it is possible to import objects from an existing infrastructure into the Terraform state file. Likewise, it should be possible to analyze a Cisco ACI fabric and describe (model) it using the language provided by NaC.

If everything works as expected, we can safely operate on a brownfield infrastructure using NaC and Terraform. Let’s walk through the process step by step.

This is an educational post: no one should execute this process in a production environment, as it is highly likely to cause service disruption.

docs.title: Analysis of a Cisco ACI Fabric
docs.text:
The first step is relatively straightforward: we need to read the objects from a Cisco ACI infrastructure that are modeled by NaC. In this example, we will limit the scope to Tenants, VRFs, and Bridge Domains (BDs).

The most direct approach is to use the APIs, which we have already discussed. This time I chose to work with Cobra, the Python SDK downloadable from any APIC at https://172.25.82.1/cobra/_downloads/

Once the *.whl files have been downloaded, they can be installed with:

pip install *.whl

Cobra is a powerful tool, but it has very limited documentation. As a result, understanding how to properly use the SDK can be challenging, and more than once I had to inspect the library’s source code to determine how to use it correctly.

Let’s start by retrieving all tenants:

# Get Tenants
fvTenant_objs = moDir.lookupByClass("fvTenant")
for tenant in fvTenant_objs:
    if tenant.name in IGNORED_TENANTS:
        # Ignore tenant
        continue
    nac_tenant_data = {}
    nac_tenant_data["name"] = tenant.name
    if tenant.descr:
        nac_tenant_data["description"] = tenant.descr

For each tenant, we must retrieve the associated VRFs:

    # Get VRFs
    fvCtx_objs = moDir.lookupByClass('fvCtx', parentDn=tenant.dn)
    if fvCtx_objs:
        nac_tenant_data["vrfs"] = []
    for vrf in fvCtx_objs:
        nac_vrf_data = {}
        nac_vrf_data["name"] = vrf.name
        nac_vrf_data["enforcement_preference"] = vrf.pcEnfPref
        if vrf.descr:
            nac_vrf_data["description"] = vrf.descr
        nac_tenant_data["vrfs"].append(nac_vrf_data)

And finally, the Bridge Domains:

    # Get BrideDomains
    fvBD_objs = moDir.lookupByClass('fvBD', parentDn=tenant.dn, subtree="children")
    if fvBD_objs:
        nac_tenant_data["bridge_domains"] = []
    for bd in fvBD_objs:
        nac_bd_data = {}
        nac_bd_data["name"] = bd.name
        nac_bd_data["multicast_arp_drop"] = parse_boolean(bd.mcastARPDrop)
        nac_bd_data["ip_dataplane_learning"] = parse_boolean(bd.ipLearning)
        nac_bd_data["unknown_unicast"] = bd.unkMacUcastAct
        if bd.descr:
            nac_bd_data["description"] = bd.descr
        nac_tenant_data["bridge_domains"].append(nac_bd_data)

        # Find VRF
        for child in bd.children:
            if child.meta.moClassName == "fvRsCtx":
                vrf = moDir.lookupByDn(child.tDn)
                nac_bd_data["vrf"] = vrf.name
                break

As shown in the code, while retrieving the objects we progressively build the NaC-formatted data structure describing Tenants, VRFs, and BDs.

Since NaC allows us to organize information arbitrarily, we generate one file per tenant:

    # Dump data
    with open(f"data/tenant-{tenant.name}.nac.yaml", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        nac_data = {"apic": {"tenants": [nac_tenant_data]}}
        yaml.dump(nac_data, fh, default_flow_style=False, sort_keys=False, allow_unicode=True)

The result is a set of NaC files describing our infrastructure:

apic:
  tenants:
  - name: NTS_TRAINING
    vrfs:
    - name: PROD
      enforcement_preference: unenforced
    bridge_domains:
    - name: FW_OUTSIDE
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: false
      unknown_unicast: flood
      vrf: PROD
    - name: APP
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: true
      unknown_unicast: flood
      vrf: PROD
    - name: WEB
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: true
      unknown_unicast: proxy
      vrf: PROD
    - name: DMZ
      multicast_arp_drop: false
      ip_dataplane_learning: true
      unknown_unicast: flood
      vrf: PROD

This is the simplest part. The next step is to import the objects from Cisco ACI into Terraform using the NaC data model.

The script used in this example is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Importing NaC objects from Cisco ACI into Terraform
Importing NaC objects from Cisco ACI into Terraform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci beginner cisco netascode terraform

In the previous post, we analyzed a Cisco ACI infrastructure and described it using the NaC data model. This is a simplification: although NaC is a very comprehensive framework, it does not support 100% of the configuration options available in Cisco ACI.

This is an educational post: no one should execute this process in a production environment, as it is highly likely to cause service disruption.

Terraform can only manage objects it is aware of. Therefore, we now need to create the Terraform representation of the objects (Tenants, VRFs, BDs) using the NaC data model.

Let’s clarify this further.

If I attempt to import the tenant NTS_TRAINING, I receive the following error:

$ terraform import aci_tenant.nts_training uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING
Error: resource address "aci_tenant.nts_training" does not exist in the configuration.

Before importing this resource, please create its configuration in the root module. For example:

resource "aci_tenant" "nts_training" {
  # (resource arguments)
}

The error essentially states that Terraform cannot find any reference to aci_tenant.nts_training. This happens because there is no .tf file defining that object. This is expected: one of the key advantages of NaC is that Terraform complexity is abstracted away.

Therefore, I must import the tenant NTS_TRAINING following the naming convention used by NaC. This information can be obtained by analyzing the Terraform plan.

For example, the plan to create the tenant NTS_TRAINING shows:

# module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant will be created
+ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvTenant" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    + class_name  = "fvTenant"
    + content     = {
        + "descr"     = null
        + "name"      = "NTS_TRAINING"
        + "nameAlias" = null
      }
    + dn          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING"
    + escape_html = true
    + id          = (known after apply)
  }

We can see that the module name is composed, among other elements, of the tenant name and the class:

module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant

The correct import command is therefore:

$ terraform import 'module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant' uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING
module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant: Importing from ID "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING"...
module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant: Import prepared!
  Prepared aci_rest_managed for import
module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant: Refreshing state... [id=uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING]

Import successful!

The resources that were imported are shown above. These resources are now in
your Terraform state and will henceforth be managed by Terraform.

We can verify the result by running Terraform plan again: the tenant object exists, but some attributes require modification:

# module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvTenant" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "ownerKey" = null
        - "ownerTag" = null
        - "userdom"  = "all" -> null
        # (3 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

This is the most critical point of the entire approach: we must ensure that the attribute values configured in Cisco ACI (and detected by Terraform) exactly match those defined via NaC for all relevant parameters:

# module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "OptimizeWanBandwidth"     = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteBumTrafficAllow" = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteL2Stretch"       = "no" -> null
        - "ipv6McastAllow"           = "no" -> null
        - "llAddr"                   = "::" -> null
        - "ownerKey"                 = null
        - "ownerTag"                 = null
        - "userdom"                  = "all" -> null
        # (19 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

To complete the process, we must apply the Terraform plan. This may lead to unpredictable situations if we do not fully understand the purpose of each attribute/value.

We must now handle the import of VRFs, BDs, and all derived objects.

In general, the Terraform plan helps us understand how many objects must be created. The data structure is already defined in the NaC files, so we only need to execute the correct import commands.

For reference, the commands to import Tenants, VRFs, BDs, and related objects are as follows:

terraform import module.aci.module.aci_tenant["NTS_TRAINING"].aci_rest_managed.fvTenant uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsBgpCtxPol uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsbgpCtxPol
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtxToExtRouteTagPol uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsctxToExtRouteTagPol
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsOspfCtxPol uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsospfCtxPol
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.vzAny uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/any
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/FW_OUTSIDE"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-FW_OUTSIDE
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/FW_OUTSIDE"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-FW_OUTSIDE/rsctx
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/APP"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-APP
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/APP"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-APP/rsctx
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB/rsctx
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/DMZ"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-DMZ
terraform import module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/DMZ"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtx uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-DMZ/rsctx

Once the process is complete, a new Terraform plan should show that some objects would be modified, but none should be created or destroyed.

The script used in this example is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Reconciling attribute drift Between NaC and Terraform
Reconciling attribute drift Between NaC and Terraform
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco netascode terraform

In the previous post, we saw how to import an infrastructure defined through NaC into Terraform. We stopped when Terraform plan reported differences in some attribute values:

# module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/WEB"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "OptimizeWanBandwidth"     = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteBumTrafficAllow" = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteL2Stretch"       = "no" -> null
        - "ipv6McastAllow"           = "no" -> null
        - "llAddr"                   = "::" -> null
        - "ownerKey"                 = null
        - "ownerTag"                 = null
        - "userdom"                  = "all" -> null
        # (19 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-WEB"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

I identified three possible scenarios:

  • The attribute is cosmetic or not relevant (e.g., annotation)
  • The attribute is not handled by our import script (ACI to NaC)
  • The attribute is not managed by NaC

Let’s examine these three cases in detail.

This is an educational post: no one should execute this process in a production environment, as it is highly likely to cause service disruption.

docs.title: Cosmetic or non-relevant attributes
docs.text:
Some attributes are purely cosmetic and have no real impact on the operation of a Cisco ACI fabric.

For example, annotation may contain a reference to who created and manages the object. By default, Ansible and Terraform set this parameter, and so does NDO. If NDO is used in the infrastructure, this parameter must be set correctly.

# module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvRsCtxToExtRouteTagPol will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvRsCtxToExtRouteTagPol" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "userdom" = "all" -> null
        # (1 unchanged element hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD/rsctxToExtRouteTagPol"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

The escape_html attribute is internal to Terraform and not relevant. Other parameters (such as userdom) may affect the visibility of the object to other Cisco ACI users or groups.

docs.title: Attributes not imported
docs.text:
Much more attention is required when an attribute is supported by NaC but was not imported from the fabric:

# module.aci.module.aci_bridge_domain["NTS_TRAINING/APP"].aci_rest_managed.fvBD will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "OptimizeWanBandwidth"     = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteBumTrafficAllow" = "no" -> null
        - "intersiteL2Stretch"       = "no" -> null
        - "ipv6McastAllow"           = "no" -> null
        - "llAddr"                   = "::" -> null
        ~ "mcastARPDrop"             = "no" -> null
        - "ownerKey"                 = null
        - "ownerTag"                 = null
        - "userdom"                  = "all" -> null
        # (18 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/BD-APP"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

In this case, we see the mcastARPDrop attribute related to a BD. If we inspect the module source code we can confirm that the attribute is supported:

resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvBD" {
  dn         = "uni/tn-${var.tenant}/BD-${var.name}"
  class_name = "fvBD"
  annotation = var.annotation
  content = {
    name                  = var.name
    nameAlias             = var.alias
    descr                 = var.description
    arpFlood              = var.arp_flooding == true ? "yes" : "no"
    hostBasedRouting      = var.advertise_host_routes == true ? "yes" : "no"
    ipLearning            = var.ip_dataplane_learning == true ? "yes" : "no"
    limitIpLearnToSubnets = var.limit_ip_learn_to_subnets == true ? "yes" : "no"
    mac                   = var.mac
    epMoveDetectMode      = var.ep_move_detection == true ? "garp" : ""
    vmac                  = var.virtual_mac
    mcastAllow            = var.l3_multicast == true ? "yes" : "no"
    multiDstPktAct        = var.multi_destination_flooding
    type                  = "regular"
    unicastRoute          = var.unicast_routing == true ? "yes" : "no"
    unkMacUcastAct        = var.unknown_unicast
    unkMcastAct           = var.unknown_ipv4_multicast
    v6unkMcastAct         = var.unknown_ipv6_multicast
    epClear               = var.clear_remote_mac_entries == true ? "yes" : "no"
    mcastARPDrop          = var.multicast_arp_drop != null ? (var.multicast_arp_drop == true ? "yes" : "no") : null
  }
}

We must therefore read the mcastARPDrop attribute from the fabric and set the multicast_arp_drop variable in the NaC data file.

The module source code effectively shows all the attributes that must be read for each fabric object.

docs.title: Attributes not managed by NaC
docs.text:
The final case involves attributes available in Cisco ACI but not managed by NaC. Although NaC is a very comprehensive framework, many attributes are not covered. It is up to us to determine whether they are not relevant (and therefore fall into the first case), whether they have no operational impact (for example, a changed default value), or whether they are critical.

# module.aci.module.aci_vrf["NTS_TRAINING/PROD"].aci_rest_managed.fvCtx will be updated in-place
~ resource "aci_rest_managed" "fvCtx" {
    + annotation  = "orchestrator:terraform"
    ~ content     = {
        - "bdEnforcedEnable" = "no" -> null
        - "knwMcastAct"      = "permit" -> null
        - "ownerKey"         = null
        - "ownerTag"         = null
        - "userdom"          = "all" -> null
        - "vrfIndex"         = "0" -> null
        # (6 unchanged elements hidden)
      }
    + escape_html = true
      id          = "uni/tn-NTS_TRAINING/ctx-PROD"
    # (2 unchanged attributes hidden)
  }

In the example, the PROD VRF includes three attributes that certainly require attention: bdEnforcedEnable, knwMcastAct, and vrfIndex.

By downloading and inspecting the module source code, we can quickly verify whether these attributes are supported. Using fgrep/egrep, we discover that these three attributes are not managed.

There are therefore two possibilities:

  • The value change is not relevant because it does not affect fabric operation
  • The value change impacts the fabric, and we must extend the Terraform module to support it

At this point, the value of professional services in handling the import of a Cisco ACI fabric into NaC becomes clear.

The script used in this example is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating configuration compliance verification for Cisco Switches
docs.text: 22 January 2025

docs.title: Automating configuration compliance verification for Cisco Switches
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced catalyst-center cisco

This article stems from a colleague’s request to automate the configuration compliance checks for hundreds of switches spread across the globe.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Ensuring configuration compliance is essential for:

  • Verifying that devices meet expected configurations.
  • Detecting unauthorized changes (out-of-process modifications).
  • Measuring compliance levels.

In this guide, we’ll outline an integration that uses templates to check device configurations and generate reports with:

  • A list of ports reviewed, showing their compliance status.
  • A summary of the number of compliant and non-compliant ports per device.

We'll focus on readability rather than advanced code optimization.

docs.title: Using Catalyst Center
docs.text:
Our scenario assumes all devices are managed via Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly Cisco DNA Center). If you don’t have a local instance, you can use the sandbox environment available at sandboxdnac2.cisco.com with the credentials:

  • User: devnetuser
  • Password: Cisco123!

If we navigate to Provision → Inventory, we get a list of managed devices:

Clicking on a device opens a small popup that lets us access its detailed page:

By going to Interfaces → Ethernet Ports → GigabitEthernet1/0/4, we can view the interface details:

We can see that the window displays some information, but it is rather limited.

Next, let’s navigate to Configuration to check the interface configuration:

From this, we can draw some initial conclusions:

  • Catalyst Center contains the configurations (running-config) for all our devices.
  • Catalyst Center provides high-level information about interface configurations, but details (e.g., STP, Port Security, QoS) are only accessible by examining the running-config.

This situation arises because we are still heavily reliant on the CLI for managing switches. It’s fair to say that these devices are CLI-first. Orchestrators like Catalyst Center tend to provide a limited view, leaving the CLI as the primary tool for accessing detailed information.

With this in mind, we can refine our approach: we’ll read the running-config of each switch and verify that each interface is configured correctly.

While we could use show commands, I would advise against this approach because:

  • There’s no guarantee that show commands exist to clearly display whether a specific configuration is present.
  • Our goal is to verify the configuration, not the operational state of the interfaces.
  • By working with the running-config, we can verify all interface configurations using a single, unified method.

docs.title: Choosing an approach: SSH, APIs, or SDK
docs.text:
When working via CLI, we now have several options:

  • Connect to each device using SSH.
  • Retrieve the running-config via Catalyst Center APIs.
  • Retrieve the running-config via the Catalyst Center SDK.

Using SSH requires downloading the running-config and storing it locally. This can be done, for example, using Netmiko or Ansible. Since we’ve already covered this approach in previous articles, it won’t be discussed here. If you choose this path, you’ll need to ensure that the running-config for all devices is obtained locally.

The Catalyst Center APIs are well documented..) There’s also a Python SDK,,) though its documentation is somewhat sparse.

Personally, if an SDK is available, I prefer to give it a try to see if it suits my needs. The advantage of an SDK is that it should handle challenges like rate-limiting (HTTP 429 errors) and pagination. However, I’ve discovered that this SDK has some limitations that are important for me, such as its inability to work through a proxy server.

Regardless of the approach we choose, we need to obtain the following:

  • A list of devices with details like hostname, site, and operating system.
  • The running-config for each device.
  • A list of interfaces for each device.

docs.title: Trial and Error
docs.text:
In general, it’s rare for documentation to be so thorough that it clearly identifies which APIs or methods are needed to achieve a specific goal. At this stage, we need to explore which APIs or methods might help us retrieve the required data.

Let’s start with the SDK and connect to the Catalyst Center:

from dnacentersdk import api

api_version = "2.3.7.6"
dnac = api.DNACenterAPI(
    base_url=config["dnac_url"],
    username=config["dnac_username"],
    password=config["dnac_password"],
    verify=config["verify_cert"],
    version=api_version,
)

We’ll store the configuration parameters in the config.yml file.

By using the dir function, we can search for potentially useful functions. For example, using dir(dnac), we notice the existence of devices, and with dir(dnac.devices), we find the functions dnac.devices.devices(), dnac.devices.get_device_by_id(), and dnac.devices.get_device_config_by_id().

The dnac.devices.devices() function provides a list of all devices, including:

  • Device ID
  • Device family

Carefully reading the output reveals that it also contains information about device health.

The dnac.devices.get_device_by_id() function returns the following for a specific device:

  • OS type
  • OS version
  • Serial number

Finally, the dnac.devices.get_device_config_by_id() function retrieves the running-config for a specific device.

Let’s now explore how to work directly with APIs. First, we perform a login and retrieve the token required for subsequent requests:

import requests

url = f"{config['dnac_url']}/dna/system/api/v1/auth/token"
response = requests.post(
    url,
    auth=(config['dnac_username'], config['dnac_password']),
    verify=config['verify_cert']
)
token = response.json()["Token"]

As before, we can now search for the necessary APIs. We will find that there’s a direct correspondence between the SDK and the APIs:

  • dnac.devices.devices() → /dna/intent/api/v1/device-health
  • dnac.devices.device_list() → /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device
  • dnac.devices.get_device_by_id() → /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device/{id}
  • dnac.devices.get_device_config_by_id() → /dna/intent/api/v1/network-device/{id}/config

Our procedure now involves the following steps:

  • Retrieve the list of all devices (device list).
  • For each device, fetch its running-config.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
At this stage, we have a data structure containing a list of devices with some details and their respective running-config. The next step is to transform the running-config into a structured list of interfaces and attributes.

As we have seen, there are several parsers available, but the one best suited for this task is TTP (Template Text Parser)..) TTP is an ideal tool for parsing a running-config and converting it into structured data.

<group name="interfaces" default="default_values">
interface {{ interface }}
 description {{ description | re(".*") }}
 switchport mode {{ swport_mode }}
 switchport access vlan {{ access_vlan | to_int}}
 switchport voice vlan {{ voice_vlan | to_int}}
 switchport nonegotiate {{ swport_negotiate | set(False) }}
 device-tracking attach-policy {{ tracking_policy }}
 load-interval {{ load_interval | to_int }}
 spanning-tree portfast {{ stp_portfast | set(True) }}
 spanning-tree guard root {{ stp_guardroot | set(True) }}
 shutdown {{ disabled | set(True) }}
! {{ _end_ }}
</group>

This template allows us to:

  • Parse text by identifying interface blocks.
  • Extract configuration details within each block, assigning values to corresponding parameters.
  • Ignore any configurations not explicitly defined in the template.

From the example, some parameters take values directly from the configuration (e.g., access_vlan), while others are set to True/False depending on the presence of specific configurations (e.g., swport_negotiate and shutdown).

To ensure parameters are always initialized, even if configurations are missing, we define a default value for each parameter:

<vars>
default_values = {
    "description": None,
    "swport_mode": None,
    "access_vlan": None,
    "voice_vlan": None,
    "swport_negotiate": True,
    "tracking_policy": None,
    "load_interval": None,
    "stp_portfast": False,
    "stp_guardroot": False,
    "disabled": False
}
</vars>

The following code applies the TTP template to each interface, saving the resulting structured data:

with open("interface.ttp", "r") as fh:
    ttp_template = fh.read()
for hostname, details in device_details.items():
    parser = ttp(
        data=device_details[hostname]["running_config"],
        template=ttp_template
    )
    parser.parse()
    device_details[hostname]["interface_config"] = parser.result()[0][0]["interfaces"]

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Our task involves verifying each interface against a defined profile. The profile can be represented either as a data structure or as an example configuration.

Since this compliance verification system will be used by network engineers, I opted to reduce complexity by representing profiles as if they were interface configurations.

ignore_value:
  - description
profiles:
  - name: ProfileAccess
    interface_regex: .*:.*Ethernet.*
    interface_template: |2
      interface GigabitEthernet0/1
       description Access Interface
       device-tracking attach-policy IPDT_MAX_10
  - name: ProfileUplink
    interface_regex: .*:.*Ethernet.*
    interface_template: |2
      interface GigabitEthernet0/1
       description Trunk Interface
       switchport trunk allowed vlan 101
       switchport mode trunk

The example above shows two profiles: each profile includes a name, a RegEx pattern to specify which interfaces the profile applies to, and a configuration template.

Our program will need to use TTP for both the profile and the interfaces to be checked, comparing their respective values.

In some cases, certain parameters must be specified but their actual value isn't important (e.g., the interface description). The ignore_value list allows specifying parameters with this characteristic.

The following code applies the same TTP template used earlier to each profile, saving the resulting structured data:

# Getting templates
for profile in config["profiles"]:
    # Get template config (use template against interface profile)
    template_parser = ttp(data=profile["interface_template"], template=ttp_template)
    template_parser.parse()
    template_config = template_parser.result()[0][0]["interfaces"]

    # Save template
    profiles[profile["name"]] = template_config

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Now, we simply need to iterate over all the interfaces, apply the first matching profile, and verify compliance. Since each interface might have multiple associated profiles, we choose to:

  • use, in order, the first profile whose RegEx matches the hostname:interface combination;
  • in any case, the verification stops at the first matching profile.

The following code searches for the corresponding profile for each interface. Once the profile is found, it is verified using the compare_interface function. In all cases, the compliance check result is recorded and we move on to the next interface.

for hostname, details in device_details.items():
    # For each device
    for interface in details["interface_config"]:
        # For each interface
        full_interface_name = f"{hostname}:{interface['interface']}"

        # Find template
        profile_name = None
        is_compliant = False
        for profile in config["profiles"]:
            if re.match(f"^{profile['interface_regex']}$", full_interface_name):
                # Profile match, update counter
                total_interfaces = total_interfaces + 1

                # Test interface compliance
                is_compliant = compare_interface(
                    profiles[profile["name"]], interface, ignore_value=config["ignore_value"]
                )
                if is_compliant:
                    # Interface is compliant, update counter
                    compliant_interfaces = compliant_interfaces + 1

                # Profile checked, proceed with next interface
                break

The function that compares two interfaces simply checks the existence of the parameters and their values, ignoring any parameters that do not require detailed verification:

def compare_interface(template, interface, ignore_value=None):
    if not ignore_value:
        # Set default
        ignore_value = []

    for key, value in template.items():
        if key not in interface:
            # template config does not exist in interface
            return False
        if key in ignore_value and interface[key] is not None:
            # tempate config value exists, value is ignored
            continue
        if interface[key] is False and value is not False:
            # template requires False
            return False
        if interface[key] is True and value is not True:
            # template requires True
            return False
        if interface[key] != value:
            # tempate config value differs from interface
            return False
    return True

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
The final step is to create a report. In a real case, this phase depends on the process we want to build. For example, we could create a non-compliance ticket for each interface or, as in this case, we can create a report in XLSX format.

The interfaces array within our script contains all the verified interfaces. The first four fields represent:

  • the device
  • the interface
  • the associated profile
  • the compliance check result

We then use the openpyxl library to create an XLSX file containing the already structured data:

wb = openpyxl.Workbook()
summary_ws = wb.active
summary_ws.title = "Summary"
interface_ws = wb.create_sheet("Interfaces")
profile_ws = wb.create_sheet("Profiles")

# Add headers
interface_ws.append(xlsx_headers)
profile_ws.append(xlsx_headers)
summary_ws.append(summary_headers)

# Add data
for line in summary:
    summary_ws.append(line)
for interface in interfaces:
    interface_ws.append(interface)
for name, profile in profiles.items():
    profile["profile"] = name
    profile_ws.append(
        profile.get(key) for key in xlsx_headers
    )

# Add filters
interface_ws.auto_filter.ref = interface_ws.dimensions
profile_ws.auto_filter.ref = profile_ws.dimensions
summary_ws.auto_filter.ref = summary_ws.dimensions

# Auto size
for ws in [summary_ws, interface_ws, profile_ws]:
    for column_cells in ws.columns:
        length = max(len(str(cell.value)) for cell in column_cells)
        ws.column_dimensions[column_cells[0].column_letter].width = length

# Save XLSX
wb.save("export.xlsx")

We chose to add a summary sheet at the beginning, summarizing the findings: the compliance level per device and the total. These two values should be calculated from the interface list.

for interface in interfaces:
    device = interface[0]
    if not current_device:
        # Initial set
        current_device = device
    has_profile = True if interface[2] else False
    is_compliant = interface[3]

    if current_device and device != current_device:
        # Add to summary and reset counters
        summary.append([
            "device",
            current_device,
            int(device_compliant_interfaces / device_total_interfaces * 100) if device_total_interfaces > 0 else "NA",
            device_compliant_interfaces,
            device_total_interfaces,
        ])
        current_device = device
        device_total_interfaces = 0
        device_compliant_interfaces = 0

    if has_profile:
        overall_total_interfaces = overall_total_interfaces + 1
        device_total_interfaces = device_total_interfaces + 1

        if is_compliant:
            overall_compliant_interfaces = overall_compliant_interfaces + 1
            device_compliant_interfaces = device_compliant_interfaces + 1

The scripts are available in my GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automatic Cisco XR provisioning with ZT
docs.text: 18 October 2023

docs.title: Automatic Cisco XR provisioning with ZT
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco ztp

This article explores how to optimize the provisioning of a hundred Cisco XR devices so that they are configured with minimal human intervention. Depending on the context, the devices might be shipped directly from the factory and configured automatically on-site, or more likely, they could be automatically configured in a lab environment, verified, and then shipped for installation. We will rely on what is known as ZTP or Zero Touch Provisioning. The ZTP protocol allows configuring a factory-delivered device without any human intervention. ZTP is vendor-specific, and specifically on Cisco XR it requires:

  • setting up a DHCP server to assign an IP address to the devices;
  • setting up a web server that generates configurations for each device;
  • powering on the devices so they can acquire an IP address via DHCP and reach the web server.

In the scenario we envision, we set up a lab environment where the devices will be unboxed, automatically configured, packaged, and shipped to the final destination, where non-technical personnel will proceed with physical installation, network cable connections, and power-on. We assume no technical skills at remote sites and no ability to send technical personnel.

Let's delve into the details.

docs.title: Lab Network Configuration
docs.text:
We set up a lab environment using a Linux system with two network interfaces: the first pnet0 will connect the system to the corporate network, and the second pnet9 will be connected to a dedicated and isolated network. The devices to be configured will then be connected to a dedicated physical switch, whose gateway is the pnet9 interface of the Linux system.

On the Linux system, we'll use Dnsmasq configured as follows:

port=0
interface=pnet9
dhcp-range=169.254.1.0,169.254.1.253,30d
dhcp-option=67,http://169.254.1.1:8080/ztp
log-dhcp

Dnsmasq will serve the 169.254.1.0/24 network by assigning free IPs to clients and maintaining the assignment for 30 days. DHCP requests will include the URL for ZTP auto-configuration. DHCP requests will be logged via syslog, typically saved in /var/log/syslog.

docs.title: Configuration Setup
docs.text:
The web server, reachable at the configured address in the previous paragraph, must:

  • make a Bash script available to all devices;
  • generate a specific configuration for each device;
  • make the correct configuration available to each device.

We'll use Flask to create a small web application capable of dynamically generating configurations for each device. The application will respond to two URLs:

  • /ztp (GET), which will make the Bash script available to Cisco XR devices;
  • /config (POST), which will make the specific configuration available to each device that must send its serial number.

Once ready, the Flask application can be run with:

flask --app ztp run -p 8080 -h 169.254.1.1

Ensure the application is listening on the correct interface and that both URLs respond correctly:

wget -q -O- http://169.254.1.1:8080/ztp
wget -q -O- --post-data="serial=1234" http://169.254.1.1:8080/config

The /ztp URL will return text similar to the following, identical for all devices:

#!/bin/bash

export CONFIG_FILE="/tmp/config.txt"
source /pkg/bin/ztp_helper.sh

SN=$(dmidecode | grep -m 1 "Serial Number:" | awk '{print $NF}')
PN=$(xrcmd "show inventory location 0/RP" | grep -m1 "PID" | awk '{print $2}')
RESULT=$(wget -O- --post-data="serial=${SN}&model=${PN}" {{ url }} > $CONFIG_FILE)

xrapply_with_reason "Initial ZTP configuration" $CONFIG_FILE

After acquiring an IP via DHCP, the device will retrieve the described script. This script fetches the serial number (via dmidecode) and the model (via show inventory). Using these parameters, the device requests the second URL to use as its initial configuration.

The /config URL will return, based on the parameters passed in POST, the minimal configuration to make the device accessible via SSH:

username cisco
 group root-lr
 password 0 cisco
!
hostname device01
!
domain name example.com
!
vrf OOB address-family ipv4 unicast
!
router static vrf OOB address-family ipv4 unicast
    0.0.0.0/0 169.254.1.1
!
interface MgmtEth0/0/CPU0/0
 vrf OOB
 ipv4 address 169.254.1.11 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
!
ssh server v2
ssh server vrf OOB
!
line default
 transport input ssh
