If the EVE-NG PRO version has a native feature (NAT Cloud) that simplifies this, in EVE-NG CE, we need to find a strategy to achieve the same result.

The goal is to configure an additional network on EVE-NG that allows us to connect the management interfaces of the devices we will use for our labs, whether they are virtual (internal to EVE-NG) or physical (PLC and other external physical devices). The diagram below summarizes our intention:

Firstly, let's clarify the networking of EVE-NG and introduce some concepts in Linux in general.

A Linux system represents its network interfaces with various names, typically prefixed (eth, ens…) associated with an identifier number. Network interfaces can represent either a physical network card or a virtual network card. In our environment, we find that the physical network card is represented by eth0, but there are other network cards named pnet.

We can view the network interfaces of the system with one of the following commands:

ifconfig -a
ip link

The configured pnet interfaces are actually virtual switches (bridges) configured by default during installation:

$ brctl show
bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
pnet0           8000.2ac1c946eac3       no              eth0
pnet1           8000.000000000000       no
pnet2           8000.000000000000       no
pnet3           8000.000000000000       no
pnet4           8000.000000000000       no
pnet5           8000.000000000000       no
pnet6           8000.000000000000       no
pnet7           8000.000000000000       no
pnet8           8000.000000000000       no
pnet9           8000.000000000000       no

In particular, we see that the bridge pnet0 is associated with the physical interface eth0. Or, in other words, anything associated with the bridge pnet0 will also be transmitted on the eth0 network. As we'll see in the web interface, we can add Cloud networks. Cloud networks are simply the pnet bridges. In particular, the pnet0 network is also used for web access. In fact, the management IP address is associated with the bridge pnet0, as we can see using one of the following commands:

ifconfig pnet0
ip address show pnet0

We can then configure an IP address on the pnet9 network and connect the management interfaces of the devices to the Cloud9 network.

EVE-NG, based on Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS, configures networks via the /etc/network/interfaces file. In particular, we need to configure the part related to the pnet9 bridge as follows:

# Cloud devices
auto pnet9
iface pnet9 inet static
    address 169.254.1.1
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    bridge_ports none
    bridge_stp off

We use the APIPA network, defined to be local. In this sense, in an Enterprise context, we have reasonable certainty of not overlapping with other networks. The remaining pnet2 - pnet9 interfaces can be deleted.

We can now reload the modified network configuration:

/etc/init.d/networking restart

If we ever want to associate a physical interface with this bridge, we need to add the line:

bridge_ports eth1

For convenience, let's choose to assign IP addresses automatically to the network interfaces connected to the Cloud9 network. To do this, we use DHCP via Dnsmasq.

The configuration of Dnsmasq is done via the configuration file /etc/dnsmasq.conf. In particular, we want to have only the DHCP service active and only for the network managed by the pnet9 interface. The configuration is therefore:

port=0
interface=pnet9
bind-interfaces
dhcp-range=169.254.1.2,169.254.1.254,3650d
log-dhcp

Upon completion, restart the service with:

systemctl restart dnsmasq

As we'll see later for the automation part, we need a stable association between the IP addresses of the devices and the devices themselves. We cannot rely on dynamic mapping provided by Dnsmasq, but we must define it statically. We can map the hostname that the device will present during the DHCP request and statically map it on Dnsmasq:

dhcp-host=SW1,169.254.1.101
dhcp-host=SW2,169.254.1.102
dhcp-host=SW3,169.254.1.103
dhcp-host=SW4,169.254.1.104

The list must obviously be completed with all the names we will use on this and future labs.

To complete our environment, the Cloud9 network must have access to the Internet. In other words, outbound traffic needs to be masqueraded (via NAT) using the IP address configured in the pnet0 interface.

We must first enable routing by modifying the file /etc/sysctl.conf:

net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

Activate the setting by executing:

sysctl -p

Configure NAT using IPTables to masquerade outbound traffic with the address of pnet0:

iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o pnet0 -j MASQUERADE

To save the changes, use:

iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4

Although not necessary, I recommend rebooting the system to ensure that everything is configured correctly.

docs.title: Import Labs
docs.text:
Now let's download the labs and make them available directly on the EVE-NG server:

git clone https://github.com/dainok/courses /opt/courses
ln -s "/opt/courses/EVE-NG labs" "/opt/unetlab/labs/DevNetOps labs"

By accessing the web interface of EVE-NG, we should now be able to see the available labs. For example, let's open Simple Network Lab.unl, power on R1, and verify the IP address and connectivity to the Internet:

Now let's verify that we can access the node from the EVE-NG server (user dev) using the admin username and cisco password:

$ ssh admin@169.254.1.21
Unable to negotiate with 169.254.1.21 port 22: no matching key exchange method found. Their offer: diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

When accessing very old devices, there may be access problems caused by outdated ciphers. We can re-enable them by acting on the ~/.ssh/config file:

Ciphers +aes128-cbc
HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
KexAlgorithms +diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1

Host *
  ServerAliveInterval 5
  ServerAliveCountMax 3

At this point, we should be able to SSH into R1.

For completeness, the repository contains the complete dnsmasq.conf file with all reserved DHCP records used in future labs. If no customizations have been made, you can update the system's configuration:

cp -a "/opt/courses/EVE-NG setup/files/dnsmasq.conf" /etc/dnsmasq.conf
systemctl restart dnsmasq

docs.title: Compile and Install Python 3.10
docs.text:
This step is not required on EVE-NG 6 because Python3.11 is available on Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04.

Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS, on which EVE-NG is based, comes with Python 3.8, which is too old to be used with recent versions of frameworks typically used for automation. The latest versions of Ansible, for example, require a higher version.

So let's proceed to download Python 3.10:

cd /usr/src
wget -q https://www.python.org/ftp/python/3.10.14/Python-3.10.14.tgz

Unpack the file, compile the sources, and install the new version:

tar xzf Python-3.10.14.tgz
cd Python-3.10.14
./configure --enable-optimizations
make
make install

After completion, the new Python interpreter will be available at /usr/local/bin/python3.10.

docs.title: Create a Development Environment
docs.text:
Now we can create a user dedicated to development:

useradd -m dev -s /bin/bash
passwd dev

We can also create a dedicated Python environment using the previously installed interpreter:

su - dev
python3.10 -m venv venv

For convenience, let's configure the shell to load the Python environment upon new login. Add to the .profile file:

source ~/venv/bin/activate

Finally, let's configure SSH authentication to occur via keys. From our desktop, copy our public key to the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file:

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub dev@172.25.82.167

Now we can connect to the EVE-NG server with the dev user without needing to enter the password. While we're at it, let's create a directory we'll use for development:

mkdir src

docs.title: Use Visual Studio Code for Remote Development
docs.text:
To complete the configuration of our environment, we need to set up Visual Studio Code to develop remotely on the EVE-NG server using the dev user created earlier.

Start the instance of Visual Studio Code installed on our desktop, go to Extensions, and install the Remote - SSH plugin.

Add a new host by going to Remote Explorer → Remotes → SSH → ➕:

  • Specify the command to connect to the host: ssh dev@172.25.82.167 -A
  • Specify where to save the new host, typically in .ssh/config

At this point, we should be able to connect to the EVE-NG server:

We can now enrich our development environment by installing the following plugins for remote use:

  • Ansible by Red Hat
  • Jinja by wholroyd
  • GitHub Actions by GitHub
  • HashiCorp Terraform by HashiCorp
  • Jinja by wholroyd
  • Pylance by Microsoft
  • Python by Microsoft
  • Terraform by Anton Kulikov
  • TextFSM Template Syntax by andytruett
  • YAML by Red Hat

docs.title: EVE-NG network interfaces explained
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

The network infrastructure that EVE-NG uses to interconnect lab nodes is somewhat obscure. Let's explore how to identify the Linux interfaces of each virtualized node for debugging or simple analysis.

Let's take the following lab as an example:

docs.title: Required Information
docs.text:
Before we begin, we need the following data:

  • User identifier (POD)
  • Lab identifier
  • Node identifiers to analyze
  • Interface identifiers to analyze
  • Network identifiers to analyze
  • Execution space identifier

docs.title: User Identifier (POD)
docs.text:
The user identifier is visible to an administrator under Management → User Management.

In this example, the POD assigned to my user is 5.

docs.title: Lab Identifier
docs.text:
The lab identifier can be found by opening the lab and navigating to Lab Details.

For instance, my lab identifier is 3b327c21-1585-499d-9a0d-4281e05f4532.

If we open the lab file with a text editor, the identifier is the id attribute of the lab object.

docs.title: Node Identifiers
docs.text:
Each node is identified by a number that can be viewed by opening the lab and navigating to Nodes.

If we open the lab file with a text editor, the identifier is the id attribute of the node object.

docs.title: Interface Identifiers
docs.text:
Each interface is identified by a number, which can be viewed by opening the lab file with a text editor. The interface identifier is the id attribute of the interface object.

Each interface is associated with a network (network_id), which represents the network to which the interface is connected.

There is a key difference between QEMU and IOL node interfaces:

  • QEMU node interfaces start from identifier 0 and increment sequentially.
  • IOL node interfaces follow the formula: ID = X + Y × 16 where X and Y are the slot and interface identifiers present in the EthernetX/Y name.

docs.title: Network Identifiers
docs.text:
Each network segment is identified by a number that can be viewed by opening the lab and navigating to Networks.

A network can be either a point-to-point link or a network object. A network object is an L2 network implemented by a Linux bridge rather than an EVE-NG node. In this view, only explicitly created networks will be displayed, while all point-to-point networks remain hidden.

If we open the lab file with a text editor, the identifier is the ID attribute of the network object.

The visibility flag determines if a network is visible from the web interface. For example, while four networks are present, only two are visible in the web interface:

  • Network R2-R7 (id=3)
  • Network R5-R7 (id=2)
  • Shared Network (id=4)
  • Mgmt Network (id=1)

When creating a point-to-point link, the network name is set using the node name and source interface.

docs.title: Execution Space Identifier
docs.text:
The execution space is represented by a number associated with an open lab. This number remains assigned until the lab is closed.

We can access the database using the following command with the password eve:

mysql -u root -p eve_ng_db

The execution space identifier can be retrieved via a database query, knowing the lab ID

mysql> SELECT * FROM lab WHERE uuid="3b327c21-1585-499d-9a0d-4281e05f4532";
+----+--------------------------------------+---------------+-----------------+-----+
| id | uuid                                 | path          | name            | pod |
+----+--------------------------------------+---------------+-----------------+-----+
|  3 | 3b327c21-1585-499d-9a0d-4281e05f4532 | /Users/Andrea | Ansible Cisco XR |   5 |
+----+--------------------------------------+---------------+-----------------+-----+

In our case, the execution space identifier is 3.

docs.title: Node Interfaces
docs.text:
At this point, we have all the necessary values to identify the interfaces in our system. Each interface is constructed as follows: vunAAABBBBCCCDD

Where:

  • AAA: Decimal execution space identifier
  • BBBB: Decimal POD identifier
  • CCC: Decimal node identifier
  • DD: Hexadecimal interface identifier

The first interface of node R2 in our lab (execution space 3, POD 5) has the prefix: vun0030005002

$ ifconfig | grep vun0030005002
vun0030005002​00: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000
vun0030005002​10: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000
vun0030005002​20: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000
vun0030005002​30: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST>  mtu 9000

Since R2 is an IOL node, its interfaces are 0, 16 (0x10), 32 (0x20), and 64 (0x30)**.

Each interface can be part of a network implemented via a Linux bridge. Linux bridges are structured as follows: vnetAAABBBBEEEE

Where:

  • AAA: Decimal execution space identifier
  • BBBB: Decimal POD identifier
  • EEE: Decimal network identifier

The network in our lab (execution space 3, POD 5, ID 4) is named: vnet00300050004

$ brctl show vnet00300050004
bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
vnet00300050004         8000.de24a99b6dc2       no                      vun003000500103
                                                        vun003000500220
                                                        vun003000500520

This network contains three interfaces:

  • vun003000500103: Execution space 3, POD 5, node 1 (R7, QEMU), interface 0x3 (Gi0/3)
  • vun003000500220: Execution space 3, POD 5, node 2 (R2, IOL), interface 0x20 (32, Eth0/2)
  • vun003000500520: Execution space 3, POD 5, node 5 (R5, IOL), interface 0x20 (32, Eth0/2)

docs.title: Troubleshooting EVE-NG nodes that fail to start
docs.text: 03 August 2025

docs.title: Troubleshooting EVE-NG nodes that fail to start
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

In this article, we will explore how to troubleshoot EVE-NG nodes that fail to start properly. The symptom is straightforward yet frustrating: when attempting to start a node, it appears to launch but then shuts down after a few seconds without any explanation.

Unfortunately, some architectural decisions made early on have made it challenging to surface these types of backend errors to the user. This was a deliberate choice, based on the assumption that with correct usage, such failures would be extremely rare. This assumption held true for the most part, but in those few error cases, users remain helpless.

Here, we will walk through the correct troubleshooting steps. We will connect to the EVE-NG system via SSH as the root user and manually replicate the backend process to identify the failure point.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Logs are located in /opt/unetlab/data/Logs (note that UNetLab was the predecessor of EVE-NG, and much of the original structure remains intact). The primary file of interest is unl_wrapper.txt, which records all operations performed by the wrapper, the program that mediates communication between the node and the backend. Specifically, the wrapper manages node start, stop, and console operations.

Run the following command:

tail -f /opt/unetlab/data/Logs/unl_wrapper.txt

Start the problematic node and observe the output. Key lines to note include:

Aug 01 10:07:03 INFO: CWD is /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/2
Aug 01 10:07:03 INFO: starting /opt/unetlab/wrappers/qemu_wrapper -C 54179 -T 5 -D 2 -t "vIOS" -F /opt/qemu-2.4.0/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 -d 0 -- -nographic -device e1000,netdev=net0,mac=50:05:00:02:00:00 -netdev tap,id=net0,ifname=vun003000500200,script=no ...

docs.title: The wrapper
docs.text:
As mentioned, the wrapper handles communication between the backend and the node. It launches the node and manages the console.

The lines above reveal:

  • The current working directory where the wrapper runs (/opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/2)
  • The wrapper executable being run (/opt/unetlab/wrappers/qemu_wrapper)
  • The command the wrapper executes to launch the node (/opt/qemu-2.4.0/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 along with parameters)

Running the wrapper directly hides any errors from the virtualization software (QEMU in this case). To diagnose, we want to launch the node directly, bypassing the wrapper. Note two simplifications here:

  • We run the node as root, which has fewer restrictions
  • We launch the node directly, without wrapper mediation

In all cases analyzed, these simplifications did not materially affect error reproduction. If an error surfaces, it is likely the root cause. If not, the issue may relate to the user permissions or the wrapper itself.

The command the wrapper uses is visible: the -F parameter specifies the binary, and all arguments after -- are passed to it. Other flags set tenant ID (-T), node ID (-D), console port (-C), and terminal title (-t). In busy EVE-NG installations, the terminal title corresponds to the node name, which helps identify the process or logs.

docs.title: Manually Starting the Node
docs.text:
To identify errors, start by SSH-ing into the EVE-NG server as the root user and navigate to the node’s working directory using the command:

cd /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/2

From there, launch the node binary directly by executing the command specified after the -F flag, including all parameters following -- except for the -d debug flag. For example:

/opt/qemu-2.4.0/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 -nographic -device e1000,netdev=net0,mac=50:05:00:02:00:00 -netdev tap,id=net0,ifname=vun003000500200,script=no ... -cpu host

Removing the -d flag ensures that error messages are output directly to the terminal. For example, in my case, the error was:

qemu-system-x86_64: -drive file=virtioa.qcow2,if=virtio,bus=0,unit=0,cache=none: Could not open 'virtioa.qcow2': No such file or directory

This indicates the disk image file virtioa.qcow2 was likely deleted after the initial node startup. Performing a wipe and restart usually resolves this by recreating the image.

docs.title: Example: Troubleshooting IOL Nodes
docs.text:
The procedure is the same for IOL nodes. For instance, logs might show:

Aug 01 10:29:58 INFO: CWD is /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/3
Aug 01 10:29:58 INFO: starting /opt/unetlab/wrappers/iol_wrapper -C 47265 -L 3 -T 5 -D 3 -t "R3" -k 0 -F /opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/x86_64_crb_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.bin -d 0 -e 1 -s 0 -- -n 1024 -q -m 1024

Change to the node directory:

cd /opt/unetlab/tmp/5/1fdf27c0-5e97-4706-a9da-1a82b01c0fde/3

Run the node binary manually (note the required instance number at the end):

/opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/x86_64_crb_linux_l2-adventerprisek9-ms.bin -n 1024 -q -m 1024 1

The appended number 1 specifies the IOL instance.

docs.title: Automating EVE-NG installation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner eve-ng

Installing an EVE-NG server is a task I encounter every time I need to prepare a new course. For this reason, I have created an Ansible playbook that, starting from an Ubuntu Linux Server 22.04 LTS installation, installs EVE-NG as seen in the previous chapters.

The playbook is available in the GitHub repository dedicated to DevNetOps courses. Therefore, let's install Ansible and retrieve the playbook from the GitHub repository:

git clone https://github.com/dainok/courses
cd courses
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cd "EVE-NG setup"

At this point, we need to modify the inventory (inventory.yml). In particular, we verify:

  • the IP address of the EVE-NG server (ansible_host);
  • that it is possible to log in via key (without password) and optionally perform privilege escalation via sudo without being prompted for a password;
  • if and how many users we want to create (dev_users).

To enable users in the sudo group to execute any command without being prompted for a password, it is necessary to modify the file /etc/sudoers with the following configuration:

%sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL

Finally, we can execute the playbook with the user with which we can log in:

./playbook-eveng6-install.yml -u ubuntu
./playbook-eveng6-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags upload
./playbook-eveng6-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags python

At the end, reboot the EVE-NG server.

If you need to install EVE-NG 5, please starts from an Ubuntu Linux Server 20.04 LTS installation and use the following playbooks:

./playbook-eveng5-install.yml -u ubuntu
./playbook-eveng5-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags upload
./playbook-eveng5-install.yml -u ubuntu --tags python

docs.title: EVE-NG Linux VM SSH troubleshooting
docs.text: 20 September 2025

docs.title: EVE-NG Linux VM SSH troubleshooting
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

Special thanks to Carlo Cianfarani for providing this post.

In this post we will explore how to troubleshoot and fix an issue on EVE-NG involving Linux VMs connected through a virtual router instance (Cisco XRd) implemented as docker container. Some time ago, indeed, I managed to extend EVE-NG to support docker containers.

docs.title: Lab scenario
docs.text:
In the scenario depicted, Linux VM ethernet interfaces (e.g. plain e1000 or paravirtualized virtio-net) are attached to two different IP subnets, each implemented by a Linux bridge. Linux VMs run on QEMU hypervisor which, at userspace level, starts a multithreaded process for each VM. Essentially, there is a main thread plus additional threads, one for each VM’s assigned vCPU.

We can check how EVE-NG networking is implemented under the hood by using:

In the above vnet0_1 and vnet0_2 are both Linux bridge implementing ethernet links connecting the VMs to the virtual router’s interfaces. vunl0_1_0 and vunl0_2_0 are Linux TAP network devices implementing the VM virtual ethernet interfaces’ backend.

vnet0_3_1 and vnet0_3_2 on the other hand are Linux veth network devices where the paired veth lives inside the docker container’s network namespace.

The following command enters the XRd container’s namespaces (PID, network and User) and confirms the associations between veth pairs.

In this lab you can successfully ping both local and remote IP addresses, however SSH to the remote VM fail! Let’s try to troubleshoot it.

When attempting SSH from Linux VM1 to VM2 we can check TcpInSegs, TcpInErrs and TcpInCsumErrors counters on VM2 keep increment of the same amount (4 packets for each run).

That means VM2 is receiving TCP SYN packets (segments) with an invalid TCP checksum. To confirm it, I used Linux ftrace framework exposed via trace-cmd frontend.

The virtual router instance connected to the Linux bridges is a Cisco XRd docker container running IOS-XR 7.10.2. From a networking perspective each docker container runs into a Linux network namespace other than the root (or default) network namespace. EVE-NG manages to create a veth pair for any ethernet link connected to it. In our scenario, a veth network device is connected to a Linux bridge within the root network namespace while the paired one lives within the container’s dedicated network namespace. By using ftrace we can dig into the Linux sk_buff kernel structures involved, by checking the value of ip_summed field we’re interested in (skb → ip_summed).

From Linux host viewpoint, ftrace reports TCP SYN packets handled from VM1 ethernet TAP backend in the RX path as seen with ip_summed set to 3 while TCP packets handled in RX path from veth device connected to the remote bridge as seen with ip_summed set to 0.

From Linux kernel C header files /include/linux/skbuff.h

Those values correspond to CHECKSUM_PARTIAL and CHECKSUM_NONE respectively. To get a clear understanding of what was really going on, I asked on stackoverflow opening this discussion.

Linux ftrace framework allows us to enable static tracepoints built inside the kernel. Here tracepoints netif_receive_skb_entry, netif_rx_entry within the relevant kernel network functions implemented by the host Linux kernel and exposed to the low-level device driver code have been enabled. Next in the reporting step the tracing file (trace.dat) has been filtered using the -F option (inessential trace entries for ARP request and reply were filtered).

According to the above trace, qemu-system-x86-11472 process with PID 11472 is the main thread (Linux lightweighted processes) running VM1’s QEMU instance. The RX path processing on vunl0_1_0 TAP interface is run in the context of this process (note that EVE-NG assigned node-id 1 to VM1 node hence the name vunl0_1_0 for the VM1virtual ethernet’s backend).

Likewise, spp-17445 is the Pid for the thread running within the XRd docker container. This thread runs the driver code handling the RX path processing for the vnet0_3_2 veth device paired with the corresponding veth device within the XRd container’s network namespace (even in this case EVE-NG assigned node-id 3 to the XRd node).

As we can see, attempting to SSH from VM1 to VM2 results in VM1 sending out TCP SYN packets having the sk_buff’s ip_summed field set to 3 (CHECKSUM_PARTIAL). That means VM1 kernel network stack is sending out TCP packets with an incomplete/incorrect TCP checksum.

After spending many hours troubleshooting, I identified the issue: by default, VM’s exposed ethernet interfaces (e.g. e1000 or virtio-net) have TCP/UDP checksum offloading enabled. Namely Linux kernel network stack assumes that the underlying “NIC hardware” will compute and fill in the correct TCP/UDP checksum into outgoing packets.

The problem is that the virtual NIC, in its TX path, does not perform that computation at all. As a result, TCP/UDP packets are sent with zeroed or corrupted checksum fields. On the receiving side, in RX path processing, they are delivered to the VM Linux kernel’s network stack that discards these invalid packets.

docs.title: The Fix
docs.text:
The solution is straightforward: disable TX checksum offloading at the virtual NIC level. This can be done from within the Linux VM as follows (note that disabling RX checksum offloading is not an option since it is not configurable).

Of course we need to do the same on the remote Linux VM:

And voilà, magically SSH to the remote VM works!

To be honest, a different kind of fix is available. According to Cisco documentation there is an optional flag (chksum) applicable for XRd interfaces. It can be set on interfaces basis by setting the relevant Linux environment variables passed to the container (XR_MGMT_INTERFACES for management interfaces and XR_INTERFACES for dataplane interfaces). It is supposed to force the virtual router to compute the relevant TCP/UDP checksum for ingress packets coming from that interface.

Let’s check the current setting for those environment variables:

From the above XR_INTERFACE environment variable, the chksum flag is clear for the first two XRd interfaces (Gi0/0/0/0 and Gi0/0/0/1) used in the lab. Let’s try to set the chksum flag for the Gi0/0/0/0 interface only (the XRd ingress interface for traffic coming from VM1 to VM2). To do it, we proceed to stop & wipe the XRd node. This way the XRd docker container is restarted from scratch.

Attempt to SSH to VM2 still fails, however we can confirm TCP packets get received from VM2 with the correct TCP checksum (TcpInErrs or TcpInCsumErrors no longer keep incrementing on VM2).

In the next step we fix the issue the other way around by setting the chksum flag for the Gi0/0/0/1 interface

And eventually it does work as well !

docs.title: EVE-NG (SW architecture and docker support)
docs.text: 22 November 2025

docs.title: EVE-NG (SW architecture and docker support)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng media

Special thanks to Carlo Cianfarani for providing this post.

This presentation provides an in-depth overview of the EVE-NG software architecture, with a particular focus on its backend components, virtualization mechanisms, and the integration of Docker-based nodes.

It walks through the main architectural layers, from the AngularJS/PHP frontend and REST API framework to the internal handling of QEMU/KVM, networking models, and wrapper functions.

The final section highlights the software modifications implemented to extend EVE-NG with Docker support, including changes in PHP modules, wrappers, and system configuration. Together, these slides aim to give a clear understanding of how EVE-NG operates internally and how its capabilities can be expanded to support advanced virtual lab scenarios.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: • EVE-NG (SW architecture and docker support)

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - Introduction
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

If you've used EVE-NG seriously — not just for a quick lab, but for building complex topologies you need to tear down and rebuild regularly — you've probably felt the friction. Every time you want to recreate a lab, you're back in the browser: create the lab, add nodes one by one, pick images from dropdowns, wire interfaces by hand, configure management access. It works, but it doesn't scale, it isn't repeatable, and it's completely impossible to version-control.

I'm a network engineer. I'm used to treating infrastructure as code. EVE-NG has a REST API, and I figured: how hard can it be to write a CLI that speaks to it properly?

This project is the answer to that question. It's still early — a proof of concept, really — but the core workflow is already useful enough that I'm sharing it.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
EVE-NG CLI is an interactive shell that connects to your EVE-NG server and lets you manage it from the terminal. Tab-completion, command history, colour-coded output. Under the hood it's all async Python, so operations that can run in parallel do.

The most powerful feature is lab import from a YAML file I call an HLD — High-Level Design. You describe your topology: nodes, images, interfaces, links. The CLI handles the rest: creates the lab, provisions every network and node, wires the interfaces, attaches the management network to NAT, and pushes startup configs for IOL devices. A 10-node lab goes from YAML to fully-wired in about five seconds.

docs.title: The full framework
docs.text:
EVE-NG CLI is one piece of a broader framework designed to make EVE-NG labs fully repeatable and code-driven. The three components are:

  • IaC-ready images: pre-configured node images that are accessible via SSH from the moment they boot, through a dedicated Out-of-Band management network. No console access required, no manual first-boot configuration.
  • EVE-NG CLI: an interactive terminal interface that builds complete labs from YAML files describing the topology — nodes, images, interfaces, links. One command, fully-wired lab.
  • Node configuration: (optional, work in progress — not yet public)

Scripts that connect to each node over the OOB network and push feature configuration described in the HLD. The topology comes up, the config follows automatically.

This post focuses on the first two. Node configuration will get its own post when it's ready for public use.

docs.title: Why share it now, at POC stage?
docs.text: Because the direction the project takes should come from people who actually use EVE-NG. I have my own workflow and my own pain points, but I'm one person. If you're an EVE-NG power user and there's a workflow you wish you could script or automate, I want to hear about it before I spend weeks building the wrong thing.

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - IaC-ready images
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

In the first post I described the three components of this framework. The EVE-NG CLI handles lab creation; node configuration (coming later) handles feature deployment. But both of those depend on one thing being true: every node in the lab must be reachable via SSH from the moment it boots, before any topology-specific configuration has been applied.

That's what IaC-ready images are for.

docs.title: What makes an image IaC-ready
docs.text:
An IaC-ready image is a standard EVE-NG node image that has been pre-configured with three things:

  • A known administrative user with SSH access enabled
  • A dedicated management VRF — keeping OOB traffic entirely separate from the lab topology
  • A management interface bound to that VRF, configured to get an IPv4 address via DHCP

When the CLI imports a lab, it attaches the OOB management network to nat0 on the EVE-NG host automatically. Every node gets a DHCP address over that network at boot — regardless of what's happening on the data-plane interfaces. From that point on, it's reachable over SSH and ready for automated configuration.

The design is intentionally minimal. The image makes no assumptions about the lab topology; it just guarantees reachability. Everything else is handled at the node configuration layer.

IOL images are a special case because IOL loads its startup configuration from an external file (not baked into the image), the CLI can push the minimal OOB config at lab creation time without any pre-configuration step. For QEMU-based images, the config must be embedded in the image itself — which is what the build process below handles.

IaC-ready images cannot be shared publicly due to copyright. Each image must be built from a legally-obtained source by the person running the framework.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Clone the repository on your EVE-NG server and install the dependencies:

ssh user@your-eveng-server
git clone https://github.com/dainok/eveng-cli
cd eveng-cli
pip install poetry
poetry install

Then install the Ansible collections required by the build playbooks:

cd playbooks
poetry run ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml

docs.title: Building IaC-ready images
docs.text:
Inside the playbooks directory there is one playbook per supported image type:

  • playbook-c8000v.yml
  • playbook-csr1000vng.yml
  • playbook-iol.yml
  • playbook-nxosv9k.yml
  • playbook-viosl2.yml
  • playbook-vios.yml
  • playbook-vyos.yml

Each playbook follows the same three-step process:

  • Searches a source directory for matching image files and copies them into /opt/unetlab/addons
  • Boots a temporary node using the copied image and applies the OOB configuration
  • Boots the configured image again and verifies it can reach both pnet0 (the EVE-NG host interface) and the internet

For Cisco images, you'll need the source files from a legally-obtained distribution. In my case I downloaded refplat-20241223-fcs-iso.zip from Cisco's software portal (CML) and extracted the contents into /opt/unetlab-downloads. Then:

cd playbooks
poetry run ./playbook-vios.yml -e search_dir=/opt/unetlab-downloads

Once complete, the configured images appear in /opt/unetlab/addons/qemu, each with the -iac suffix in their name — for example, vios-adventerprisek9-m.spa.159-3.m9-iac. That suffix is how the CLI (and you) can tell at a glance which images support IaC and which don't.

To build all supported images at once, there is a convenience script used in CI before each release:

./rebuild_all_templates.sh

This wipes all existing -iac images and rebuilds them from scratch — useful both for testing and for an initial full setup.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a playbook fails, you can run the three steps manually to isolate where the problem is.

Step 1 — Copy the image only (skip configuration):

poetry run ./playbook-vios.yml -e search_dir=/opt/unetlab-downloads -e template_config=false

Step 2 — Apply the OOB configuration to an already-copied image:

poetry run config_scripts/vios_config.py vios-adventerprisek9-m.spa.159-3.m9-iac

Step 3 — Verify reachability of the configured image:

poetry run config_scripts/vios_test.py vios-adventerprisek9-m.spa.159-3.m9-iac

Running these in sequence lets you pinpoint whether the failure is in image discovery, in the configuration step, or in the connectivity verification.

Once your IaC-ready images are in place, you can reference them from the -iac suffix in your HLD YAML files — and the EVE-NG CLI will pick them automatically when importing a lab. The next post will cover the HLD format in detail.

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - HLD files
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

The primary reason EVE-NG CLI exists is to let you build labs from code. Every other command in the shell — folder navigation, image listing, lab inspection — is there to support that core workflow. The real feature is this: describe your network topology in a text file, run one command, and have a fully-wired lab on the server in seconds.

That text file is the HLD — High-Level Design.

docs.title: The HLD format
docs.text:
An HLD file is a structured YAML document. At its core, it contains a groups key, which holds one or more node groups. Each group defines a set of nodes that share the same image and are wired together in a specific topology.

You can define as many groups as you need and connect them to each other in arbitrary ways — which makes it possible to describe anything from a simple linear chain to a complex multi-tier network in a single file.

groups:
  - template: "*linux-adv*-iac.bin"
    prefix: R
    count: 4
    topology: linear
    features:
      - loopback:name=Loopback0
interfaces:
  - match: Loopback0
    address: 192.168.0.0/16
    mask: 32
    features:
      - ospf:area=0
  - match: Ethernet
    address: 10.0.0.0/8
    mask: auto
    features:
      - ospf:area=0

Every node in every group is connected to the OOB management network (attached to nat0) by default. If you want to exclude a group from OOB — for example, a group of devices that have no management interface — set use_oob: false on that group.

Optional per-group parameters:

  • ram — amount of RAM to allocate to each node (MB)
  • cpu — number of vCPUs to assign to each node

The features and interfaces keys are reserved for the upcoming node configuration layer, which will push advanced configuration (OSPF, BGP, MPLS, etc.) to nodes after first boot. That part of the framework is not yet released.

Example topology files are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Topology: linear
docs.text:
Nodes are connected in a chain — each node linked to the next. Use count to set the number of nodes.

Useful for simulating a simple WAN backbone, a sequence of routers along a path, or any scenario where traffic flows in a single direction along a chain.

docs.title: Topology: ring
docs.text:
Nodes are connected in a closed loop — the last node connects back to the first. Use count to set the number of nodes.

A natural fit for OSPF ring topologies, resilient metro networks, or anywhere you need a loop with no single point of failure.

docs.title: Topology: full-mesh
docs.text:
Every node is connected directly to every other node. Use count to set the number of nodes.

Ideal for BGP full-mesh iBGP scenarios, or any topology where all nodes need direct adjacency.

docs.title: Topology: hub-spoke / spine-leaf / star
docs.text:
This topology type creates a two-tier structure. A set of nodes acts as hubs; the rest are spokes, each connected to all hubs. Required parameters:

  • hubs — number of hub nodes
  • count — number of spoke nodes
  • connect_hubs — set to true to interconnect hubs in full-mesh; false to leave them isolated

The same topology type covers three different patterns depending on how you configure it:

Hub-spoke — multiple hubs, connected to each other, each spoke connected to all hubs. A classic WAN or DMVPN layout.

Spine-leaf — multiple hubs (spines) that are *not* interconnected (connect_hubs: false), each leaf connected to all spines. The standard data centre fabric topology.

Star — a single hub (hubs: 1), all spokes connected to it. Simple and effective for scenarios with a central aggregation point.

docs.title: Topology: defined
docs.text:
For anything that doesn't fit a regular pattern, the defined topology lets you specify connectivity explicitly. You provide a list of links, each containing the names of the nodes to connect, separated by a comma.

Node names are built from the group's prefix and a sequential number (R1, R2, SW1, etc.).

The defined topology is also the mechanism for connecting nodes across different groups:

This makes it possible to model multi-tier topologies — core, distribution, access — entirely within a single HLD file.

The HLD format is still evolving. If you have a topology that's hard to express with the current types, or a use case that would benefit from a new topology mode, open an issue on GitHub or leave a comment below.

docs.title: EVE-NG CLI - Usage and HLD Import
EVE-NG CLI - Usage and HLD Import
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced eve-ng

EVE-NG CLI is still in its early stages. The core workflow — building a lab from an HLD file — is fully functional. For everything else (starting and stopping nodes, connecting to consoles, advanced lab management), the EVE-NG web interface remains the right tool for now. This post covers what the CLI supports today and how to use it.

docs.title: Starting the CLI
docs.text:
The CLI needs to reach an EVE-NG server. You can provide credentials interactively at startup, but the cleanest approach is to set them as environment variables before launching:

export EVENG_ADDRESS='10.0.0.1'
export EVENG_USERNAME='admin'
export EVENG_PASSWORD='eve'

Then launch the CLI with:

poetry run eveng_cli/main.py

Once connected, you'll see the CLI prompt. At any point, type help to get the full list of available commands with their arguments and descriptions.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
The image ls command lists every node image available on the EVE-NG server — template name, image type, and whether it has been built as an IaC-ready image (indicated by the -iac suffix):

This is useful to check which images are available before writing an HLD file, and to confirm that IaC-ready builds completed successfully.

docs.title: Folders
docs.text:
The folder command lets you browse and manage the folder tree on the EVE-NG server.

The last folder you navigated to is saved in the session cache as the current path, so subsequent commands that need a path can use it as a default. Both absolute and relative paths are supported.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text:
The lab command covers lab creation, inspection, and deletion.

Importing a lab from an HLD file: this is the primary workflow. Start by navigating to the folder where you want the lab to be created:

folder ls /Users/Andrea

Then import the lab by pointing to a local HLD file:

lab add eveng_cli/tests/hld/hld-1-linear-vios.yml

The lab name is taken directly from the filename (without the .yml extension). The CLI then runs through the full import pipeline — creating networks, provisioning nodes, wiring interfaces, attaching the OOB network to nat0, and pushing startup configs for IOL nodes — printing a progress line for each step.

Once created, you can inspect the lab to verify its metadata and node status:

This shows the lab name, ID, filename, version, and author, followed by a table of all nodes with their current status, type, image, and resource allocation.

docs.title: What's missing
docs.text: A few commands are present in the shell but not yet implemented — most notably lab rm. These will be added in upcoming releases. For operations not yet covered by the CLI, the EVE-NG web interface remains fully usable alongside it: the CLI and the browser talk to the same API and the same data, so you can mix both freely.

docs.title: Key steps for Real-World success
docs.text: 27 November 2024

docs.title: Key steps for Real-World success
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner fundamentals

Before launching any automation project, even before opening our editor, we need to define the essential steps for project success. Equally important is understanding the most common reasons automation projects can fail.

There's often a large gap between expectations and reality in the field. This gap has driven me to create a practical approach drawn from my field experience.

In an ideal world, the devices we work with are modern, standardized, and compatible across the board, making tools, frameworks, and orchestrators the perfect fit for rapid operational improvements. However, in reality, we often encounter a mix of newer devices and those that reached end-of-support years ago, each with unique configurations that demand a highly precise and nuanced approach.

Formal training can’t fully prepare you for these scenarios, as their specific nature defies standardization in traditional courses. But ignoring these issues is no longer an option: the shortage of qualified personnel means that traditional infrastructure management has become unsustainable. Specific training projects can greatly improve operations in a short time. Here, automation is key in gradually bringing infrastructure back under control.

docs.title: Key factors for project success
docs.text:
Certain factors contribute significantly to the success of automation projects:

  • Understand the scenario: Process automation vs Task Automation
  • Engage decision-makers: Operational improvements require involvement from key stakeholders. Without their engagement and support, it’s nearly impossible to achieve lasting improvements.
  • Standardize processes and define use cases: Automation requires a clear process. We must be able to define and standardize each step we plan to automate.
  • Modeling: Part of the design phase, this step is crucial and often underappreciated. It’s essential to map out and visualize each process, as this groundwork shapes the entire project.
  • Configuration approach: Choosing between a golden configuration or a differential approach impacts the project deeply, and it's often a long-term commitment.
  • Inventory: the inventory isn’t just a device list, it’s a structured set of input data for specific configurations.
  • Maintain an up-to-date lab: Each automation project should include a test environment for continual development and validation.
  • Prepare for large-scale outages: Automation at scale means errors, if not managed, can have significant repercussions. Accounting for potential issues is crucial.
  • Document thoroughly: Proper documentation ensures that automated processes remain maintainable.
  • Write reusable code: Writing reusable code helps to broaden the project scope over time.
  • Standardize the development environment: Standardized, certified environments ensure a reliable automation platform.

These factors are listed by importance and align with their typical order of occurrence in a project.

docs.title: Single task automation
docs.text:
I call single task automation an activity that arises from a purely personal need, aimed at automating a series of activities (tasks) of the individual themselves. In most cases, automation in a company starts like this: there are repetitive tasks, and if the person performing them is particularly creative, they will write a small software to automate those tasks. Let’s look at its characteristics:

  • One-shot;
  • Based on procedural scripts, written to solve a task, and generally not reusable;
  • Aimed at personal use;
  • Does not involve the team but remains confined to the individual;
  • Not included in any procedure;
  • Closely linked to the person who developed it.

In short:

  • Easy to implement (pro);
  • Does not scale, causing a proliferation of scripts, and is limited to specific tasks (con).

What characterizes this type of automation the most is its short lifecycle: born out of the individual’s need and almost never reaching the level of a process, once the author changes roles or companies, the automation ceases.

I can affirm that, despite the very high number of hours saved, 80% of my automation projects died as soon as I changed roles or companies.

docs.title: Process automation
docs.text:
I call process automation the automation, possibly arising from single task automation, which is accepted at the company level and therefore becomes the way to perform one or more specific tasks. The scripts are documented, maintained, and used by a team of people. But not only that: the scripts are the only authorized way to perform associated tasks. Let’s see its characteristics:

  • Automation is based on company-approved and vulnerability-monitored frameworks;
  • People cannot act except through approved scripts, and in emergency situations, this could be a problem;
  • Compared to total freedom, scripts offer little or no freedom of movement, and in emergency situations, this could be a problem;
  • Script changes are only allowed with prior authorization and testing;
  • Automation is approved by the company and defined as a standard.

In short:

  • The process is defined, standardized, less subject to human errors, and, especially thanks to some frameworks, self-documented (pro);
  • Automation development is generally slower due to the number of people involved in defining the process, standardization, and development. In the long run, automation removes expertise, as people get used to using scripts and lose sight of the underlying world.

docs.title: Engaging Decision-Makers
docs.text: In my experience, the push for operational improvements often comes from individual contributors. Yet automation projects will fail unless process owners are involved from the beginning. Effective operations often involve multiple teams, and changing established workflows requires organizational buy-in. Ultimately, once automation is in place, those resisting the transition will need the guidance and support of decision-makers to adapt.

docs.title: Design... first and foremost
docs.text:
A “learning by doing” approach, where one begins scripting while exploring framework capabilities, can lead to working solutions but often falls short of reusability or optimization. At some point, we face two options: we either scrap it and rebuild with the gained knowledge, or we continue with the current approach, accepting technical debt, a concept well covered by Gene Kim’s books. Over time, that debt will grow into a larger challenge if left unchecked.

While I consider “learning by doing” invaluable, we must also recognize the need for a structured approach to more complex projects. Thoughtful design enables us to approach automation challenges with an unbiased perspective. Here, asking the right questions allows us to develop reusable, maintainable solutions:

  • Who will use this automation? People, programs?
  • How will they access it? Through CLI, orchestrators, APIs?
  • What parameters will they need?
  • When will it be used? Daily, in emergencies, at high frequencies?
  • Why is it needed? For provisioning, troubleshooting, compliance?

docs.title: Standardize Processes and Define Use Cases
docs.text: Building automation requires a transformation from manual to automatic processes. Before coding, it’s critical to analyze the current process thoroughly, but, like modeling, this phase is often overlooked. In practice, I often find myself piecing together operational processes based on client patterns. Without predefined, standardized procedures, automation risks devolving into an endless list of new features.

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
Modeling defines the infrastructure (the target of automation) as a data structure, akin to defining a database schema in application development. Choices made here should be as general as possible while accommodating the tools we plan to use. Consider an example: defining an ACL to restrict access to devices:

10.0.7.0/24
10.15.0/24
172.15.0/24

In our scenario, ACLs manage primary, secondary, and decommissioned sites, and each ACL is “permit” only, using an implicit deny at the end. However, this ACL structure won’t work directly with Ansible’s cisco.ios.ios_acls module, which requires specific network and wildcard inputs. We can either:

  • Simplify our data model to align with the Ansible module requirements, making it less readable and limiting its flexibility, or
  • Use advanced techniques to bridge the data model with our framework of choice, such as Jinja filters in Ansible.

docs.title: Configuration Approach
docs.text:
Choosing between a golden-config or an incremental approach depends not only on device capabilities but also on operational workflow. This choice is pivotal; once selected, changing it often requires extensive redevelopment.

Golden-config allows for total configuration control but is complex, whereas the incremental approach is more adaptable but cannot track all unauthorized changes.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text: In Ansible, an inventory goes beyond a device list. It includes all parameters required to configure each device. A well-designed inventory depends on several factors, such as device list, input variables, and configuration approach.

docs.title: Up-to-date Lab
docs.text: Automation projects require a continuous test environment. Each update must be validated in a lab before going live in production.

docs.title: Prepare for large-scale outages
docs.text: Automation is essential for managing infrastructure at scale, but any error could impact multiple devices. A robust testing framework reduces but doesn’t eliminate this risk, so procedures for large-scale recovery should be established.

docs.title: Development environment
docs.text:
The development environment should be standardized, fully documented, and reproducible. For Ansible projects, it’s advisable to define Python dependencies in a requirements.txt file and Ansible collections in a requirements.yml file, enabling an isolated Python environment exclusively for Ansible.

Tracking environment changes is essential. I personally prefer Git for this, alongside tools like:

  • .gitignore for keeping the environment clean,
  • linters to ensure consistent code syntax, and
  • pipelines to validate every change.

docs.title: Simplifying the Data Structure
docs.text: 19 October 2025

docs.title: Simplifying the Data Structure
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals

In all the automation projects I’ve worked on, the operations teams usually don’t have the skills needed to effectively manage the automation framework itself.

In other words, the data structures behind Ansible, Terraform, and NaC are often too complex for operations teams to handle directly. They are difficult to understand and increase the risk of mistakes.

And let’s not forget: an error introduced into an automation system will instantly propagate at scale. The first priority of any automation system must be to prevent errors that could compromise the infrastructure.

docs.title: A Hybrid Approach
docs.text:
Before starting an automation project, I always try to identify a data structure that the operations team can manage, and define what their day-to-day responsibilities should be.

In most cases, their tasks are limited to creating and deleting objects (networks, addresses). This information often lives in an IPAM system, or sometimes just in Excel spreadsheets. From an Infrastructure-as-Code perspective, I prefer using text-based data structures that can be stored and versioned in systems like GitHub or GitLab. Very often, I rely on CSV or YAML files stored alongside the automation code.

However, reading data from a CSV and converting it into a structure compatible with Ansible, Terraform, or NaC can be quite challenging. My approach is therefore to build a parser that reads the data from one or more sources and generates the native data structures required by Ansible, Terraform, NaC, or even a combination of these.

This approach, also adopted by other colleagues, offers several advantages:

  • The parser can be modified freely, since the generated files make it easy to detect whether changes have introduced errors.
  • It allows generating data structures for multiple frameworks (and thus redundancy) from a single source of truth.
  • Compliance checks can be embedded within the parser to validate the resulting data structures.
  • It is fully compatible with CI/CD workflows.

docs.title: Review of SNMP Fundamentals
docs.text: 04 December 2024

docs.title: Review of SNMP Fundamentals
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals snmp

SNMP is a protocol developed to manage network devices. Initially, it was designed to configure devices, monitor them, and receive push alerts. SNMP was first conceived in 1988 and has evolved over time.

SNMP aimed to be a standard interface to devices, regardless of the vendor. It partially succeeded by formalizing a set of interfaces, but it also failed because each vendor was allowed to extend the data structure by adding interfaces necessary to characterize their specific devices.

SNMP security was a problem for several years, to the extent that the implementation of device configuration functionalities was significantly limited.

Although SNMP has been a vital protocol for network monitoring, its complexity, initial insecurity, and centralized architecture led to the development of alternative solutions.

In this post, we review the SNMP ecosystem and how to implement and use it in versions 2 and 3.

docs.title: MIB
docs.text:
MIB is the modeling language that defines the data structure used by SNMP. MIB (Management Information Base) defines a tree-structured data format that includes all objects manageable via SNMP. Each object has a unique OID (Object Identifier): through the OID, it is possible to access a specific object.

The tree consists of a standard part and a custom part. Each company can define its own objects by attaching them to the enterprises branch. Since each object must be unique, any company that needs to define its own objects should request a free Private Enterprise Number from IANA. To date, more than 6000 companies have customized the use of SNMP. There are two dangerous consequences:

  • it is difficult to find a repository that contains all the updated MIBs;
  • some MIBs may be incompatible with others because they are based on different versions.

If we want to retrieve the hostname of a system via SNMP, we can use the sysName object defined in the SNMPv2-MIB. sysName has ID 5, starting from system, which has ID 1. system attaches to mib-2, which has ID 1 and is part of mgmt. Moving up the tree, we find that the OID for sysName is: iso.org.dod.internet.mgmt.mib-2.system.5, translated to 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.

sysName is defined as a string that can be accessed in both read and write modes.

sysName OBJECT-TYPE
    SYNTAX DisplayString (SIZE (0..255))
    MAX-ACCESS read-write
    STATUS current

Read/Write are the only two permissions possible in SNMP. Security in the first two versions of SNMP was quite weak, so the write operation was disabled on almost all devices. The introduction of SNMPv3 corrected security issues, but SNMP remained a monitoring protocol rather than a configuration one.

On Linux, we can download MIBs using the download-mibs command, included in the snmp-mibs-downloader package:

apt-get -y install snmp snmp-mibs-downloader
download-mibs

At this point, we should be able to translate OIDs correctly between textual and numeric formats:

snmptranslate -m ALL -TB sysNa
snmptranslate -m ALL .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5
snmptranslate -m ALL -On SNMPv2-MIB::sysName
snmptranslate -m ALL -Os .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5
snmptranslate -m ALL -Of .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5

The snmptranslate command converts a numeric OID into a textual OID. The options used in the commands above are:

  • -m ALL to use all available MIBs
  • -TB to search for an OID using a keyword
  • -On to print a textual OID in numeric form
  • -Os to print only the last element of the OID in textual form
  • -Of to print the full textual OID

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
A query allows us to read the value of one or more objects. The device must be configured to allow us to read that specific value. Here are some examples for SNMPv2 and SNMPv3.

Configuration for SNMPv2 is quite simple: it requires setting a community and the type of access. In the example below, we use the community public, knowing that in a production environment, a much more complex string should be used:

snmp-server community public RO

We can further enrich the configuration by setting the location and contact fields:

snmp-server location Calisota
snmp-server contact Andrea Dainese
snmp-server ifindex persist

The ifindex persist setting allows interfaces to retain an ID even after a reboot.

We can read the value of a specific OID:

$ snmpget -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 sysName
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName = No Such Instance currently exists at this OID

In this case, the device reports that the OID sysName does not exist. The reason is that the complete OID is sysName.0:

$ snmpget -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 sysName.0
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: R1.example.com

For this reason, I tend to use snmpwalk, which does not stop at the requested OID but traverses all the branches it finds:

$ snmpwalk -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 sysName
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: R1.example.com

Additionally, we notice that the downloaded MIBs contain an error reported with each command. This example shows how complex it is to maintain an integral and error-free MIB repository.

Traditional monitoring systems perform regular polling via SNMP, checking parameters that help determine the device's behavior. There are two consequences:

  • as the number of devices increases, continuous polling overloads the monitoring system;
  • continuous polling consumes device resources even when there are no significant changes.

docs.title: Set
docs.text:
The set action allows us to assign a value to one or more OIDs. The device must be set up to authenticate and accept this type of operation. In its simplest form (SNMPv2), it requires configuring a community with read-write permissions.

snmp-server community private RW

In the example above, we configured a Cisco device to accept write operations using the community private. Of course, in a production environment, the community should be a sufficiently complex string. As mentioned earlier, due to the protocol's inherent weaknesses, this type of implementation is rarely seen.

Once we have configured a privileged community, we can, for example, set the new hostname via SNMP:

$ snmpset -m ALL -v 2c -c private 169.254.1.118 sysName.0 s R1NEW.example.com
Bad operator (INTEGER): At line 73 in /usr/share/snmp/mibs/ietf/SNMPv2-PDU
SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0 = STRING: R1NEW.example.com

The operation only changes the hostname value. If we connect to the device, we discover that the configuration has not been saved. Saving the configuration via SNMP requires specific actions that depend on the device in use.

In the following sections, we will see how to proceed operationally to save the configuration via SNMP.

docs.title: Finding and using a MIB
docs.text:
First, we need to check if the save operation is possible via SNMP. We previously mentioned that the operation is not standard: if an OID exists, it is likely located within the private.enterprises branch.

We start by searching Google for cisco mib locator, leading us to Cisco's official page that manages the MIB archive for all devices:

If we search for config, we find that there is a CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB. We download it along with its dependencies, CISCO-SMI and CISCO-ST-TC, and integrate the three files into the /usr/share/snmp/mibs directory.

If the repository is correct, we should be able to verify an OID:

snmptranslate -m ALL -TB ccCopyProtocol

We see that the process was one of trial and error:

  • we hypothesized the existence of an OID for saving the configuration;
  • we used Google to find the Cisco MIB archive;
  • we assumed that the string config would be present in the MIB we needed;
  • we downloaded dependencies until we had a functioning command.

If we now analyze the CISCO-CONFIG-COPY-MIB, we see that:

This MIB facilitates writing of configuration files of an SNMP Agent running Cisco's IOS in the following ways: to and from the net, copying running configurations to startup configurations and vice-versa, and copying a configuration (running or startup) to and from the local IOS file system.

The MIB is correct; we just need to understand how to use it.

If we continue reading, we find the following OIDs:

  • ccCopyProtocol: sets the protocol for transferring the configuration, which can be ignored in our case.
  • ccCopySourceFileType: contains the source file type. The values are described in the ConfigFileType OID, specifically runningConfig=4.
  • ccCopyDestFileType: contains the destination file type. The values are described in the ConfigFileType OID, specifically startupConfig=3.
  • ccCopyEntryRowStatus: allows initiating the copy (createAndGo=4).
  • ccCopyState: contains the result of the copy operation, and the values are described in the ConfigCopyState OID (waiting=1 running=2, successful=3, failed=4).
  • ConfigCopyFailCause: contains the reason for the failure of the copy operation.

To save the configuration (copy running-config startup-config), we need to set the following OIDs using a random index:

  • ccCopySourceFileType.777 i 4
  • ccCopyDestFileType.777 i 3
  • ccCopyEntryRowStatus.777 i 4

We can use a single command:

snmpset -m ALL -v 2c -c private 169.254.1.118 ccCopySourceFileType.777 i 4 ccCopyDestFileType.777 i 3 ccCopyEntryRowStatus.777 i 4

We can then check the outcome of the operation:

snmpget -m ALL -v 2c -c public 169.254.1.118 ccCopyState.777

docs.title: SNMP Table
docs.text:
In some cases, certain OIDs can be represented together as a table. When this is possible, there is usually a specific OID that refers to this concept.

In the case above, there is the ccCopyTable OID, which can be queried using the snmptable utility:

snmptable -m ALL -v 2c -c public -Cf , 169.254.1.118 ccCopyTable

In the example above, we print the table using a comma as a separator.

A more famous example involves printing the interface table:

snmptable -m ALL -v 2c -c public -Cf , 169.254.1.118 ifTable

docs.title: Trap
docs.text:
In addition to allowing access to device data, SNMP enables the notification (trap) of events to an external server. The external server must be equipped with the necessary MIBs to translate the event so that it is interpretable by people.

We can install a simple daemon that will receive traps sent by the devices:

apt-get -y install snmptrapd

The device must be configured to send traps to a specific host:

snmp-server host 169.254.1.1 version 2c public

We can choose which traps to enable, or enable them all indiscriminately:

snmp-server enable traps

The daemon must be configured to accept traps with the set community (public).

Configure the snmptrapd daemon via the /etc/snmp/snmptrapd.conf file:

authCommunity log,execute,net public
traphandle default logger

In this way, we accept traps with the public community and send all traps to the syslog using the logger command.

Restart the daemon:

systemctl restart snmptrapd

At this point, the received traps will be forwarded to the syslog daemon:

Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: <UNKNOWN>
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: UDP: [169.254.1.118]:54361->[169.254.1.1]:162
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 1:1:18:10.81
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.4.1.0 iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.2.0.1
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.1.1.6.1.3.16 1
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.1.1.6.1.4.16 2
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.1.1.6.1.5.16 3
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.18.1.3.0 169.254.1.118
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.18.1.4.0 "public"
Oct 16 17:54:01 eve-ng Debian-snmp: iso.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.4.3.0 iso.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.43.2

We can see that the OIDs are numerical and difficult to read.

In the real world, the daemon is associated with a series of handlers that trigger notifications or actions via workflows.

docs.title: SNMPv3
docs.text:
So far, we have focused on SNMPv2. Its simplicity is also its main weakness: most field implementations use very simple communities, and the protocol does not provide for communities to be encrypted.

SNMPv3 allows you to operate on two levels: authentication and encryption. There are three possible security levels:

  • noAuthNoPriv: the channel is neither authenticated nor encrypted
  • authNoPriv: the channel is authenticated (via MD5 or SHA) but not encrypted
  • authPriv: the channel is authenticated (via MD5 or SHA) and encrypted (using DES)

Additionally, it is possible to restrict access to the OID tree, specifying which branches to include or exclude.

The configuration of devices is therefore more complex and requires creating:

  • a view that includes or excludes the OIDs
  • a group associated with a security level and the required privilege (read or write)
  • a user associated with the group that meets the requirements of the associated security level
snmp-server view ROOT iso included
snmp-server group PUB v3 noauth read ROOT
snmp-server group MONITOR v3 auth read ROOT
snmp-server group SECRET v3 priv read ROOT write ROOT
snmp-server user APP1 PUB v3 auth sha password1
snmp-server user APP2 MONITOR v3 auth sha password2
snmp-server user APP3 SECRET v3 auth sha password3 priv aes 256 secretpass3

We can then use the three users to perform queries:

snmpwalk -m ALL -v 3 -l noAuthNoPriv -u APP1 169.254.1.118 sysName
snmpwalk -m ALL -v 3 -l authNoPriv -u APP2 -a SHA -A password2 169.254.1.118 sysName
snmpwalk -m ALL -v 3 -l authPriv -u APP3 -a SHA -A password3 -x AES-256-C -X secretpass3 169.254.1.118 sysName

docs.title: Parsing text with TextFSM
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals

TextFSM is a framework developed by Google that enables the transformation (parsing) of human-readable text into structured, machine-readable output.

TextFSM, available as a Python module, is one of the essential tools when automating a network device that requires CLI interaction, allowing us to interpret the output in order to make decisions.

Let’s look at an example: we want to analyze the interfaces of a switch and shut down the ones that are not connected.

The following output is human-readable, but it cannot be used directly within a script.

MGMTSWITCH1#show interfaces status

Port        Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1     to SRV1:eth1-1     connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/2     to SRV2:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/3                        disabled     1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/4     to SRV3:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/5                        notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/6     to ESXi2:vmnic0    connected    trunk      a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/7     to SRV4:CIMC       connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/8     to Router:Gi0/0    connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/9                        notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/10                       notconnect   1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX

TextFSM helps convert the above output into a structured format:

[['Gi1/0/1',
  'to SRV1:eth1-1',
  'connected',
  '58',
  'a-full',
  'a-1000',
  '10/100/1000BaseTX'],
 ['Gi1/0/2',
  'to SRV2:mgmt0',
  'notconnect',
  '58',
  'auto',
  'auto',
  '10/100/1000BaseTX'],
 ['Gi1/0/3', ' ', 'disabled', '1', 'auto', 'auto', '10/100/1000BaseTX'],
 ['Gi1/0/4',
  'to SRV3:mgmt0',
  'notconnect',
  '58',
  'auto',
  'auto',
  '10/100/1000BaseTX'],

docs.title: Finite State Machine
docs.text:
TextFSM operates as a finite state machine (FSM), starting from the Start state and implicitly ending at the EOF state, which is reached at the end of the file.

The process can be summarized as follows:

  • The first line of the input text is read
  • The line is matched against a set of rules, starting from the top
  • If a rule matches, the corresponding action is executed and the line is "consumed"
  • The next line of the input is read and matched against the rule set again, starting from the top
  • Once the entire input has been processed, the FSM terminates and returns the structured output

The actions, described below, can modify the default behavior of the FSM.

docs.title: Rule Actions
docs.text:
A simple template contains a set of rules within the Start state, which is mandatory. The Start state is the entry point of the FSM and processes the rules defined within it, starting from the first.

Each rule consists of a regular expression followed by one or more optional actions. Actions can be categorized as follows:

  • Line Action: allows control over the selection of the next input line and, consequently, which rule will be applied next.
  • Record Action: allows control over how the extracted values are stored in a record.
  • State Transition: allows moving to a different state.

Consider the following example:

Gi1/0/1
Gi1/0/2
Gi1/0/3
Gi1/0/4
Gi1/0/5
Gi1/0/6
Gi1/0/7
Gi1/0/8
Gi1/0/9
Gi1/0/10

The corresponding template is as follows:

Value SLOT (\S+)
Value MODULE (\S+)
Value PORT (\S+)

Start
  ^\s*Gi${SLOT}/${MODULE}/${PORT}\s*$$ -> Record
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error "unexpected line"

In this example, we have three rules within the Start state:

  • The first rule matches the text Gi1/0/1 and extracts the fields SLOT, MODULE, and PORT. When this rule matches, the Record action is used.
  • The second rule matches any line containing zero or more spaces. The default action is NoRecord.
  • The third rule triggers an error if a line is encountered that doesn't match any of the previous rules. This approach is considered a best practice to catch template-related errors as early as possible.

docs.title: TextFSM Line Actions
docs.text:
As previously discussed, each TextFSM rule can trigger three types of actions: Line Actions, Record Actions, and State Transitions.

Line Actions define the behavior of the FSM after processing the current input line:

  • Next (default): finishes processing the current line, reads the next one, and resumes matching from the first rule in the current state.
  • Continue: retains the current line and does not reset matching to the first rule. Instead, it continues processing as if no match occurred (although variable assignments still take place).

The Continue action is often used together with Record (e.g., Continue.Record) when a line both starts a new record and contains values that need to be captured into fields.

Consider the following example:

PING 10.0.0.1:
  size=64 icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.211 ms

PING 10.0.0.2:
  size=64 icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.011 ms

The associated template:

Value DESTINATION (\S+)
Value SIZE (\S+)
Value SEQ (\S+)
Value TTL (\S+)
Value RTT (\S+)

Start
  ^PING.*$$ -> Continue.Record
  ^PING ${DESTINATION}:\s*$$
  ^\s*size=${SIZE} icmp_seq=${SEQ} ttl=${TTL} time=${RTT} ms\s*$$
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

In this example:

  • The first rule detects the beginning of a new record (and implicitly closes the previous one).
  • The second rule is triggered on the same input line and saves the field values into the new record.
  • The first record contains all null fields and is therefore discarded by the FSM.

Continue is frequently used when a field consists of a list of values located on the same line.

Consider the following example:

vlan 1 Gi1/0/1
vlan 2
vlan 3 Gi1/0/2, Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/5
vlan 4 Gi1/0/6, Gi1/0/7

The corresponding template:

Value VLAN (\S+)
Value List INTERFACES ([^,]+)

Start
  ^vlan.* -> Continue.Record
  ^vlan ${VLAN} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){1} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){2} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){3} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){4} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan.*
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

In this example, a more comprehensive approach is used:

  • As seen in the previous example, the first rule is used to close the current record.
  • From the second rule onward, the line is evaluated by multiple rules thanks to the use of the Continue action.
  • The second rule captures the VLAN.
  • The third rule saves the first interface associated with the VLAN.
  • The fourth to seventh rules save the subsequent interfaces.
  • The eighth rule consumes the entire line, whose values were already saved by the previous rules.
  • The interface RegEx, assuming interface names cannot be known in advance, matches a substring up to the next comma, which acts as a delimiter.
  • The same RegEx, including the comma, is reused in rules 4 through 7 to progressively shift the captured value.

docs.title: TextFSM Rule Actions
docs.text:
As discussed earlier, each TextFSM rule can trigger three types of actions: Line Actions, Rule Actions, and State Transitions.

The available Rule Actions are:

  • NoRecord (default): the FSM moves to the next line of input and re-evaluates the rules from the beginning of the current state, using the same record.
  • Record: the collected values are saved into a record. Field options (explained later) can affect whether the record is stored, for example, a record missing a Required field will not be saved.
  • Clear: clears all fields of the current, unsaved record that are not marked as Filldown.
  • Clearall: clears all fields of the current, unsaved record, including those marked as Filldown.
  • Error: raises an error and stops the FSM execution. An optional error message can be provided.

When both a Line Action and a Rule Action are present, they must be separated by a dot: e.g., Continue.Record, Next.NoRecord. Default actions can always be omitted if not explicitly needed.

docs.title: State Transition
docs.text:
The final action type allows the FSM to transition between states. As noted, the initial state is always Start and must be explicitly defined. The final state is implicitly EOF, reached once the entire input has been processed. Additionally, a special state called End can be invoked to terminate execution early.

You can define as many states as needed, and create rules to move between them.

A state transition consumes the current input line, and you cannot use Continue in combination with a state transition. This restriction ensures the FSM remains loop-free.

Consider the following example:

vlan 1 Gi1/0/1
vlan 2
vlan 3 Gi1/0/2, Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4, Gi1/0/5
vlan 4 Gi1/0/6, Gi1/0/7

The corresponding template:

Value VLAN (\S+)
Value List INTERFACES ([^,]+)

Start
  ^vlan.* -> Continue.Record
  ^vlan ${VLAN} -> Continue
