  ^vlan \S+ ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){1} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){2} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){3} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan \S+ (?:[^,]+,){4} ${INTERFACES} -> Continue
  ^vlan.*
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

This example is similar to the previous one, but in this case, we identify lines that separate sections. The header allows us to use a dedicated state for VLAN analysis.

docs.title: Value definitions
docs.text:
Now that we’ve clarified how the FSM works, we can dive deeper into how values (fields) are defined in templates. Values are declared in the first section of the template, and each field follows this structure:

Value [option[,option...]] name regex
  • Value: indicates that the line defines a field.
  • option: modifies the field's behavior within the FSM.
  • name: specifies the field's name.
  • regex: defines how TextFSM extracts the value using a regular expression.

Available options include:

  • Required: the record is only considered valid if this field is populated. Otherwise, the record is discarded.
  • Filldown: the field's value is retained for subsequent records unless it is redefined or cleared. This is useful when a field, once defined, applies to multiple following records.
  • Fillup: similar to Filldown, but applies the value to previously captured records that do not yet have a value for this field.
  • Key: declares that the field contributes to the unique identifier of a row.
  • List: specifies that the field contains a list; matched values will be appended to this list.

The most complex part often lies in crafting suitable regular expressions (RegEx). Here are a few common examples:

  • \S+: a sequence of non-whitespace characters
  • *\s+: a sequence of whitespace characters
  • *[^,]+: any sequence of characters excluding commas
  • \d+: a sequence of digits
  • [A-Fa-f0-9]+: a hexadecimal string
  • ([0-9a-fA-F]{2}:){5}[0-9a-fA-F]{2}: a MAC address in the format 01:23:45:67:89:ab (matches five xx: groups followed by a final xx)
  • \d+(\.\d+){3}: an IP address in the format 10.23.45.167 (starts with digits, then matches three .xxx occurrences)
  • up|down|administratively down: a string that matches exactly one of these specific states

Using an online RegEx testing tool can be very helpful for quickly validating your expressions.

docs.text:

  • A Beginner's Guide to TextFSM for Network Automation
  • TextFSM - Changing a state
  • TextFSM sandbox
  • RegEx sandbox
  • Collection of TextFSM templates by Network to Code

The input text and the associated template are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: TextFSM parsing non-tabular text
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced fundamentals

Many network devices provide two commands to retrieve specific information: the first command returns a summarized output in tabular format, while the second command provides a more detailed view, typically in a non-tabular format where each entry is separated into a specific section.

Although the tabular format is more human-readable, non-tabular text is significantly easier for a machine to interpret.

Let’s look at an example: the show interfaces command displays detailed information about the interfaces configured on a switch.

GigabitEthernet1/0/1 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
  Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is ecbd.1d38.a901 (bia ecbd.1d38.a901)
  Description: to SRV1:eth1-1
  MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec,
     reliability 255/255, txload 1/255, rxload 1/255
  Encapsulation ARPA, loopback not set
  Keepalive set (10 sec)
  Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is 10/100/1000BaseTX
  input flow-control is on, output flow-control is unsupported
  ARP type: ARPA, ARP Timeout 04:00:00
  Last input 27w3d, output 00:00:01, output hang never
  Last clearing of "show interface" counters never
  Input queue: 0/2000/0/0 (size/max/drops/flushes); Total output drops: 0
  Queueing strategy: fifo
  Output queue: 0/40 (size/max)
  30 second input rate 0 bits/sec, 0 packets/sec
  30 second output rate 1000 bits/sec, 1 packets/sec
     4416551 packets input, 760890620 bytes, 0 no buffer
     Received 254313 broadcasts (23 multicasts)
     0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
     0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     0 watchdog, 23 multicast, 0 pause input
     0 input packets with dribble condition detected
     35009046 packets output, 5719203205 bytes, 0 underruns
     Output 10138785 broadcasts (0 multicasts)

The first step is to identify the pieces of information we’re interested in, each of which must be associated with a RegEx. Here are a few examples:

  • Interface, which is mandatory and serves as the key: \w+/\d+/\d+
  • Bandwidth, which is a string delimited by a comma: [^,]+
  • Description, which is a generic string ending at the end of the line: .+
  • Line status, which is one of several possible strings: up|down|administratively down
  • MAC address, which consists of three hexadecimal sequences separated by dots: ([0-9a-f.]{4}\.){2}[0-9a-f]{4}
  • MTU, which is a number: \d+
  • Protocol status, which is one of several possible strings: up|down
  • Interface type, which is a string delimited by a comma: [^,]+

The value definitions in the template will appear as follows:

Value Key,Required INTERFACE (\w+/\d+/\d+)
Value BANDWIDTH ([^,]+)
Value DESCRIPTION (.+)
Value LINE_STATUS (up|down|administratively down)
Value MAC (([0-9a-f.]{4}\.){2}[0-9a-f]{4})
Value MTU (\d+)
Value PROTOCOL_STATUS (up|down)
Value TYPE ([^,]+)

Next, we need to analyze the structure of the input text to determine where to insert the Record command required to store the data for each interface.

Each interface's information is grouped within a specific paragraph that begins with the interface name. Since the output starts with an interface name, we must work within the Start state (note that we cannot use a state transition associated with the Continue action).

The line that specifies the interface name also signals the end of the previous record. A first attempt might be to create the following rule:

^${INTERFACE} is .\*$$ -> Record

However, this rule has a clear flaw: the record is closed, but the data describing the interface appears afterwards.

The correct approach is as follows: when a new interface line is read, we must close the previous record and use the same line to populate fields for the new record:

^\w+/\d+/\d+ is -> Continue.Record
^${INTERFACE} is .\*$$

The first rule uses the same pattern as the second, but it doesn’t assign any field values. It simply closes the previous record and passes the line to the next rule that opens the new record.

We can now insert the subsequent rules to parse the remaining part of the text:

Start
  ^\w+/\d+/\d+ is -> Continue.Record
  ^${INTERFACE} is ${LINE_STATUS}, line protocol is ${PROTOCOL_STATUS} .*$$
  ^\s+Hardware is ${TYPE}, address is ${MAC} .*$$
  ^\s+Description: ${DESCRIPTION}$$
  ^\s+MTU ${MTU} bytes, BW ${BANDWIDTH}, .*$$
  ^\s+reliability
  ^\s+Encapsulation
  ^\s+Keepalive

The last three rules consume lines that are not of interest. As a best practice, all lines should be consumed, and an error should be raised if unexpected text is encountered.

Start
  ^\w+/\d+/\d+ is -> Continue.Record
  ^${INTERFACE} is ${LINE_STATUS}, line protocol is ${PROTOCOL_STATUS} .*$$
  ^\s+Hardware is ${TYPE}, address is ${MAC} .*$$
  ^\s+Description: ${DESCRIPTION}$$
  ^\s+MTU ${MTU} bytes, BW ${BANDWIDTH}, .*$$
  ^\s+reliability
  ^\s+Encapsulation
  ^\s+Keepalive
  ^\s+\w+-duplex
  ^\s+input
  ^\s+ARP
  ^\s+Last
  ^\s+Input
  ^\s+Queueing
  ^\s+Output
  ^\s+\d+ \w+ input
  ^\s+\d+ \w+ output
  ^\s+Received
  ^\s+\d+ runts
  ^\s+\d+ input
  ^\s+\d+ watchdog
  ^\s+\d+ output
  ^\s+\d+ unknown
  ^\s+\d+ babbles
  ^\s+\d+ lost
  ^. -> Error

The input text and associated template are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: TextFSM parsing tabular text
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced

In the previous post, we discussed how to structure the output of the show interfaces command. Now, for educational purposes, let’s examine how to structure the equivalent command that returns output in tabular format: show interfaces status.

Port        Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/1     to SRV1:eth1-1     connected    58         a-full a-1000 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/2     to SRV2:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/3                        disabled     1            auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi1/0/4     to SRV3:mgmt0      notconnect   58           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX

The first step is to identify the relevant pieces of information, each of which must be associated with a RegEx:

  • Interface, which is mandatory and also serves as the key: \w+/\d+/\d+
  • Name (description), which is an optional, generic string that may include spaces: .+?
  • Status, which is one of several possible strings: connected|notconnect|disabled
  • VLAN, which is a number: \d+
  • Duplex, which is a non-space string: \S+
  • Speed, which is a non-space string: \S+

The value definitions in the template will appear as follows:

Value Key,Required INTERFACE (\w+/\d+/\d+)
Value DESCRIPTION (.+?)
Value DUPLEX (\S+)
Value SPEED (\S+)
Value STATUS (connected|notconnect|disabled)
Value VLAN (\d+)

The structure of the input text is simpler than in the previous example: each line represents a record.

^${INTERFACE} -> Record

The table includes a header, which can either be consumed or used to define a specific state.

Our template will therefore include only the Start and Interface states. Since each line corresponds to a record, we need only a minimal number of rules:

Start
  ^Port -> Interface
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

Interface
  ^${INTERFACE}\s+${DESCRIPTION}\s+${STATUS}\s+${VLAN}\s+${DUPLEX}\s+${SPEED}\s+.*$$ -> Record
  ^\s*$$
  ^. -> Error

The input text and the associated template are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Pexpect as a tool of last resort
docs.text: 15 February 2026

docs.title: Pexpect as a tool of last resort
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced pexpect

Twenty years ago, when I started automating tasks on the distributed network I was managing, there were practically no automation tools available. I started with Expect, which is still my lifesaving tool today. When I have no other way to interact with a system, Expect is my last resort.

Since I’ve now moved all my development to Python, I use Pexpect, which allows me to integrate automation into an ecosystem I already know well.

docs.title: Preconfiguring templates for EVE-NG
docs.text:
The goal I set for myself, part of a larger project, is to preconfigure templates for EVE-NG. Specifically, I need to:

  • import new templates;
  • preconfigure each template so that the first interface always belongs to a management VRF, receives an IP address via DHCP, has a privileged user preconfigured, and has SSH enabled;
  • verify that the generated images work as expected (ping, login);
  • verify the entire process in CI/CD mode after every significant change.

The problem was divided into four parts:

  • Ansible searches for the required files and prepares the environments under /opt/unetlab/addons/qemu;
  • a script configures each image;
  • a script runs an instance and verifies network reachability (ping) and login;
  • Pytest takes care of creating temporary instances, configuring them, and verifying them.

In this article, we focus on the two scripts that, using Pexpect, handle image configuration and testing.

docs.title: Starting the node
docs.text:
In our case, we need to start a command (QEMU) and make decisions based on the output displayed on the screen.

cmd = get_start_qemu_node_cmd(template, **kwargs)
child = pexpect.spawn(
    cmd,
    encoding=None,
    timeout=10,
    echo=False,
)
child.logfile = TeeLogger()

In particular, we treat the output as a stream of bytes. This is necessary because most nodes do not output plain text, but rather a byte stream that may include special characters (screen clears, colors, etc.).

The TeeLogger class was required to correctly handle the output and, optionally, save it to a file:

class TeeLogger:
    """Print output in stdout and in file."""

    def __init__(self, log_file=None):
        self.raw = None
        if log_file:
            self.raw = open(log_file, 'wb')

    def write(self, data):
        if isinstance(data, bytes):
            if self.raw:
                self.raw.write(data)
                self.raw.flush()
            text = data.decode(errors='ignore')
        else:
            if self.raw:
                self.raw.write(data.encode(errors='ignore'))
                self.raw.flush()
            text = data

        sys.stdout.write(text)
        sys.stdout.flush()

At this point, all that remains is to execute the process:

# Starting node
child = start_qemu_node(template, boot_from_cd=False, **NODE_CONFIG)

# Close before exit
def cleanup():
    """Cleanup before exit."""
    child.kill(signal.SIGTERM)

atexit.register(cleanup)

The cleanup function is called every time the script completes, whether successfully or with errors. Since we do not want the QEMU process to survive the script, cleanup terminates QEMU before the script exits.

docs.title: Managing the interactive session
docs.text:
We are now ready to manage the image boot process and configure it as desired. Pexpect allows us to detect a string sent by QEMU and execute actions accordingly.

First, for example, we want to send ENTER as soon as the bootloader screen appears.

# Boot menu
child.expect(rb'GNU GRUB', timeout=300)
child.sendline('')

If we are configuring a vIOS image, the next step is to exit the interactive configuration:

# Skip initial configuration
expect_output(
    child,
    'Would you like to enter the initial configuration dialog',
    ERRORS,
    timeout=300,
)
send_cmd(child, 'no')

In this case, we used two helper functions that simplify workflow management.

The expect_output function allows us to wait for a specific text and raise an exception in case of errors or timeouts:

def expect_output(child, expected, errors, timeout=10):
    if isinstance(expected, (bytes, str)):
        expected = [expected]

    patterns = list(expected) + list(errors)
    output = b''

    try:
        res = child.expect(patterns, timeout=timeout)
        output += child.before

        if res < len(expected):
            while True:
                # Consume the rest of the line
                try:
                    child.expect(rb'.+', timeout=0.1)
                    output += child.before
                except pexpect.TIMEOUT:
                    break
            return res, output

        err = errors[res - len(expected)]
        raise RuntimeError(f'Command error {err!r} (expected={expected})')
    except pexpect.TIMEOUT:
        raise pexpect.TIMEOUT(
            f'Timeout occurred (expected={expected}, timeout={timeout})'
        )
    except pexpect.EOF:
        raise RuntimeError(f'EOF reached (expected={expected})')

The send_cmd function, instead, allows us to display the text sent to QEMU in green, making the process easier to read:

GREEN = '\033[92m'
RESET = '\033[0m'

def send_cmd(child, text, delay=1):
    """Send command using to pexpect process."""
    time.sleep(delay)
    print(f'{GREEN}{text}↵{RESET}')
    child.send(text.encode() + b'\r')

We can then configure the image:

for line in [
    'configure terminal',
    f'username {NODE_CREDENTIALS["username"]} privilege 15 password {NODE_CREDENTIALS["password"]}',
    'hostname vios',
    'ip domain name example.com',
    'crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048',
    'ip ssh version 2',
    'line vty 0 15',
    'login local',
    'transport input ssh',
    'vrf definition mgmt',
    'address-family ipv4',
    'interface GigabitEthernet0/0',
    'vrf forwarding mgmt',
    'ip address dhcp',
    'no shutdown',
]:
    send_cmd(child, line)
    expect_output(child, CONFIG_PROMPT, ERRORS)
send_cmd(child, 'end')

And save the configuration before exiting:

# Save configuration
expect_output(child, EXEC_PROMPT, ERRORS)
send_cmd(child, 'write memory')
expect_output(child, '[OK]', ERRORS)
time.sleep(5)

docs.title: Automated reachability tests for EVE-NG templates
docs.text: 22 February 2026

docs.title: Automated reachability tests for EVE-NG templates
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced pexpect

As in the previous post, we now want to start a QEMU node and verify that:

  • the management interface receives an IP address via DHCP;
  • it is possible to ping the Internet through the management interface;
  • it is possible to log into the node via SSH with privileged access.

docs.title: Waiting for DHCP configuration
docs.text:
If we were doing this manually, we would check the interface status until we find a configured IP address. After a few minutes, we would probably suspect a network issue and stop the test.

We need to do exactly the same thing using Pexpect:

# Wait for IP address
ip_address = None
expect_output(child, EXEC_PROMPT, ERRORS)
for _ in range(10):
    try:
        send_cmd(child, 'show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0')
        _, output = expect_output(child, EXEC_PROMPT, ERRORS)
        match = re.search(rb'Internet address is (\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})', output)
        if match:
            ip_address = match.group(1).decode()
            break
    except pexpect.TIMEOUT:
        pass

if not ip_address:
    raise RuntimeError('IP Address not found')

The script performs 10 attempts with a 10-second pause between each one. If no IP address is configured after 10 attempts, the script fails.

docs.title: Reachability test
docs.text:
At this point, we perform a connectivity test using ping:

# Test reachability
send_cmd(child, 'ping vrf mgmt 8.8.8.8 repeat 5 source GigabitEthernet0/0')
expect_output(child, '!!', ERRORS)

Here as well, we wait for a confirmation which, in the case of Cisco IOS-XE devices, means receiving at least two ! characters as a response.

docs.title: Login test
docs.text:
To perform the login test, we use the IP address detected earlier and test access from the current system to the QEMU node. The most suitable library for this task is Paramiko:

ssh_client = paramiko.SSHClient()
ssh_client.set_missing_host_key_policy(paramiko.AutoAddPolicy())
try:
    ssh_client.connect(
        hostname=ip_address,
        username=NODE_CREDENTIALS['username'],
        password=NODE_CREDENTIALS['password'],
        timeout=10,
        look_for_keys=False,
    )
except Exception:
    raise RuntimeError('Cannot connect via SSH')

In this specific case, we do not verify the host key, as the system is disposable.

docs.text: Manually running the script allows us to observe the entire testing process:

docs.text:
At this point, we can optionally consolidate all these steps into a single CI/CD validation pipeline, which can be executed on every change or whenever a new image is introduced.

The scripts are available in the GitHub repository dedicated to DevNetOps courses.

docs.title: Collecting information from a network infrastructure
Collecting information from a network infrastructure
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco

During an assessment, you need to gather information from network devices, structure the data, organize it, and prepare reports according to stakeholder requirements. If we approach this manually, the operational cost is very high. Automating it is not complex, but you need to understand how all the pieces fit together.

This series of articles is inspired by a real project. Let's look at the requirements:

  • collecting information from dozens of devices
  • the data to collect is partially known, with more potentially added later
  • data collection must be schedulable and recurring
  • it must be possible to compare differences between two time intervals
  • some reports must be generated whose structure is not known in advance
  • extremely limited time to implement the automation

There are certainly products that meet some of these requirements, but some are so loosely defined that they demand a level of flexibility rarely found in off-the-shelf solutions. We therefore need a fast — if not immediate — approach that gets us to the result.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
The problem is actually quite straightforward: let's separate the discovery phase from the reporting phase for simplicity.

For discovery, we will proceed as follows:

  • given an inventory of all devices (Cisco IOS XE)
  • we will log into them and retrieve all necessary information by running a set of commands from a predefined list
  • we will save the raw output of each command to a dedicated file
  • we will use ntc-templates to convert the raw format to JSON
  • all outputs from a single scan will be saved in a specific directory
  • device scanning must run in parallel across multiple devices

For the reporting phase, we will proceed as follows:

  • we will analyze only the data needed for the report, reading the JSON files
  • we will insert the relevant data into a SQLite database
  • we will generate reports based on the specifications defined during the project

The following reports will definitely be included:

  • connected endpoints, in terms of MAC address, vendor, IP address, device and port the endpoint is connected to, and VLAN
  • physical interfaces, in terms of device, interface, CDP and LLDP neighbors, and total number of connected MAC addresses

docs.title: Gathering structured network data with Netmiko and NTC Templates
Gathering structured network data with Netmiko and NTC Templates
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco

In the previous post we planned how to automatically collect information from a large number of devices. Let's now walk through how to address each requirement step by step, keeping in mind that, due to the tight timeline, the automation will be spaghetti code that is not easily reusable.

docs.title: Inventory
docs.text:
Any automation requires a configuration file to store global parameters, and a place to store the credentials needed to access the devices. In our case, we chose to save the configuration in a config.yaml file.

The inventory in particular is described by a list containing the FQDN and IP of each device:

inventory:
  - fqdn: switch11.example.com
    ip: 172.25.80.11
  - fqdn: switch12.example.com
    ip: 172.25.80.12
  - fqdn: switch13.example.com
    ip: 172.25.80.13

In our case, using only the FQDN was not sufficient because:

  • not all device FQDNs were resolvable via DNS
  • using only IP addresses to identify devices was not practical

docs.title: Data to collect
docs.text:
Similarly to the previous point, we chose to use config.yaml to specify all the data to retrieve from the devices.

commands:
  - show authentication sessions
  - show cdp neighbors detail
  - show dot1x all
  - show interfaces
  - show interfaces status
  - show interfaces switchport
  - show interfaces trunk
  - show inventory
  - show ip arp
  - show ip interface
  - show lldp neighbors detail
  - show logging last 200
  - show mac address-table dynamic
  - show running-config
  - show spanning-tree
  - show standby
  - show version
  - show vlan
  - show vrf

All data needed for the assessment can be retrieved via show commands. Specifying the full list of commands to run on each device is therefore straightforward:

  • adding or removing a command is within anyone's reach
  • commands not supported by specific devices will simply produce empty or error output, which can then be ignored

docs.title: Device Access
docs.text:
We established that the automation must access the devices via SSH, execute a command, collect the output, convert it to JSON, and save both the raw and JSON output to file.

This is achieved as follows:

  • Netmiko handles device access and command execution
  • TextFSM with NTC Templates converts the output to JSON

We use Netmiko to connect to a device:

ip_address = device.get("ip")
hostname = device.get("fqdn").upper()
netmiko_cfg = {
    'device_type': "cisco_ios",
    'host': ip_address,
    'username': secrets.get("username"),
    'password': secrets.get("password"),
}
try:
    ssh = ConnectHandler(**netmiko_cfg)
except NetmikoTimeoutException:
    print(f"{hostname} ({ip_address}): CONNECTING (TIMEOUT)")
    return device, 'Timeout'

Once connected, before running any commands, we set up the environment — specifically, we create the directory structure that will hold the output files and disable terminal paging on the connected device:

device_dir = f"output/{timestamp}/{hostname}"
timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d-%H:%M:%S")
os.makedirs("output", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(f"output/{timestamp}", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs(device_dir, exist_ok=True)
ssh.send_command("terminal length 0")

We then execute each command:

for command in config.get("commands"):
    try:
        output = ssh.send_command(command, read_timeout=read_timeout)
    except ReadTimeout:
        print(f"{hostname} ({ip_address}): GETTING {command} (READTIMEOUT)")
        return device, 'ReadTimeout'

We save the raw output to a dedicated TXT file:

filename = f"{device_dir}/{slugify(command)}"
with open(f"{filename}.txt", "w") as fh:
    fh.write(output)

parsed_output = None

We then convert the output to JSON and save it to a dedicated file, but only if the conversion was successful:

parsed_output = None
try:
    parsed_output = get_structured_data(output, platform=platform, command=command)
except TextFSMError:
    pass
if isinstance(parsed_output, dict) or isinstance(parsed_output, list):
    with open(f"{filename}.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        json.dump(
            parsed_output,
            fh,
            indent=2,
        )

Remember to disconnect from the device after the last command has been executed:

ssh.disconnect()

docs.title: Building network reports from structured JSON data
Building network reports from structured JSON data
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco

In the previous post we saw how to collect information from dozens of devices and convert it, where possible, to JSON format.

Now we need to read the necessary information, store it, and generate the required reports. We do not know in advance exactly which reports will be requested, but we can reasonably expect the following will be needed:

  • MAC address, IP address, and VLAN for each connected endpoint
  • CDP and LLDP neighbors for all physical interfaces across all devices
  • Number of MAC addresses connected on each physical interface

All of this information is collected by our discovery script — we just need to read it, save it to a database, update it after each scan, and generate the reports.

docs.title: Standardization
docs.text:
To correlate the data, we need to define a standard and apply it consistently. In our case, two fields need to be standardized: MAC address format and interface name.

Cisco uses a proprietary format to represent MAC addresses. We want to standardize it so we can cross-reference it with external data — specifically to look up the vendor as defined in the IEEE database.

We create a function to convert a MAC address from Cisco format to the standard format:

def cisco_to_standard_mac(mac: str) -> str:
    """Convert a MAC Address from Cisco to standard format."""
    hex_digits = re.sub(r'[^0-9a-fA-F]', '', mac).lower()
    if len(hex_digits) != 12:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid MAC address: {mac}")
    return ":".join(hex_digits[i:i+2] for i in range(0, 12, 2))

We can then look up the vendor using, for example, the database provided by MAC Lookup.

The second point of attention is interface naming: Cisco uses both the full name and an abbreviated form. Going from the full name (e.g. GigabitEthernet0/1) to the abbreviated form (e.g. Gi0/1) is straightforward, but the reverse can be tricky. We therefore choose to always use the abbreviated name, converting the full name when necessary:

def truncate_interface_name(iface: str) -> str:
    """Truncate an Interface name so we can match rows on tables."""
    if iface.startswith("FiveGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("FiveGigabitEthernet", "Fi")
    if iface.startswith("FortyGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("FortyGigabitEthernet", "Fo")
    if iface.startswith("GigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("GigabitEthernet", "Gi")
    if iface.startswith("TenGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("TenGigabitEthernet", "Te")
    if iface.startswith("TwentyFiveGigE"):
        iface = iface.replace("TwentyFiveGigE", "Twe")
    if iface.startswith("TwoGigabitEthernet"):
        iface = iface.replace("TwoGigabitEthernet", "Tw")
    return iface

This allows us to correlate data from verbose outputs (e.g. show interfaces) with data from table outputs (e.g. show mac address-table).

docs.title: Vendor Lookup
docs.text:
During an assessment, it can be very useful to understand how many devices belong to a specific vendor. We have already seen how to standardize the MAC address format. We now load the database provided by MAC Lookup into memory so we can use it for each MAC address:

# Load MAC Address lookup table
with open("maclookup-20260204.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    vendor_list = json.load(f)
vendor_map = []
for entry in vendor_list:
    prefix = entry["macPrefix"].lower()
    vendor_map.append((prefix, entry["vendorName"]))
vendor_map.sort(key=lambda x: -len(x[0]))

docs.title: Loading Data
docs.text:
We now need to scan the directory containing the JSON outputs and look for the following files:

  • show-mac-address-table-dynamic.json
  • show-ip-arp.json
  • show-cdp-neighbors-detail.json
  • show-lldp-neighbors-detail.json

For each file type, we load the data into the SQLite database:

for json_file in arp_table_json_files:
    # Get discovery data (timestamp, device)
    timestamp_str = str(json_file).split("/")[1]
    timestamp_dt = datetime.strptime(timestamp_str, "%Y-%m-%d-%H:%M:%S")
    device = str(json_file).split("/")[2]
    vrf = str(json_file).split("/")[3].split("-")[4]

    with json_file.open(encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        # Load output file
        arp_table_data = json.load(fh)
        for row in arp_table_data:
            # Load entry
            ip_address = row["ip_address"]
            mac_address = row["mac_address"]
            iface = row["interface"]
            if mac_address == "Incomplete":
                # Skip incomplete MAC address
                continue
            mac_address = cisco_to_standard_mac(mac_address)

            # Add to bulk database operation
            arp_table_rows.append((
                device,
                mac_address,
                ip_address,
                iface,
                vrf,
                timestamp_dt,
                timestamp_dt
            ))

On large infrastructures, working with individual objects one at a time is not feasible — we need to prepare a list of operations and execute them all at once (bulk operations):

cursor.executemany("""
INSERT INTO arp_table (
    device,
    mac_address,
    ip_address,
    interface,
    vrf,
    created_at,
    updated_at
) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT(device, mac_address, ip_address, interface, vrf)
DO UPDATE SET
    updated_at = excluded.updated_at
WHERE excluded.updated_at > arp_table.updated_at;
""", arp_table_rows)
conn.commit()

docs.title: Creating Reports
docs.text:
Once all the data is in the database, generating reports is straightforward. We choose to produce them in CSV format, which is flexible and easy to work with:

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT device, interface, vrf, mac_address, ip_address, vendor, " \
    "vendor_prefix, created_at, updated_at FROM arp_table")
rows = cursor.fetchall()
with open(ARP_TABLE_CSV_FILE, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as fh:
    writer = csv.writer(fh, delimiter=";", quotechar='"', quoting=csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL)
    writer.writerow(["Device", "Interface", "VRF", "MAC Address", "IP Address",
                     "Vendor", "Vendor Prefix", "First Seen", "Last Seen"])
    writer.writerows(rows)

docs.title: Optimizing a network assessment automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco

In the previous posts we covered how to automate an infrastructure assessment and how to manage the data to generate meaningful reports. This post closes the series with some considerations for optimizing the automation.

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
Netmiko generally operates sequentially — it connects to one device only after the previous one is complete. In the past I have used Nornir and consider it a very efficient scheduler. However, Nornir has its own logic and is not immediately intuitive to grasp.

Again due to the very tight timeline, I preferred a quick-and-dirty solution: concurrent.futures.

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
    futures = [executor.submit(worker, device)
               for device in config.get("inventory")]

    for future in as_completed(futures):
        device, result = future.result()

The worker function encapsulates all the steps for connecting to a device, executing the commands, and handling the output. The number of parallel executions can be set via the max_workers parameter.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Access credentials can be read from a file or from an environment variable. An environment variable is generally the preferred choice, but the decision depends heavily on where the automation is being run.

In principle the system should be hardened and secure, but on a project with very tight deadlines it is easy for this step to be underestimated. That said, we can do our best by using a restricted account capable of running only show commands.

docs.title: JSON Conversion
docs.text:
The conversion of each command's output to JSON format deserves a brief explanation.

Netmiko handles this conversion automatically via the use_textfsm parameter. However, in our example we took a different approach, managing the conversion manually through the get_structured_data function.

The reason is straightforward and comes from prior experience: we always want the raw output of each command to be available. This is useful during troubleshooting or when we need to verify the exact output of a command. Furthermore, the JSON conversion performed by the ntc_templates library could introduce errors that we cannot anticipate at this stage. By saving the original command output, we can later verify whether any errors occurred and correct them if needed.

docs.title: MAC Address Randomization
docs.text:
Endpoint devices increasingly use pseudo-random MAC addresses when connecting to wireless networks. These MAC addresses can be identified by analyzing their format.

In our assessment we choose to set the vendor to *Unknown* for such addresses. To do this, we create a function that detects whether a MAC address is of the randomized type:

def mac_to_vendor(mac: str) -> str:
    parts = mac.split(":")
    first_byte = int(parts[0], 16)
    if first_byte & 0x02:
        return "Locally Administered", None

    for prefix, vendor in vendor_map:
        if mac.startswith(prefix):
            return vendor, prefix
    return "Unknown", None

docs.title: Preotecting Your Development Environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco digital-self-defence

For quite some time now, I've been closely and with growing concern following the evolution of attacks targeting open-source libraries — attacks specifically designed to compromise the software supply chain. The concept is straightforward: certain libraries, developed and maintained by individuals or small teams, are distributed across millions of systems worldwide. Compromising one of these libraries means gaining control over an enormous network of machines.

The most notorious attack of this kind involved the XZ Utils library (2024). The specific characteristics of that attack strongly suggest it was state-sponsored. Fortunately, it was intercepted in its early stages — because the potential impact would have been catastrophic.

Other notable attacks of the same nature targeted PyTorch (2022), Colors and Faker (2022), and Axios (2026).

The last incident — the Axios compromise — is what finally convinced me to fundamentally change my development workflow. Today, there is no reliable way to know whether the libraries we use, directly or transitively, contain malicious code. By the time we find out, it will simply be too late.

In my work, I frequently develop software integrations for multiple clients in parallel. If I were to use a compromised library in any one project, my machine would be compromised — and with it, every client integration I'm actively working on.

Given the increasing frequency of these events, and what I believe lies ahead, I concluded that the risk was no longer acceptable. A change in approach was necessary.

docs.title: Sandboxing (macOS)
docs.text:
Coming from the Linux world, I had a strong appreciation for Firejail: simple to configure, easy to use, and a solid model to follow when looking for an equivalent on macOS — my current platform.

Few people know that macOS includes a native sandbox. It is poorly documented, its long-term support is uncertain, but it exists — and in my opinion it's here to stay. On first read, it reminded me a great deal of Firejail, and it became my first candidate.

The appeal of a native sandbox was clear: it would let me stay on my existing operating system without introducing additional infrastructure layers (which we'll explore later).

To use the sandbox, you need to create a profile — a configuration file that defines what is and is not permitted. Here's a basic example:

(version 1)
(allow default)

(deny network*)

(allow file-read-metadata
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]")
)

(deny file-read*
    (regex "^/Users/")
)
(allow file-read*
    (regex "^/dev")
    (regex "^/private")
    (regex "^/usr/bin")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.cache/pre-commit")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.ansible")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.gitconfig")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.ssh/known_hosts")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.terraform.d")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/src/")
)

The profile starts by inheriting sandbox defaults, then extends them as needed. In this example, I allow the sandbox to read metadata from the entire Users directory, but restrict file content access to specific subdirectories only.

One immediate limitation becomes apparent: to avoid creating a separate profile for every development environment, I would need a generalized profile — but that means broader permissions, which defeats the purpose.

Write permissions can be configured in a similar fashion:

(deny file-write*)
(allow file-write*
    (regex "^/dev")
    (regex "^/private")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.cache/pre-commit")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/.terraform.d")
    (regex "^/Users/[^/]+/src/")
)

All malware, to function, needs outbound network access. My profile therefore disables networking entirely.

However, this makes many essential tools unusable — including package managers like pip and poetry. To address this, I created a second, identical profile with one addition:

(allow network*)

With the profiles in place, you can execute a command inside the sandbox using:

sandbox-exec -f .profile.sb bash

$ sandbox-exec -f /Users/dainese/src/personal/template/.profile.sb bash

The default interactive shell is now zsh.
To update your account to use zsh, please run `chsh -s /bin/zsh`.
For more details, please visit https://support.apple.com/kb/HT208050.
localhost:~ dainese$ ls /Users/dainese/
ls: /Users/dainese/: Operation not permitted

The shell runs inside the sandbox and is blocked from executing operations that would otherwise be permitted on the host system.

For convenience, I defined two shell aliases:

  • sb — launches a sandbox using the no-network profile
  • sbn — launches a sandbox using the network-enabled profile
alias sb='sandbox-exec -f /Users/dainese/src/personal/template/.profile.sb'
alias sbn='sandbox-exec -f /Users/dainese/src/personal/template/.profile-w-network.sb'

The final piece is logging. To understand what the sandbox is blocking — and refine the profile accordingly — you can stream sandbox events in real time using the log utility:

log stream --style compact --predicate 'sender=="Sandbox" && eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "python"'

$ log stream --style compact --predicate 'sender=="Sandbox" && eventMessage CONTAINS[c] "python"'
Filtering the log data using "sender == "Sandbox" AND composedMessage CONTAINS[c] "python""
Timestamp               Ty Process[PID:TID]
2026-06-06 09:39:19.294 E  kernel[0:59ffbf] (Sandbox) Sandbox: python3.12(49222) deny(1) file-read-data /Users/dainese

In this specific case, the sandbox reports that the running process is attempting to access /Users/dainese.

After several weeks of use, I concluded that the sandbox was not the right approach. I was forced to add too many exceptions to avoid impacting project timelines — and every exception was a potential vulnerability. I needed a more flexible solution, one better aligned with my actual workflow.

docs.title: From Sandbox to Containers
docs.text:
My IDE of choice is Visual Studio Code. VSCode offers native Docker integration, enabling the entire development and testing lifecycle to run inside containers. I spent several days evaluating this feature, but ultimately discarded it: the setup felt unnecessarily complex, and — critically — it required per-project customization.

To be more precise: in my day-to-day work, the scope of what I develop varies enormously. It can range from complex integrations involving multiple heterogeneous environments (Python, Terraform, external services) to simple throwaway scripts written in under an hour and never touched again.

Both scenarios require external libraries. Both scenarios must be handled without significant overhead. I cannot afford to spend an hour configuring an environment for a task that takes thirty minutes to complete.

So I returned to containers — via Docker. I had previously avoided this solution on macOS because execution is not native (due to processor architecture differences), and it requires running a virtual machine as the Docker host. As it turns out, this architectural constraint is actually an advantage: compared to a native Linux environment, it introduces an additional isolation layer between macOS and the container.

The question was simply: how flexible is Docker on macOS in practice?

docs.title: Containers via Docker Desktop
docs.text:
The standard solution for running Docker on macOS is Docker Desktop — essentially a management interface for the underlying virtual machine that acts as the Docker host, along with image and container management.

The first step is to define which local macOS directories will be visible to containers. This is configured under Settings → Resources → File Sharing → Virtual File Shares.

In my setup, all source code lives under a single root directory (src), organized into subdirectories: personal, 3rd-party(external collaborative projects), and nts (company projects).

The next step is building a base image that includes everything needed for development. I wrote a simple Dockerfile that defines the build steps:

FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV POETRY_HOME="/opt/poetry"
ENV POETRY_NO_INTERACTION=1
ENV POETRY_VERSION=2.3.4
ENV POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_IN_PROJECT=true
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV PRE_COMMIT_HOME=/src/.cache/pre-commit

ENV PATH="$POETRY_HOME/bin:$PATH"

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl git libatomic1 make openssh-client tree && curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 - && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Non-root user for security
RUN useradd -m dev
USER dev

# Add relaxed SSH client config
RUN mkdir -p /home/dev/.ssh && chmod 700 /home/dev/.ssh
COPY --chown=dev:dev ssh_config /home/dev/.ssh/config
RUN chmod 600 /home/dev/.ssh/config

WORKDIR /src

Key decisions in the image:

  • Base image: Python 3.12-slim
  • Environment variables common to all my projects
  • Development utility packages
  • A non-root user with a relaxed SSH configuration

Because some of my integrations target legacy devices, I occasionally need a weakened SSH configuration to maintain compatibility:

KexAlgorithms +diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1,diffie-hellman-group14-sha1
HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa
Ciphers +aes128-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes256-ctr
MACs hmac-sha1,hmac-sha1-96

Host *
  ServerAliveInterval 5
  ServerAliveCountMax 3
  ForwardAgent yes

Build the image with:

docker build --no-cache -t python-dev .

Once the build is complete, spin up a container with:

docker run -ti --rm -u dev python-dev:latest bash

At this point, all the pieces are in place. Let's put them together.

docs.title: Practical Examples
docs.text:
My four core use cases are:

  • Run a one-off command
  • Get an interactive shell inside a container for multi-step operations, optionally chaining output
  • Same as above, but with a long-running server process (e.g., Django)
  • Open additional shells inside an already-running container for cross-validation

In all four cases, I need:

  • Access to the macOS filesystem, where Visual Studio Code is running
  • A persistent environment (Python venv, Poetry, pre-commit) that doesn't need to be rebuilt from scratch each time

A container with a mapped local directory can be launched as follows:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev python-dev:latest bash

Flag breakdown:

  • --rm — removes the container immediately after exit, ensuring a clean state every time
  • -v .:/src — mounts the current macOS directory as /src inside the container; -w /src sets it as the working directory
  • -u dev — runs as the non-root dev user
  • -t and -i — allocate a TTY and keep stdin open, making the container shell feel local

To expose a TCP port, use the -p flag to map a local port to the container.

docs.title: Use case 1 — One-off command
docs.text:
Navigate to the project directory and run:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev python-dev:latest poetry run ./build.py

The build script executes via Poetry inside the container. The container is immediately destroyed afterward.

docs.title: Use case 2 — Interactive shell
docs.text:
Navigate to the project directory and run:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev python-dev:latest bash

From here, you can work continuously inside the container:

docs.title: Use case 3 — Server process
docs.text:
Navigate to the project directory and run:

docker run -ti --rm -v .:/src -w /src -u dev -p 8000:8000 python-dev:latest bash

Port 8000 on the container is now reachable via port 8000 on macOS:

docs.title: Use case 4 — Additional shell in an existing container
docs.text:
Retrive the container ID from docker ps and run:

docker exec -ti 172d5701bbc6 bash

Any environment requiring persistence must write to /src — the only persistent directory. Code written there is saved to the macOS filesystem, but is never executed by macOS directly. Python virtual environments, pip, and Poetry are all installed and run by the Linux container; they are not macOS-executable binaries. All dependencies and packages are scoped entirely to the container.

This approach covers 100% of my current use cases. It isolates each project's development environment, and keeps my macOS system clean of packages whose origin cannot be verified or controlled.

docs.title: Extensions, Libraries, and Plugins
docs.text:
Some residual attack surface remains. In my case: Visual Studio Code extensions, browser extensions, and a small number of Homebrew packages.

I've been operating under a zero-trust philosophy for some time now. I install only the extensions that are strictly necessary, sourced exclusively from verified, reputable vendors. Browser extensions are kept to an absolute minimum and installed only in a dedicated browser that has no access to credentials. I maintain a separate browser for security-sensitive tasks, and another for general browsing and anonymous research.

Third-party software is used sparingly — only when essential and when containerization is not a viable option.

The risk of inadvertently running malicious software cannot be eliminated entirely. But with this setup, the attack surface has been dramatically reduced.

docs.title: Git fundamentals for developers and IT professionals
docs.text: 06 September 2024

docs.title: Git fundamentals for developers and IT professionals
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese fundamentals git intermediate media

Git is a distributed version control software created by Linus Torvalds to manage the Linux kernel source code. Personally, I use Git, along with GitHub, to manage:

  • The source code for the software I develop;
  • The source code and compiled files for my website;
  • The source code for the books I’ve written;
  • My notes, written with Obsidian.

Git allows me to track every change and, overall, the evolution of a repository. It’s well-suited to handle any file that can be represented as text. This is why, for the past few years, I’ve been using Markdown to write text and have embraced the Documentation as Code approach.

Git is a vital tool that should be mastered by anyone working in IT, but it’s essential for developers.

Before getting started, here are some important considerations:

  • Storage: Git saves every version of every file. For text files, we know that changes can be represented by just the lines that have been modified, but for binary files, a revision often means saving a full copy of the file. So, keep in mind that a repository may grow in size, and it might require maintenance to reduce the space used, which will improve its performance.
  • Clean Structure: Especially when working in a team, it's important to adopt a common workflow. The repository should only contain the files necessary to recreate the environment and avoid cache, compiled, or temporary files.
  • Security: Since Git saves permanent copies of all files added to the repository, be cautious about including files with sensitive information like passwords. While you can remove references to such files locally, this process isn’t fully effective on third-party platforms like GitHub.

In this series of posts, we’ll explore the fundamentals of Git. For those interested in learning more, I recommend the following resources:

  • Pro Git Book by Scott Chacon and Ben Straub
  • GIT for Beginners by Anthony Baire

docs.title: Working Locally
docs.text:
Let’s start working with Git by creating a local repository. Any empty or non-empty directory can be initialized as a Git repository:

$ mkdir test
$ cd test
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/dainese/src/test/.git/
localhost:test dainese$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)

The commands above create a .git directory, which contains all the information for the repository. As long as this directory remains intact, the contents of the repository are safe.

When we add a file like README.md, it will be marked as untracked. To include this file in the Git repository, we need to add it to the staging area (also called the index) using the add command. Only then can we commit it:

$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        README.md

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
$ git add README.md
$ git commit -m "Add readme file"
[main (root-commit) 18ded90] Add readme file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 README.md

We can think of a commit as a snapshot of the current environment. This snapshot is given a unique identifier (SHA-1 hash), which allows us to track it:

$ git log
commit 18ded90e0116a6c228b6a61a9229ff119a1f77f1 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:24:05 2024 +0200

    Add readme file

We can see that the commit is associated with the main branch. The term HEAD indicates our current position. HEAD is essentially a pointer to the commit we are working on.

By using the first six characters of the commit ID, we can view its details:

$ git show 18ded90
commit 18ded90e0116a6c228b6a61a9229ff119a1f77f1 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:24:05 2024 +0200

    Add readme file

diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..62c8d0b
--- /dev/null
+++ b/README.md
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+Readme file

docs.title: Staging Area (Index)
docs.text:
We’ve seen that there is a staging area called the index. The staging area reflects the changes that will be consolidated with a commit. We can work with the staging area using the following commands:

  • git add: adds a file to the staging area
  • git rm: removes a file from the staging area and deletes it
  • git reset: removes a file from the staging area but does not delete it
  • git checkout: restores a file from the staging area (the file must not have been added)
  • git diff: shows the differences between the file in the staging area and the current file

docs.title: Local Branches
docs.text:
When my workspace contains a dataset on which I’m always adding, I tend to work with a single branch. For example, my notes, source code, and the compiled version of my website are all stored in repositories with a single branch.

When working on more complex projects, I need to use multiple branches. Generally:

  • My main branch contains the latest version of the code I consider stable;
  • I maintain branches for major previous releases for historical purposes;
  • When I need to make changes, I create a dedicated branch, which will be merged into the main branch once all tests pass successfully.

Let’s see how to create a new branch:

$ git checkout -b add_doc
Switched to a new branch 'add_doc'

As an example, we add a file to the branch and create additional branches:

$ echo "Doc file" > HOWTO.md
$ git add HOWTO.md
$ git commit -m "Add howto file"
[add_doc c12d12e] Add howto file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 HOWTO.md
$ git checkout main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git checkout -b add_examples
Switched to a new branch 'add_examples'
$ echo "Example file" > EXAMPLES.md
$ git add EXAMPLES.md
$ git commit -m "Add example file"
[add_examples 8645356] Add example file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 EXAMPLES.md

A branch is a pointer to a commit. When we create a branch, we can specify the pointer (ID, tag, branch), or use the one we are currently on, as we did in the examples above.

Each commit can depend on:

  • 0 parents, if it's the initial commit
  • 1 parent, if it’s an ordinary commit
  • 2 or more parents, if it’s the result of a merge

Let’s check the current state of our repository:

$ git log --all
commit 86453561ff929c6d6decf6c14b798df7072e59d7 (add_examples)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:28:08 2024 +0200

    Add example file

commit c12d12e8c24d89dfd81505562635e11166d6304d (add_doc)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:27:27 2024 +0200

    Add howto file

commit 18ded90e0116a6c228b6a61a9229ff119a1f77f1 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Andrea Dainese <andrea.dainese@pm.me>
Date:   Fri Aug 23 15:24:05 2024 +0200

    Add readme file

We have three commits, one for each branch, and we’re currently in the main branch. We can merge the add_doc branch into main:

$ git merge c12d12e8c24d89dfd81505562635e11166d6304d
Updating 18ded90..c12d12e
Fast-forward
 HOWTO.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 HOWTO.md

In this example, we used the ID, but we could have used the branch name.

We can view all branches with the git branch command or delete a specific branch with git branch -d add_doc.

docs.title: Merge Conflicts
docs.text:
In the previous example, the branches worked on separate files, so no conflicts occurred. However, it’s common to work simultaneously on the same files, and in such cases, the merge command will notify us of conflicts:

$ git merge fce3122f882e68f922a718dbdf6ba6a675bec2b7
Auto-merging import.py
CONFLICT (add/add): Merge conflict in import.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

We can check the status:

$ git status
On branch main
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Changes to be committed:
        new file:   file2.py

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
        both added:      import.py

In this case, the file file2.py has been added to the staging area, but import.py has been modified by both branches and requires manual intervention. Examining import.py, we see a structure similar to the following:

<<<<<<< HEAD
import file1

o = file1.obj()
=======
import file2

o = file2.obj()
>>>>>>> fce3122f882e68f922a718dbdf6ba6a675bec2b7

We need to manually correct the file, add it to the staging area, and commit the changes.

docs.title: Understanding HEAD
docs.text:
We’ve seen that HEAD is a pointer to a commit. Generally, HEAD always points to the latest commit of a branch, so we can say that HEAD always points to a branch.

If, for any reason, we decide to work on a specific commit that is not the latest of a branch (i.e., it doesn’t point to a branch), we are in a detached HEAD state.

We can end up in a detached state in the following cases:

  • Checking out a specific Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA-1) commit hash
  • Checking out a remote branch without fetching it first

To make changes from a detached state, you need to create a new branch.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
• Pro Git
  • Git for Beginners

docs.title: Collaborating with Git by working with remote repositories and forks
docs.text: 10 September 2024

docs.title: Collaborating with Git by working with remote repositories and forks
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese fundamentals git intermediate

In the previous post, we covered the basics of using Git locally. Now, let’s dive into real-world scenarios and learn how to collaborate using Git with remote repositories.

When working with remote repositories, we gain access to some new functionalities:

  • clone: allows us to create a local copy of a remote repository.
  • pull: lets us update our local branch with changes from the remote.
  • push: enables us to update the remote branch with our local changes.

Typically, pull and push actions are not allowed directly on the main branch. This forces us to always create a new branch for our changes, which we’ll then merge into the main branch.

Moreover, we often don’t have permission to create branches on repositories we don’t own. This requires us to create a fork, which is a copy of the entire repository we want to work on. We can then create a branch on this new repository, make our changes, and request (via a Pull Request or PR) that the original repository merges our changes.

But let’s take it step by step.

docs.title: Origin
docs.text:
First, let’s clone a repository of our choice:

$ git clone https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates
Cloning into 'ntc-templates'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 20633, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (3872/3872), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (1262/1262), done.
remote: Total 20633 (delta 3069), reused 2953 (delta 2607), pack-reused 16761 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (20633/20633), 5.68 MiB | 11.11 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (11629/11629), done.

Once inside the directory, we can check which remote repositories our local repository is linked to:

$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (push)

origin is the default name used when cloning a remote repository. We can specify a different name using the -o flag if desired.

docs.title: Fork
docs.text:
In the world of network automation, we’ll often need to fix or improve the code of publicly available frameworks, which is the essence of open source. The repository I’ve chosen to guide you through using Git includes 46 contributions of mine so far. I’m sure many of you will find opportunities to contribute to this project as well.

The NTC Templates repository isn’t mine, and I don’t have the right to write directly to it. What we can do is create a fork of the repository. On GitHub, you need to visit the repository via a web browser, expand the Fork menu, and create a new fork:

This creates a copy of the repository under our user account. Keep in mind that this copy is independent of the original repository, meaning any changes made will be separate.

Next, let’s clone the repository associated with our user account:

$ git clone https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates
Cloning into 'ntc-templates'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 16045, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (3368/3368), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (322/322), done.
remote: Total 16045 (delta 3210), reused 3046 (delta 3046), pack-reused 12677 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (16045/16045), 3.95 MiB | 9.51 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (9387/9387), done.

In this repository, we can create a branch and make all the changes we discussed in the previous post. To update our remote repository, we need to push the changes, and at least the first time, we must specify which remote our branch (test) is associated with:

$ git push --set-upstream origin test
Enumerating objects: 4, done.
Counting objects: 100% (4/4), done.
Delta compression using up to 12 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (2/2), done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 273 bytes | 273.00 KiB/s, done.
Total 3 (delta 1), reused 1 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (1/1), completed with 1 local object.
remote:
remote: Create a pull request for 'test' on GitHub by visiting:
remote:      https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates/pull/new/test
remote:
To https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates
 * [new branch]      test -> test
branch 'test' set up to track 'origin/test'.

We can check which remotes are associated with each branch:

$ git branch -vv
  master d0f4bff [origin/master] cisco_ios_show_interfaces_switchport: Edge case (#1665)
* test   7c5e49f [origin/test] Just a test

Finally, let’s add a new remote, linking our local repository to the original repository as well:

$ git remote add upstream https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates (push)
upstream        https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (fetch)
upstream        https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates (push)

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
The fetch command allows us to synchronize our local repository with the metadata of a remote repository. It doesn’t transfer files but lets us check if there are any changes available.

For example, we can use the fetch command if we need to sync our local repository with the original one (upstream):

$ git fetch upstream
remote: Enumerating objects: 5207, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (2208/2208), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (1037/1037), done.
remote: Total 5207 (delta 1490), reused 1514 (delta 1168), pack-reused 2999 (from 1)
Receiving objects: 100% (5207/5207), 1.90 MiB | 8.76 MiB/s, done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (2651/2651), completed with 176 local objects.
From https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates
 * [new branch]      asa-show-acl-brief         -> upstream/asa-show-acl-brief
 * [new branch]      asa_show_run_object_network -> upstream/asa_show_run_object_network
 * [new branch]      feature/cisco_xr_l2vpn_mac -> upstream/feature/cisco_xr_l2vpn_mac

Branches created in the original repository after the fork are now available locally.

docs.title: Branch
docs.text:
As we’ve seen, our local repository is connected to two remote repositories. A branch can exist in one or more of these repositories. After using the fetch command, we can now view the branches:

$ git branch -a
  all
  master
* test
  upstream
  remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/master
  remotes/origin/add_allied_telesis
  remotes/origin/allied_telesis_show_arp
  remotes/origin/allied_telesis_show_etherchannel_summary
  remotes/origin/allied_telesis_show_interface

Remote branches are prefixed with remotes. As mentioned in the previous post, we can use checkout to switch to a specific remote branch, but this will put us in a detached state since the branch isn’t available locally.

If we need to modify a remote branch, we should associate it with a local branch (by convention, we use the same name):

localhost:ntc-templates dainese$ git branch add_allied_telesis remotes/origin/add_allied_telesis
branch 'add_allied_telesis' set up to track 'origin/add_allied_telesis'.

docs.title: Advanced Git commands
docs.text: 19 September 2024

docs.title: Advanced Git commands
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced git

In the last two posts, we covered most of the essential Git features. Now, let's dive into some additional functionalities that might come in handy.

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
The .gitignore file is used to specify which files or directories should never be included in your Git repository. This file is tailored to each repository and typically excludes:

  • Cache files
  • Compiled files
  • Temporary files
  • Password files

You can either start with GitHub’s suggested templates or create your own using the correct format.

docs.title: Stashing your work
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to put aside your current work to focus on something more urgent. If you’ve made changes but aren’t ready to commit, switching branches won’t work because Git doesn’t know how to handle uncommitted changes.

$ git checkout master
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
        file1.py
        file2.py

This is where stash comes in. It saves all your changes, including those staged for commit, and allows you to retrieve them later:

$ git stash
Saved working directory and index state WIP on test4: 47f10c2 update

Now you can safely switch branches. To retrieve the stashed changes later:

$ git stash pop
On branch test4
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   file5.py

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   file1.py
        modified:   file2.py

Dropped refs/stash@{0} (add5e575a2620fee2141b1c97ab4ba8bc5d245f9)

You can also list all stashed changes with:

$ git stash list
stash@{0}: WIP on test4: 47f10c2 update
stash@{1}: WIP on master: 25372f7 merge

docs.title: Deleting Remote Branches
docs.text:
While local branches can be deleted with the branch command, deleting a remote branch involves a push:

$ git push origin --delete allied_telesis_show_arp
To https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates
 - [deleted]         allied_telesis_show_arp

docs.title: Rebase
docs.text:
Rebase lets you integrate changes in a way similar to merge, but it reapplies a series of commits starting from a different base, effectively rewriting the history of the repository. Be cautious, this can cause inconsistencies, especially in public repos where multiple people collaborate.

For example, in a repo with main and branches fix3 and fix4 waiting to be merged:

If we merge the fix3 branch, we notice that the commit IDs have been preserved:

The rebase operation, on the other hand, allows us to modify the repository history by reapplying the commits from the fix3 branch:

We can see that the commit ID for "add readme" has changed, which creates inconsistencies for users who haven't performed the rebase operation.

docs.title: Squashing commits
docs.text:
When merging, all commits from a branch are typically preserved. Over time, this can create unnecessary overhead. You can instead consolidate multiple commits into one:

$ git merge --squash fix3
Squash commit -- not updating HEAD
Automatic merge went well; stopped before committing as requested

This prepares the commit without applying it, so you can review before finalizing. After squashing, the entire history of the branch is condensed into a single commit.

Using the repository from the previous example, we can see that the fix3 branch is not connected to the main branch:

At the end of the merge, we can delete the fix3 branch as it is no longer needed.

docs.title: Reinitializing a repository
docs.text:
Sometimes, you may want to reset your repository and wipe out its history, for example, when making a private repo public. Here’s how you can do that:

mv .git/config config.git
rm -rf .git
git init -b master
mv config.git .git/config
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git push -u --force origin master

Here are the steps in detail:

  • saved the repository configuration
  • deleted the repository structure
  • reinitialized the repository
  • added all content to the staging area
  • made the first commit
  • pushed the changes, overwriting the remote state

It’s important to note that when using services like GitHub, commits can still be recovered if their ID is known. To completely erase a repository’s history on GitHub, the repository must be deleted and recreated.

docs.title: Undoing the last commit
docs.text:
You can undo your last commit without losing your changes using:

git reset --soft HEAD~1

This only works if you haven’t pushed the commit yet. Once pushed, the commit remains recoverable via its ID.

docs.title: Recovering a deleted file
docs.text:
Git tracks everything, so even if you commit a file that shouldn’t have been added and then delete it, it’s still retrievable. To list deleted files:

localhost:test dainese$ git log --diff-filter D --pretty="format:" --name-only
password.txt

Then, find the commit ID:

localhost:test dainese$ git rev-list HEAD -n 1 -- password.txt
a73306c8511fbedad06a687cc342c1d50c9035f3

And recover the file:

$ git checkout a73306c8511fbedad06a687cc342c1d50c9035f3^ password.txt
Updated 1 path from 652f7ba

I’ve created a simple script that automates this process, available in my GitHub repository.

docs.title: Permanently Removing Deleted Files
docs.text:
We have seen that a Git repository always keeps references to deleted files. There is a handy tool that removes deleted files from the history:

If we use bfg on the repository, the files will also be removed from the history:

bfg --delete-files password.txt

As you can see, the commit IDs have changed:

However, the commit ID still exists, and if the ID is known, it can be recovered:

$ git checkout 2fb4ce83b0015c4a44b45be2f5339613ddabe71f
localhost:test dainese$ ls password.txt
password.txt

To fix this, we need to clean the cache:

$ git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now --aggressive
Enumerating objects: 5, done.
Counting objects: 100% (5/5), done.
Delta compression using up to 12 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Writing objects: 100% (5/5), done.
Total 5 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0

The last operation, however, cannot be performed on remote repositories like GitHub.

docs.title: Updating a Fork
docs.text:
As we’ve seen, once you fork a repository, it no longer gets updated. If you need to submit a patch after a long time, it’s important to start from an updated repository. You can either delete the fork and refork it, or update it. Here's how to update it:

git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/master master
git rebase upstream/master
git push origin

As you can see, we are updating the master branch from the upstream remote. Any other branches, either local or on other remotes (like origin), will remain unchanged.

docs.title: Updating a branch
docs.text:
When working on a branch for a long time, it may diverge significantly from the main branch, whether local or remote:

git fetch origin
git merge origin/main

docs.title: Selective merge
docs.text:
In some cases, you may need to perform a selective merge, picking specific commits. Let’s take an example we've seen before:

Now, we want to merge only one commit from the fix3 branch:

$ git cherry-pick d09ad27123063a6414de0b3de5c3d7a0c2afb2cb
[main 2c57f06] add file4
 Date: Fri Sep 13 14:47:10 2024 +0200
 1 file changed, 0 insertions(+), 0 deletions(-)
 create mode 100644 file4.py

After the merge, the situation will look like this:

docs.title: Tag
docs.text:
We can use tags to mark a commit, which will then be associated with a release. Here's how to create a tag:

git tag 0.1
git tag
git push origin --tags

docs.title: Contributing to NTC Templates with Git and GitHub
docs.text: 25 September 2024

docs.title: Contributing to NTC Templates with Git and GitHub
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced git

Let's finally see how to contribute to an open-source project. We'll use the NTC-Templates project as a practical example, for which I have already developed 46 patches.

Let's assume we've already made the necessary changes, and now we want to propose them for official inclusion in the NTC Templates repository.

docs.title: Configure git
docs.text:
Configure some git mandatory options:

git config --global user.email "andrea.dainese@pm.me"
git config --global user.name "Andrea Dainese"

docs.title: Fork, clone, update and merge the latest changes
docs.text:
Fork the NTC Templates GitHub repository via the web and clone the repository locally:

git clone https://github.com/dainok/ntc-templates

Add the original upstream:

git remote add upstream https://github.com/networktocode/ntc-templates

If the repository is already present, we can either update it or recreate it. In previous posts, we’ve already covered both options.

docs.title: Make changes
docs.text:
Our changes should be contained in a specific branch:

git checkout -b fix_for_old_hp_procurve

The NTC Templates project requires that each template is accompanied by a series of validation tests. These tests are used to prevent regression errors. A regression error is caused by a patch that, in fact, breaks something that previously worked. To avoid this, it has been decided to include input files and the expected output for each template.

Thus, our patch includes:

  • templates: ntc_templates/templates/hp_procurve_show_mac-address.textfsm
  • raw output: tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.raw
  • parsed output: tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.yml

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
For convenience, I always prefer to run a series of local tests: this allows me to be faster and avoid using unnecessary external resources.

Prepare Python virtual environment:

sudo apt-get install python3-venv python3-pip
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install tox textfsm ntc_templates pyyaml

When I develop or modify a template, I always create a small script to quickly perform a functionality test. The script takes the input file and returns the result after processing it with the TextFSM engine:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import textfsm
import pprint

template_file = "ntc_templates/templates/hp_procurve_show_mac-address.textfsm"
raw_output_file = "tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.raw"

with open(template_file) as fd_t, open(raw_output_file) as fd_o:
    re_table = textfsm.TextFSM(fd_t)
    parsed_header = re_table.header
    parsed_output = re_table.ParseText(fd_o.read())

pprint.pprint(parsed_header)
pprint.pprint(parsed_output)

Or we can use NTC Templates libraries:

#!/usr/bin/env python3

import pprint
from ntc_templates.parse import parse_output

platform = "hp_procurve"
command = "show mac-address"
raw_output_file = "tests/hp_procurve/show_mac-address/hp_procurve_show_mac-address2.raw"

data = open(raw_output_file, "r").read()
parsed_output = parse_output(platform=platform, command=command, data=data)

pprint.pprint(parsed_output)

Both scripts are available in the GitHub repository.

Currently, NTC Templates uses poetry to run tests during the CI/CD pipeline. To perform the same tests, install poetry and run the tests:

curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 -
poetry install
poetry run pytest

Before proceeding, we need to achieve 100% success.

docs.title: Commit and Pull Request
docs.text:
Add files, commit and create the pull request from the original repository.

The CI/CD pipeline will run, and if all tests are completed successfully, it will soon be included in the official repository.

As an example, you can see one of the PRs that have already been approved.

docs.title: GitLab as the backbone of IaC
docs.text: 25 January 2026

docs.title: GitLab as the backbone of IaC
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco git gitlab

GitLab has become the de facto standard for managing the software lifecycle within enterprises. It offers a huge number of features, adapts to almost any requirement, and for this reason it is a broad and complex piece of software. When talking about automation, we will use GitLab as the foundation for provisioning our infrastructure as code (IaC).

In the series of posts related to Cisco NDO and Cisco ACI, we saw how NaC (NetAsCode) allows us to easily configure our fabric in an IaC model. In those articles we also saw how an additional parser helps us implement input data validation and define configurations starting from simplified data structures designed specifically for our infrastructure.

The next step is to move the validation, build, and configuration process into a CI/CD pipeline, where:

  • Continuous Integration (CI): change requests are validated before becoming part of the infrastructure configuration
  • Continuous Deployment (CD): after approval by an authorized operator, configurations are pushed to production devices

The entire system is not limited to Cisco NDO / ACI environments, but can be extended to any ecosystem that can be configured programmatically, and in particular with Terraform. In this specific case, I implemented a pipeline that configures Cisco NDO, Cisco ACI, Cisco Intersight, and VMware vSphere environments.

docs.title: Installing GitLab
docs.text:
In my case, I installed GitLab Community Edition on an Ubuntu Linux 24.04 VM:

curl -s https://packages.gitlab.com/install/repositories/gitlab/gitlab-ce/script.deb.sh | bash

At the end of the installation, we can log in using the root user and the password contained in the file /etc/gitlab/initial_root_password.

Before using GitLab, we may need to set the URL in the /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb file:

external_url 'http://172.24.9.183:8060/'

At this point we can validate and apply the configuration:

gitlab-ctl check-config
gitlab-ctl deploy-page
gitlab-ctl reconfigure

docs.title: Creating a repository
docs.text:
We now need to create a repository that will contain the source code and manage the CI/CD process. Through the web interface we can create a new repository, and via the CLI we can upload all the code we have already developed:

The CI/CD process we designed works only if a Merge Request (MR) is created for every change. In other words, users must work on a copy of the code that will be integrated into the main repository (main) only after all tests have successfully completed. It sounds more complicated than it actually is.
