However, we must protect the repository so that direct changes to the main branch are not allowed. To do this, go to Settings → Repository → Branch rules and protect the main branch:

We also need to ensure that only working code is merged into the main branch. In Settings → Merge requests, make sure that the related pipeline must complete successfully before a merge is allowed:

docs.title: Credential management
docs.text:
The process we previously created was designed to use a local directory. We therefore need to adapt it to be used within a CI/CD pipeline.

In particular, credentials can no longer be stored in clear text. They must be loaded as environment variables.

In Settings → CI/CD → Variables, we can insert all the required variables. In this specific case, we have 6 credentials (Intersight, APIC, vCenter):

The variables are not marked as protected because we want to use them even in pipelines triggered by each commit. Assuming that only authorized users have access to this repository, the risk is acceptable.

Environment variables can then be read as follows:

provider "aci" {
  url      = var.url
  username = var.MI_USERNAME
  password = var.MI_PASSWORD
  insecure = var.insecure
}

docs.title: Terraform state file
docs.text:
The second important change to our build process concerns the Terraform state file. The tfstate files can no longer be stored inside the same repository; instead, they must be stored independently, ensuring that only one pipeline can run at a time.

GitLab allows us to store tfstate files directly within the repository itself. We simply need to configure Terraform to use the HTTP backend as follows:

terraform {
  backend "http" {
    address        = "http://172.24.9.183:8060/api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/site-mi"
    lock_address   = "http://172.24.9.183:8060/api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/site-mi/lock"
    unlock_address = "http://172.24.9.183:8060/api/v4/projects/1/terraform/state/site-mi/lock"
    lock_method    = "POST"
    unlock_method  = "DELETE"
  }
}

By default, Terraform would use the LOCK method, which GitLab does not support. This configuration instructs Terraform to use the POST method on a specific lock file.

To correctly configure the backend, we need to obtain the project ID. Go to Settings → General → Naming, description, topics and view the project ID associated with our repository:

Once the backend is configured, we must instruct Terraform to upload the local tfstate to the backend. To do this, run:

terraform init -reconfigure

docs.title: GitLab runner
docs.text:
The final step is to add one or more runners. A GitLab runner allows GitLab to execute the operations described in a CI/CD pipeline.

Go to Settings → CI/CD → Runners → Project runners → Show runner installation and registration instructions

Copy the command used to register a runner.

Then connect to the GitLab VM via SSH, install Docker, and install the runner using the following steps:

curl -L "https://packages.gitlab.com/install/repositories/runner/gitlab-runner/script.deb.sh" | sudo bash
sudo apt install gitlab-runner -y

Then register the runner using the previously copied command:

sudo gitlab-runner register --url http://172.24.9.183:8060/ --registration-token GR1348941sYrX_7fqAqS7CpeQxnXV

Enter an executor: docker

Enter the default Docker image: alpine:latest

docs.title: Designing a GitLab CI/CD pipeline for IaC
docs.text: 01 February 2026

docs.title: Designing a GitLab CI/CD pipeline for IaC
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco git gitlab

Our CI/CD process is defined in GitLab through the .gitlab-ci.yml file, which resides in the root of our repository.

As mentioned earlier, a pipeline is triggered on every commit to validate the code. Specifically, the following checks are performed:

  • formatting of all files (linting)
  • syntax and consistency of our infrastructure files (CSV files)
  • creation of the infrastructure change plan (build + Terraform plan)

At this point, the user can create a Merge Request (MR) which, after a manual review, is approved.

After approval, a second pipeline is triggered to apply the changes to the infrastructure.

docs.title: Check stage
docs.text:
In the check stage, we take care of building the Python + Poetry environment required for execution. In this stage, validation tests are executed and the infrastructure files are built:

validate-data:
  stage: check
  image: python:3.11
  before_script:
    - pip install --no-cache-dir poetry
    - poetry --version
    - poetry config virtualenvs.in-project true
    - poetry install --no-interaction --no-ansi --with dev
    - poetry env info --path
  script:
    - poetry run pre-commit run -a
    - poetry run ./build-nac-data.py
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - nac-data/
      - site-mi/
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

I usually use pre-commit to run validation tests. This allows any developer to verify the test results before committing code and waiting for the pipeline outcome.

The build phase generates files in the nac-data and site-mi directories. These two directories are treated as artifacts and made available to subsequent stages.

docs.title: Plan stage
docs.text:
In the plan stage, the pipeline uses the artifacts created previously and runs Terraform to confirm the changes that would be applied in production.

mi-apic-plan:
  stage: plan
  image:
    name: hashicorp/terraform:1.14.3
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    TF_HTTP_USERNAME: "gitlab-ci-token"
    TF_HTTP_PASSWORD: $CI_JOB_TOKEN
  dependencies:
    - validate-data
  script:
    - cd site-mi
    - terraform init
    - terraform plan -out=tfplan
    - terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - site-mi/.terraform.lock.hcl
      - site-mi/.terraform/
      - site-mi/plan.txt
      - site-mi/tfplan
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

The Terraform state file is stored in GitLab using the HTTP backend. Access is managed through a user and token that are always available within the GitLab pipeline. We can see the result under Operate → Terraform states:

docs.title: Apply stage
docs.text:
The final stage is executed only in the case of a merge request (a commit on the main branch). In this stage, Terraform is executed to apply the plan displayed in the previous stage (plan).

mi-apic-apply:
  stage: apply
  image:
    name: hashicorp/terraform:1.14.3
    entrypoint: [""]
  variables:
    TF_HTTP_USERNAME: "gitlab-ci-token"
    TF_HTTP_PASSWORD: $CI_JOB_TOKEN
  dependencies:
    - mi-apic-plan
    - validate-data
  script:
    - cd site-mi
    - terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan
  # when: manual
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"

Since it is not possible to link validation pipelines (executed on every commit) with deployment pipelines (executed on every merge request), the two pipelines are independent and, unfortunately, redundant:

  • on every commit, the CI pipeline is executed (check + plan stages), allowing the code to be integrated into the main branch via a merge request
  • on every merge request, the CD pipeline is executed (check + plan + apply stages), applying the configuration to the infrastructure

In this example, we chose to use the merge action as the boundary between validation and application. Other variations are possible, for example by using the when option to define additional control points.

docs.title: Multiple infrastructures
docs.text:
In my case, the infrastructure consists of Cisco NDO, Cisco ACI, Cisco Intersight (UCS), and VMware vSphere. The complete pipeline defines plan and apply jobs for each site and for each environment.

stages:
  - check
  - plan
  - apply
validate-data:
  stage: check
mi-apic-plan:
  stage: plan
mi-apic-apply:
  stage: apply
mi-vcenter-plan:
  stage: plan
mi-vcenter-apply:
  stage: apply
intersight-plan:
  stage: plan
intersight-apply:
  stage: apply

Each commit and merge request executes all 8 jobs. Here too, optimizations are possible by running only the jobs impacted by changes to the infrastructure files.

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD + IaC in action
docs.text: 08 February 2026

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD + IaC in action
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese aci advanced cisco git gitlab

Let’s now see, in practical terms, how to make changes to our infrastructure using GitLab and the pipeline we have created.

We access our GitLab repository, open a file to be modified, and edit it using the Web IDE:

We modify the infrastructure files in the same way we would when using Visual Studio Code:

Once finished, we go to source control and use the Create a new branch and commit function, using add-vlan-1510 as the name of the new branch:

Remember that the main branch is protected and direct commits to main are disabled.

We then return to our repository and go to Build → Pipelines to monitor the progress of the jobs:

In this case, we made a mistake. By looking at the details, we can see that the job stopped during data validation:

280  16:46:56 ValueError: With network 1509, VLAN is duplicated on site MI
281  16:46:56 Cleaning up project directory and file based variables
282  16:46:57 ERROR: Job failed: exit code 1

We defined a duplicated VLAN. We modify our code again, fix the error, and check the new execution:

All jobs have completed successfully, indicating that the data has been validated and that a plan has been prepared for each environment. We can open the plan jobs to review the operations that Terraform will execute:

If we are satisfied, we can go to Code → Merge requests and create a new MR:

Up to this point, no changes have been applied: the main branch is intact, all modifications are contained in a dedicated branch, and the infrastructure has not been reconfigured:

When we press merge:

  • the changes are integrated into the main branch
  • a new pipeline is triggered, which once again executes all jobs and applies the changes to the infrastructure, without any further confirmation

We return to Build → Pipelines and wait for the jobs to complete:

If we now check the status of the three environments, we can verify that they have been reconfigured and now include VLAN 1510.

On the APIC, the BD and EPG have been created:

On Intersight, the VLAN range has been updated:

And on vCenter, the port group has been created:

docs.title: Diving into OAuth 2.0
docs.text: 21 August 2024

docs.title: Diving into OAuth 2.0
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese fundamentals intermediate oauth

In this post, we’ll delve into some key concepts of the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework. Understanding OAuth 2.0 is crucial for working with APIs that are protected by this mechanism. OAuth 2.0 defines four main roles:

  • Resource Owner: the entity (often a person) that grants access to a protected resource.
  • Resource Server: the server hosting the protected resource.
  • Client: the application that needs to access a protected resource and is authorized by the resource owner.
  • Authorization Server: the server that issues an access token to the client after the resource owner has authenticated and authorized the client’s access to the protected resource.

From our perspective, the resource server and authorization server can be a single entity and typically exist within the same security perimeter.

OAuth 2.0 supports various workflows, known as grant types. Four types of workflows are defined, but two are the most commonly used:

  • Authorization Code (3-legged): Preferred when the client is a web application running on a server and the resource server is owned by a third party.
  • Client Credentials (2-legged): Necessary for machine-to-machine interactions. In this scenario, the client is also the resource owner, meaning no user authorization is needed.

docs.title: Authorization Code (3-legged)
docs.text:
This is the most common scenario when dealing with web applications that need to access third-party data, and we are asked to authorize this access. Let’s consider a practical example: logging into LinkedIn using our Google account.

Start by opening a clean browser and logging into Google, then access LinkedIn via Google. Google will ask you to authorize LinkedIn to access your Google data (name, email, profile picture):

Refer to this diagram to understand what happens behind the scenes:

  • (1) The user (resource owner) wants to access LinkedIn (OAuth Client) via the browser.
  • (2) LinkedIn redirects the user to Google (Authorization Server) via the pop-up, passing the client_id parameter that identifies LinkedIn as a registered application with Google.
  • (3, 4, 5) The user opens the Google pop-up, authenticates, and authorizes LinkedIn to access their Google data.
  • (6) Through the user, Google sends an authorization code to LinkedIn.
  • (7) LinkedIn uses the authorization code to request an access token from Google.
  • (8) Google verifies the authorization code and sends an access token to LinkedIn.
  • (9, 10) LinkedIn uses the access token to access Google’s resources.

Remember, in real-world scenarios, the resource server and authorization server are usually a single entity.

docs.title: Client Credentials (2-legged)
docs.text:
This approach is used when dealing with machine-to-machine communication via APIs. In this case, there is no resource owner. The client can act as the resource owner or be considered trustworthy based on the credentials it uses. No user authorization is required.

Refer to this diagram to see how it works:

  • (1) The application (client) requests an access token from the authorization server.
  • (1) The server (authorization server) verifies the application’s credentials and issues an access token.
  • (2) The application uses the access token to access resources.

Again, in real-world scenarios, the resource server and authorization server are typically a single entity.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
For more technical details on the OAuth 2.0 Framework, check out the following links:

  • The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: The official OAuth 2.0 Framework specifications (RFC 6749).
  • Diagrams And Movies Of All The OAuth 2.0 Flows: Takahiko Kawasaki has created excellent diagrams for all four workflows.
  • OAuth Flows: IBM DataPower Gateway’s documentation provides a great overview of the OAuth 2.0 Framework. It includes the two diagrams used above, which are incredibly well done.

docs.title: OAuth Authorization Code flow with Patreon
docs.text: 24 August 2024

docs.title: OAuth Authorization Code flow with Patreon
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese fundamentals intermediate oauth

In our previous post, we introduced the OAuth 2.0 Framework. Now, let's dive into a practical example using the Authorization Code flow (3-legged).

The term "authorization code" refers to the fact that, in the process, we exchange a temporary token (authorization code) for an access token, which will grant us access to protected resources.

docs.title: Patreon Integration
docs.text: Our example focuses on Patreon, where we aim to automate certain tasks using Patreon's API. According to the documentation, authentication must be done via OAuth, and the full procedure for OAuth implementation is outlined there.

docs.title: Registering a New Application
docs.text:
First, we need to register a new application on Patreon. Head over to Clients & API Keys → Create Client:

  • Name: Test API
  • Description: Testing API via OAuth
  • App Category: Member Benefits
  • Redirect URIs: http://localhost:5000/callback
  • Client API Version: 2

After confirming, your client application should look like this:

docs.title: Developing the WebApp
docs.text:
Next, we'll create a simple WebApp that implements the workflow we've discussed:

In this scenario:

  • We act as the Resource Owner.
  • The WebApp we develop is the OAuth Client.
  • Patreon serves as both the Authorization and Resource Server.

The flow is as follows:

  • (1) The user (resource owner) accesses the WebApp (OAuth Client) via a browser.
  • (2) The WebApp redirects the user to Patreon (Authorization Server) via a pop-up.
  • (3, 4, 5) The user authenticates on Patreon and authorizes the WebApp to access their Patreon data.
  • (6) Patreon sends an authorization code to the WebApp through the user.
  • (7) The WebApp uses the authorization code to request an access token from Patreon.
  • (8) Patreon verifies the authorization code and sends an access token to the WebApp.
  • (9, 10) The WebApp uses the access token to access Patreon's resources.

docs.title: Setting Up the WebApp with Flask
docs.text:
We’ll build the WebApp using Flask. It will save all necessary access data in a secrets.yml file. The functions for saving and reading the configuration look like this:

def save_config():
    config = {
        "client_id": app.config.get("client_id"),
        "client_secret": app.config.get("client_secret"),
        "access_token": app.config.get("access_token"),
    }
    with open("secrets.yml", "w") as fh:
        yaml.dump(config, fh, default_flow_style=False)


def read_config():
    try:
        with open("secrets.yml", "r") as fh:
            config = yaml.safe_load(fh)
    except FileNotFoundError as err:
        config = {}
    app.config.update(
        client_id=config.get("client_id"),
        client_secret=config.get("client_secret"),
        access_token=config.get("access_token"),
    )

To start the WebApp, run:

flask run

Open your browser and go to http://localhost:5000 to configure the WebApp using the Client ID and Client Secret obtained earlier. These credentials are typically stored within the application and are not accessible to the user:

After configuration, you'll see a link to access Patreon and authorize the WebApp. The documentation specifies that this link must include three parameters:

  • response_type: code (meaning that the application is initiating the authorization code flow)
  • client_id: the Client ID obtained during Patreon setup
  • redirect_uri: the URL where Patreon will send the authorization code after the user authorizes our WebApp.
  • scope (optional): indicating which permissions the application is requesting.
  • state (optional): used as CSRF.

Once the application is authorized, Patreon redirects the user to the callback URL, passing the authorization code and the state (see above). Since Patreon does not directly interact with the WebApp, we can create internal applications that are not externally accessible.

When the WebApp receives the authorization code from the user, it sends it to Patreon. Patreon verifies the code and returns an access token to the WebApp. The WebApp is sending to the Authorization Server:

  • code: the access code received from the authorization server through the user’s redirection.
  • grant_type: authorization_code
  • client_id: the Client ID obtained during Patreon setup
  • client_secret: the Client Secret obtained during Patreon setup

The WebApp will use the received access token to access Patreon's data:

headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {app.config['access_token']}"}
uri = "https://www.patreon.com/api/oauth2/api/current_user"
req = requests.get(uri, headers=headers)

The source code for the WebApp is available in this GitHub repository.

docs.title: OAuth Client Credentials flow with Patreon
docs.text: 26 August 2024

docs.title: OAuth Client Credentials flow with Patreon
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals oauth

In the previous post, we covered how to implement the Authorization Code flow (3-legged) using the OAuth 2.0 Framework. Now, let's explore a practical example of the Client Credentials flow (2-legged).

docs.title: Patreon
docs.text:
We'll continue using Patreon as our platform, building on what we discussed earlier.

First, we need to register a new application on Patreon. Go to Clients & API Keys → Create Client:

  • Name: Test API
  • Description: Testing API via OAuth
  • App Category: Member Benefits
  • Redirect URIs: http://localhost:5000/callback
  • Client API Version: 2

After confirming, your client application should look like this:

According to the official documentation, if you're working with the API, you can use the Creator's Access Token.

Next, we'll create a simple WebApp to implement the workflow described above:

In this scenario:

  • The script we develop acts as the OAuth Client.
  • Patreon serves as both the Authorization and Resource Server.

The flow is as follows:

  • (1) The server (authorization server) authenticates the script (OAuth client).
  • (2) The script can then access resources (Resource Server).

Authentication in this case is straightforward, relying entirely on a token (Creator's Access Token) obtained during the initial setup. These credentials are typically stored within the application and are not accessible to the user.

In real-world scenarios, the resource server and authorization server are typically a single entity. If that weren’t the case, the script would need to send the Client ID and Client Secret to the authorization server (as discussed in the previous post) to obtain the Access Token needed to access the resources.

As with the previous example, you'll need to include the access token in the HTTP header for any API request:

headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {config['access_token']}"}
uri = "https://www.patreon.com/api/oauth2/api/current_user"
req = requests.get(uri, headers=headers)

The source code for the WebApp is available in this GitHub repository.

docs.title: Simplifying documentation with Markdown and CI CD
docs.text: 05 February 2025

docs.title: Simplifying documentation with Markdown and CI CD
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced documentation

In every company I've encountered, documentation is a recurring challenge. It's a complex topic: creating documentation is labor-intensive, but keeping it up to date is even more demanding. This often leads to outdated or non-existent documentation.

For years, I’ve worked on improving documentation processes. My approach focuses on enhancing tools to make them more efficient and incorporating automation. In many cases, documentation can be derived directly from infrastructure, minimizing manual data collection and allowing people to focus on analysis, commentary, and summarization.

While it might seem like a small detail, I believe a different approach to documentation could bring significant benefits to organizations.

docs.title: What makes great documentation?
docs.text:
No matter what platform a company uses, it should support all types of documentation: process, technical, or compliance. Choosing the right tool requires considering the needs of all teams. I recommend the following key features:

  • Export to PDF.
  • Support for macros, even complex ones.
  • Integration with APIs.
  • Metadata for each document: author, date, confidentiality level.

docs.title: Why I avoid traditional word processors
docs.text:
The most commonly used tool for writing documents is Microsoft Word. In some cases, I’ve also seen LibreOffice or Wiki-style collaborative systems.

Microsoft Word is undoubtedly powerful, offering countless features. However, its complexity often results in these features being underutilized.

Personally, I avoid traditional word processors for several reasons:

  • Incompatible with version control: Their binary data structure doesn't work well with tools like Git.
  • Mixing layout and content: Formatting and content are intertwined, complicating workflows.
  • Inconsistent layouts: Achieving uniform formatting can be unnecessarily time-consuming.

I find the combination of content creation and formatting to be inefficient. Authors should focus on writing, not how their text looks, to save valuable time.

docs.title: Not everything needs to be documented
docs.text:
Over-documentation often highlights deeper process issues. Here are key points for organizations to consider:

  • Base skills: Employees should have fundamental skills. Documentation isn’t a substitute for basic training.
  • Documentation ≠ Reporting: Documentation should be concise and essential for the company’s operations, unlike extensive reports.
  • Readability: Hundreds of unreadable pages are a waste of time. Keep it simple and practical.
  • Regular updates: Allocate time for maintaining and updating documentation.
  • Standardization over Customization: If every product requires unique documentation, consider standardizing products instead of creating endless variations.

docs.title: The perfect tool for my documentation workflow
docs.text:
If you’ve read the previous section, you’ll understand why my ideal tool isn’t Microsoft Word or similar platforms. Instead, my perfect tool allows me to write in Markdown while dynamically integrating external content.

In a corporate setting, I’ve successfully adapted to using XWiki in the past.

For my personal projects, where we’ll focus, I rely on Markdown files stored in Git repositories. This setup allows me to manage document revisions seamlessly. Recently, I’ve been using Obsidian, though the specific tool isn’t critical.

All the documentation I create for myself, whether for my website, books, notes, or courses, is written in Markdown and saved on Git. This workflow ensures I can focus entirely on the content without being distracted by formatting.

Of course, presentations and spreadsheets require a different approach.

docs.title: Markdown: the ideal language for simple and effective documentation
docs.text:
Markdown is a lightweight markup language created in 2004. It’s designed for formatting documents, and its simplicity makes it incredibly effective. Markdown files can easily be converted into HTML, which can then be styled using CSS.

One of Markdown's key advantages is its readability, even in its raw form, Markdown is structured in a way that’s easy to read.

Markdown files are plain text, which means they work seamlessly with any text-searching tools and can be easily versioned using Git or similar systems.

One of Markdown’s downsides is the lack of an official standard. This can create confusion and, at times, compatibility issues between tools. Specifically:

  • Inconsistent syntax: For example, headings can be defined with # or =.
  • Limited feature support: Some tools don’t support all Markdown features, such as tables.
  • Proprietary extensions: Certain tools introduce unique features that aren’t universally compatible.

Despite these drawbacks, Markdown remains my ideal tool for documentation. Here’s why:

  • Focus on content: It enables writers to prioritize the message over the layout.
  • Comprehensive formatting options: It supports essential elements like headings, paragraphs, bullet and numbered lists, images, tables, bold/italic/underlined text, links, code blocks, and quotes.
  • Custom functionality: It can be extended to meet specific needs, providing flexibility for diverse projects.

Markdown's simplicity and adaptability make it an invaluable tool for creators who want to streamline their workflows. Whether you’re building documentation, writing a book, or organizing notes, Markdown empowers you to focus on what truly matters: your content.

docs.title: My Ideal Workflow for Publishing
docs.text:
After extensive testing, I’ve developed an ideal workflow:

The same content is used to generate both the printed book in PDF format and the electronic version in ePub format. After various tests, I decided to use Pandoc for generating the ePub version and WeasyPrint for generating the PDFs. The PDFs, styled differently, are used both for sharing digital documents and creating printed ones.

Both scripts are available in my GitHub repository, along with the style sheets and an example book in both ePub and PDF formats.

docs.title: Electronic Version (ePub)
docs.text:
The process for generating the electronic version is super straightforward: Pandoc takes a template, converts the text directly from Markdown, and applies style sheets specifically designed for the ePub format. Pandoc also handles adding the cover and generating the table of contents (ToC).

The command I use to create an ePub from Markdown looks like this:

pandoc --from markdown-smart --to epub3 --toc --toc-depth=1 --css=css/fonts.css --css=css/common.css --css=css/epub.css --css=css/style.css --template=default.epub3 --epub-cover-image=cover.jpg --output book.epub --metadata-file=metadata.yml

I’ve split the style sheets into multiple files because some of them are also used for producing the printed version. The epub.css file, however, contains all the styles specific to the electronic version.

The metadata file includes all the information that gets embedded in the ePub file. In my case, it also includes specific details (like toc-title) that Pandoc needs to generate the ePub.

belongs-to-collection: Sample Books
creator:
  - role: author
    text: Andrea Dainese
description: null
rights: © 2024 Andrea Dainese
title:
  - text: Sample Book
    type: main
toc-title: Table of contents

The toc-title parameter, in particular, isn’t documented.

Pandoc comes with a set of templates for generating files in the most common formats using default settings that work well in most cases. For ePub, the default template works perfectly as it is.

docs.title: Printed Version (PDF)
docs.text:
The process for generating the printed version is more complex because the style needs to be manually enriched with:

  • page numbers,
  • page breaks,
  • headers and footers,
  • and a table of contents (ToC).

So far, I haven’t found a way to generate a PDF with an acceptable style directly from Markdown. After various tests, I decided to use the WeasyPrint suite. Specifically:

  • Using the Markdown library, I convert the content into HTML.
  • I manually create a single HTML file by adding the header, footer, ToC, and individual chapters that were previously converted.
  • From Python, I use WeasyPrint to generate the PDF from the HTML file and apply the ecessary style sheets.
weasyprint.HTML(f"{book_folder}.html").write_pdf(
    f"../{book_folder}.pdf",
    stylesheets=[
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/common/css/fonts.css"),
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/common/css/common.css"),
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/book/css/paper_size.css"),
        weasyprint.CSS(filename="../templates/book/css/style.css"),
    ],
    font_config=font_config,
)

Compared to other libraries, WeasyPrint gave me satisfying results, even when working with very complex style sheets.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
Once the publishing process is automated, we can integrate it into a CI/CD pipeline where, with each change/commit, a series of checks are triggered, followed by the publication.

In a business context, the pipeline could, for example:

  • require confirmation/validation from a third party,
  • notify stakeholders of a new version of a document,
  • automatically highlight differences compared to the previous version.

For my personal content, my pipeline includes:

  • checking the structure, integrity, and compliance of the YAML files I use to describe each book,
  • checking the structure, integrity, and compliance of the style sheets (CSS),
  • checking the structure, integrity, and compliance of each Markdown file,
  • checking the spelling in each Markdown file.

These four steps are checked before every commit using pre-commit, and they’re also verified server-side after the push, via the CI pipeline.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Writing presentations with Markdown
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced documentation

Previously, we discussed improving documentation management by focusing on content rather than tools. Specifically, we explored how high-quality documents can be generated using Markdown, CSS, and WeasyPrint.

When it comes to documents, optimization is not just about streamlining content writing but also about automating parts of the process. Many business reports, for instance, can be automatically generated, requiring analysts only to provide data commentary.

For my personal productivity, I faced a similar challenge: improving slide creation in the same way.

docs.title: Microsoft PowerPoint
docs.text:
My experience with PowerPoint has been largely negative, and I see that many share this sentiment. While it theoretically supports master templates and offers a wide range of features, practical use reveals significant issues. Transferring content between presentations with different formats becomes an error-prone process, making it difficult to maintain consistent styling.

In enterprise environments, it is common to encounter presentations with mismatched and outdated styles. Centralizing templates at the organizational level is virtually impossible.

docs.title: Google Slides
docs.text:
Google Slides impressed me with its simplicity. Its essential feature set is sufficient for my needs, allowing for clean presentations with consistent styles. Moving content between different presentations is also relatively easy.

However...

From a strategic perspective, I am moving towards a cloud-exit approach. Google uses a proprietary format that is only fully functional within its ecosystem. While I can export presentations in other formats, this reintroduces the very same issues I sought to avoid.

docs.title: Slides as Code
docs.text:
Several tools allow slide creation using Markdown, including:

  • Slidev
  • Marp
  • Reveal.js

Many of these are built on Node.js, which I am not familiar with. Additionally, some lack features essential to my workflow. I also wanted to avoid reliance on a framework that I could not fully control.

Thus, I returned to the approach I had already developed for document generation: Markdown, CSS, and WeasyPrint.

docs.title: Styling Considerations
docs.text:
Documents typically follow a structured format (unless designing highly customized brochures). CSS, especially as implemented in WeasyPrint, offers a high degree of customization, though it is not a perfect solution. Laying out a webpage on a screen differs significantly from typesetting a PDF document.

The compromises necessary for document formatting were largely acceptable. However, designing a presentation is an entirely different challenge, as slides are inherently more artistic.

That said, my presentations are usually technical, with a simple layout comprising text and images. For my use case, efficiency in structuring slides outweighs the need for pixel-perfect element positioning.

docs.title: Defining the Presentation Structure
docs.text:
Similar to my document generation workflow, I used YAML to define the core parameters of each presentation:

title: Sample Presentation
subtitile: Recipes and real world examples by the creator of UNetLab
version: 1
language: en
logo: main
logos:
  main: ../templates/slides/images/logo-ad.png
  small: ../templates/slides/images/logo-ad-small.png
footer: © Andrea Dainese - No AI were harmed during the making of these slides.

This structure allows me to associate different logos with different layouts. A dictionary is used to store logo options, with a primary logo set as the default.

Each slide includes metadata that specifies the layout and associated logo:

---
layout: title
logo: main
---
# Sample Presentation

## Recipes and real world examples by the creator of UNetLab

The slide content itself is written in Markdown.

While Markdown has limitations (many of which are actually its strengths) I needed flexibility. To address this, I incorporated HTML support:

---
layout: main
logo: small
---
# #WhoAmI

## Andrea Dainese

- Senior Network & Security Architect with 20+ years’ experience in securing complex IT and OT infrastructures
- Focused on cyber security strategies, GDPR/ISO 27001 compliance and Automation
- Cisco (CCIE), VMware, Red Hat... certified
- Father of [Unified Networking Lab (UNetLab)](https://www.adainese.it/blog/2019/01/01/unified-networking-lab-unetlab-the-story/)
- Privacy and digital security evangelist

[https://adainese.it](https://adainese.it)
{: .right}

In this example, I use the attr_list extension to assign a .right class, aligning my website link to the right. Additionally, key links are displayed using FontAwesome icons directly embedded in HTML.

This approach fully met my requirements, enabling me to store presentations as Markdown in a Git repository and render them into PDFs using a simple script that I completely control.

Any style updates are instantly reflected across all presentations.

docs.title: Template Processing
docs.text:
The script reads individual slides (one per file) and compiles them into a single HTML file using a Jinja template:

<body>
    {% for slide in slides %}
    <section id="{{ slide.id }}" class="slide {{ slide.meta.layout }}-slide">
        <div class="content">
            {% if slide.logo %}<div class="logo"><img src="{{ slide.logo }}" /></div>{% endif %}
            {{ slide.content | safe }}
        </div>
        {% if footer %}<div class="footer">{{ footer }}</div>{% endif %}
        <div class="page_counter">{{ loop.index }} / {{ slides | length }}</div>
    </section>
    {% endfor %}
</body>
</html>

Each slide is wrapped in a <section> element, with an optional footer and slide number.

The CSS styles are linked based on metadata defined in each slide file.

docs.title: Generating the PDF
docs.text:
To compile the final presentation, we combine Markdown content, the Jinja template, stylesheets, and fonts into a single PDF.

Read each Markdown file and store the content:

md = markdown.Markdown(
    extensions=[
        "markdown.extensions.meta",
        "markdown.extensions.fenced_code",
        "markdown.extensions.codehilite",
        "markdown.extensions.footnotes",
        "markdown.extensions.tables",
        "markdown.extensions.attr_list",
        "markdown.extensions.md_in_html",
        "markdown_captions",
        "pymdownx.tilde",
        "pymdownx.caret",
    ]
)
slide_body = md.convert(md_document)
slide_meta = md.Meta

Use Jinja to generate the HTML presentation:

html_document = template.render(
    language=language,
    title=title,
    subtitle=subtitle,
    slides=slides,
    stylesheets=stylesheets,
    footer=footer,
)
with open("presentation.html", "w") as fh:
    fh.write(html_document)

Render the final PDF using WeasyPrint:

weasyprint.HTML("presentation.html").write_pdf(
    "../Sample Presentation.pdf",
    stylesheets=stylesheets,
    font_config=font_config,
    presentational_hints=True,
)

The output is visually indistinguishable from a PowerPoint-generated PDF, but with the advantages of version control, automation, and full styling control. By leveraging a simple, scriptable workflow, I have significantly streamlined my slide creation process while maintaining flexibility and consistency.

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
Once the publishing process is automated, we can integrate it into a CI/CD pipeline where, with each change/commit, a series of checks are triggered, followed by the publication.

In a business context, the pipeline could, for example:

  • require confirmation/validation from a third party,
  • notify stakeholders of a new version of a document,
  • automatically highlight differences compared to the previous version.

For my personal content, my pipeline includes:

  • checking the structure, integrity, and compliance of the YAML files I use to describe each book,
  • checking the structure, integrity, and compliance of the style sheets (CSS),
  • checking the structure, integrity, and compliance of each Markdown file,
  • checking the spelling in each Markdown file.

These four steps are checked before every commit using pre-commit, and they’re also verified server-side after the push, via the CI pipeline.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: An introduction to workflow and process automation with n8n and Camunda
docs.text: 07 December 2025

docs.title: An introduction to workflow and process automation with n8n and Camunda
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner camunda n8n

In a corporate environment, the natural evolution of network automation is to plug itself directly into business processes, speeding them up and making them more cost-effective.

Over the past few years, I’ve often come across Camunda. Camunda is an open-source platform for business process automation and orchestration that helps coordinate complex workflows involving people, systems, and devices.

In other words, Camunda lets us design business processes, orchestrate them, automate them, and monitor them:

Camunda is built to handle complex, long-running processes represented using the BPMN (Business Process Model and Notation) standard. Different processes can communicate with each other by passing variables across workflows.

Even though it’s a great product, I personally find it quite complex. Between 2019 and 2020, n8n was released, a tool with similar goals but much simpler to use.

n8n is a low-code/no-code automation platform that lets you build workflows connecting different applications, thanks to its 1000+ ready-made integrations. Each workflow runs independently from the others.

So while Camunda and n8n may look similar at first glance, they’re actually very different tools. NTConsult provides a great overview of how they compare:

Use Camunda when:

  • The process involves human tasks, SLAs, escalations, or manual approvals.
  • Execution spans hours, days, or weeks (e.g., onboarding, credit approvals).
  • You need audit trails, versioning, and strict governance (e.g., AML, KYC).
  • You expect high concurrency or thousands of parallel instances.
  • You're coordinating multiple systems, events, and services with full traceability.

Use n8n when:

  • You need quick automations triggered by events, APIs, or schedules.
  • Execution is short (seconds or minutes).
  • You’re building internal tools, notifications, or SaaS integrations.
  • You want low-code speed for non-developers or DevOps workflows.
  • You’re automating infrastructure tasks like provisioning or cleanup.

Our focus here is workflow automation, that is, automating a set of tasks that belong to a broader business process. For this reason, we’ll start working with n8n because:

  • it’s very easy to learn
  • it comes with lots of ready-to-use integrations
  • it’s the right tool for automating sequences of operational tasks

docs.title: Automating user management with n8n and AI Agents
docs.text: 14 December 2025

docs.title: Automating user management with n8n and AI Agents
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate n8n

One of the most repetitive and resource-intensive operational tasks for IT teams is managing users, groups, and roles. This process is almost always triggered by HR following an organizational change. HR submits a service request ticket to IT for each individual operation.

If we analyze this workflow, it’s clear that it is highly inefficient: it requires asynchronous coordination between two teams, HR and IT. Conceptually, HR could interact directly with Microsoft Active Directory, the most common platform for managing users, groups, and roles. In practice, however, this rarely happens. The reason is obvious: Microsoft Active Directory is the backbone of the company, it is complex, and no one outside IT wants to deal with it.

The proposed solution is to create a natural language interface that allows HR to interact with Active Directory in a simple and secure way by:

  • Creating a new user when someone joins the company
  • Assigning and modifying groups and roles for existing users
  • Disabling users when someone leaves the organization
  • Searching and retrieving information about users and groups

docs.title: Installing n8n
docs.text:
n8n can be installed either as a Docker container or via npx. In this example, we use:

npx n8n
[license SDK] Skipping renewal on init: license cert is not initialized
Version: 1.119.1

Editor is now accessible via:
http://localhost:5678

Press "o" to open in Browser.

This provides access to the n8n web interface at http://localhost:5678/. The first step is to register the initial account:

During registration, you can optionally provide a valid email to receive a free license that unlocks some premium features.

At this point, n8n is installed and operational, although this setup is suitable for development purposes, not for production environments.

docs.title: Workflow Overview
docs.text:
We aim to create a workflow that allows an operator, via a natural language agent (bot), to:

  • Retrieve a list of users
  • Get details of a specific user
  • Search for a user
  • Create a user and assign a role (standard, staff, admin)
  • Disable a user
  • Activate a user

Before executing any modification, the bot should request explicit confirmation.

We will use n8n, Django, and Django REST Framework to create this simple workflow. The workflow requires two main components:

  • Chat Trigger: provides the chat interface and triggers the workflow
  • AI Agent: interacts with the user in natural language and performs actions

The AI Agent requires access to:

  • An LLM engine (we use Google Gemini)
  • A storage system for historical interaction data (we use Simple Memory)
  • Tools to execute operations (we use HTTP Request Tool to interact with Django via API)

docs.title: Chat Trigger Configuration
docs.text:
For this prototype:

  • We use Hosted Mode
  • Make the chat publicly accessible
  • No authentication is required

docs.title: AI Agent (IAM Bot) Setup
docs.text:
To configure the agent, we need to:

  • Configure a prompt
  • Associate an LLM engine
  • Define storage for historical interactions
  • Associate operational tools

Associating an LLM Engine: n8n provides a list of supported models. We simply select Google Gemini, add the credentials, and the engine is ready.

Configuring Storage: we add a storage module to allow the agent to utilize past interactions. The main configuration is the number of previous interactions to store:

Associating Tools (HTTP Request Tool): the agent requires “hands” to act in our context. It’s best to create minimalist tools to simplify the agent and reduce potential risks.

We interact with Django user database via REST API. The tools we create include:

  • GetUserList: GET http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/
  • GetUserDetail: GET http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/{{ $fromAI('id') }}
  • SearchUser: GET http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/?search={{ $fromAI('search') }}
  • CreateUser: POST http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/ first_name={{ $fromAI('first_name') }}, last_name={{ $fromAI('last_name') }}, username={{ $fromAI('username') }}, is_active=True, is_staff={{ $fromAI('is_staff') }}, is_superuser={{ $fromAI('is_superuser') }}
  • DisableUser: PATCH http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/{{ $fromAI('id') }}/ is_active=False
  • ActivateUser: PATCH http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/user/{{ $fromAI('id') }}/ is_active=True

The $fromAI() syntax allows seamless data transfer from the agent conversation to API calls.

docs.title: Building the AI Agent
docs.text:
The final step is to assemble the agent with the user, LLM engine, and tools. The key task is prompt design, which instructs the agent to act correctly.

For this MVP, we focus on a functional setup:

  • Use LLM to draft an initial prompt
  • Clearly define agent capabilities and permissions
  • Define user data structure
  • List all available tools with parameters and formats
  • Set operational rules
  • Define AI style and behavior
  • Provide example scenarios

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
We can now test the platform via the workflow’s chat window to validate functionality in real-time:

After fixing issues, we can inspect the data structure exchanged between nodes:

Finally, we can run the workflow in a more professional chat environment:

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
n8n was chosen for its simplicity, allowing rapid prototyping. However:

  • The same workflow could be implemented via a web form, less interactive but faster and more efficient.
  • A full Python-based solution with on-prem LLM is possible but significantly more complex.

Important note: This prototype does not log the user initiating the request or the action performed. For production, non-repudiation is critical: each workflow execution must record the requester, the chat interaction, and the resulting modification.

The final prompt and code are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Approaching OT/ICS Cybersecurity
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance intermediate ot-ics

A few days ago, together with Rocco Sicilia and FESTO Academy, I presented a webinar on OT/ICS Cybersecurity approach. We are often spending time increasing Cybersecurity awareness, and that webinar was focused to gives Cybersecurity fundamentals to OT managers.

docs.title: Understanding the Attacker's point of view
docs.text:
The main discussion was about the Threat Actors, I mean, the attackers. Understanding the attackers gives us the big picture about the different business models they have (the "why", using a definition by Simon Sinek). We focused on:

  • the evolving Cybercrime phenomena;
  • the value the attacker is looking for;
  • types of attackers, goals, and budgets;

Then we discussed some popular Cyberattacks: from WannaCry and NotPetya (2017) which I consider IT attacks to OT/ICS specific attacks: Stuxnet (Iran, 2010), BlackEnergy (Ukraine, 2015), Triton (Saudi Arabia, 2017), Florida city's water supply (2021), Colonial Pipeline (2021), and the recent Viasat attack (2022).

Even if IT and OT attacks have different targets, we reviewed how attackers are used to breach in enterprises: three out of four Threat Vectors are based on human behavior, one Threat Vector only is technology-based.

docs.title: Why (do we interconnect critical devices to Internet?)
docs.text:
Based on the previous paragraph the question is legitimate and the answer is obvious: the Industry 4.0 era is based on fast and automatic interactions (data exchanges). Data can be automatically transmitted between components, plants, systems, suppliers, customers... The more automatic and fast the process is, the more profitable the business is.

Cyberspace provides tools, methods, and interactions to get more opportunities.

But at the same time:

It is considered the fifth theater of warfare.

Place ourselves out of Cyberspace or interconnecting everything without considering the consequences are extreme solutions. We need to find the right balance between them.

Find the correct proportion between freedom, even unconscious, and security

docs.title: Peculiarities of OT/ICS devices
docs.text:
The next chapter was about OT/ICS peculiarities. The audience was already aware, but we presented them from an IT perspective:

  • designed for "availability": the same term is used in the IT world with a different meaning;
  • extremely sensitive to Ethernet disruptions and overloads: remember that Ethernet networks can fail by design (STP convergence);
  • communications do not guarantee confidentiality, integrity, and availability: those are fundamentals attributes in IT security;
  • long term life: compared to the IT world, we can see plants 20 years old;
  • not subject to the same life cycle as IT components: production OT/ICS components (including HMI) are usually "untouchable".

Based on our experiences, we presented seven common issues:

  • Shadow OT: nobody knows exactly what is installed in plant networks and why (e.g. WiFi networks, cloud base telemetry, vulnerable devices, default passwords, remote access devices...). That leads to unmanaged Risk.
  • Weak and sensitive protocols: OT/ICS protocols don't follow the CIA triage used in IT, but they run on Ethernet networks. That leads to unexpected behaviors.
  • Long term life devices: 5 years old plants installed and not maintained are vulnerable to well-known attacks. OT/ICS plants tend to be Legacy, weak and harmful.
  • Remote maintenance: remote 3rd party operators can connect to critical plants anytime and acts locally, watch sensitive production processes and information (espionage and sabotage).
  • Removable storage: 3rd party operators are used to upgrading software via untrusted USB keys. It's not uncommon that malware spread via USB even today.

The list is not intended to be complete, of course; those are the main issues that industries are reporting to us.

docs.title: How (should we approach Cybersecurity in OT/ICS environments?)
docs.text:
Without reinventing the wheel, there are many standards and frameworks which can be used: Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity (NIST), CIS Controls, UNI ISO 31000:2018 Risk management — Guidelines, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations (800-171 and 800-172) and Secure Architecture for Industrial Control Systems (Purdue Model) were discussed during the webinar.

Special mention for the IEC62443 standard: it should be taken into account for both integrators and customers. Even if we still don't have regulations for medical and industry sectors, IEC62443 is supposed to be a sort of guideline.

The purpose of this phase is to plan a strategy taking into accounts

docs.title: What (should we do in practice?)
docs.text:
Cybersecurity is a process and is implemented with organization and technical measures. In practice we want to build a continuous improvement process, starting from the first major issue: Shadow OT.

We cannot protect what we don't know.

The first step requires assessing the OT/ICS infrastructure, and finding out what is installed, the purpose, the business impact, the weakness or robustness... Then we can move on to the supplier, partners, 3rd parties, and employees and evaluate the Cybersecurity risk.

We can suppose a 4-phases improvement process:

  • Check: measures the Cybersecurity posture (get qualitative or quantitative values regarding the many Cybersecurity aspects).
  • Act: analyze the associated Risk and highlight the unacceptable ones.
  • Plan: define a strategy to mitigate the unacceptable risks, taking into account standards and regulations.
  • Do: govern and supervise the implementation.

It's a PDCA cycle, but I'm starting from the third phase because I assume the first two steps are already been completed during the first iteration. It is expected that the next CHECK phase will get better KPI (Key Performance Indicators).

docs.title: IT - OT Convergence
docs.text:
An interesting discussion was about IT and OT convergence: should we go for it?

I consider IT and OT two different worlds with different values and rules. In my opinion, they cannot converge and they shouldn't. If IT guys follow the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad, the OT guys are following a sort of Safety, Reliability, and Productivity triad. Moreover, if uniqueness is something to avoid in IT (we don't want to reinvent the wheel), customization is expected in OT/ICS.

But the IT and OT Cybersecurity must converge. Moreover, Cybersecurity must be a common overlay for all organization departments. The IT and OT Cybersecurity convergence point is defined by:

  • Safety first.
  • A Risk-based approach.
  • Open mindset and dialogue with stakeholders.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Preparing a webinar or a training path is a good way to review concepts and organize them in a coherent flow. I hope auditors could get a different point of view regarding OT/ICS security. Slides are available and the additional session will be delivered in the future.

docs.title: Assume breach design
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced design governance

There is much discussion around Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), but it seems the concept of Assume Breach Design has yet to be formalized. Or, at least, a Google search does not yield results. The term Assume Breach Paradigm is used, and I want to apply it to infrastructure design. So, I am appropriating (in a manner of speaking) the term and explaining why changing the mindset could be beneficial.

As always, the idea stems from field experience, when I realize that infrastructure design, from a cybersecurity perspective, follows a traditional approach. In the 1990s and 2000s, it was common to implement a DMZ network, a server network, and sometimes a client network. Policies were designed based on application needs and were never formalized. This approach, still frequently used today, relies on the classic 3-tier architecture of web applications: clients, servers, and databases, which had to be implemented separately. From a security standpoint, this led to logically separating these components through a firewall.

What I see today is precisely the consequence of this: systems are separated based on an application logic, not a security logic. The result is that companies have security zones that separate application components (Internet, DMZ, client, server, OT, Guest), and policies derive from application needs, not security requirements.

A case in point: server networks typically contain the backend and databases for the entire company. If one is compromised, the whole network is at risk.

A second equally telling example: I imagine anyone who has implemented firewall policies based on an application request. The vast majority of firewall policies originate from application needs, and their impact is rarely evaluated because rejecting the request is not an option.

docs.title: Policy Design
docs.text:
The first attempt at a mindset shift was almost ten years ago. I was in a position to influence the network and security architecture of the company I was working for, and following the advice of an ISO27001 auditor, I formalized the interactions between different security zones.

The idea was to publish a manifesto so that everyone in the company would know the rules governing the firewalls.

Here are some examples:

  • The server network cannot receive connections from the Internet;
  • The DMZ network can access the server network only through HTTP/HTTPS protocols;
  • Server and DMZ networks could only access the Internet on a specific list of addresses/protocols.

All rules were designed to reduce the risk of compromise or lateral movement. But there were some fundamental errors.

The first error (mine) was that the evaluation was conducted by me, and at the time, my experience was primarily in defensive security. A few years later, when I began working on offensive security as well, I realized that while the approach was correct, the assumptions were incomplete.

The second error (company-wide) was failing to give this work the importance it deserved. It was seen as an obstacle created by a paranoid technician rather than a document meant to design secure applications within the company.

Specifically, the 3-tier paradigm was converted to Client (Internet) - Reverse Proxy (DMZ) - Server. It goes without saying that a reverse proxy, without any functionality other than forwarding connections from the Internet to the internal network, has the sole consequence of exposing the internal network directly to the Internet. This should be obvious, but even today, I find several configurations like this.

The last consequence was that when I left that company, the manifesto was shelved and forgotten.

docs.title: A Technical Matter
docs.text:
Anyway, the experience helped me over the years to provide an approach to technical teams that needed to organize firewall policies. Shifting the focus from policy to the needs of the systems before deciding where to place them helps prevent problems rather than chasing them.

The formalization of policies never worked because it was seen by companies as a technical issue, not related to the business.

Particularly, the words a CEO said to me a few years ago were illuminating: cybersecurity is a technical problem, and thus it is entrusted to the CIO.

docs.title: The Purpose of the DMZ
docs.text:
Another factor that drove me to rethink the approach to defending companies is my frequent task of analyzing firewall policies to bring order and logic. Almost always, I find NAT rules that allow direct access from the Internet to internal systems. Often these are necessities related to specific applications, IoT systems, cameras, or building automation in general.

In all these cases, there is a DMZ, which prompts me to ask what the purpose of having a DMZ is if internal systems are still directly exposed.

What I discovered is that the DMZ is often created without a clear understanding of the concept behind it.

Originally, the DMZ network was intended to be the most at-risk segment of the infrastructure: the policies governing traffic to and from the DMZ were meant to be particularly stringent. Some might call this the Zero Trust approach today.

Going back many years, systems in the DMZ network did not have Internet access. This was because if a system was compromised, it could not communicate outward.

Over the years, this paradigm has crumbled (like many others) because many application frameworks require external resources (XML schemas, telemetry, licenses).

The concept of "containment" in the DMZ has gradually eroded, and today a DMZ network risks becoming just another network. Quite frequently, I find:

  • Databases residing in the DMZ;
  • DMZ networks that can access the Internet indiscriminately;
  • Internal systems that can access the DMZ indiscriminately;
  • Unrestricted Internet access from the DMZ and internal networks;
  • Weak systems exposed on the Internet, residing in the DMZ or even internal networks;
  • Reverse proxies that map internal systems to the Internet without providing any security mechanism.

I could go on, but I believe the point is clear.

docs.title: Defense in Depth
docs.text:
The idea behind the Defense in Depth paradigm is to protect a system from cyberattacks using a multi-layered approach. In other words, we should not rely on a single protection (the firewall), but foresee multiple layers that can act together if one or more protections fail.

To be clear, a defense layer could consist of:

  • Firewall
  • VPN
  • Anti-malware
  • MFA
  • Monitoring
  • Vulnerability scanner
  • IDS/IPS
  • Physical security

Defense in Depth is promoted by the NSA, which advises associating each layer with one or more of the five cybersecurity functions as defined in the cybersecurity framework formalized by NIST.

I find the Defense In Depth approach absolutely correct, but, in my opinion, it risks being too technical and thus disconnected from the business. In a way, it was the mistake I made: not being able to speak to the business side, I could not secure the space I needed.

docs.title: Zero Trust Architecture
docs.text:
ZTA, unfortunately, is becoming a mantra. ZTA is defined by NIST in the document SP 800-207, which should be studied before discussing ZTA. I will try to summarize some points useful for my reflections, quoting directly from the original document.

That is, authorized and approved subjects (combination of user, application (or service), and device) can access the data to the exclusion of all other subjects (i.e., attackers). To take this one step further, the word "resource" can be substituted for "data" so that ZT and ZTA are about resource access (e.g., printers, compute resources, Internet of Things IoT actuators) and not just data access.

ZTA pertains to data access, where the data can reside on any system, including printers, IoT systems, and, of course, servers, databases, and so on. The subject is, therefore, digital data in any form.

Access to resources is determined by dynamic policy—including the observable state of client identity, application/service, and the requesting asset—and may include other behavioral and environmental attributes.

Data access is determined by dynamic policies built on who is requesting the data, who holds the data. Policies may consider other environmental or behavioral attributes.

Requesting asset state can include device characteristics such as software versions installed, network location, time/date of request, previously observed behavior, and installed credentials. Behavioral attributes include, but not limited to, automated subject analytics, device analytics, and measured deviations from observed usage patterns.

Today we build policies based on the identity of the source and destination. The destination identity typically consists of an IP address and port. The source identity is slightly more complex, considering not only the IP address but also the associated user. In more complex infrastructures, the source is also validated according to specific requirements concerning patch status and the presence of anti-malware.

We rarely use attributes related to location and time. Even less frequently, we use behavioral attributes (e.g., if the client behaves differently from expected).

The ZTA approach would require allowing access to data only when strictly necessary. To achieve this, we would need to:

  • Identify the source in terms of device, user, application requesting the data, the client's location, the time of the request, the source's behavior, and compliance status;
  • Identify the means by which the request arrives (Internet, VPN, private network, encryption...);
  • Identify the requested data and the operation being requested.

Although technologies capable of implementing almost all (but not all) features required by

ZTA exist, it is still not a paradigm widely implemented today.

The reason, in my opinion, is always the same: ZTA is seen as a technical approach, detached from the business.

docs.title: Assume Breach Design
docs.text:
Let's move on to the assume breach paradigm applied to design. The core idea is quite simple: my architectural choices are guided by the assessment of the risk of a potential breach. We could call it risk-based design, but in my opinion, the term would be less effective.

There are two important premises:

  • It is necessary to be able to thoroughly assess the possible attack paths against the infrastructure.
  • It is necessary to be able to evaluate the impact of potential breaches on the business.

The first point requires specific offensive skills that are different from those of someone who designs and defends an infrastructure. Those who do not make use of these skills will make substantial mistakes in designing defenses.

The second point requires the ability to conduct a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) for each attack scenario.

Only after these assessments can we determine which defenses to implement. In this sense, Defense in Depth and ZTA are consequences of Assume Breach Design, not its premises.

Let's return to the example of particularly large server networks that contain backends and databases for all company applications. The consequence of this design is that if one is compromised, the attacker can move relatively easily to all critical business systems. If we correctly assess this scenario, we realize that it is unacceptable. At this point, we can implement a microsegmentation technology and try to reduce the traffic flows between these hosts. But we can also consider monitoring technologies that allow us to identify traffic anomalies. Both approaches have pros and cons, and there is no one-size-fits-all solution. The assessment of business risk helps us determine the available budget, and consequently, we can select the solution that best fits our context.

I can, therefore, break down ZTA into parts and decide where it is important. The decision is based on a risk analysis of attack scenarios: in other words, Assume Breach Design.

docs.title: Post Breach
docs.text:
All the infrastructures I know have grown gradually and without structure. In other words, there is never any documentation that describes how the infrastructure, in terms of servers and applications, was created. On the one hand, the task would be impossible with traditional tools, while on the other, the assume breach paradigm forces us to think about how we would respond to an attack.

In almost all cases (and I am being optimistic), if we notice an ongoing attack within our infrastructure, we are not able to say for sure how far the attack has spread. In other words, we do not know how to eradicate the attack from the infrastructure unless we completely rebuild it.

The Infrastructure as Code paradigm can help us build our infrastructure (or part of it) starting from text files. The use of microservices and containers allows us to do the same in the application domain. If we start to embrace this mindset, we realize that we can rebuild the entire infrastructure at any moment, and the build process can serve as documentation.

The advantages are immediate: documentation, standardization, compliance... However, the complexity of the tools remains a barrier to adoption for many organizations. The rigidity of the infrastructure is actually an apparent problem that reveals the underlying operational chaos.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The Assume Breach Design approach aims to bring business back to the center of decision-making. The infrastructure exists to serve one purpose: the company's business. The protections that technical teams decide on today are implemented to safeguard the company's business.

Putting business back at the center means shifting cybersecurity from being a technical matter to a business necessity.

For too many years, I have seen IT departments considered as a black hole that absorbs budget. The effects of this mindset are clear to everyone. Maybe it's time for a change.

docs.title: Crisis management
docs.text: 10 February 2021

docs.title: Crisis management
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance incident-management intermediate

Note: This article was originally written a few months ago but never published. I've now revisited it, adding some updated reflections.

This period has taught us many lessons at different levels. Today I want to focus on one in particular: the importance of having a plan for emergencies.

Referring to an investigative report by Report — "Virus and State Secrets" — one of the main weaknesses that severely impacted the ability to respond was the absence of an emergency plan that was:

  • shared with all the people involved;
  • clear and complete, down to the details;
  • comprehensive, covering a wide range of scenarios.

In recent weeks, an additional factor has emerged: the reliability of the supply chain during global crises.

docs.title: Shared
docs.text:
When an emergency occurs, people need to know that a plan exists and that it specifies exactly what actions to take.

In Incident Response engagements, I've often found emergency plans tucked away in drawers—never communicated, let alone practiced.

But awareness alone is not enough: people must internalize the plan so they can act as a team, not as individuals driven by panic or anxiety. One of the most important and fascinating aspects of my job is training staff through simulated scenarios with increasing levels of stress.

Borrowing the concept of Kata from martial arts—later adopted by Toyota in organizational management—we know that only by repeatedly practicing behaviors can we truly internalize them and apply them effectively when it really matters.

docs.title: Clarity and Completeness
docs.text:
An emergency plan must be clear and complete. In high-stress situations, people can't be expected to think calmly and rationally. They must follow a predefined plan that includes every necessary detail.

Examples of seemingly obvious yet essential information include:

  • roles and responsibilities of team members;
  • internal and external communication procedures;
  • how to file a report with law enforcement;
  • how to assess and, if needed, notify a Data Breach to the Data Protection Authority.

While some of these steps may appear "obvious" and easy to look up online, under stress people forget, misjudge, or waste time. In fact, during real crises it's common to see confusion and disorganization—even forgetting basics like the network topology, device locations, or how to access them.

This is not about "experience." It's about the ability to work under stress.

Here again, training is key: if the plan clearly defines roles and procedures, and people are trained accordingly, the team is much more likely to perform effectively.

Realistic training also serves to test how individuals react under pressure. The goal is not that everyone stays calm, but that leadership at all levels—board, line managers, team leaders—can guide and reassure the team in a moment of crisis.

As highlighted in Report, chains of command must function, because people need structured points of reference.

docs.title: Comprehensive Scenarios
docs.text:
While it's impossible to anticipate every possible crisis, a good risk assessment helps identify the most critical scenarios. That assessment is the foundation for building targeted emergency plans.

Today, most cyber threats revolve around ransomware: attackers exfiltrate sensitive data and then attempt to render infrastructure unusable.

Clearly, an attack on a telecom network is very different from an attack on an ICS/OT system, a database, or a file-sharing platform hosting next season's product catalog. Just as the attacks differ, so must the response plans. Reacting to an attempt to poison a water treatment plant requires entirely different actions than handling the outage of a call center's phone system.

docs.title: Equipment Availability
docs.text:
Preparedness also depends on the scenarios considered in the crisis plan. If scenarios are missing or unrealistic, you'll end up improvising under pressure.

As COVID-19 showed, effective operations require tested and ready-to-use equipment. In a health emergency, that might mean stockpiled medical gear and medicines. In a cyber crisis, it means having "clean" workstations available—functional, charged, with all necessary accessories (network cables, serial adapters, Wi-Fi/4G connectivity, etc.).

Without planning, the result is what we saw: governments rushing to procure medical equipment mid-crisis, and companies scrambling to buy laptops to hastily enable remote work.

docs.title: Supply Chain Reliability
docs.text:
One lesson that wasn't highlighted in Report, but has since become clear, is the fragility of the supply chain during global crises.

The slow and uneven distribution of vaccines revealed how suppliers may struggle to meet expectations—or, in some cases, prioritize certain entities over others.

When selecting suppliers, organizations must now consider not only technical and contractual factors but also geopolitical ones: in times of crisis, political decisions may override contractual obligations, prioritizing some regions or countries over others based on commercial, economic, or strategic interests.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
Observation is essential for understanding the world around us—but to be useful, it must be detached and objective. This allows us to see the many parallels between the physical and digital worlds.

As COVID-19 has shown, real-world crises can teach us valuable lessons for cyber crisis management, making companies more resilient to inevitable future challenges.

The ultimate goal is not just to make organizations safer, but also more competitive. Reliability is now a differentiator in the marketplace, and in these times, it can make all the difference.

Successfully surviving a cyber attack is one of the best credentials an organization can show—arguably stronger than simply claiming never to have faced one.

docs.title: Cybersecurity: fashion or strategy
docs.text: 12 October 2024

docs.title: Cybersecurity: fashion or strategy
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner governance

I couldn't find a suitable title for this post, in which I try to gather various insights that I've received in the past few days and that I've planned, sooner or later, to discuss together with Rocco Sicilia.

I start with the provocation: the world of Cybersecurity has certainly been under the spotlight for some years now. Provocatively (we'll see the reasons later), I would define it as "trendy". There are various hypes that follow one another in creating needs/fears with the aim of selling solutions and services. There's nothing wrong with this, but we need to distinguish acting out of "trendiness" from strategic action.

Acting out of "trendiness" is an impulse, aesthetic, sometimes very personal, often done out of emulation, and fundamentally it's difficult to trace the motivation behind some choices. Because it's precisely an impulse. Translated, for the purpose of this post, security measures chosen on impulse are not guided by a strategy and, we have already talked about this several times, they are often ineffective. This mode is extremely widespread and easy to identify: if I ask "why" a security measure (NAC, firewall, Security Awareness Training Software...) was implemented, the answer tends to be (I exaggerate and simplify) "because". Almost always, these security measures chosen on impulse are not integrated into a process and are not monitored we have also talked about this.

Strategic action (summarized) starts with an analysis and inserts security measures into a higher design. Each measure is chosen and inserted with a specific purpose and measured as such. There may be exceptions but they are well documented and temporary (with a certain date). Because an exception weakens the protections we have implemented.

A real example that touches on the fundamentals: the firewall. All companies have a firewall, whether it's perimeter, dual bastion... But almost no company defines policies: policies are made by technicians and are often hated because they limit others' work. Strategic action starts from the purpose of one's infrastructure, which is to support the business. As such, it must provide services that are implemented through servers. These servers, to function, have connectivity needs and therefore risks. Risks are mitigated by dividing servers into areas and these areas can only communicate with each other under certain rules, which are translated into firewall policies. In the ideal world, I should NEVER find systems publicly exposed and positioned in networks considered secure. However, I find them and they are often historical relics, abandoned, unchecked but, precisely exposed for "historical reasons".

Because, in companies, security is done by technicians, there is no strength to bring the world of Cybersecurity to the corporate level.

And then the CISO arrives.

The responsibility for Cybersecurity is dumped onto the CISO. And I mean "dumped": namely, the problem, once relegated to technicians, is now relegated to a manager so that the company can continue to forget about it. Let's start with the basics:

  • a CISO who doesn't report to the board cannot do his job;
  • a CISO who doesn't have a budget cannot do his job;
  • a CISO who doesn't have veto power cannot do his job;
  • a CISO who is not consulted before any technological choice cannot do his job.

It has been said many times: Cybersecurity is a corporate problem, but everyone keeps pretending otherwise. A couple of years ago, I had the opportunity to interview some CEOs of enterprises close to me. The answers were enlightening because they allowed me to enter their mindset and understand their needs.
