Obviously, the approach is imprecise, incomplete, and partly incorrect (we will see why later). However, the contribution it brings to organizations is significant:

  • thousands of vulnerabilities are now weighted based on the security measures in place, making it possible to define priorities;
  • security measures are considered, allowing for discussions about whether untouchable assets should be moved to separate zones;
  • the impact of a complete attack is considered, not just that of the vulnerable asset;
  • it allows for defining justifications for why certain assets might remain unpatched.

This approach, sometimes referred to as risk-based vulnerability assessment, is gaining increasing traction. Specifically, I am observing that the compliance and insurance sectors are welcoming a risk-based approach and evaluating it positively.

In other words, it is justified for critical vulnerabilities to exist, provided they are managed with a risk-based approach.

docs.title: Predicting the future
docs.text:
In a pragmatic approach, a vulnerability is considered as such if it can be exploited. Many vulnerabilities require such specific conditions that, in practice, exploitation becomes unfeasible. The CVSS value takes into account the complexity of the attack, but it does so with only two possibilities: low and high.

FIRST has defined a parameter that represents the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days:

EPSS is a measure of exploitability. Specifically, EPSS is estimating the probability of observing any exploitation attempts against a vulnerability in the next 30 days.

The value of EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), variable over time, helps us define the SLA to mitigate each vulnerability associated with a CVE.

docs.title: Mitigating a vulnerability
docs.text:
At this point, we should have a list of vulnerabilities with associated risk, net of security measures (Inherent Risk), and a mitigation factor that represents the security measures in place (EDR, firewall, awareness, etc.). The combination of these two factors allows us to determine the risk that a vulnerability will be exploited, considering the security measures (Residual Risk).

Before sorting this list in descending order of risk and starting to compile the remediation plan, we are missing one last factor: risk appetite (Risk Appetite). This factor indicates the level of risk that our organization considers acceptable. Once defined, all vulnerabilities with a Residual Risk below this factor are automatically ignored. If we have any doubts, it means our risk model has some flaws.

We have now obtained a list of real, exploitable vulnerabilities for which the risk is not considered acceptable. We must therefore define actions to reduce the risk of each vulnerability.

Risk can be:

  • resolved, for example by updating the vulnerable software or shutting it down;
  • mitigated, by implementing a new security measure (e.g., moving the vulnerable system to a higher security zone);
  • transferred, for example through insurance or third parties.

docs.title: Patching
docs.text:
Often, a vulnerability can be resolved by installing an update. However, we must ask ourselves when this action should be taken. I have seen organizations with monthly patching policies, at best. In the worst cases, systems are updated once a year or even less frequently.

First, each system and application should have a well-defined maintenance window.

Second, we must associate a specific SLA with risk categories: the higher the risk, the faster the updates must be installed, and consequently, the maintenance windows must be scheduled at shorter intervals. Paradoxically, the more critical a system is from a business perspective, the more frequently it must be taken offline for maintenance.

For this reason, organizations tend to perform what I call "blind patching," which focuses not on risk but on systems that are easiest to update. This is the exact reason that causes the accumulation of hundreds or thousands of vulnerabilities in many companies.

An additional consideration on patching activities is often their lack of proper "dignity." People responsible for patching do so at their own risk:

  • if everything goes well, they receive no recognition;
  • if something goes wrong, they are blamed for the disruption and are responsible for restoring the service.

In this environment, people will avoid taking on patching tasks, causing further delays. If we think that the lack of patching is a resource problem, we will soon discover that the real issue is that no one wants to press the button and take on the associated responsibility.

From an organizational perspective, it is unrealistic to have a cross-functional team responsible for software updates. Each system serves an application necessary for the business. In this sense, applications and systems have an assigned owner who guarantees the service. If we want the process to work, we cannot decouple the application responsibility from the update responsibility.

The final consideration concerns the maximum time to mitigate a vulnerability. This time depends on conditions that change over time (as we have already discussed with EPSS). It is worth citing a Cloudflare report.

CVEs exploited as fast as 22 minutes after proof-of-concept published

22 minutes is an impossible time frame to manage these vulnerabilities manually. In 22 minutes, we might not even notice the new vulnerability. We need to think about a different approach.

docs.title: Mitigating Risk
docs.text:
We have already stated that patching is one of the possibilities for managing software vulnerabilities. However, there are many cases where patching cannot be performed. The typical reasons are:

  • The application cannot be stopped frequently enough to allow continuous patching;
  • The application is no longer supported, and updates are no longer available;
  • The application is no longer sold and/or the vendor no longer exists.

There are also more operational reasons, such as:

  • No one wants to take responsibility for updating a mission-critical application;
  • There is no proper rollback system;
  • The risk of encountering issues is higher than the risk of leaving the application as is.

This situation is common in ICS/OT environments, especially in production, medical, naval, utilities, oil & gas sectors... But, on closer inspection, every company has applications that cannot be updated.

We must also consider that, very often, business processes are tied to a specific application. The evolution of this application is often faster than the speed at which business processes can evolve. A prime example: the company relies on a specific CRM with customizations that are key to business processes. Subsequent major releases of that CRM do not guarantee full portability of customizations, forcing the company to spend time and resources chasing each successive release.

It thus becomes clear that if we use patching as the only method to resolve software vulnerabilities, we will always have a set of unmanageable objects.

If we return to a risk-based approach, things change.

If we know the risk associated with each application (and thus each asset), we can isolate it in a specific security zone protected by adequate security measures. For example, if we have industrial systems that are particularly vulnerable and important at the same time, we can isolate them in a secure zone. Communications to and from this zone can be limited and controlled to reduce the risk of compromise.

We have just described the Purdue model (SANS Secure Architecture for Industrial Control Systems), which suggests creating a containment zone between the IT and OT worlds.

It is not certain that the Purdue Model can be implemented in your company, and it likely cannot, but we can use that idea to separate critical, non-upgradable applications from those that are manageable. By optimizing security measures, we can create a sufficiently strong barrier to protect even the most fragile devices.

Security measures can include:

  • Firewalls with particularly stringent rules;
  • Web Application Firewall (WAF);
  • EDR / XDR;
  • Behavioral analysis;
  • Active monitoring services;
  • NAC (Network Access Control);
  • Microsegmentation;
  • Network probes;
  • Honeypots;
  • ...

In practice, my advice is to start with a well-structured asset inventory. Each asset should be characterized based on its impact on business operations (see NIS2) and personal data (GDPR). Each asset should also have a defined maintenance window: this value is key to understanding how much we can operate on an asset without impacting the business.

Where the maintenance window is insufficient to ensure proper maintenance, we need to mitigate the potential risk of compromise by enhancing security measures.

We can then define the necessary security zones protected by additional security measures. Ideally, these security measures can be represented by a numerical factor, which can be used to calculate residual risk. This way, for each security zone, there will be a mitigation factor associated with the assets contained within that zone.

This approach allows us to extend traditional vulnerability scanning tools by including the context, i.e., the protection derived from the security zone in which the assets reside.

docs.title: VA Scanner
docs.text:
The most common system today for identifying software vulnerabilities within an organization is Vulnerability Assessment (VA). Specifically, we are talking about Vulnerability Scanner applications that scan the network for known vulnerabilities. Vulnerabilities are detected through signatures: if a service announces its version and it is vulnerable, the scanner will report that service as vulnerable.

It is clear that these tools are often overrated.

docs.title: Generic Risk
docs.text:
Vulnerability scanners provide a report of detected vulnerabilities, associating a risk with each vulnerability. However, this risk factor is obviously incomplete: it lacks context.

However, we have already seen how to assess risk by associating specific information about the asset and the available security measures.

docs.title: Limited Coverage
docs.text:
The effectiveness of a scanner, or its ability to find all vulnerabilities present in the infrastructure, is tied to the signature database that the scanner uses. No scanner can have 100% coverage for two reasons:

  • The software landscape is highly diverse, and there are products (like WordPress) that can be extended by a vast ecosystem of plugins;
  • Almost every organization has custom applications.

While the utility of a Vulnerability Scanner is undeniable because it allows for the analysis of thousands of devices in a very short time, it is also true that there must be plans for deeper analysis of well-known applications that may not be covered by the scanner.

It is also worth mentioning that many companies turn to different vendors to perform VA, hoping to gain better coverage over time. It is obvious that if all companies use the same scanner, the result will be the same. At most, the interpretation may vary.

docs.title: Local Vulnerabilities
docs.text: In almost all cases, Vulnerability Assessments are limited to network scanning. This means that all local vulnerabilities—such as those that could be exploited to escalate privileges after gaining local access—are completely overlooked.

docs.title: Annual Scanning
docs.text:
If Vulnerability Assessments are conducted to detect vulnerabilities, we must consider the maximum time that may pass from when a vulnerability becomes public (and starts being exploited) to when we become aware of it.

We have seen that active exploitation of a vulnerability can occur within minutes of its discovery. Therefore, conducting annual, semi-annual, quarterly, or even monthly scans makes little sense.

docs.title: Detection vs. Verification
docs.text:
Vulnerability scanning systems are not meant to discover vulnerabilities; rather, they are intended to check the vulnerability management process.

In other words, if the vulnerability management process is functioning correctly, the scanner's report will almost always (if not always) be redundant.

docs.title: Vulnerability Management
docs.text:
The vulnerability management process brings together all the considerations we've made so far and formalizes the operational procedures. The process begins when a new vulnerability is detected, and this can happen through various sources:

  • Reports;
  • Automated tools;
  • Individuals.

Each report will be analyzed and evaluated to understand the associated risk. If the inherent risk, reassessed based on the existing security measures, exceeds the activation threshold, the change management process will need to be triggered to further mitigate the vulnerability.

To summarize:

  • Patch Management: Involves updating software to supported versions. Updates to resolve functional bugs are part of this process.
  • Application Lifecycle Management: Involves the removal or migration of obsolete applications that have reached the end of their lifecycle.
  • Vulnerability Management: Involves reducing the risk associated with known vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text:
We have seen that the time interval between the discovery of a technical vulnerability and its exploitation "in the wild" is very small. On the other hand, technical vulnerabilities are constant, and managing updates to address them requires significant effort. We have also seen that the most critical systems are the hardest to update, both due to the difficulty of halting them and the reluctance to modify critical systems that are functioning.

We cannot today think of addressing the vulnerability management process without using automatic or semi-automatic systems. The most basic form of automation, usually applied to end-user devices, involves a weekly update. More complex workflows involve, upon confirmation, updating systems first on test groups, then on groups with increasing criticality.

My experience tells me that the more a process is defined and automated within the organization, the less likely people are to question it. In other words, if a system stops functioning due to someone manually updating the system, the responsibility will fall on that person. But if a system is updated through an automated organizational process, any malfunctions are accepted and managed.

docs.title: Immutable OS and Containers
docs.text:
"Immutable" systems do not allow for modifications. In other words, an immutable system is created, configured, typically through an automated process, and then destroyed without anyone modifying it. Containers behave the same way in this regard.

Likewise, immutable systems and containers are not updated but are instead destroyed and recreated from an updated base template.

This approach, used by organizations with a strong DevOps culture, is ideal for:

  • Managing system changes, including updates;
  • Creating test groups with increasing criticality;
  • Applying updates on a daily/hourly basis;
  • Performing rollbacks to the previous version in a matter of seconds.

docs.title: SBOM and Vulnerabilities in Templates
docs.text:
Those who develop, and even those who use open-source software, should monitor the vulnerabilities of the libraries that their main application depends on. This may seem, and indeed is, a monumental task. However, it can be tackled by structuring an automated process to perform these checks.

The goal is to prevent situations like the one seen with Log4Shell.

One potential approach involves using the CycloneDX utility to get a list of the libraries used by a specific software in a standard format (SBOM or Software Bill of Materials). This list can then be used by a second utility to analyze any vulnerabilities:

cyclonedx-npm package.json.bak_00.md > sbom.json
bomber scan sbom.json

The mechanism is certainly improvable, but it is a first step in structuring a process to monitor, as much as possible, the applications installed within the organization.

docs.title: Post patching (Threat Hunting)
docs.text:
We reach the end of this long post by considering the vulnerability lifecycle:

Once a vulnerability is resolved, we must ask ourselves a key question: is it possible that this vulnerability has already been exploited? How should we proceed?

The answer is not simple and depends heavily on the vulnerability. In some cases, there are Indicators of Compromise (IoC) associated with the vulnerability that help us determine whether the vulnerability has already been exploited, but in many cases, these indicators are not available.

Ideally, organizations regularly perform an activity (Threat Hunting) aimed at detecting silent threats already within the organization that, for some reason, were not detected or blocked by other security systems.

Our vulnerability management process could therefore trigger specific Threat Hunting activities for the vulnerability we are managing. For example, we might want to initiate in-depth analyses for particularly critical vulnerabilities, with an EPSS score above 70%.

docs.title: What does it take to secure any SME organization
What does it take to secure any SME organization
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese governance intermediate

Managing Cybersecurity is expensive, we all know that. But not managing it is also more expensive. Given my experience, an SME recovers from a critical Cyberattack in 5-10 days, if it can recover (yes I also personally know companies that lost everything because of a Cyberattack).

So how we can conjugate an SME with a minimal effective Cybersecurity strategy?

To plan a strategy, we need to fully understand common Cyberattacks and Threat actors.

docs.title: SME, Threat Actors, and Cyberattacks
docs.text:
First, let's try to describe an SME:

  • privately owned (I often find a single owner);
  • manufacturing sector;
  • a maximum of 150 employees (most of them are working in production);
  • a maximum of $50 million annual receipts;
  • very small or outsourced IT department;
  • low IT budget;
  • low Cybersecurity awareness (management often doesn't want to be bored with security topics);
  • increasing security compliance requirements.

SMEs need to protect:

  • production;
  • CRM;
  • intellectual property.

Threat actors targeting SMEs probably want to:

  • compromise and ask for ransom (usually);
  • steal intellectual properties (seldom);
  • sabotage them (rarely).

Based on the above assumptions, the most frequent type of Cyberattack is a ransomware-based attack.

docs.title: Lifecycle of a ransomware attack
docs.text:
The New Zealand CERT describes the Lifecycle of a ransomware attack.

In short, we have 4 ways the attacker gets inside organizations:

  • Phishing
  • Password guessing
  • Exploit vulnerability
  • Email

We should notice that 3 out 4 are person based attacks: attackers, using social engineering techniques, try to:

  • steal valid credentials persuading people to insert them in malicious web portals;
  • guess the password using a public data breach and assuming people reuses passwords;
  • persuade people to download and execute malware to take control of computers inside the organization.

docs.title: Designing an effective Cybersecurity strategy
docs.text:
Based on the most probable attack, we can now design an effective Cybersecurity strategy to reduce the risk. Always remind that we are talking about SMEs, so our budget is limited.

We can mitigate the risk of an attacker getting inside the organization as following:

  • Techincal measures:
  • Multi-Factor Authentication: we want MFA for email access and remote access VPNs (mitigate Phishing, Password guessing).
  • Antispam: we want to filter out malicious emails (mitigate Phishing, Email).
  • Logging: we want to detect invalid login attempts (mitigate Password guessing).
  • Security Assessment: we want to detect vulnerabilities via VA, DAST, and PT (mitigate Exploit vulnerability).
  • Patching: we want up-to-date applications and because the IT department is very small we want it to happen automatically (mitigate Exploit vulnerability).
  • Endpoint Detection Response: we want a good EDR to stop malware (mitigate Email);
  • Segregation: we want well-configured network/host-based firewalls which drop incoming and outgoing malicious connections (mitigate last attack phases);
  • Data Protection: we want that in the worst-case scenario, we can get our data back (mitigate the last attack phase);
  • Organizational measures:
  • Policies and procedures: we want to enforce password security (mitigate Password guessing).
  • Training: we want to test how employees are good at detecting social engineering attacks (mitigate Phishing, Email).

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: I think that is the minimal set of technical and organizational measures that any organization should implement to reduce the risk of Cyberattacks. Even very small organizations should evaluate the security controls described above.

docs.title: Leveraging Nautobot as a SSOT
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner nautobot

Every company should move away from using Excel sheets as databases for managing infrastructure and switch to a structured system as the foundation for operational workflows.

The goal is to have a single repository that contains all the infrastructure data, including:

  • VLANs, IP networks, IP addresses, VRFs (IPAM)
  • Sites, physical and virtual devices
  • Rack configuration and cabling

This type of data structure is often referred to as SSOT or Single Source Of Truth, implying that this database:

  • Reflects what is configured in the infrastructure
  • Serves as the source for various workflows

In reality, things are a bit different: a SSOT, as defined here, isn’t truly a “source” but more of a destination. For instance:

  • VLANs, IP networks, IP addresses, and VRFs are configured within devices. It’s always possible to create a new VLAN inside a device without updating the SSOT.
  • VMs are configured within virtual environments (e.g., ESXi). You can always add a VM locally to a host (e.g., ESXi) that isn’t visible to the orchestrator (e.g., vCenter) or the SSOT.

That’s why I prefer using the term Single Pane Of Glass (SPOG). A SPOG is essentially a dashboard that collects data from external sources and presents it in an integrated and coherent manner. From a SPOG, you can execute workflows to alter the state of systems.

To summarize:

  • Having a unified data structure that shows the state of the infrastructure is essential for reducing operational costs
  • It’s not accurate to refer to it strictly as a SSOT (Single Source Of Truth)
  • We should approach the problem by developing a SPOG (Single Pane Of Glass)
  • A SPOG should be fed or at least verified with real data from the infrastructure (often from individual devices)
  • We can associate workflows with the SPOG to make changes to the infrastructure

From here on, we’ll use the term SSOT interchangeably with SPOG for simplicity, now that we’ve clarified the differences.

Here’s a clarifying example:

  • We use Nautobot (or Netbox) as the SSOT
  • Feed Netbox with data from devices in the infrastructure
  • Define profiles to associate with switch interfaces
  • By changing the profile associated with an interface in Nautobot, the switch configuration is automatically updated

In upcoming posts, we’ll cover how to implement this workflow from scratch. The implementation will be done in a development environment. We won’t cover how to transition the development environment to production.

docs.title: Choosing the foundation for our SSOT
Choosing the foundation for our SSOT
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner nautobot

The first topic we need to address is selecting the software that will serve as the foundation for our SSOT (Single Source of Truth). Our ultimate goal is to create a data structure that consolidates all the critical information about our infrastructure, such as:

  • VLANs, IP networks, IP addresses, VRFs (IPAM)
  • Sites, physical and virtual devices
  • Rack configuration and cabling

Essentially, we’re looking for an IPAM (IP Address Management) tool that can also store various other types of data. Since this data structure will be the base for executing some automated workflows, it needs to be:

  • Well-documented
  • Designed with an API-First approach
  • Open source
  • Extensible via plugins
  • Written in a widely used automation programming language (Python)

We have two main candidates: Nautobot and Netbox. Nautobot is a fork of Netbox created in 2021. The primary reason behind Nautobot’s development was to evolve the product into a platform for automating processes within organizations.

Both products are currently undergoing significant restructuring, often with substantial breaking changes. This decision will impact the future of our integration:

  • Our implementation must keep up with product updates: it’s crucial that our integration doesn’t hinder future updates to our SSOT.
  • The closer we stick to the product’s official features, the fewer customizations we’ll need to make, simplifying future updates.
  • Fewer customizations mean fewer problems → we’ll use more standard constructs.
  • It must support interface roles.

We have demo versions of both products available:

  • demo.netbox.dev: registration required.
  • demo.nautobot.com: username demo, password nautobot.
  • next.demo.nautobot.com: username demo, password nautobot.

From the demos, we can see that the next version of Nautobot offers the ability to assign roles to interfaces, a feature not available in the current versions of Netbox or Nautobot. There was a bug in the demo, but it should be resolved and integrated into the demo now.

Therefore, the decision is clear: Nautobot, in its upcoming version, will be the product we use to implement our SSOT.

docs.title: Installing Nautobot in your lab environment
Installing Nautobot in your lab environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner nautobot

In this guide, we'll walk through installing Nautobot in a lab environment. For production installation, please refer to the official documentation. Nautobot requires Python versions between 3.8 and 3.11. First, ensure you have the correct Python version:

$ python3 -V
Python 3.11.9

Next, create a dedicated Python environment:

mkdir /opt/nautobot
python3.11 -m venv /opt/nautobot/venv
source /opt/nautobot/venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip wheel setuptools
pip install --no-binary=pyuwsgi nautobot

We will use PostgreSQL as the database. After installing PostgreSQL, create a dedicated database and user for Nautobot:

$ psql postgres
create user nautobot with password '42f5de36abff';
create database nautobot;
grant all privileges on database nautobot to nautobot;

Configure Nautobot using the following environment variables:

export NAUTOBOT_ROOT=/opt/nautobot
export NAUTOBOT_DB_HOST=localhost
export NAUTOBOT_DB_NAME=nautobot
export NAUTOBOT_DB_USER=nautobot
export NAUTOBOT_DB_PASSWORD=42f5de36abff
export NAUTOBOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=\*
export NAUTOBOT_DEBUG=True

Initialize the basic configuration, which will be saved to /opt/nautobot/nautobot_config.py:

nautobot-server init

Update the database:

nautobot-server migrate

Create the first administrative user:

nautobot-server createsuperuser

Finally, start the Nautobot server:

nautobot-server runserver

You can now access Nautobot at http://localhost:8000/ using the admin user credentials you created earlier.

docs.title: Installing a Development Version of Nautobot
docs.text:
As discussed, the feature we need (interface roles) is available in the next version of Nautobot. Let's follow the official guide to install it.

First, activate the previously created Python environment:

cd /opt/nautobot
source venv/bin/activate

Uninstall the current version of Nautobot:

pip uninstall -y nautobot

Download the next version from GitHub:

git clone --depth 1 --branch next https://github.com/nautobot/nautobot

Install the newly downloaded version:

cd nautobot
poetry install

Update the database:

nautobot-server migrate

Start Nautobot:

nautobot-server runserver

docs.title: Populating our SSOT with Automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate nautobot

Now, we need to populate our Single Source of Truth (SSOT). Manually adding interfaces for each device is impractical. Hence, automating this process by reading device configurations and creating corresponding SSOT objects is essential.

Currently, there's no official system for automatic device discovery. This led me to develop NetDoc years ago, though it's currently exclusive to Netbox.

Let's create a simple automation to efficiently handle this task.

Tools We'll Use:

  • Netmiko for device connectivity and information retrieval.
  • NTC Templates to parse information into structured data.
  • Nautobot’s REST API to create SSOT objects.

Assuming the device is manually created in our SSOT for convenience, our automation will focus solely on populating interfaces.

Let's proceed step-by-step to develop our automation.

docs.title: Parameters Needed for Our Automation
docs.text:
Our automation requires the following parameters to function effectively:

  • nautobot_base_url: The URL to access Nautobot.
  • nautobot_apikey: The API key for making REST API requests to Nautobot.
  • host: The IP address of the physical device to be read.
  • username: The username used to access the physical device.
  • password: The password used to access the physical device.

You can create the API key on Nautobot by navigating to User → Profile → API Tokens → Add a token.

In the example script, some parameters are interactively read while others are statically defined within the code. Please note, this script serves as a simple example and should not be used securely in production environments.

docs.title: Connecting to the device and retrieving information
docs.text:
Next, we need to establish a connection to the device and retrieve necessary information. In this example, let's assume the device is a Cisco IOS XE switch, and the required data can be obtained using the following two commands:

  • show version: to retrieve the device hostname.
  • show interfaces: to retrieve all configured interfaces and any additional parameters.
with ConnectHandler(**data) as net_connect:
    show_version = net_connect.send_command("show version", use_textfsm=True)
    show_interfaces = net_connect.send_command("show interfaces", use_textfsm=True)

The use_textfsm parameter allows us to immediately transform the human-readable output into structured data. This transformation (parsing) is performed using the Google TextFSM library and NTC Templates.

docs.title: Processing retrieved data
docs.text:
Now that we have obtained the data we need in a structured format, our next step is to clean it up and extract only the following parameters:

  • Hostname (standardized to uppercase).
  • Interface name, description, and link status.
device_name = show_version[0]["hostname"].upper()
device_interfaces = {
    item["interface"]: {
        "description": item["description"],
        "status": "Active" if item["link_status"] == "up" else "Decommissioning",
    }
    for item in show_interfaces
}

docs.title: Updating data on Nautobot
docs.text:
We are now ready to update the data on Nautobot. To do this, we need to:

  • Retrieve the device ID by its name. Let's assume the device has already been manually created within Nautobot.
  • Add interfaces associated with the device only if they do not already exist.

First, let's make a call to retrieve all devices by filtering their name:

# Ingesting data to Nautobot
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Token {nautobot_apikey}",
    "Accept": "application/json",
}

# Get device ID
url = f"{nautobot_base_url}/api/dcim/devices/?name={device_name}"
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30).json()
if req["count"] < 1:
    raise ValueError(f"{device_name} not found")
device_id = req["results"][0]["id"]

If the device exists, we use the device_id to retrieve interfaces associated with this device. If the interface does not exist, we create it:

# Ingesting data to Nautobot
headers = {
    "Authorization": f"Token {nautobot_apikey}",
    "Accept": "application/json",
}

# Get device ID
url = f"{nautobot_base_url}/api/dcim/devices/?name={device_name}"
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=30).json()
if req["count"] < 1:
    raise ValueError(f"{device_name} not found")
device_id = req["results"][0]["id"]

In both cases, we assume that Nautobot's structure does not allow multiple devices with the same name or multiple interfaces with the same name within the same device.

docs.title: Preparing to Execute the Script
docs.text:
Before running the script, we need to create the device on Nautobot. Here's the step-by-step process.

Create a Device Role: navigate to Organization → Roles → Add, with Content Type = dcim|device:

Create a Manufacturer: go to Devices → Manufacturers → Add:

Create a Device Type: in Devices → Device Type → Add, associate it with the previously created Manufacturer:

Create a Location Type: set up a Location Type in Organization → Location Type → Add, with Content Type = dcim|device:

Create a Location: add a Location in Organization → Locations → Add, associating it with the previously created Location Type:

Create the Device: finally, in

, associate the Device Role, Device Type, and Location, using the hostname in uppercase:

docs.title: Running the Script
docs.text:
Now, we can execute the script. If everything works correctly, the device on Nautobot will be populated with all its interfaces:

This process ensures that the device is properly set up within Nautobot before proceeding with the automation script to populate its interfaces.

The script can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: Integrating Ansible with Nautobot
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible intermediate nautobot

Integrating Ansible with Nautobot involves two main aspects:

  • Reading information from Nautobot using Ansible.
  • Running Ansible playbooks to update device configurations.

Let's focus on the first point: to make Nautobot's information available in Ansible, we need to use a dynamic inventory. Network to Code provides a specific Ansible collection for Nautobot that includes an inventory plugin. You can install this collection with:

ansible-galaxy collection install networktocode.nautobot

Before configuring the inventory, ensure the following information is completed in Nautobot for your device:

  • IP address for device access
  • Username and password for device access
  • Connection method used by Ansible to access the device
  • Device interfaces with associated profiles

docs.title: Configure primary IP address
docs.text:
To configure the management IP address, follow these steps:

Create a network prefix: Navigate to IPAM → Prefixes → Add:

Create an IP address: Go to IPAM → IP Addresses → Add:

Associate the IP address with a device interface: Go to Devices → Devices → select the device → Interfaces → edit the management interface → IP Addresses and select the newly created IP address:

Set the interface's IP address as the primary address: Go to Devices → Devices → select the device → Primary IPv4 → select the correct IP address:

docs.title: Device custom attributes
docs.text:
Next, create two custom attributes to define the parameters Ansible will use to connect to the devices.

Go to Extensibility → Custom Fields and add the connection and network_os attributes, both associated with the dcim|device type:

Now, populate the attributes for each device:

  • connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
  • network_os: cisco.ios.ios

docs.title: Interface profiles
docs.text:
Define the profiles to be associated with the interfaces. Assume we have three profiles initially:

  • access: for interfaces connecting PCs
  • isl: for inter-switch link interfaces
  • trunk: for interfaces connecting servers or firewalls

Go to Organization → Roles → Add and add the three profiles of type dcim|interface:

Finally, associate some interfaces with the newly defined roles by going to Devices → Devices → select the device → Interfaces:

docs.title: Ansible Inventory
docs.text:
Define the Ansible inventory file that will read configurations from Nautobot. Following the official documentation we can create an inventory.yml file configured to return the necessary information:

plugin: networktocode.nautobot.inventory
api_endpoint: http://localhost:8000
token: ced15098774a01a54fb7f4fcfadba56e9e68a8c0
validate_certs: false
config_context: false
interfaces: true
compose:
  ansible_connection: custom_fields.connection
  ansible_network_os: custom_fields.network_os
keyed_groups:
  - key: device_types
    prefix: type
  - key: manufacturers
    prefix: manufacturers
  - key: location
    prefix: location
  - key: device_roles
    prefix: role

This simple configuration isn't suitable for a production environment, but it allows us to:

  • Retrieve a list of devices with the parameters needed by Ansible.
  • Retrieve the list of interfaces for each device with the associated profile.
  • Group devices into three different groups.

Verify the inventory functionality with the command:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list

The output should include:

  • For each device, the variables ansible_connection, ansible_host, and ansible_network_os.
  • For each device, the interfaces list containing all interfaces.
  • For each interface, the variables description, enabled, role, and status.

The Ansible inventory can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: The Ansible role breakdown
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible nautobot

Now, we need to translate the interface roles defined in Nautobot into specific configurations for the switches. To achieve this, we will create an Ansible role that utilizes the inventory described in the previous post to configure the interfaces of each device.

docs.title: Fetch Running Configuration
docs.text:
First, we retrieve the current running configuration from the switch:

- name: GETTING RUNNING CONFIGURATION
  cisco.ios.ios_command:
    commands:
      - show running-config
  register: show_running_config

Optimizing show running-config improves overall performance.

docs.title: Create data structures
docs.text:
Next, we generate data structures with necessary details from Nautobot:

- name: SETTING INTERFACE PROFILES
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    interface_profiles: >-
      {
        {% for interface in interfaces %}
          {% if interface.role %}
            "{{ interface.name }}": "{{ interface.role.name }}",
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      }
    interface_cfgs: >-
      [
        {% for interface in interfaces %}
          {% if interface.role %}
            {
              "name": "{{ interface.name }}",
              {% if interface.enabled %}
                "description": "{{ interface.description }} ({{ interface.role.name }})",
                "enabled": true,
              {% else %}
                "enabled": false,
              {% endif %}
            },
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      ]
  • interface_profiles links each interface to its profile.
  • interface_cfgs holds configurations for the ios_interfaces module .

Interfaces are processed only if they have an associated profile.

docs.title: Limit data structure (optional)
docs.text:
Optionally, we can limit the data structure to a single interface via command line:

- name: FILTERING INTERFACES
  ansible.builtin.set_fact:
    interface_profiles: >-
      {
        {% for interface_name, profile in interface_profiles.items() %}
          {% if interface_name == interface_limit %}
            "{{ interface_name }}": "{{ profile }}",
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      }
    interface_cfgs: >-
      [
        {% for interface in interface_cfgs %}
          {% if interface.name == interface_limit %}
            {{ interface }},
          {% endif %}
        {% endfor %}
      ]
  when: interface_limit is defined

docs.title: Apply interface profile configuration
docs.text:
For each interface, an external configuration file is included:

- name: ATTACHING PROFILE TO INTERFACE
  ansible.builtin.include_tasks: "profile_{{ interface.value }}.yml"
  with_dict: "{{ interface_profiles }}"
  loop_control:
    loop_var: interface

The profile file uses the ios_config module to apply configuration commands:

- name: "APPLYING PROFILE ISL TO INTERFACE {{ interface.key }}"
  cisco.ios.ios_config:
    config: "{{ show_running_config.stdout.0 }}"
    lines:
      - switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
      - switchport mode trunk
      - switchport nonegotiate
      - udld port aggressive
    parents: "interface {{ interface.key }}"
    before: "default interface {{ interface.key }}"

This step is the slowest, so optimizations are crucial.

docs.title: Set interface description and state
docs.text:
Finally, we apply the prepared configuration data:

- name: "SETTING INTERFACE STATUS"
  cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
    config: "{{ interface_cfgs }}"
    state: merged

This task manages the interface state (shutdown and no shutdown) using the native module.

docs.title: Running the playbook
docs.text:
Execute the playbook on all devices or limit it to a specific interface:

./playbook-interface-configuration.yml
./playbook-interface-configuration.yml --extra-vars interface_limit=GigabitEthernet1/0/47 --limit MGMTSWITCH1

By following these steps, you'll efficiently automate your network interface configurations using Ansible and Nautobot.

The Ansible role can be downloaded from GitHub.

docs.title: Orchestrating Ansible playbooks for Nautobot integration
Orchestrating Ansible playbooks for Nautobot integration
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese ansible beginner nautobot

Currently, it is not possible to execute Ansible playbooks directly from Nautobot. There are some proposals, but nothing concrete has been implemented yet.

The only option is to use an external orchestrator to run the playbook regularly or upon operator request. Here are some options:

  • Crontab: schedule playbook runs at regular intervals.
  • Ansible Tower: A web-based solution for managing and scheduling Ansible playbooks.
  • AWX: The open-source version of Ansible Tower.
  • Spacelift: A flexible CI/CD platform for infrastructure as code.

Each of these tools offers unique features and capabilities, allowing you to choose the best fit for your environment and requirements.

docs.title: Key insights from developing Nautobot and Ansible integrations
Key insights from developing Nautobot and Ansible integrations
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible behind-the-scene nautobot

Beyond the topics discussed in previous posts, my work on this project focused on four key areas:

  • The data structure of Nautobot
  • Nautobot's REST API
  • Integrating Ansible with Nautobot
  • Running Ansible playbooks from Nautobot

Let's dive into the challenges encountered and the solutions omitted from previous posts.

docs.title: Nautobot's data structure
docs.text:
Effectively using Nautobot requires careful planning of the data structure to avoid costly changes later. Understanding this structure allows for simplifications in automation scripts.

Each object in Nautobot is identified by a UUID, such as 2170a207-43b2-422a-a90d-51a4908b85fb. This choice allows any attribute to be changed without issues. Since the device identifier is a UUID and not a name, we must consider:

  • Can two devices have the same name?
  • Can two interfaces on the same device have the same name?

Quick tests reveal that the answer is no to both questions, allowing for safe simplifications in automation scripts.

docs.title: Django shell
docs.text:
Nautobot is built on Django, a Python-based web application framework. Django provides a shell for easy interaction with the data structure.

The decision had to be made whether to develop automations using the shell or the REST API.

The shell can be invoked using the command:

nautobot-server shell

For example, to retrieve the list of interfaces associated with a device, you can use this simple script:

from nautobot.dcim import models

models.Interface.objects.filter(device__name="MGMTSWITCH1")

While this option is appealing, it is important to note that the shell is only available locally to the instance running Nautobot. In environments where Nautobot is running in containers, accessing the shell can be complex or impossible.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
REST APIs are useful when well-documented, which is not the case with Nautobot. The documentation includes examples, and local installations provide API call documentation (http://localhost:8000/api/docs/)..) However, some features like filtering are poorly documented, requiring trial and error.

The device_id filter worked, but device_name returned an error:

{"device_name": ["Unknown filter field"]}

After numerous attempts, I discovered a 2023 bug. Eventually, I realized the API filters are actually FilterSets, allowing device to filter by name or label.

The equivalent code is:

url = "http://localhost:8000/api/dcim/interfaces/?device=MGMTSWITCH1"

req = requests.get(url, headers=headers).json()

Remember to handle pagination.

docs.title: Django shell o REST API
docs.text: Deciding between the shell and REST API, I chose the REST API for broader compatibility despite the difficulties.

docs.title: Integrating Ansible with Nautobot
docs.text:
network.toCode() provides a specific Ansible collection for Nautobot. I needed a solution to use Nautobot as an Ansible inventory without creating one from scratch.

The plugin documentation offers a good starting point with examples.

The challenge is defining a data structure that includes:

  • Ansible-specific parameters (ansible_connection, ansible_network_os, ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_ssh_pass)
  • A group identifying devices
  • A list of interfaces with profiles for each device

Three options exist:

  • The inventory contains all necessary information from Nautobot.
  • Playbook defines information except for the group with correct variables.
  • A mix of both.

I opted to move information to Nautobot to experiment with custom fields. In practice, usernames and passwords are stored in a vault; for simplicity, I hardcoded them in the playbook.

After testing, I found the correct combination. Two custom fields map to variables:

compose:
  ansible_connection: custom_fields.connection
  ansible_network_os: custom_fields.network_os

Each device is associated with three groups based on attributes:

keyed_groups:
- key: device_types
  prefix: type
- key: manufacturers
  prefix: manufacturers
- key: location
  prefix: location

compose and keyed_groups are standard Ansible features that required some trial and error. I used the following command to test:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --list

docs.title: The Ansible Playbook
docs.text:
Creating an optimized Ansible playbook requires experience. I reused a previously developed role with slight modifications.

First, I read the configuration from Nautobot and created two data structures:

  • interface_profiles: maps interfaces to profiles.
  • interface_cfgs: contains the data structure for the ios_interfaces module.

This approach was necessary as the ios_l2_interfaces module does not support all needed parameters. Using the ios_config module for interface configuration and ios_interfaces for specific parameters (description and status) was the solution.

This results in a simple CLI command list that any network engineer can read and modify:

lines:
- switchport access vlan 53
- switchport voice vlan 54
- no cdp enable
- no lldp receive
- no lldp transmit
- spanning-tree bpduguard enable
- spanning-tree portfast edge
- switchport mode access
- switchport nonegotiate

I used Jinja to create the data structure for better performance:

ansible.builtin.set_fact:
  interface_profiles: >-
    {
      {% for interface_name, profile in interface_profiles.items() %}
        {% if interface_name == interface_limit %}
          "{{ interface_name }}": "{{ profile }}",
        {% endif %}
      {% endfor %}
    }

Verify the data structure as JSON using the debug command to avoid issues like missing commas:

ok: [MGMTSWITCH1] => {
"msg": "{\n\"GigabitEthernet1/0/44\": \"interface_access\"\n\"GigabitEthernet1/0/45\": \"
interface_isl\"\n\"GigabitEthernet1/0/47\": \"interface_trunk\"\n}"

}

Once corrected

ok: [MGMTSWITCH1] => {
    "msg": {
        "GigabitEthernet1/0/44": "interface_access",
        "GigabitEthernet1/0/45": "interface_isl",
        "GigabitEthernet1/0/47": "interface_trunk"
    }
}

The next step is enabling playbook execution for a specific interface:

./playbook-interface-configuration.yml --extra-vars interface_limit=GigabitEthernet1/0/47

I cleaned the data structures to keep only the filtered element. Profile association is done using include_tasks, optimal for network engineers who deal with profiles for each interface.

Finally, description and interface status are configured using the ios_interfaces module, simplifying shutdown and no shutdown command management.

docs.title: Introduction to OT/ICS
docs.text: 12 February 2025

docs.title: Introduction to OT/ICS
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals ot-ics

Operational Technology (OT) encompasses the systems responsible for monitoring and controlling industrial operations. Within OT, Industrial Control Systems (ICS) refer specifically to technologies used for automating and managing industrial processes.

While IT professionals have decades of experience securing networks, systems, and applications, cybersecurity in OT/ICS is a relatively new concern. In industrial environments, availability takes priority over integrity and confidentiality, meaning that ICS software is often designed for speed and efficiency rather than security. This fundamental difference makes OT/ICS systems uniquely vulnerable to cyber threats.

docs.title: OT (Operational Technology)
docs.text:
Operational Technology (OT) refers to the hardware and software used to monitor, control, and automate industrial processes, critical infrastructure, and manufacturing plants. OT is distinct from IT (Information Technology) because its primary focus is on ensuring operational continuity and physical safety, whereas IT is concerned with data management and cybersecurity.

Key OT Components:

  • Industrial Control Systems (ICS)
  • Sensors and Actuators
  • Supervisory and Control Systems (SCADA, DCS)
  • Embedded Devices (PLC, RTU)
  • Industrial Networks (Industrial Ethernet, MODBUS, Profibus, etc.)

docs.title: ICS (Industrial Control Systems)
docs.text:
Industrial Control Systems (ICS) are a subset of OT that includes all technologies used to monitor and control automated industrial processes. ICS are deployed in manufacturing, energy, transportation, utilities, and other critical industries to ensure safe and efficient operations.

Types of ICS:

  • SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition)
  • DCS (Distributed Control System)
  • PLC (Programmable Logic Controller)
  • RTU (Remote Terminal Unit)

docs.title: SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition)
docs.text:
SCADA is a supervisory system used to monitor and control industrial processes distributed over large geographical areas, such as power grids, pipelines, and water treatment plants. SCADA collects data from remote sensors and devices, allowing operators to make real-time decisions.

Key SCADA Components:

  • Supervisory Computers: Centralized servers that collect and process data from field devices (PLCs, RTUs) and provide visualization tools for operators.
  • Human-Machine Interface (HMI): The graphical interface used by operators to monitor and control industrial processes.
  • Communication Networks: Infrastructure connecting SCADA components (Ethernet, serial, radio, cellular, satellite).
  • Remote Terminal Units (RTU): Remote field devices that collect data from sensors and transmit it to the SCADA system.
  • Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC): Controllers responsible for executing real-time logic and automation tasks.

docs.title: DCS (Distributed Control System)
docs.text:
A DCS is an automation system designed for real-time process control in large, localized industrial facilities, such as oil refineries, chemical plants, and power plants. Unlike SCADA, which is optimized for wide-area monitoring, DCS systems are designed for tightly integrated process control within a single site.

Key DCS Components:

  • Process Control Units (PCU): Localized control units that manage industrial processes in real time.
  • Field Devices (Sensors, Actuators, Valves, etc.): Directly interface with physical processes.
  • Engineering Workstations: Used for configuring and optimizing control logic.
  • Operator Consoles (HMI): Interfaces for monitoring and managing plant operations.
  • Industrial Communication Networks: Used to connect different DCS components (e.g., Fieldbus, Profibus, OPC-UA).

docs.title: PLC (Programmable Logic Controller)
docs.text:
A PLC is a specialized industrial computer used to control machinery and processes in manufacturing and automation environments. PLCs are essential components of both SCADA and DCS systems, as they provide real-time monitoring and decision-making.

Key PLC Features:

  • Real-Time operation: Executes logic based on inputs from sensors and generates outputs to control machinery.
  • Modular architecture: Allows customization with input/output (I/O) modules.
  • Industrial protocol support: Communicates via MODBUS, PROFINET, EtherCAT, and other protocols.
  • High reliability: Designed for continuous operation in harsh environments.

docs.title: Summary of key differences
docs.text: System Primary Function Best for Geographical Scope Control Approach OT Industrial operations & automation Manufacturing, utilities, energy Local and global Ensures uptime and safety ICS Monitoring & controlling industrial processes Industrial environments Local and global Integrates SCADA, DCS, PLC, RTU SCADA Supervisory control & data acquisition Remote monitoring (e.g., power grids, pipelines) Large-scale, geographically distributed Centralized monitoring DCS Real-time process automation & control Complex, high-precision manufacturing (e.g., chemical plants, oil refineries) Localized within a facility Distributed control with redundancy PLC Logic execution & machine control Automated processes (e.g., assembly lines, robotic systems) Localized control Executes predefined automation logic

docs.title: IT vs. OT: Key Differences
docs.text:
While Information Technology (IT) and Operational Technology (OT) are increasingly interconnected, they have fundamental differences in priorities, lifecycle management, and security approaches:

  • System Lifecycle: IT systems typically have a 3-5 year lifecycle, with frequent upgrades and replacements. OT systems, however, are built for longevity, often operating for 10-30 years without major changes.
  • Patching and Updates: In IT, regular software updates and patches are standard to mitigate security vulnerabilities. In OT, however, patching is infrequent or even impossible, as system downtime can disrupt critical industrial processes.
  • Security vs. Safety: IT security focuses on protecting data (confidentiality, integrity, availability). OT prioritizes safety and operational continuity, where system availability is more important than data protection.
  • Risk Approach: IT deals with cybersecurity risks, such as data breaches and malware. OT must consider both cyber and physical risks, as failures can lead to equipment damage, environmental hazards, or even loss of life.
  • Data Protection vs. Availability: IT prioritizes data confidentiality and integrity (ensuring information is secure and accurate). OT prioritizes availability and uptime, ensuring industrial systems run without interruption.

These differences make OT environments harder to secure, requiring specialized cybersecurity strategies that balance safety, reliability, and risk management.

docs.title: Final Thoughts
docs.text:
Understanding the differences between OT, ICS, SCADA, DCS, and PLCs is essential for anyone working in industrial automation, cybersecurity, or operational technology. As IT and OT continue to converge, securing these systems against cyber threats becomes increasingly important.

In Simple Terms:

  • Industrial operations rely on sophisticated, mission-critical computer systems (SCADA).
  • In OT/ICS environments, security is not the top priority, availability and uptime come first.
  • Operators can manually override plant operations using a mouse, keyboard, or touchscreen, both locally and remotely.
  • Malicious software can manipulate plant behavior in the same way an authorized operator would through the HMI.

For a deeper understanding, refer to the Guide to Industrial Control Systems (ICS) Security (NIST 800-82).

docs.title: Introduction to Modbus protocol
docs.text: 19 February 2025

docs.title: Introduction to Modbus protocol
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

Modbus is a widely used industrial communication protocol originally developed by Modicon (now part of Schneider Electric) in 1979. It is open, royalty-free, and simple to implement, making it one of the most popular protocols for connecting Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs), Remote Terminal Units (RTUs), sensors, and other industrial devices.

Modbus is primarily used for data exchange in supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems and distributed control systems (DCS). The protocol is designed for high reliability and deterministic communication, which is essential in industrial automation environments.

docs.title: Modbus Protocol Overview
docs.text:
Modbus operates using a master-slave (or client-server) architecture, where:

  • The Master (Client) initiates requests, reading from or writing to devices.
  • The Slaves (Servers) respond to the requests but do not initiate communication independently.

A master device (such as an HMI or SCADA system) communicates with one or more slave devices (such as PLCs, RTUs, or field devices) over a network. Each slave is assigned a unique 8-bit address (ranging from 1 to 247 in RTU mode). Modbus RTU (Remote Terminal Unit) is usually used via RS-485 (serial network).

Modbus TCP (Modbus over TCP/IP):

  • Encapsulates Modbus RTU messages inside TCP/IP packets for transmission over Ethernet networks:
  • Uses port 502 as the standard Modbus TCP communication port.
  • Does not require timing-based message separation like RTU, making it easier to integrate with modern IT networks.
  • Allows multiple clients to communicate with a single server, unlike Modbus RTU, which supports only one master.

Modbus data is organized into "registers," which store information in predefined formats. Each register type serves a specific purpose:

Register Numbers Type Address Name Data Type Value Range 1-9999 Read-Write %IX Status/Coil (State controls) bool 0 or 1 10001-19999 Read-Only %QX Input Contact (State information) bool 0 or 1 30001-39999 Read-Only %QW Input Registers (Numerical values) uint, word 0 to 32767 40001-49999 Read-Write %IW Holding Registers (Numerical values) uint, word 0 to 32767

Holding registers and input registers handle analog values, while coils and discrete inputs manage binary (on/off) signals.

docs.title: Modbus Function Codes
docs.text:
Modbus uses function codes to perform operations on registers and coils. These function codes specify whether data is being read or written and determine the type of data being accessed.

Function Code Description Register Type 1 Read Coil Coil (Discrete Output) 2 Read Discrete Input Discrete Input 3 Read Holding Registers Holding Register (16-bit) 4 Read Input Registers Input Register (16-bit) 5 Write Single Coil Coil (Discrete Output) 6 Write Single Holding Register Holding Register (16-bit) 15 Write Multiple Coils Coil (Discrete Output) 16 Write Multiple Holding Registers Holding Register (16-bit)

Each request consists of:

  • Function Code (e.g., 03 for reading holding registers)
  • Start Address (the register or coil address)
  • Number of Registers or Coils
  • Data (for write operations)
  • Error Checking (CRC for RTU, checksum for ASCII, or TCP checksum for Modbus TCP)

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Modbus remains one of the most widely used industrial communication protocols due to its simplicity, reliability, and interoperability. However, as IT and OT networks continue to converge, securing Modbus communication is critical to preventing cyber threats and operational disruptions.

Despite its widespread use, Modbus lacks built-in security mechanisms, making it vulnerable to cyber threats such as:

  • Eavesdropping (Modbus traffic can be intercepted and read)
  • Unauthorized Commands (No authentication, allowing unauthorized devices to issue commands)
  • Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attacks (Attackers can modify Modbus traffic)

For more information see Modbus 101 - Introduction to Modbus.

docs.title: Why build an OT/ICS Cybersecurity lab?
docs.text: 29 January 2025

docs.title: Why build an OT/ICS Cybersecurity lab?
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals ot-ics

For several years now, I have been deeply interested in the security challenges of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Operational Technology (OT). Living in a region renowned for its manufacturing excellence, many of my clients operate in this domain. This proximity has allowed me to witness firsthand the evolving landscape of ICS/OT security.

When I first started discussing the application of cybersecurity to ICS/OT systems, I quickly realized I was ahead of the curve. At the time, the primary focus for ICS/OT environments was ensuring operational continuity. OT managers were more concerned with uptime, process efficiency, and reliability than the potential risks posed by cyber threats.

However, the landscape has been gradually shifting. Traditionally isolated ICS/OT systems have started interacting more closely with IT environments. This trend accelerated significantly around 2020, when it became common practice to connect ICS/OT systems to the internet for real-time remote support and monitoring.

This convergence of IT and OT domains has brought both opportunities and challenges. On the one hand, connectivity enhances efficiency and reduces response times for troubleshooting. On the other hand, it exposes previously isolated systems to cyber threats that they were not originally designed to handle.

To deepen my understanding, experiment with ICS/OT-specific security solutions, and provide meaningful demonstrations to clients and stakeholders, I realized I needed dedicated environments, part physical, part virtual. These labs serve as controlled spaces to test vulnerabilities, evaluate defensive mechanisms, and simulate real-world attack scenarios.

In this series of posts, I will explore the various approaches to creating ICS/OT labs. From hardware configurations to virtualized environments, and from affordable setups to more advanced scenarios, I aim to provide a practical guide for anyone interested in this field.

docs.title: An ICS lab with VirtuaPlant
docs.text: 26 February 2025

docs.title: An ICS lab with VirtuaPlant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

VirtuaPlant is an Industrial Control Systems (ICS) simulator developed by Jan Seidl in 2015. Unlike most PLC simulators, which only allow reading and writing tags, VirtuaPlant introduces real-world-like control logic, making it a more advanced and interactive learning tool.

By leveraging a game library and a 2D physics engine, VirtuaPlant provides a graphical user interface (GUI) that simulates the physical world behind the control system. This approach helps users visualize industrial processes and understand how control systems interact with real-world mechanics.

Originally, VirtuaPlant included only one scenario, but later, an external contributor (GitHub user prjpet) added an additional scenario, further expanding its capabilities.

The biggest issue with VirtuaPlant today is that it has been stagnant since 2015. Installing it on modern systems is extremely difficult due to outdated OS requirements, dependencies, and libraries, many of which are now deprecated.

To overcome these challenges, I have made several modifications to the project and converted it into a Docker container. This makes installation and deployment much easier on modern systems.

The Dockerfiles required for this setup are available in my GitHub repository. These will serve as the foundation for building our ICS/OT security lab.

docs.title: Installing VirtuaPlant Bottle Filling plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

The first scenario available in VirtuaPlant simulates a basic bottle-filling plant. This scenario includes a graphical Human-Machine Interface (HMI) that allows users to interact with the simulated industrial process.

The simulation and HMI communicate using the Modbus protocol. The simulation acts as a basic PLC, handling both control logic and plant visualization.

Both the simulation and HMI are graphical applications developed in Python 2.7 using the Pygame library. Since they rely on Linux-based systems, both components must be run on Linux machines.

docs.title: Installing the Simulation (PLC) Container
docs.text:
Before installing the scenario, ensure you have two Linux systems with Docker installed. I used the latest Ubuntu LTS version and followed the official Docker installation guide. Once the systems are ready, install the PLC simulation container on the first machine using:

docker run --name plc --rm -d -p 443:6901 -p 502:5020 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-bottle-filling-plc:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest PLC simulation container for the Bottle Filling Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container once it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes ports 443 (for the web interface), and 502 (for Modbus communication with the PLC).
  • Sets a password for VNC access.

After a few moments, you can access the PLC simulation by entering the host system’s IP address in a web browser, using port 443:

Use the username kasm_user and the password set in the Docker command to log in.

Once logged in, you’ll see the simulation environment ready to start:

Press ESC at any time to restart the simulation.

docs.title: Installing the HMI Container
docs.text:
Next, install the HMI container on the second Linux machine:

docker run --name hmi --rm -d -p 443:6901 -e PLC=172.26.104.12 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-bottle-filling-hmi:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest HMI simulation container for the Bottle Filling Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container once stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 443 for web-based interaction.
  • Defines the PLC's IP address (-e PLC=<PLC_IP>) to establish communication.
  • Sets a password for access.

Open the HMI web interface using the second machine’s host IP and port 443, login with kasm_user and the password set during container execution:

Press "Run" to start the plant simulation. If everything is configured correctly, the bottle-filling plant will begin operating.

docs.title: Attacking the Bottle Filling plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese attack intermediate ot-ics

This scenario serves as an introduction to attacking a Modbus-based PLC. The goal is to gradually understand the system’s behavior by monitoring the PLC registers before executing an attack.

docs.title: Reconnaissance phase
docs.text:
Before launching an attack, it is crucial to analyze the plant’s behavior. This involves monitoring the PLC registers to identify active ones and understand how they are utilized.

For this purpose, I developed a small tool that continuously monitors Modbus registers to determine which ones are in use. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

To monitor the PLC behavior for 15 seconds, execute:

./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -t holding -k 15

From our observations, only holding registers are used, specifically registers 1, 2, 3, 4, and 16. Notably, register 16 holds a value of 1, warranting further investigation.

We also identified that these registers store binary information (0 or 1), despite Modbus offering dedicated boolean registers for this purpose.

The system operates in three phases:

  • Initialization: The conveyor moves the first bottle under the nozzle.
  • Filling: The nozzle opens, filling the bottle.
  • Moving: The conveyor moves the next bottle into position.

This cycle repeats indefinitely. During a real-world attack, the adversary would likely lack physical visibility of the system’s operation. However, for this lab, we simplify the analysis.

From the three phases described above, we can observe:

  • Sensors: Used to read the state of the plant. There are two sensors: bottle presence and full bottle.
  • Actuators: Used to alter the state of the plant. There are three actuators: roller and nozzle.

After observing the plant behavior and associated states for a certain period, we can define that:

  • The only registers in use are holding registers.
  • Five holding registers are used.
  • Holding registers store binary information using 0 and 1.
  • Registers 1, 3, and 16 are set when the roller is moving the bottle and the nozzle is closed.
  • Registers 2, 4, and 16 are set when the roller is stopped and the nozzle is filling a bottle.
  • When analyzing a newly started plant, we find that only registers 3 and 16 are set.

From this, we can deduce that:

  • Register 16 (actuator) defines the plant state (on/off).
  • Register 3 (actuator) defines the conveyor state (on/off).
  • Consequently, Register 1 (red sensor) defines whether the bottle is full.
  • Registers 2 and 4 change value together.

They are associated with the nozzle actuator and the green bottle presence sensor, but require further analysis.

docs.title: Attack Phase
docs.text:
An attack on a PLC assumes that register values can be overwritten and that the PLC reacts accordingly. Unlike traditional IT systems, PLCs often rely on external inputs without strict validation, making them susceptible to register manipulation.

In a targeted attack on a PLC, we assume that we can overwrite register values and that the PLC will act accordingly. This might seem paradoxical to those coming from IT: does the PLC act based on overwritten external values (from the attacker) instead of executing its programmed logic?

The answer is that the attacker manipulates the PLC’s memory registers, much like in a buffer overflow attack.

In the previous phase, we observed that only holding registers with values 0 and 1 are used, specifically:

  • Register 1: Red sensor, defines whether the bottle is full.
  • Register 2: Requires verification.
  • Register 3: Actuator, defines the conveyor state (on/off).
  • Register 4: Requires verification.
  • Register 16: Actuator, defines the plant state (on/off).

Now, let’s attempt to force register values by continuously overwriting them. For this purpose, I have developed a small tool that does exactly that: it continuously writes a specific value to one or more Modbus registers of a PLC. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

First let's check register 4:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 4 1

We observe that the nozzle remains permanently open:

We can then complete our analysis:

  • Register 1: Red sensor, defines whether the bottle is full.
  • Register 2: Green sensor, defines whether the bottle is in position.
  • Register 3: Actuator, defines the conveyor state (on/off).
  • Register 4: Actuator, defines the nozzle state (open/closed).
  • Register 16: Actuator, defines the plant state (on/off).

Now, we can plan various attack scenarios by manipulating the actuators.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Plant permanently off
docs.text:
Regardless of sensor states, the plant remains off, even if an operator manually intervenes via HMI.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 16 0

Effect: The production line remains halted.

docs.title: Scenario 2: Nozzle Open and Conveyor Stopped
docs.text:
In this attack, the plant is active, the nozzle remains open, but the conveyor does not operate.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 3 0 -s h 4 1 -s h 16 1

Effect: Water waste and potential flooding of the facility.

In this scenario, the attack script competes with the PLC: the script attempts to stop the motor, while the PLC tries to activate it as soon as the sensor detects a full bottle.

A more advanced version of the attack also manipulates the two sensors:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 1 0 -s h 2 1 -s h 3 0 -s h 4 1 -s h 16 1

The effect is more stable:

If the operator tries to turn off the plant via HMI, the action has no effect.

docs.title: Scenario 3: Conveyor Active and Nozzle Closed
docs.text:
In this attack, the plant is active, the nozzle remains closed, and the conveyor is continuously running:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.12 -p 502 -s h 1 0 -s h 2 0 -s h 3 1 -s h 4 0 -s h 16 1

Effect: The production line produces empty bottles.

Again, if the operator attempts to shut down the plant via HMI, the action has no effect.

docs.title: Installing VirtuaPlant Oil Refinery plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

Originally, VirtuaPlant included only one scenario, but later, an external contributor (GitHub user prjpet) added an additional scenario, further expanding its capabilities.

he simulation and HMI communicate using the Modbus protocol. The simulation acts as a basic PLC, handling both control logic and plant visualization.

Both the simulation and HMI are graphical applications developed in Python 2.7 using the Pygame library. Since they rely on Linux-based systems, both components must be run on Linux machines.

docs.title: Installing the Simulation (PLC) Container
docs.text:
Before installing the scenario, ensure you have two Linux systems with Docker installed. I used the latest Ubuntu LTS version and followed the official Docker installation guide. Once the systems are ready, install the PLC simulation container on the first machine using:

docker run --name plc --rm -d -p 443:6901 -p 502:5020 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-oil-refinery-plc:22

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest PLC simulation container for the Oil Refinery Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container once it is stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes ports 443 (for the web interface), and 502 (for Modbus communication with the PLC).
  • Sets a password for VNC access.

After a few moments, you can access the PLC simulation by entering the host system’s IP address in a web browser, using port 443:

Use the username kasm_user and the password set in the Docker command to log in.

Once logged in, you’ll see the simulation environment ready to start:

Press ESC at any time to restart the simulation.

docs.title: Installing the HMI Container
docs.text:
Next, install the HMI container on the second Linux machine:

docker run --name hmi --rm -d -p 443:6901 -e PLC=172.26.104.22 -e VNC_PW=password dainok/virtuaplant-oil-refinery-hmi:22

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest HMI simulation container for the Oil Refinery Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container once stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 443 for web-based interaction.
  • Defines the PLC's IP address (-e PLC=<PLC_IP>) to establish communication.
  • Sets a password for access.

Open the HMI web interface using the second machine’s host IP and port 443, login with kasm_user and the password set during container execution:

Press "Run" to start the plant simulation. If everything is configured correctly, the oil refinery plant will begin operating.

docs.title: Attacking the Oil Refinery plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced attack ot-ics

We have already explored how to attack the Bottle Filling system. This article follows up on that analysis but in a significantly more complex scenario.

docs.title: Reconnaissance phase
docs.text:
The Bottle Filling system operated automatically. However, this system requires supervision by an operator who interacts with it via an HMI. Specifically, the operator determines when to transition from one processing phase to another.

We will analyze how the PLC registers change while interacting with the HMI.

For this purpose, I developed a small tool that continuously monitors Modbus registers to determine which ones are in use. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

We acknowledge that a real attack would be much more complex, as the attacker does not have visual feedback from the HMI or the system itself.

To continuously monitor the PLC behavior, we execute:

./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -t holding

System Idle: when the system is idle, all registers report a value of 0.

Filling Tank: as soon as the feed pump is activated, register 1 is set to 1. When the crude oil level reaches the sensor, register 1 returns to 0, and register 2 is set to 1.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 1:  Actuator, defines the state of the feed pump (open/closed)
  • Register 2: Sensor, detects if the tank is full (tank level sensor)

Tank drainage: when the discharge valve is opened, register 2 remains unchanged, register 3 is set to 1, and registers 6 and 7 increment.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 3: Actuator, controls the tank discharge valve (open/closed)
  • Register 6: Sensor, requires further investigation
  • Register 7: Sensor, requires further investigation

Water discharge: when the water discharge valve is opened, registers 2 and 3 remain unchanged, register 8 is set to 1, and register 6 increments.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 6: Sensor, measures the amount of discharged water
  • Register 8: Actuator, controls the water discharge valve (open/closed)

Oil discharge: when the oil discharge valve is opened, registers 2, 3, and 8 remain unchanged, register 4 is set to 1, and register 7 increments rapidly.

From this, we deduce:

  • Register 4: Actuator, controls the oil discharge valve (open/closed)
  • Register 7: Sensor, measures the amount of produced oil

docs.title: Attack Phase
docs.text:
Before planning possible attacks, let’s summarize the findings from our reconnaissance:

  • Register 1: Actuator, controls the feed pump (open/closed)
  • Register 2: Sensor, detects if the tank is full (tank level sensor)
  • Register 3: Actuator, controls the tank discharge valve (open/closed)
  • Register 4: Actuator, controls the oil discharge valve (open/closed)
  • Register 6: Sensor, measures the amount of discharged water
  • Register 7: Sensor, measures the amount of produced oil
  • Register 8: Actuator, controls the water discharge valve (open/closed)

Registers 6 and 7 are the only ones with incremental values.

Now, let’s attempt to force register values by continuously overwriting them. For this purpose, I have developed a small tool that continuously writes a specific value to one or more Modbus registers of a PLC. The tool is available in my GitHub repository.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Feed Pump Forced Closed
docs.text:
Regardless of sensor states, the feed pump remains closed, even if an operator manually intervenes via HMI.
