./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 0

Effect: The production line remains halted.

docs.title: Scenario 2: feed pump Open and Tank Level Sensor Disabled
docs.text:
Regardless of the crude oil level in the tank, the pump remains open.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 1 -s h 2 0

Effect: The crude oil overflows from the tank, flooding the facility.

docs.title: Scenario 3: Oil Discharge Valve Forced Closed
docs.text:
The feed pump is forced open, the water discharge valve is forced open, while the oil discharge valve is forced closed.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 1 -s h 3 1 -s h 4 0 -s h 8 1

Effect: All the oil is discharged through the water pipeline, contaminating it.

docs.title: Scenario 4: Altered Product
docs.text:
The feed pump is forced open, the water discharge valve is forced closed, while the oil discharge valve is forced open.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 1 1 -s h 3 1 -s h 4 1 -s h 8 0

Effect: The oil is not properly refined.

docs.title: Scenario 5: Unknown Production Data
docs.text:
The values of the two sensors are overwritten with arbitrary values.

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.22 -p 502 -s h 6 999 -s h 7 111

Effect: It becomes impossible to accurately determine the amount of refined oil. Operators and all processes relying on this data are compromised.

docs.title: An ICS lab with GRFICSv2
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner ot-ics

GRFICSv2 (Graphical Realism Framework for Industrial Control Simulations) is an Industrial Control Systems (ICS) simulator developed by Fortiphyd and released in 2020. Unlike VirtuaPlant, GRFICSv2 integrates an HMI, a PLC, and a simulation environment. The simulation emulates a chemical plant that is controlled and monitored by simulated remote I/O devices via a simple JSON API.

docs.title: Officially Released Components
docs.text:
The following components are distributed as OVA (Open Virtual Appliance) files compatible with VirtualBox:

  • Simulation: The ChemicalPlant VM executes a detailed chemical process simulation. The simulated remote I/O devices interact with the system through a JSON API and are controlled by the PLC VM using the Modbus protocol.
  • PLC: The plc_2 VM is a customized version of OpenPLC (GitHub), relying on an outdated version of the libmodbus library, which contains known buffer overflow vulnerabilities.
  • HMI: The ScadaBR VM hosts an operator interface (HMI) developed with ScadaBR, an open-source SCADA software. This HMI allows operators to monitor process data collected by the PLC and send control commands.
  • pfSense Firewall/Router: The pfSense VM serves as a firewall and router, managing network security and routing between the DMZ and the ICS network.
  • Engineering Workstation (EWS): The Ubuntu 16.04 VM acts as the engineering workstation, equipped with tools for programming OpenPLC and positioned within the ICS network.

docs.title: Network Configuration
docs.text:
GRFICSv2 requires two VirtualBox networks to be configured:

Adapter Name Type Gateway Address vboxnet0 DMZ VirtualBox Host-Only Ethernet Adapter 192.168.90.100/24 vboxnet1 ICS VirtualBox Host-Only Ethernet Adapter 192.168.95.1/24

Each of the five VMs should be assigned to these networks as follows:

VM Adapter Network Address Credentials Simulation 2 ICS 192.168.95.10 simulation/Fortiphyd PLC 1 ICS 192.168.95.2 user/password HMI 1 DMZ 192.168.90.5 scadabr/scadabradmin/admin EWS 1 ICS 192.168.95.5 workstation/password FW 1 DMZ 192.168.90.100 admin/pfsense FW 2 ICS 192.168.95.1 admin/pfsense

docs.title: Limitations & Enhancements
docs.text:
The primary limitation of GRFICSv2 is its dependency on VirtualBox, which restricts the integration of third-party appliances and services. To improve flexibility and deployment, I have converted GRFICSv2 into a Docker-based system, simplifying installation and making it more compatible with modern environments.

While the Docker implementation is not yet flawless, GRFICSv2 remains a valuable tool for gaining hands-on experience with PLC, HMI, and engineering workstation environments.

The necessary Dockerfiles for this setup can be found in my GitHub repository. These files serve as the foundation for building an ICS/OT security lab.

docs.title: Installing the GRFICSv2 Chemical plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate ot-ics

As we have seen, the GRFICSv2 simulator consists of four main components: HMI, PLC, Simulator, and EWS.

In a real-world ICS environment, the HMI, PLC, and Simulator are connected to the field network, where a gateway facilitates communication between the OT network and the field devices. The EWS (Engineering Workstation), on the other hand, is located within the OT network and communicates with the HMI and PLC through the router/gateway.

We can organize these components in a way that best suits our needs. The following instructions describe how to configure all components within the same OT network, similar to what we previously did with VirtuaPlant.

The communication between HMI, PLC, and the simulator uses the Modbus protocol. Unlike real-world systems, the HMI is implemented as a web-based interface. The EWS system, which is typically Windows-based, is represented here by a Linux system equipped with the OpenPLC SDK.

The complete scenario consists of four distinct VMs, although it is possible to run all components on the same Docker host.

docs.title: Installing the Chemical Plant Container
docs.text:
Before setting up the environment, ensure you have two Linux systems with Docker installed. I used the latest Ubuntu LTS version and followed the official Docker installation guide.

Once the systems are ready, install the PLC simulation container on the first machine using:

docker run --name simulation --rm -d -p 80:80 -p 5020:5020 -p 5021:5021 -p 5022:5022 -p 5023:5023 -p 5024:5024 -p 5025:5025 dainok/grficsv2-simulation:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest Chemical Plant simulation container.
  • Automatically removes the container when stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes ports: 80 (for the web interface), 502X (for Modbus communication with the PLC).

After a few moments, you can access the simulator web interface by entering the host system’s IP address in a web browser using port 80.

docs.title: Installing the PLC Container
docs.text:
The PLC is implemented using OpenPLCv2. While a newer version of OpenPLC exists, the differences were too significant, so the only way to ensure compatibility was to retain this outdated version.

Install the PLC container on the second machine using:

docker run --name plc -d -p 502:502 -p 80:8080 -e SIM=172.26.104.33 dainok/grficsv2-plc:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest PLC container for the Chemical Plant.
  • Does not automatically delete the container when stopped (--rm is omitted).
  • Exposes ports: 80 (for the web interface), 502 (for Modbus communication with the simulator).
  • Configures OpenPLC to connect to the simulator at IP address 172.26.104.33.

After a few moments, you can access the PLC web interface using the host system’s IP address in a web browser, on port 80.

docs.title: Installing the HMI Container
docs.text:
Next, install the HMI container on the third Linux machine:

docker run --name hmi --rm -d -p 80:8080 dainok/grficsv2-hmi:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest HMI container for the Chemical Plant.
  • Automatically removes the container once stopped (--rm).
  • Exposes port 80 for web-based interaction.

After a few moments, open the HMI web interface using the host IP and port 80. Log in with:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: admin

docs.title: Configuring the PLC connection in HMI
docs.text:
Navigate to Data Sources and edit the PLC source.

Modify the host address, setting it to the Docker host’s IP where OpenPLC is running.

Save the configuration and return to the main screen. The HMI should now display real-time values from the PLC.

Finally, press the Start button to activate the plant. If everything is configured correctly, the production process will begin.

You should notice an increase in product quantity over time. If there is no change, or if pressure slowly decreases, something is wrong. In that case, restart both the PLC and Simulation containers:

  • Stop both containers.
  • Restart the simulation first.
  • Wait a few seconds, then restart the PLC.

docs.title: Installing the EWS Container
docs.text:
Finally, install the Engineering Workstation (EWS) container on the fourth Linux machine:

docker run --name ews -d -p 443:6901 --privileged --shm-size=512m -e VNC_PW=password dainok/ews:latest

This command:

  • Downloads and runs the latest EWS container for the Chemical Plant.
  • Does not automatically delete the container when stopped (--rm is omitted).
  • Exposes port 443 for web-based access.
  • Sets a password for login.

Open the EWS web interface using the machine’s host IP and port 443, login with kasm_user and the password set during container execution:

The EWS is an Ubuntu Linux 22.04 system with the following pre-installed software:

  • OpenPLC Editor: For developing and modifying PLC programs.
  • Web Browser: For uploading software to OpenPLC.

docs.title: Uploading a PLC Program
docs.text:
In Applications → Development, you will find the OpenPLC Editor application. Inside the Documents folder, the project grficsv2-simplified_te is already available and preloaded onto the PLC.

If needed, you can load the project and generate the program for OpenPLC:

Open a web browser and connect to the PLC, then upload the program by clicking Upload Program:

The program will be uploaded, compiled, and executed in OpenPLC.

Since this is an older OpenPLC version, issues may occur. If you face any problems, try restarting the PLC container.

docs.title: Attacking the Chemical plant
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate ot-ics

Compared to VirtuaPlant, this scenario is more complex and allows us to explore potential attacks on a PLC in greater detail.

docs.title: Reconnaissance Phase
docs.text:
As done previously, we analyze the holding and coil registers:

./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.32 -t holding


./modbus_monitor.py -i 172.26.104.32 -t coil

For coil registers, we observe that only register 0 is set.

docs.title: Attack Phase
docs.text:
Coil registers store binary values, making them ideal for controlling the operational state of the entire plant.

We can modify coil 0 and verify that it stops the plant:

./modbus_write.py -i 172.26.104.32 -s c 0 1

At this point, the HMI will no longer be able to start the plant, as any interaction will be immediately overridden by the attack.

docs.title: Uploading a Malicious Program
docs.text:
Unlike VirtuaPlant, where the PLC was simulated, this scenario features a real PLC, along with its associated Engineering Workstation (EWS). The EWS is typically used to develop, test, and deploy PLC programs.

If an attacker gains access to the EWS, they can analyze the existing program, modify it, and upload a malicious version to the PLC.

In real-world environments, PLCs often have a hardware switch that must be in the correct position to allow software overwrites. However, in every facility I have visited, these switches were always left in "Program Mode", effectively nullifying this security measure.

Let's assume the attacker gains control of the EWS and can upload the grficsv2-simplified_te program.

  • Inside the Function Blocks, there is a function called pressure_control.
  • At the top, we can see all the defined variables, including pressure_sp (setpoint).
  • This variable is initialized to 58981.
  • The attacker modifies it to 65535, causing the pressure to rise uncontrollably.

Once the program is compiled and uploaded to the PLC, the pressure will slowly increase, placing stress on the plant:

Eventually, the pressure reaches a critical point, causing the plant to explode:

You can find the original training videos Fortiphyd ICS Training - GRFICS on their YouTube channel.

docs.title: Industrial network segmentation with VLAN Insertion
Industrial network segmentation with VLAN Insertion
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced media ot-ics palo-alto-networks

In real-world industrial environments, it is common to have all OT/ICS devices configured with IP addresses belonging to a single large network. This setup allows different production lines or plants to potentially communicate without any filtering.

Additionally, user PCs are often part of the same network for various purposes. Unfortunately, these PCs are more susceptible to malware due to inconsistent adherence to corporate policies. A malware infection within an OT/ICS network can easily spread due to weak security defenses.

Our laboratory implements two different plants: the Bottle Filling Plant and the Oil Refinery Plant. In our setup, these two plants should not communicate with each other, even though they reside on the same IP network.

The goal is to segment the OT/ICS network transparently, minimizing disruptions.

Observations after VLAN insertion implementation:

  • No IP address changes required
  • Minimal downtime
  • Increased network visibility
  • Clear separation between IT and OT resources
  • Ability to apply customized policies to different zones
  • Capability for deep packet inspection on a per-zone basis
  • Faster identification and isolation of potential issues
  • Scalability up or down as needed

docs.title: Grouping OT/ICS Devices Without Reconfiguration
docs.text:
Our laboratory includes the following devices:

Plant Role Address VLAN Bottle Filling Plant HMI 172.26.104.11/24 104 Bottle Filling Plant PLC 172.26.104.12/24 104 Oil Refinery Plant HMI 172.26.104.21/24 104 Oil Refinery Plant PLC 172.26.104.22/24 104

To segment the network transparently, we will deploy Palo Alto Networks firewalls configured with VLAN Insertion. This feature groups devices into specific VLANs and enforces communication policies between them.

After segmentation, the devices will be organized into two groups, each containing all necessary components for its respective plant:

Plant Role Address Group (VLAN) Bottle Filling Plant HMI 172.26.104.11/24 102 Bottle Filling Plant PLC 172.26.104.12/24 102 Oil Refinery Plant HMI 172.26.104.21/24 103 Oil Refinery Plant PLC 172.26.104.22/24 103

While it is technically possible to separate HMI and PLC devices into different groups with the firewall controlling their communication, this approach may not be feasible in a real-world setting, as OT managers typically prefer to keep HMI and PLC units in the same physical location without additional security layers in between.

docs.title: Switch Configuration
docs.text:
Currently, all ICS/OT devices reside in VLAN 104. This VLAN will be retained for routing purposes while the devices are moved to their final VLANs without changing their IP addresses.

We create the necessary VLANs on the switch:

  • VLAN 102: LAB_SEC_OT_L2_1
  • VLAN 103: LAB_SEC_OT_L2_2

Additional requirements:

  • Configure a loop prevention algorithm on the switches.
  • Ensure the firewall is connected via a trunk port carrying VLANs 102 and 103.

Once all ICS/OT devices have been migrated and connectivity verified, VLAN 104 can be removed.

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text: We now enable VLAN Insertion on the firewall.

docs.title: Step 1: Create security zones
docs.text:
Navigate to Network → Zones → Add and create the following zones:

  • LAB_SEC_OT_L2_1 (Layer 2)
  • LAB_SEC_OT_L2_2 (Layer 2)

docs.title: Step 2: Create subinterfaces
docs.text:
Each ICS/OT group is assigned a subinterface with:

  • The correct VLAN tag
  • The appropriate security zone

Navigate to Network → Interfaces → Add and create the subinterfaces.

docs.title: Step 3: create VLAN interface
docs.text: Navigate to Network → Interfaces → VLAN → Add and create a VLAN interface.

docs.title: Step 4: Create VLAN Mapping
docs.text:
Navigate to: Network → VLANs → Add and associate the VLAN interface and subinterfaces.

This configuration maps network 172.24.106.0/24 onto VLANs 102 and 103, enforcing security policies accordingly.

Once all configurations are applied, policy rules committed, and devices moved to the correct VLANs, the segmentation process is complete.

docs.title: Policy considerations
docs.text:
Policies uses L2 or L3 zones as following:

  • Inter-VLAN communication: Source/destination is the Layer 3 zone assigned to the VLAN interface.
  • Intra-VLAN communication: Source/destination is the Layer 2 zone assigned to the subinterfaces.

docs.title: Virtual firewall considerations
docs.text:
If you are using a virtual device, keep in mind that the firewall behaves like a switch, manipulating incoming and outgoing frames. Therefore, the virtual network must be configured to allow:

  • Promiscuous mode: to receive frames not specifically addressed to the firewall’s network interface.
  • Forged transmit: to forward (transmit) frames originating from other devices.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: • Applying VLAN Insertion in ICS/SCADA

docs.title: Industrial network segmentation with Private VLANs
Industrial network segmentation with Private VLANs
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced cisco ot-ics

We have explored how to transparently segment an OT/ICS network into groups using VLAN Insertion from Palo Alto Networks. The flexibility of this feature has allowed us to divide our lab environments into groups without the need to reconfigure IP addresses. Additionally, this solution enables us to define policies to allow specific communications between groups when necessary.

Since the early 2000s, a standard feature has been available to achieve a similar outcome: Private VLAN, also known as port isolation, which allows devices to be segmented into port groups.

docs.title: Private VLAN
docs.text:
Private VLANs are defined in RFC5517 as VLAN-based "forced forwarding." In other words, frame forwarding is determined at the VLAN level.

Two types of VLANs are defined:

  • Primary VLAN: This VLAN handles traffic common to all groups.
  • Secondary VLAN: This VLAN is associated with port groups and can be either Isolated or Community. In an Isolated VLAN, each port can communicate only with the primary VLAN. In a Community VLAN, each port can communicate with the primary VLAN and all ports within the same Community VLAN.

There are three types of ports:

  • Promiscuous Access Port (P-Port): This port can communicate with any other port, regardless of VLAN assignment.
  • Host Isolated Access Port (I-Port): This port is associated with an Isolated VLAN and can only communicate with P-Ports.
  • Host Community Access Port (C-Port): This port is associated with a Community VLAN and can communicate with P-Ports and all other C-Ports within the same VLAN

In a real-world environment, multiple interconnected switches would likely be present. Additionally, the network gateway is often a firewall that may not be VLAN-aware.

From an operational standpoint, it is highly recommended to use switches of the same model and automate the PVLAN configuration to minimize human error.

docs.title: Broadcast traffic
docs.text:
A switch configured with PVLAN must handle broadcast traffic uniquely. For instance, consider ARP requests: a single request must be propagated across ports, even those within different secondary VLANs.

  • Broadcast traffic from a promiscuous port is forwarded to all ports within the primary VLAN, including those in isolated and community VLANs.
  • Broadcast traffic from an isolated port is forwarded only to promiscuous ports in the primary VLAN associated with the isolated port.
  • Broadcast traffic from community ports is forwarded to all ports within the same community and all associated promiscuous ports. It is not forwarded to other communities within the primary VLAN or to isolated ports.

docs.title: PVLAN trunks
docs.text:
In a distributed network, inter-switch links (ISL) configured as trunks are necessary. Trunking allows multiple VLANs to be transported and is essential for secondary PVLANs (Community and Isolated VLANs).

  • Regular PVLAN Trunk: When both switches support PVLAN, regular trunks can be used. Each switch recognizes and properly handles PVLANs.
  • Promiscuous PVLAN Trunk: Used when connecting a device that must communicate with all ports, such as a firewall or router. Here, the switch replaces the secondary PVLAN ID with the primary PVLAN ID when sending a frame.
  • Isolated PVLAN Trunk: Used when the connected device handles only isolated ports. The switch replaces the primary PVLAN ID with the isolated secondary PVLAN ID when sending a frame.

For isolated PVLAN trunks, the switch is responsible for isolating ports within the isolated PVLAN, which can be enforced using the switchport protected command.

docs.title: Segregating a plant with PVLAN
docs.text:
Compared to VLAN Insertion, Private VLANs offer less flexibility: groups can either communicate fully or not at all. Selectively allowing or blocking specific communications is not possible. Therefore, before deploying PVLANs in OT/ICS environments, it is crucial to identify required communications.

To transparently segment our ICS/OT devices, we configured them into separate Community VLANs:

Plant Role Address VLAN Bottle Filling Plant HMI 172.26.104.11/24 110 Bottle Filling Plant PLC 172.26.104.12/24 110 Oil Refinery Plant HMI 172.26.104.21/24 110 Oil Refinery Plant PLC 172.26.104.22/24 110

docs.title: Switch configuration
docs.text:
All ICS/OT devices reside in VLAN 110, which will be maintained for routing and promiscuous ports. Devices will be moved to the final VLAN without changing their IP addressing.

First, configure the secondary Community VLANs:

vlan 111
  name LAB_SEC_OT_SEC_1
  private-vlan community
vlan 112
  name LAB_SEC_OT_SEC_2
  private-vlan community

Next, define the primary VLAN associated with the secondary VLANs:

vlan 110
  name LAB_SEC_OT_L3
  private-vlan primary
  private-vlan association 111-112

docs.title: Host access ports (C-Port and I-Port)
docs.text:
We use a host port when an endpoint device is directly connected to the access port of the switch. In private VLANs, host ports are part of the secondary VLANs, which can be either community VLANs or isolated VLANs. Configuring a private VLAN host port involves two steps. First, the port is defined as a private VLAN host port, and then a host association is configured between the primary and secondary VLANs.

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 switchport private-vlan host-association 110 111
 switchport mode private-vlan host

This configuration places the port in primary VLAN 110 and secondary VLAN 111 (Community), making it a C-Port.

docs.title: Promiscuous access ports (P-Port)
docs.text:
We use a promiscuous port when a device is directly connected to the access port of the switch. This device, typically a gateway, needs to communicate with all host ports, both community and isolated. In a private VLAN domain, promiscuous ports are part of the primary VLAN. Configuring a promiscuous port involves two steps. First, the port is defined as a promiscuous port, and then the mapping between the secondary VLAN and the primary VLAN is configured.

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport private-vlan mapping 110 111-112
 switchport mode private-vlan promiscuous

docs.title: Promiscuous Trunk Port
docs.text:
We use a Promiscuous Trunk Port when a device that does not support PVLAN, typically a gateway, is directly connected to a trunk port of the switch. In a private VLAN domain, promiscuous trunk ports are part of the primary VLAN. Promiscuous trunk ports can carry multiple primary VLANs, and multiple secondary VLANs under a given primary VLAN can be mapped to a promiscuous trunk port

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport private-vlan trunk allowed vlan 102-104,110
 switchport private-vlan mapping 110 111-112
 switchport mode private-vlan trunk promiscuous

In this case, we have configured a trunk to the gateway. VLANs 102, 103, and 104 are regular VLANs. VLANs 111 and 112 are secondary PVLANs associated with the primary VLAN 110. VLAN 110 is allowed on the trunk because, in a promiscuous trunk port, traffic destined for a secondary VLAN is mapped using the tag of the associated primary VLAN.

docs.title: Isolated Trunk Port
docs.text:
This is not our case, but if we need to configure a trunk port connected to a device that does not support PVLAN and manages devices on an isolated VLAN, a different syntax must be used:

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 switchport private-vlan trunk allowed vlan 102-104,110
 switchport private-vlan association 110 113
 switchport mode private-vlan trunk secondary

Upstream devices must be aware that VLAN 113 is isolated to properly manage broadcast and unicast traffic.

By implementing PVLANs with uniform switch models and using promiscuous PVLAN trunks only for gateways, network complexity can be minimized while ensuring proper segmentation of OT/ICS environments.

docs.title: Introducing Cortex XSOAR
docs.text: 12 August 2024

docs.title: Introducing Cortex XSOAR
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cortex-xsoar palo-alto-networks

Cortex XSOAR is a comprehensive orchestration and automation system that unifies all the components of your security infrastructure. It seamlessly integrates with your third-party security and incident management vendors, allowing you to trigger events that automatically become incidents within Cortex XSOAR.

Once these incidents are created, Cortex XSOAR enables you to run playbooks that enrich the incidents with valuable information from other connected products. This enriched data helps you build a complete picture of the situation, ensuring that nothing is overlooked.

Automation and rules can be applied to these incidents, determining whether they require further investigation or can be safely closed. This intelligent filtering allows your security analysts to focus on the minority of incidents that genuinely need attention, significantly enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of your security operations.

This learning path follows the Cortex XSOAR Customer Success Engineering Training course and provides details on creating a lab and tackling each lesson.

docs.title: Incident Lifecycle
docs.text:
This learning path follows the incident lifecycle:

The lifecycle begins with strategic planning. During this phase, you assess your organization’s security needs, define objectives, and determine the necessary integrations and workflows that Cortex XSOAR will manage.

This phase allows us to design the workflow for incident management. While it’s true that the planning phase typically comes first, my perspective is different. Before designing a workflow, we need to understand the capabilities of the product. Therefore, the lesson dedicated to planning is postponed until the end: first, we learn how the product works and what its features are, and then, with this knowledge, we approach the design phase.

docs.title: Setting Up Your Cortex XSOAR Lab Environment
docs.text: 12 August 2024

docs.title: Setting Up Your Cortex XSOAR Lab Environment
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cortex-xsoar palo-alto-networks

In this post, we’ll guide you through setting up a lab environment for experimenting with Palo Alto Networks' Cortex XSOAR. This tutorial aligns with the content from the video XSOAR Engineer Training - Part 2: Incident Types & Fields.

docs.title: Download and Install Cortex XSOAR
docs.text:
Start by downloading the trial version of XSOAR. You'll receive a file, approximately 1GB in size, named something like demistoserver-6.12-857430.sh. This file needs to be copied to a Linux system. I’m using Ubuntu Linux 22.04 for this setup.

Run the installation with the root user:

bash /tmp/demistoserver-6.12-857430.sh

The installation process is straightforward and will prompt you to set credentials for accessing XSOAR via the web interface.

Once the installation is complete, you can access XSOAR via the web using the credentials you set up. You’ll see a pop-up notifying you that the license is missing:

The Community Edition provides a 30-day full-featured license, giving you a complete experience to explore Cortex XSOAR’s capabilities. Simply press Cancel and continue with the setup.

docs.title: Update Installed Content Packs
docs.text: Navigate to Marketplace → Installed Content Packs. Select all content packs that need updating and click Update. You might receive a warning that updates could introduce breaking changes. Since this is a new installation, proceed with the updates.

docs.title: Install the Sample Event Generator Plugin
docs.text:
We need a plugin to generate some sample events. While normally events would be collected from a SIEM, we’ll use a simpler alternative for our lab setup.

Go to Marketplace → Browse and search for JSON Sample Incident Generator. Install the JSON Sample Incident Generator package, which includes an integration. This integration allows you to generate custom events within XSOAR.

Next, navigate to Settings → Integrations → Sample Incident Generator → Add Instance and configure the instance as follows:

  • Name: JSONSampleIncidentGenerator_url_events
  • Do not fetch
  • The raw JSON string to use as the sample data: Paste the content from this GitHub repository.

Click Test, then Save & Exit.

If you don’t see the integration, try refreshing your browser.

docs.title: Configuring Incident Classification in Cortex XSOAR
docs.text: 19 August 2024

docs.title: Configuring Incident Classification in Cortex XSOAR
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner cortex-xsoar palo-alto-networks

In this post, we’ll set up the classification feature, which allows us to transform events into specific incident types. This guide expands on the content covered in the videos XSOAR Engineer Training - Part 2: Incident Types & Fields and XSOAR Engineer Training - Part 3: Classification and Mapping.

docs.title: Set Up Incident Classifier
docs.text:
Navigate to Settings → Objects Setup → Classification & Mapping → New Incident Classifier. At the top, select the JSONSampleIncidentGenerator_url_events instance we created in the previous post. This allows us to work with sample events.

On the right, you’ll see a list of existing incident types in XSOAR:

There’s already a PAN-OS URL Log Incident type, but since our events don’t originate from PAN-OS, we’ll create a new incident type specific to the data we’re analyzing.

Go to Settings → Objects Setup → Incidents → Types and select PAN-OS URL Log Incident. Use the Detach button to modify the object and explore its structure. After making your changes, click Reattach to restore the original state.

docs.title: Create a New Incident Type
docs.text:
Create a new incident type with the following settings:

  • Name: URL Alerts
  • Run playbook automatically: Set (best practice)
  • Post process using: Unset (script executed before closing the incident)

Now, define the fields that need to be populated. Go to Indicators Extraction Rules and check if a field for URL categories exists. If not, proceed to save and exit.

docs.title: Create Custom Fields
docs.text:
Go to Settings → Objects Setup → Incidents → Incidents Fields and create two new custom fields:

  • URL Category: Short text
  • Suspicious URL: Short text

We chose not to use the URL type because it would make the field clickable, which is not desirable for suspicious URLs: they should be treated as plain text.

docs.title: Define Indicator Extraction Rules
docs.text:
Return to Settings → Objects Setup → Incidents → Types → URL Alerts → Edit → Indicators Extraction Rules. These rules define how indicators are extracted from each event and populate the incident. Indicator extraction can be:

  • Inline: Playbooks execute after indicator extraction is complete (blocking).
  • Out of Band: Indicator extraction and playbook execution run in parallel (non-blocking).
  • None: No indicator extraction.

Best practices suggest using None when possible, and Inline when the playbook depends on the indicators.

Add the following fields:

  • Suspicious URL: Add URL and Domain
  • Source IP: Add IP
  • Source Username: Add Email

This ensures that the three fields generate associated indicators: URL, Domain, IP, and Email.

docs.title: Finalize the Classifier
docs.text:
Go back to Settings → Objects Setup → Classification & Mapping → New Incident Classifier and select the JSONSampleIncidentGenerator_url_events instance.

When selecting a sample event in the type field, you’ll see options like url allowed and url blocked. Drag these two values to the right column under the URL Alerts incident type. This categorizes all url allowed and url blocked incidents as URL Alerts.

At the bottom, you can choose how to classify events that don’t fall into these categories. In our case, it’s unnecessary, but we’ll select URL Alerts anyway.

Save the classifier as URLAlertClassifier.

docs.title: Configure the Sample Incident Generator
docs.text:
Go to Settings → Integrations → Sample Incident Generator → ⚙️ and configure:

  • Fetches incidents
  • Classifier: URLAlertClassifier
  • Incidents Fetch Interval: 00:01 (events from the JSON will be generated every minute)

After a few minutes, stop the fetching (Do not fetch) and go to Incidents:

You’ll notice that the events are categorized as URL Alerts, but the indicators aren’t extracted correctly.

Delete all incidents and move on to the next step.

docs.title: Introduction to Palo Alto firewall automation
Introduction to Palo Alto firewall automation
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner fundamentals palo-alto-networks

The automation of firewalls is still a relatively under-discussed topic compared to the automation of network devices. This is likely due to complexity: firewall policies tend to be a long list of rules, created by different people, for different (application) purposes, and aggregated together. The order of these rules is often crucial and has direct performance impacts. Creating a model to describe them is far from simple. While other tasks can be automated, in my experience, they are of relatively minor importance.

Let’s take a step back and identify the activities a security engineer performs throughout the lifecycle of a firewall:

  • Provisioning: These are one-time or occasional tasks that configure the foundation of a firewall (IP addressing, routing, VLANs, DNS, NTP, licenses, etc.).
  • Rules: These tasks involve adding, modifying, or deleting rules in response to changes in the services passing through one or more firewalls.
  • Maintenance: These tasks allow us to monitor the status of a firewall or perform troubleshooting in case of anomalies or unexpected behaviors.

In the context of Palo Alto Networks firewalls, we can interact with them using the following methods:

  • Web User Interface
  • Command Line Interface (CLI) via SSH
  • XML API
  • External Dynamic Lists
  • SDKs (Python, PHP)
  • Frameworks (Ansible, Terraform)
  • Direct configuration changes

In complex environments, Panorama is often used to centrally manage all firewalls. Panorama can be interacted with through all the same methods described for individual firewalls.

Except for the Web User Interface, all other interfaces enable the creation of automations and integrations.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via CLI
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via CLI
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner palo-alto-networks

The first method we will discuss is called screen scraping, a topic already covered in the past. We use the screen scraping approach when automating devices that are designed to be managed via CLI, without APIs that allow us to cover all the scenarios we are interested in. Screen scraping is commonly used when dealing with network devices.

As we will see later, Palo Alto Networks firewalls offer XML-based APIs that make the screen scraping approach less attractive unless for very specific cases.

For Palo Alto Networks firewalls, screen scraping can be useful for performing specific actions related to monitoring and troubleshooting.

Let’s look at a couple of examples.

The first example is a request from a client several years ago. The client wanted to implement a device locator that would allow them to identify the location of a device based on its MAC address or IP address. It was necessary to gather the MAC address table and the ARP table from all devices. For the ARP table, we needed to retrieve the output of the show arp all command and convert it into machine-readable format (parsing): this is screen scraping.

We will use two tools:

  • netmiko to connect to the devices, execute the command, and collect the output.
  • NTC Templates to transform the output into JSON format.

The sample script is quite simple:

  • It defines the necessary data to connect to the device.
  • It defines the command to execute.
  • It connects to the device, sends the command, and uses NTC Templates to structure the output.
device = {
    "device_type": "paloalto_panos",
    "ip": "172.25.10.4",
    "username": "admin",
    "password": getpass(),
    "fast_cli": False,
}
net_connect = ConnectHandler(**device)
result = net_connect.send_command("show arp all", use_textfsm=True)

Netmiko offers a wide range of connectors for managing different devices. The device must specify a type using the vendor and operating system. The full list is available in the GitHub source. In our case, we selected paloalto_panos.

Generally, it is not necessary to specify additional options, but it seems that there is still a bug regarding prompt recognition. When using the screen scraping approach, it is normal to encounter anomalies caused by interpreting the output.

Finally, we use NTC Templates to transform the text into JSON format. NTC Templates can be used by installing the Python package:

pip install ntc-templates

Or by using a local repository and setting the NET_TEXTFSM environment variable:

export NET_TEXTFSM=/Users/dainese/src/ntc-templates/ntc_templates/templates

The output of the script will be as follows:

In this specific case, the output was added to a database, which, through a web interface, allowed the user to know the location of a specific MAC address.

The script is available on GitHub.

docs.title: Configuration command with Netmiko
docs.text:
We can use Netmiko for some basic configurations. For example, we can remove default configurations or add basic settings (NTP, DNS, etc.). Netmiko may offer a simpler solution to implement and maintain compared to full Python scripts.

Let's look at a simple script to delete the default configuration:

commands = [
    'delete rulebase security rules "rule1"',
    "delete network virtual-wire default-vwire",
    "delete zone trust network virtual-wire",
    "delete zone untrust network virtual-wire",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/1 virtual-wire",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/2 virtual-wire",
    "delete zone trust",
    "delete zone untrust",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/1",
    "delete network interface ethernet ethernet1/2",
    "commit",
]
net_connect = ConnectHandler(**device)
net_connect.send_config_set(commands)
net_connect.disconnect()

The script is available on GitHub.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via XML API
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via XML API
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced palo-alto-networks

Palo Alto Networks firewalls provide XML-based APIs for interacting with the system. To use the API, the first step is to generate an API key that will authenticate our requests:

curl -k -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" -X POST https://firewall/api/?type=keygen -d 'user=admin&password=password'

Alternatively, a simple Python script can be used:

headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
}
data = {
    "user": "admin",
    "password": getpass(),
}
url = "https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=keygen"
req = requests.post(url, headers=headers, data=data, verify=False)

At this point, we can use the XML API to perform any operation typically executed via the web interface or CLI. The token must be passed as a GET parameter in every API request. Documentation is available directly on the firewall at: https://172.25.10.4/php/rest/browse.php

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Operational Commands via XML API
docs.text:
Let’s revisit the example from the previous post and retrieve the ARP table. Documentation provides the XML call to execute: https://172.25.10.4/php/rest/browse.php/op::show::arp

The script is straightforward:

headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
}
url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=op&cmd=<show><arp><entry name = 'all'/></arp></show>&key="
url = url + getpass()
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
req.raise_for_status()

The output is the ARP table in XML format:

<response status="success"><result>
  <dp>dp0</dp>
  <timeout>1800</timeout>
  <total>13</total>
  <entries>
    <entry>
      <interface>ethernet1/1.581</interface>
      <ip>172.25.81.254</ip>
      <mac>fc:10:1a:ce:e3:12</mac>
      <port>ethernet1/1</port>
      <status>  c  </status>
      <ttl>916</ttl>
    </entry>
    <entry>
      <interface>ethernet1/1.100</interface>
      <ip>172.26.100.11</ip>
      <mac>00:50:56:9d:4b:0b</mac>
      <port>ethernet1/1</port>
      <status>  c  </status>
      <ttl>877</ttl>
    </entry>

XML is not the most Python-friendly format. The official documentation warns about various risks:

However, we can treat the XML output from the firewall as trusted and proceed using the ElementTree library.

Compared to JSON, navigating XML requires more experience. The example below shows how to extract data from the XML response returned by the firewall:

root = ET.fromstring(req.text)
for entry in root.iterfind(".//result/entries/"):
    interface = entry.find('interface').text
    ip = entry.find('ip').text
    mac = entry.find('mac').text
    print(f"{interface},{ip},{mac}")

The script output is similar to the following:

ethernet1/1.581,172.25.81.254,fc:10:1a:ce:e3:12
ethernet1/1.100,172.26.100.11,00:50:56:9d:4b:0b
ethernet1/1.101,172.26.101.11,00:50:56:9d:1e:d1
vlan.104,172.26.104.11,00:50:56:9d:fb:39
vlan.104,172.26.104.12,00:50:56:9d:e3:96
vlan.104,172.26.104.21,00:50:56:9d:90:e2
vlan.104,172.26.104.22,00:50:56:9d:8a:13
vlan.104,172.26.104.31,00:50:56:9d:d6:b7
vlan.104,172.26.104.32,00:50:56:9d:a3:60
vlan.104,172.26.104.33,00:50:56:9d:1c:ea
vlan.104,172.26.104.34,00:50:56:9d:cd:11
vlan.104,172.26.104.41,00:50:56:9d:8f:7e
vlan.104,172.26.104.42,00:50:56:9d:47:26

Referencing the documentation, we also explore the show interface command:

The payload to retrieve all interfaces is as follows:

<show><interface>all</interface></show>

Note the syntax difference compared to the show arp command.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via XML API
docs.text:
Palo Alto Networks firewalls can be configured via either XML API or REST API. Documentation is available directly on the firewall: https://172.25.10.4/php/rest/browse.php/config

As an example, let’s configure Google's two DNS servers on the firewall. The documentation is somewhat limited:

Expanding our research, we find working examples to guide script creation:

# xpath = "/config/shared/address/entry" # Shared (Panorama)
xpath = "/config/devices/entry[@name='localhost.localdomain']/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address/entry"

# Create elements
for name, ip in addresses.items():
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=config&action=set&xpath={xpath}"
    url = url + f"[@name='{name}']&element=<ip-netmask>{ip}</ip-netmask>"
    url = url + f"&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()

Key points:

  • The URL must include the path specifying whether the object is created under shared or within vsys1.
  • The payload is sent via GET along with the required parameters: attributes are marked with @, and the XML content is passed in the element variable.
  • The token is provided via the key parameter.
  • In case of malformed payloads or attributes, the HTTP status is always 200; the error is contained in the response body:
<response status="error" code="13"><msg><line>set failed, may need to override template object first</line></msg></response>

Similarly, we can retrieve configured objects:

xpaths = [
    "/config/shared/address/entry", # Shared (Panorama)
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address", # VSYS
]
for xpath in xpaths:
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=config&action=get&xpath={xpath}&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()
    root = ET.fromstring(req.text)
    for entry in root.iterfind(find_path):
        name = entry.attrib["name"]
        address = entry.find("ip-netmask").text
        print(f"{name},{address}")

Note that the paths for "shared" and "vsys" differ from those used during object creation.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Commit via XML API
docs.text:
After modifying the firewall configuration, a commit operation is required. This consists of:

  • Executing the commit
  • Retrieving the job ID
  • Waiting for the job to complete
  • Verifying the job result

We use the XML API to automate the entire process. Note that REST APIs are currently not supported for this operation:

url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=commit&cmd=<commit></commit>&key={token}"
req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
req.raise_for_status()

The job ID is included in the response

job = root.find("./result/job")
job_id = None
if job is not None:
    # msg = root.find("./result/msg")
    job_id = job.text
else:
    msg = root.find("./msg")

We then wait for the job to complete:

while progress < 100:
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/api/?type=op&cmd=<show><jobs><id>{job_id}</id></jobs></show>&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()
    root = ET.fromstring(req.text)
    result_el = root.find("./result/job/result")
    if result_el is not None:
        result = result_el.text
    progress = int(root.find("./result/job/progress").text)
    print(f"Job ID {job_id}: {progress}%")
    time.sleep(5)

The final result should be OK.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via XML API
docs.text:
Let’s now see how to delete the default configuration using the XML API. As a reminder, the documentation is hosted locally on the firewall: https://172.24.1.34/php/rest/browse.php

As previously noted, documentation is minimal:

Further searches won’t help much, as the task is quite specific. Before scripting, we must better understand the XML-based API structure.

Let’s export and analyze the firewall configuration:

      <vsys>
        <entry name="vsys1">
          <application/>
          <application-group/>
          <zone>
            <entry name="trust">
              <network>
                <virtual-wire>
                  <member>ethernet1/1</member>
                </virtual-wire>
              </network>
            </entry>
            <entry name="untrust">
              <network>
                <virtual-wire>
                  <member>ethernet1/2</member>
                </virtual-wire>
              </network>
            </entry>
          </zone>

We see that XML represents a hierarchical structure. In this example, vsys contains child elements like application, application-group, and zone. zone in turn contains two child elements representing the security zones. In an XML document, elements can be referenced using XPath. For specifics, refer to the official Palo Alto Networks documentation.

Two important concepts to understand:

  • Attributes: Defined within the element as parameters. For example, vsys/entry includes an attribute name=vsys1. Attributes are referenced using the @ symbol.
  • Values: These are the text content of elements. For example, the member element in the first zone has the value ethernet1/1.

We must define the full paths of the elements to delete. By analyzing the configuration, we can extract the complete list:

xpaths = [
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='rule1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/virtual-wire/entry[@name='default-vwire']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='trust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='untrust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/2']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/2']",
]

Unlike the CLI method, we notice two operations are needed for the import path. Interfaces must be removed from the import section before deletion.

Lastly, when selecting the devices/entry path, we do not explicitly specify localhost.localdomain. Since our environment contains only one entry, this is acceptable due to the uniqueness of the element.

The complete script is as follows:

# Defining paths
xpaths = [
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='rule1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/virtual-wire/entry[@name='default-vwire']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='trust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='untrust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/2']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/2']",
]
# Deleting objects
for xpath in xpaths:
    url = f"https://172.24.1.34/api/?type=config&action=delete&xpath={xpath}&key={token}"
    req = requests.get(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    # req.raise_for_status()

Note that for XML API calls, the HTTP status code will always be 200. The actual result is contained in the response payload. If successful, the response will be:

<response status="success" code="20"><msg>command succeeded</msg></response>

If the element does not exist:

<response status="success" code="7"><msg>Object doesn't exist</msg></response>

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Finding the Correct Command
docs.text:
As we've seen, the XML API documentation is not very comprehensive. One recurring issue is identifying the correct syntax to execute a command. There is a very simple method to convert a CLI command to its XML equivalent. Let’s see how to do this with the command used to display the ARP table:

We used the following commands:

  • debug cli on: enables translation of each CLI command into its XML equivalent.
  • set cli op-command-xml-output on: allows viewing the output of operational commands in XML format.

There is also a third command:

  • set cli config-output-format xml: this allows viewing the configuration in XML format instead of the traditional set format.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via REST API
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via REST API
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced palo-alto-networks

Palo Alto Networks firewalls were originally designed around XML APIs. JSON-based REST APIs were introduced later and, as a result, the implementation is currently incomplete and, as we’ll see, prone to certain errors. As noted earlier, the API documentation is available directly on the firewall: https://172.25.10.4/restapi-doc

My recommendation is to use the REST API only for specific, well-tested tasks. In all other cases, it is preferable to rely on the XML API.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via REST API
docs.text:
Currently, REST APIs can only be used for configuration tasks. All other operations, including commit, must still be performed using the XML API.

Let’s take the same example from the previous section and create Google’s two DNS servers on the firewall. While REST API documentation is more comprehensive, it’s sometimes incomplete and not always easy to interpret:

If we attempt to use the API without carefully reading the documentation, we receive the following error:

{"code":3,"message":"Missing Query Parameter: name","details":[{"@type":"CauseInfo","causes":[{"code":7,"module":"pan_api","description":"Missing Query Parameter: name"}]}]}

Here is a working example:

# Create elements
for name, ip in addresses.items():
    url = f"https://172.25.10.4/restapi/v10.2/Objects/Addresses?name={name}&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1"
    data = {
        "entry": {
            "@name": name,
            "ip-netmask": ip,
        },
    }
    req = requests.post(url, json=data, headers=headers, verify=False)
    req.raise_for_status()

The documentation lists the query parameters, but examples often omit them. In particular:

  • The URL must include both the name and location parameters. If the location is vsys, the vsys name must also be specified.
  • The payload is sent via a POST request along with the required parameters; its structure is similar to the XML example from earlier.
  • The token is passed in the X-PAN-KEY header.
  • If the payload or parameters are incorrect, the HTTP status code is 400.

We also note a violation of the principle of minimization: the name parameter is redundantly used in both the URL and the request body.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via REST API
docs.text:
Let’s now remove the default configuration using the REST API. The script is relatively simple, but we first need to identify the appropriate API endpoints. The documentation is available locally on the firewall: https://172.24.1.34/restapi-doc/

The APIs to be called using the DELETE method are as follows:

urls = [
    f"{base_url}/Policies/SecurityRules?name=rule1&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/VirtualWires?name=default-vwire",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=trust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=untrust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/1", # Validation error
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/2", # Validation error
]

Finding the correct API for zone deletion took some time, as it is not documented. The last two API calls generate an error that does not occur in the web interface:

{"code":9,"message":"Reference Not Zero","details":[{"@type":"CauseInfo","causes":[{"code":10,"module":"panui_mgmt","description":"Reference Not Zero: ethernet1\/1 cannot be deleted because of references from:. import -> network -> interface. import -> network -> interface. import -> network -> interface. import -> network -> interface."}]}]}

As a result, the script lacks part of the logic compared to what is done via CLI or the web interface. This happens because REST APIs are effectively a wrapper over the XML API, and this layer still contains limitations and bugs. The final script remains simple nonetheless

# Defining API
base_url = "https://172.24.1.34/restapi/v10.2"
urls = [
    f"{base_url}/Policies/SecurityRules?name=rule1&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/VirtualWires?name=default-vwire",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=trust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    f"{base_url}/Network/Zones?name=untrust&location=vsys&vsys=vsys1",
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/1", # Validation error
    # f"{base_url}/Network/EthernetInterfaces?name=ethernet1/2", # Validation error
]
# Deleting objects
for url in urls:
    req = requests.delete(url, headers=headers, verify=False)
    # req.raise_for_status()

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN-OS SDK
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN-OS SDK
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced palo-alto-networks

In previous posts, we explored how to automate certain operations on Palo Alto Networks firewalls using XML API and REST API directly. According to the official documentation, there are ready-to-use libraries available for several programming languages (PHP, Go, Python).

Personally, I believe Python is the most suitable language for writing automations and integrations. For this reason, we will focus on the Python SDKs. There are two libraries available:

  • pan-python: developed and maintained personally by Kevin Steves. This library allows low-level operations on PAN-OS systems.
  • pan-os-python: officially developed and maintained by Palo Alto Networks, it enables high-level interaction with firewalls, similar to the CLI or Web interface. This library depends on specific versions of pan-python.

The pan-os-python library is officially maintained by Palo Alto Networks. It depends on the pan-python library but is not compatible with its latest version. pan-os-python allows interaction with firewalls and Panorama similarly to the Web interface.

The documentation is available online, and the relationships between APIs are described through diagrams.

On some systems, you may encounter the following error:

from distutils.version import LooseVersion # Used by PanOSVersion class ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'distutils'

In this case, you need to install a specific version of setuptools:

pip install setuptools>=75.1.0

The library organises various methods into the following classes:

  • base
  • device
  • errors
  • firewall
  • ha
  • network
  • objects
  • panorama
  • plugins
  • policies
  • predefined
  • updater
  • userid

docs.title: Operational Commands via pan-os-python
docs.text:
Let’s revisit the previous example and print the ARP table. According to the documentation, we can use the same syntax as the CLI:

However, doing so will result in the following error:

panos.errors.PanDeviceXapiError: show -> arp -> all has unexpected text. show -> arp is unexpected show is unexpected

Upon closer inspection, we learn that the library translates CLI syntax into XML format. This translation is not available for all commands, and in such cases, the XML format must be used:

As previously shown, we can translate commands from CLI format to XML format using: debug cli on.

At this point, the script becomes almost identical to the one shown earlier:

token = getpass("Token: ")
fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Getting elements
root = fw.op("<show><arp><entry name='all'/></arp></show>", cmd_xml=False)
for entry in root.iterfind(".//result/entries/"):
    interface = entry.find("interface").text
    ip = entry.find("ip").text
    mac = entry.find("mac").text
    print(f"{interface},{ip},{mac}")

The library returns an ElementTree object, which can be handled as previously discussed.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via pan-os-python
docs.text:
Modifying the firewall configuration via SDK becomes simpler once the library’s operation is understood. Here is an example:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Create elements
for name, ip in addresses.items():
    fw.add(AddressObject(name=name, value=ip, type="ip-netmask")).create()

First, we have the Firewall class, which allows us to define access parameters. This class does not perform any actions itself, it simply defines the configuration to access the firewall.

We then have the AddressObject class, which enables management of Address-type objects. In the example, we create two ip-netmask objects containing Google DNS addresses. The script updates the configuration but does not commit the changes.

Similarly, we can read configured objects:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Getting configured elements
for entry in AddressObject.refreshall(fw):
    name = entry.name
    address = entry.value
    location = entry.vsys
    print(f"{name},{address},{location}")

In this case, the refreshall method retrieves the configuration from the firewall, returning the Address objects section.

The scripts are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Commit via pan-os-python
docs.text:
The Firewall class includes a convenient method for committing changes. As previously discussed, the commit is an asynchronous job. We must wait for its completion and verify the exit code:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Commit
job_id = fw.commit()
if job_id:
    result = fw.syncjob(job_id)
    if not result["success"]:
        print("ERROR: failed to commit.")

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via pan-os-python
docs.text:
Finally, let’s see how to delete the default configuration using the pan-os-python library. With the previous examples, we now understand how the library works. The challenge is identifying the appropriate classes for different object types:

  • SecurityRule (child of Rulebase),
  • VirtualWire,
  • Zone,
  • EthernetInterface.

Once the correct classes are identified, the script becomes straightforward:

fw = Firewall("172.24.1.34", api_key=token)

# Delete default rule
rulebase = Rulebase.refreshall(fw)
for rule in SecurityRule.refreshall(rulebase):
    if rule.name == "rule1":
        rule.delete()

# Delete default vwire
for vwire in VirtualWire.refreshall(fw):
    if vwire.name == "default-vwire":
        vwire.delete()

# Delete default zones
for zone in Zone.refreshall(fw):
    if zone.name in ["trust", "untrust"]:
        zone.delete()

# Delete default interfaces
for intf in EthernetInterface.refreshall(fw):
    if intf.name in ["ethernet1/1", "ethernet1/2"]:
        intf.delete()

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN SDK
Automating Palo Alto Firewall via Python PAN SDK
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced palo-alto-networks

In the previous post, we explored the official pan-os-python library maintained by Palo Alto Networks. We also noted that this library builds upon the personal work of Kevin Steves, who developed the pan-python library, enabling low-level operations on PAN-OS systems. Kevin also included several command-line tools to perform operations via CLI instead of Python.

The documentation is available online in reStructuredText format. The following modules are supported:

  • pan.afapi: provides CLI access to AutoFocus via panafapi
  • pan.licapi: manages PAN-OS licenses via CLI using panlicapi
  • pan.wfapi: interfaces with WildFire via CLI using panwfapi
  • pan.xapi: enables operations via the XML API, accessible via CLI with panconf and panxapi

As we’ll see in the examples, PAN SDK essentially provides an interface to the XML API, with some added conveniences. The upcoming examples will resemble those from the XML API post.

PAN SDK relies on Python's ElementTree, which reminds us:

A large number of log entries can cause a memory exception which may not be possible to catch.

docs.title: Operational Commands via pan-python
docs.text:
Let’s revisit a previous example and print the ARP table. The documentation is quite minimal and lacks examples. First, we create an api object with the firewall connection details:

ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
ctx.check_hostname = False
ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
fw = xapi.PanXapi(hostname="172.24.1.34", api_key=token, ssl_context=ctx)

We can now issue a command to print the ARP table:

fw.op(cmd="<show><arp><entry name='all'/></arp></show>", cmd_xml=False)
root = fw.element_root
for entry in root.iterfind(".//result/entries/"):
    interface = entry.find("interface").text
    ip = entry.find("ip").text
    mac = entry.find("mac").text
    print(f"{interface},{ip},{mac}")

The command syntax is identical to what we covered in the XML API post.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Configuration Commands via pan-python
docs.text:
Let’s now look at how to add objects to the firewall configuration. According to the documentation, the supported methods include set(), get(), edit(), delete(), move(), rename(), and clone().

As previously discussed, this example also follows the XML API syntax:

for name, ip in addresses.items():
    # xpath = "/config/shared/address/entry" # Shared (Panorama)
    xpath = "/config/devices/entry[@name='localhost.localdomain']/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address/entry" # VSYS
    xpath = xpath + f"[@name='{name}']"
    element = f"<ip-netmask>{ip}</ip-netmask>"
    fw.set(xpath=xpath, element=element)

The configured addresses can be printed in a similar way:

xpaths = [
    "/config/shared/address/entry", # Shared (Panorama)
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/address", # VSYS
]
for xpath in xpaths:
    if "/shared/" in xpath:
        location = "Shared"
        find_path = ".//result/"
    else:
        location = "VSYS"
        find_path = ".//result/address/"

    fw.get(xpath=xpath)
    root = fw.element_root
    for entry in root.iterfind(find_path):
        name = entry.attrib["name"]
        address = entry.find("ip-netmask").text
        print(f"{name},{address},{location}")

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Commit via pan-python
docs.text:
The xapi class includes the commit() method, which manages commit operations and the associated job:

cmd = "<commit></commit>"
fw.commit(cmd=cmd, sync=True)
if "no changes to commit" in fw.status_detail:
    pass
elif fw.status != "success" or "successfully" not in fw.status_detail:
    print("ERROR: failed to commit.")

As shown, the code isn't particularly clean since it checks both the job status and its textual description. Alternatively, an asynchronous commit can be used along with the job() method to manually verify status:

cmd = "<commit></commit>"
fw.commit(cmd=cmd, sync=False)
root = fw.element_root
job = root.find("./result/job")
job_id = None
if job is not None:
    # msg = root.find("./result/msg")
    job_id = job.text
else:
    msg = root.find("./msg")

# Wait for job
if job_id:
    progress = 0
    result = None
    while progress < 100:
        fw.op(cmd=f"<show><jobs><id>{job_id}</id></jobs></show>", cmd_xml=False)
        root = fw.element_root
        result_el = root.find("./result/job/result")
        if result_el is not None:
            result = result_el.text
        progress = int(root.find("./result/job/progress").text)
        print(f"Job ID {job_id}: {progress}%")
        time.sleep(5)

    if result != "OK":
        print("ERROR: failed to commit.")

This example is similar to the one covered using the XML API.

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Removing Default Configuration via pan-python
docs.text:
Finally, let’s see how to remove the default configuration using the pan-python library. From the previous examples, we’ve learned the similarities between XML API and pan-python:

token = getpass("Token: ")
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
ctx.check_hostname = False
ctx.verify_mode = ssl.CERT_NONE
fw = xapi.PanXapi(hostname="172.24.1.34", api_key=token, ssl_context=ctx)

# Defining paths
xpaths = [
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/rulebase/security/rules/entry[@name='rule1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/virtual-wire/entry[@name='default-vwire']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='trust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/zone/entry[@name='untrust']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/vsys/entry[@name='vsys1']/import/network/interface/member[text()='ethernet1/2']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/1']",
    "/config/devices/entry/network/interface/ethernet/entry[@name='ethernet1/2']",
]
for xpath in xpaths:
    fw.delete(xpath=xpath)

The script is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating operations with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 31 August 2025

docs.title: Automating operations with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner palo-alto-networks scm

Management of Palo Alto Networks firewalls is gradually shifting from traditional on-premises administration, either directly or via Panorama, to a cloud-based model. The product enabling centralized, cloud-based management of Palo Alto Networks firewall infrastructures is Strata Cloud Manager (SCM).

This management paradigm introduces several fundamental changes:

  • Data format: Panorama was XML-based, while SCM uses JSON.
  • Configuration model: Panorama relied on Device Groups, Templates, and Template Stacks. SCM uses *configuration scopes*, where *snippets* are reusable scopes that can be applied to folders or devices.
  • Variables: Variables existed in Panorama but with limited scope. SCM extends them, allowing usage even within security policies.

The approach to structuring complex infrastructures changes significantly. Our focus here is not on designing the architecture, but on creating automation to make migrations and ongoing operations more efficient.

We will not cover how to work manually within SCM; instead, we will explore how to interact with SCM through its API.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
There is no official CLI for SCM. However, Calvin Remsburg has developed a personal CLI module and an accompanying SDK enabling command-line management.

While the project is worth reviewing, several caveats apply:

  • It is a personal project, not an official tool.
  • It does not cover all operational scenarios.
  • It can be complex to use.
  • It was developed using Claude by Anthropic.

In my view, SCM-CLI can assist in automating certain tasks. However, I prefer using official tools or building my own so I can maintain them freely. The reasoning is simple: when working with APIs or SDKs, encountering bugs is common. Having vendor support or full control to implement workarounds is essential.

docs.title: Ansible
docs.text: Calvin Remsburg has also developed an Ansible module, built on pan-scm-sdk. The same considerations mentioned for the CLI apply here.

docs.title: Terraform
docs.text:
Palo Alto Networks has released an official Terraform provider, but it comes with no guarantees, the software is provided *as is*. The current version (0.11.0) indicates the provider is still considered unstable.

The associated GitHub repository shows active development, but many features are still missing.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Before writing any code, it is critical to understand the ecosystem and its inherent complexity.

SCM is a web-based application that builds its interface through multiple API calls:

Inspection via browser developer tools reveals that the web interface does not always use the same APIs exposed to developers. For instance, there is no trace of calls to /config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces in the interface's network activity.

In some cases, such as viewing interface details, we can identify the specific API calls used to populate the page. However, as we will see, the web UI uses a different backend API system, making it largely irrelevant for automation purposes.

Therefore, when automating SCM, we must rely entirely on the official API documentation. From experience, this significantly increases complexity and development time because:

  • Documentation is never fully complete.
  • Documentation is rarely up to date.
  • Examples for specific use cases are often missing.
  • Iterative testing is required to develop reliable automations.

docs.title: Recommended Approach
docs.text:
In an ideal scenario, web applications follow an API-First design, where the UI consumes the same APIs available to developers. This ensures consistency and reduces automation complexity.

With SCM, a hybrid approach is often necessary:

  • Rely on official documentation despite its limitations.
  • Use both the web UI and APIs in parallel to understand the exact impact of each operation and the structure of the objects involved.

docs.title: Authenticating to the Strata Cloud Manager API
docs.text: 07 September 2025

docs.title: Authenticating to the Strata Cloud Manager API
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner palo-alto-networks scm

According to the official documentation, before making any API calls, you must first obtain an access token using your username, password, and tenant service group.

This token can then be used to authorize subsequent API requests.

http_username = f"{username}@{tenant_id}.iam.panserviceaccount.com"
basic_auth = HTTPBasicAuth(http_username, password)
data = {
    "grant_type": "client_credentials",
    "scope": f"tsg_id:{tenant_id}",
}
url = "https://auth.apps.paloaltonetworks.com/oauth2/access_token"
req = requests.post(url, auth=basic_auth, headers=headers, data=data)
req.raise_for_status()
token = req.json()["access_token"]

Along with the token, the API also returns its validity period, 900 seconds (15 minutes), which must be taken into account when designing automations.

The token itself is a JSON Web Token (JWT), a standardized, encoded JSON object. By decoding it, you can inspect the claims and metadata it contains:

docs.title: Example: Retrieving the List of Registered Devices
docs.text:
As a first example, let's retrieve the list of devices registered in SCM.

From the API documentation homepage, use the search bar to locate the relevant endpoint:

As shown earlier, the first step is to authenticate and generate a token valid for 15 minutes:

# Get token
headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
}
http_username = f"{username}@{tenant_id}.iam.panserviceaccount.com"
basic_auth = HTTPBasicAuth(http_username, password)
data = {
    "grant_type": "client_credentials",
    "scope": f"tsg_id:{tenant_id}",
}
url = "https://auth.apps.paloaltonetworks.com/oauth2/access_token"
req = requests.post(url, auth=basic_auth, headers=headers, data=data)
req.raise_for_status()
token = req.json()["access_token"]

Next, use the list-devices API endpoint to retrieve the inventory:

# Get devices
headers = {
    "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"
}
req = requests.get("https://api.strata.paloaltonetworks.com/config/setup/v1/devices", headers=headers)
req.raise_for_status()
pprint(req.json())

The response will contain the device list in JSON format:

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Optimizing Strata Cloud Manager API usage
docs.text: 14 September 2025

docs.title: Optimizing Strata Cloud Manager API usage
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced palo-alto-networks scm

Before moving forward, let’s review our current approach to invoking the API:

  • We are using the requests library.
  • We must first generate an authentication token.
  • Many parameters are repeatedly passed in multiple calls.
  • We must verify whether the token has expired.

We can improve this workflow by creating a lightweight extension of the requests library.

This extension should handle token management automatically, including renewal when needed.

It would also be beneficial to centralize header and URL handling to keep our code clean and concise.

docs.title: Implementing a Custom API Client
docs.text:
To achieve this, we will create a new class called APIClient:

class APIClient(requests.Session):
    """APIClient is a specialized HTTP client for interacting with the Palo Alto Networks API."""

    def __init__(self, tenant_id: int, username: str, password: str) -> None:
        """Initialize the APIClient and perform the first authentication."""

        # Initialize the parent requests.Session
        super().__init__()

        # Authentication endpoint for Palo Alto Networks
        self.auth_url = "https://auth.apps.paloaltonetworks.com/oauth2/access_token"

        # Store credentials and tenant information
        self.tenant_id = tenant_id
        self.username = username
        self.__password = password

        # Will hold the Bearer token once authenticated
        self.__token = None

        # Perform the initial authentication right away
        self.__authenticate()

This class must handle the following:

  • TSG ID (also referred to as *tenant ID*)
  • Username
  • Password
  • Token, including generation and renewal logic

Since the authentication URL is always the same, we can define it directly within the code.

When an APIClient object is initialized, the authentication process is triggered:

  def __authenticate(self) -> None:
    """Authenticate with the Palo Alto endpoint and store the Bearer token."""

    # Build HTTP Basic Auth
    basic_auth = HTTPBasicAuth(
      f"{self.username}@{self.tenant_id}.iam.panserviceaccount.com",
      self.__password,
    )

    # Headers for the token request
    headers = {
      "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
    }

    # Body parameters for client credentials grant
    data = {
      "grant_type": "client_credentials",
      "scope": f"tsg_id:{self.tenant_id}",
    }

    # Send the POST request to the auth server
    req = requests.post(self.auth_url, auth=basic_auth, headers=headers, data=data)
    req.raise_for_status()

    # Save the access token for later requests
    self.__token = req.json()["access_token"]

As seen earlier, the authentication function calls a specific API to obtain a token and stores it for later use.

docs.title: Overriding Requests for SCM
docs.text:
To integrate seamlessly with SCM, we override the request method in our client to add the required intelligence:

  def request(self, method: str, url: str, **kwargs) -> Response:
    """Send an HTTP request with automatic Bearer token handling."""

    # Ensure the headers dictionary exists
    if "headers" not in kwargs:
      kwargs["headers"] = {}

    # Add Authorization header with the current Bearer token
    kwargs["headers"]["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self.__token}"

    # Accept JSON responses by default
    kwargs["headers"]["Accept"] = "application/json"

    # For POST/PUT requests, set Content-Type to application/json
    if method.lower() in ["post", "put"]:
      kwargs["headers"]["Content-Type"] = "application/json"

    # If the given URL is just a path, prefix it with the API base URL
    if url.startswith("/"):
      url = f"https://api.strata.paloaltonetworks.com{url}"

    # Execute the request
    req = super().request(method, url, **kwargs)

    # Retry once if token expired
    if req.status_code == 401 and req.json()["message"] == "Invalid Request Token.":
      # Token expired
      self.__authenticate()
      # Retry once
      kwargs["headers"]["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self.__token}"
      req = super().request(method, url, **kwargs)

    return req

The key logic is at the end:

  • The request is executed.
  • If the token has expired, the client re-authenticates and retries the request.

docs.title: Additional Optimizations
docs.text:
This approach streamlines our work by:

  • Automatically injecting the token into every request.
