  • Dynamically generating headers and adapting them when sending payload data.
  • Building the request URL with the FQDN if it is not already included.

With this improvement, the previous device-listing example can now be rewritten using the new client:

client = APIClient(
    tenant_id=tenant_id,
    username=username,
    password=password,
)
req = client.get("/config/setup/v1/devices")
req.raise_for_status()
pprint(req.json())

The result: we’ve cut the code roughly in half, making it cleaner and more maintainable.

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Retrieving firewall interfaces with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 21 September 2025

docs.title: Retrieving firewall interfaces with Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner palo-alto-networks scm

Let’s look at a second example that illustrates both the functionality and the complexity of SCM’s APIs.

In this scenario, we want to retrieve the Ethernet interfaces of the firewalls. A quick search in the documentation leads us to the correct API endpoint.

Using the custom class we created earlier, the code is straightforward:

# Get interfaces
req = client.get(f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces")
req.raise_for_status()
interfaces = req.json()
pprint(interfaces)

However, this returns no results.

docs.title: Understanding API Parameters
docs.text:
Reviewing the documentation reveals that certain parameters can be specified, though they are not mandatory.

From a logical standpoint, requesting a list of interfaces without specifying the target firewall is incomplete. It also makes sense for the firewall to be identified by its ID rather than its hostname (since hostnames can change).

By adapting the code to request interfaces for each device ID, we get:

# Get devices
req = client.get("/config/setup/v1/devices")
req.raise_for_status()
devices = req.json()

# For each device, get interfaces
for device in devices["data"]:
    device_id = device["id"]
    device_hostname = device["hostname"]

    req = client.get(f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces?device={device_id}")
    req.raise_for_status()
    interfaces = req.json()

docs.text:

docs.title: Modifying an object in Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text: 28 September 2025

docs.title: Modifying an object in Strata Cloud Manager
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate palo-alto-networks scm

This example is particularly relevant because it directly impacts operational workflows.

Before diving into the example, let’s review the HTTP methods used in REST APIs. HTTP defines five default methods that map to CRUD operations: Create, Read, Update, Delete:

  • GET: Retrieve a resource
  • POST: Create a new resource
  • DELETE: Remove a resource
  • PUT and PATCH: Update an existing resource

The difference between PUT and PATCH is crucial:

  • PATCH updates only the specified fields.
  • PUT replaces the entire resource with the provided fields.

docs.title: Example: Updating Interface Comments
docs.text:
As an example, let’s modify the comment for the interfaces associated with a firewall.

It’s important to note that SCM APIs implement only the PUT method, PATCH is not supported.

This means you cannot update just a single attribute (such as the comment).

# Edit comment (WRONG)
interface_details = {
    "comment": f"{interface_name} managed via API ({api_timestamp})"
}
req = client.put(interface_url, json=interface_details)
req.raise_for_status()

If you attempt to set only the comment field using PUT, the result will be an interface reset to default settings, with only the comment preserved. This happens because PUT overwrites the resource entirely with the supplied data.

docs.title: Workaround for the Missing PATCH Method
docs.text:
Since PATCH is unavailable, the correct approach is to:

  • Retrieve the full interface structure via GET.
  • Modify the desired attribute (in this case, the comment).
  • Apply the updated structure back using PUT.
# Get interface details
interface_url = f"/config/network/v1/ethernet-interfaces/{interface_id}"
req = client.get(interface_url)
req.raise_for_status()
interface_details = req.json()

# Edit comment
interface_name = interface_details["name"]
interface_details["comment"] = f"{interface_name} managed via API ({api_timestamp})"
req = client.put(interface_url, json=interface_details)
req.raise_for_status()

The full example code is available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Networks firewalls
docs.text: 02 February 2022

docs.title: Automating Palo Alto Networks firewalls
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced ansible palo-alto-networks

I spent a few Twitch sessions speaking about the automation of Palo Alto Networks firewalls. We used different approaches than the one used with Cisco devices. Initially, we developed a few simple Ansible playbooks. In the last sessions, we developed a very small Django web application to programmatically enable and disable network flows.

docs.title: Ansible with Palo Alto Networks firewall
docs.text:
The Palo Alto Networks module for Ansible has some prerequisites:

pip install pan-os-python pan-python pandevice xmltodict requests requests_toolbelt

Then install PAN-OS Ansible collection:

ansible-galaxy collection install paloaltonetworks.panos

The interpreter_python on ansible.cfg file must point to the interpreter with the PanOS libraries installed. This is important if you're using a virtual environment.

Firewall credentials are not passed in the standard way, but a specific dictionary must be passed to each task. We populated the dictionary from Ansible parameters as following:

- set_fact:
    provider:
        ip_address: "{{ ansible_host }}"
        password: "{{ ansible_password }}"
        username: "{{ ansible_user }}"

docs.title: Getting facts
docs.text:
The Palo Alto Network module is not using the gather_facts parameter; instead, it's defining a custom task to retrieve facts:

* paloaltonetworks.panos.panos_facts:
    provider: "{{ provider }}"

docs.title: Sending operational commands
docs.text:
The module panos_op allows sending commands to the firewall. The module translates the given command into XML and uses the XML API. Some commands can fail so the best way is to specify commands using the XML syntax. The following command is failing:

cmd: 'show arp management' # Fails with "show -> arp has unexpected text."

The following command is working:

cmd: "<show><arp><entry name='management'/></arp></show>"
cmd_is_xml: true

The API browser, available on the Firewall using the /api URL can help to find out the right request. The above API is available at /php/rest/browse.php/op::show::arp.

We used panos_op to get system info and the ARP table.

Because operational commands are sent in the XML format, the output is automatically converted to JSON from the Ansible module. Remember that XML can be converted to JSON/YAML and back, but mind that XML attributes will be usually lost.

docs.title: Sending configuration commands
docs.text:
We wrote the fourth playbook to test configuration commands. There are many configuration commands available from the Ansible module but we are limited to configuring some management interface parameters.

We discussed a few about how to "zero-touch provision" a Palo Alto Network firewalls. Even if we didn't test the scenario, we agreed that we could write a working playbook.

docs.title: Configuration templating
docs.text:
Even if configuration commands could be used to manage a lot of firewall features, we tested a different approach: configuration templating. Because Palo Alto Network firewalls have the commit feature, in my opinion, this is the best approach.

My idea is:

  • prepare a configuration template (Jinja2);
  • build the firewall configuration from the template using an external configuration file (model);
  • upload the firewall configuration file and enable it.

The fifth playbook implement this approach.

Pros and cons of this approach:

  • the entire firewall configuration can be stored in a CMDB file (pro);
  • the firewall configuration is always consistent (pro);
  • we can configure almost everything (pro);
  • we don't need to make checks before inserting a specific configuration in a running firewall (pro);
  • we need to spend a lot of time designing our firewall model (cons).

docs.title: Programming the firewall using external feeds
docs.text:
Many firewalls can read external feeds: the content can be used as a source or destination in access lists. This approach is perfect to allow temporary access. In the last session we created a small web application using Django.

The application provides feeds containing IP addresses. Each IP address has an expiration date. Once the IP address is expired, it is removed from the feed.

docs.title: Installing Django
docs.text:
Install Django into a Python environment (see S01E01):

pip install Django==4.0.1

docs.title: Creating the Django application
docs.text:
Create the first Django project and an application within it:

django-admin startproject feedapp
cd feedapp
django-admin startapp edlprovider
./manage.py migrate

By default, the database is an SQLite file stored under the Django root folder. The app must be loaded in the settings.py file stored in the feedapp folder:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    "edlprovider",
]

Create the admin user:

./manage.py createsuperuser

docs.title: Modeling
docs.text:
In the simplest version of our application, we can expect that:

  • an admin user is adding one or more EDL objects (list of IP addresses);
  • an admin user is adding one or more IP addresses to one EDL object;
  • possibly an expiration time can be set to each IP address;
  • unexpired IP addresses will be available in a text list under a specific, non-guessable, URL.

In other words, we have two objects:

  • EDL with ID, name, URL;
  • IP with name, expiration date (optional), associated EDL.

When the model is complete, we need to update the migration scripts and upgrade the database schema:

./manage.py makemigrations
./manage.py migrate

docs.title: Admin page
docs.text:
By default, Django provides an admin page for each model. It can be enabled by adding in the admin.py file:

admin.site.register(models.EDL)
admin.site.register(models.IPAddress)

Open the Django application using the URL /admin, and add one EDL with at least one IP address.

docs.title: Printing EDLs
docs.text:
The view.py file is used to serve custom HTTP requests. We need to print the content of each EDL if a GET is requesting the EDL id (slug). The URL is defined in the rrapp/urls.py file.

All IP addresses linked to a specific EDL are printed in text format if the expiration date is in the future.

docs.title: Starting the server
docs.text:
In the settings.py file you can configure Django to serve any client. This is an insecure configuration. Add * to the ALLOWED_HOSTS:

ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']

Start the application:

./manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000

The Django application is now reachable. Use the /admin URL and log in with the superuser credentials created before.

docs.title: Using the EDL from a PANW firewall
docs.text:
Once an EDL is populated, it can be used as a source or destination on ACLs.

EDL can be debugged with the following commands:

admin@fw> request system external-list stats type ip name EDL1
admin@fw> request system external-list show type ip name EDL1
admin@fw> request system external-list refresh type ip name EDL1

Last note: when an IP address is removed from an EDL, the session is not cleared. In other words, the established sessions are maintained, and new sessions are dropped.

A script should clear sessions related to expired IP addresses:

admin@fw> clear session all filter rule TestEDL1 destination 192.168.28.152

Mind also that firewall usually probes URLs every 5 minutes, so the clear command should be executed 5 minutes after the expiration date. The web application should be extended to track requests and if they have been cleared.

docs.title: Introduction to MISP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner misp

MISP (Malware Information Sharing Platform) is an open-source software solution for collecting, storing, distributing, and sharing cybersecurity indicators and threat intelligence related to cybersecurity incident analysis and malware analysis. MISP is designed for incident analysts, security professionals, ICT specialists, and malware reverse engineers to support their daily operations and efficiently share structured information.

Launched in 2011 to manage Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in a structured manner, MISP has since evolved and is now used by national CERTs and NATO, which gave the platform its name. Today, MISP is also utilized by organizations like ACN and various entities that require structured IoC management.

Additionally, MISP has been used by the European Payments Council (EPC) to share timely information aimed at preventing and intercepting fraudulent activities in payment transactions. For further details, refer to the CIPA note.

docs.title: A Threat Intelligence Tool
docs.text:
Threat intelligence or "threat intel" refers to actionable insights into current or emerging cybersecurity threats, which helps individuals and organizations better understand past, present, and future risks.

Threat intelligence is more than just IoC management. It may also provide insights into the motivations behind emerging threats, such as geopolitical tensions between nations. On a more granular level, it can involve specific data, such as IP addresses associated with suspicious activities.

MISP supports threat intelligence activities by:

  • Comprehensive IoC management (Indicators of Compromise).
  • Implementing a flexible and precise taxonomy system using tagging, which helps define each piece of stored data. (GitHub).
  • Integrating a variety of feeds available by default in any MISP installation.
  • Extending functionalities through third-party tools and integrations.
  • Utilizing open protocols and data structures.

docs.title: Automation-Oriented
docs.text:
MISP is designed to integrate seamlessly into automated or semi-supervised processes.

It provides complete APIs that allow for custom integrations with third-party solutions. PyMISP enables native integration of MISP into Python projects.

IoCs can be exported in multiple formats, including various native IDS formats, OpenIOC, plain text, CSV, MISP JSON, STIX (XML and JSON versions 1 and 2), NIDS exports (Suricata, Snort, and Bro/Zeek), RPZ zones, and cache formats for forensic tools. Additional formats, such as PDF, can be easily added through the misp-modules or customized as built-in export modules.

docs.title: Installing MISP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner misp

Installing MISP is relatively straightforward and is well documented in the user guide. For some reason, the user guide does not yet mention Ubuntu 24.04, although the installation script is available in the repository.

apt-get update
apt-get upgrade -y
wget -O /tmp/INSTALL.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MISP/MISP/refs/heads/2.5/INSTALL/INSTALL.ubuntu2404.sh
bash /tmp/INSTALL.sh

At this point, the installation begins, displaying each step as it proceeds:

At the end, credentials to access the platform are shown:

By default, the platform is accessible at https://misp.local. If the system is reachable through a different FQDN, you can update the /var/www/MISP/app/Config/config.php file:

<?php
$config = array (
  'debug' => 0,
  'MISP' =>
  array (
    # 'baseurl' => 'https://misp.local',
    'baseurl' => 'https://172.24.1.18',

You should also modify the /etc/apache2/sites-available/misp-ssl.conf file, which handles HTTPS redirection:

<VirtualHost _default_:80>
    ServerAdmin admin@misp.local
    ServerName misp.local

    # Redirect permanent / https://misp.local
    Redirect permanent / https://172.24.1.18

    LogLevel warn
    ErrorLog /var/log/apache2/misp.local_error.log
    CustomLog /var/log/apache2/misp.local_access.log combined
    ServerSignature Off
</VirtualHost>

Reload the configuration:

apachectl graceful

Then log in using the credentials displayed during installation.

docs.title: Enabling feeds
docs.text:
We can now enable one or more default feeds in MISP. Go to Sync Actions → Feeds:

Edit the feeds and enable them. Returning to the event list, you’ll now see events imported from the feeds:

docs.title: Creating an Event
docs.text:
Next, let's create an event. Navigate to Event Actions → Add Event, using a SPAM email as the base:

When creating an event, the following parameters are required:

  • Distribution refers to event sharing: Your organization only (0), This community only (1), Connected communities (2), All communities (3), Sharing group (4), Inherit Event (5).
  • Analysis indicates the threat analysis status: Initial (0), Ongoing (1), Complete (2).
  • Threat level: High (1), Medium (2), Low (3), Undefined (4).

Once the event is created, you can associate attributes that best describe the threat. Since we’re analyzing an email, we’ll include:

  • Subject
  • IP address of the sending server
  • Destination email address
  • Source email address
  • Any links contained in the email
  • Any attachments found in the email

When creating an attribute, the following parameters are required:

  • Category of the attribute, which in this case will be *Payload delivery*
  • Type of the attribute, chosen from a predefined list based on the most appropriate match
  • Distribution, referring to the attribute sharing level

The final step is to properly tag the event and its attributes. Best practices suggest tagging the event itself, and only tagging individual attributes when strictly necessary. If an appropriate cluster exists, you can also use MISP Galaxy (GitHub).

You can also assign the appropriate TLP level. The TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) was created to support the proper sharing of sensitive information. TLP uses a series of labels to define who may share the information:

  • TLP:CLEAR: Information can be freely shared without restriction, subject to copyright or proprietary considerations.
  • TLP:GREEN: Information can be shared with peers and partner organizations, but not publicly.
  • TLP:AMBER: Information carries potential privacy, reputational, or operational risk and may only be shared within the recipient’s organization and its clients.
  • TLP:AMBER+STRICT: Same as TLP:AMBER, but sharing is restricted to the recipient organization only.
  • TLP:RED: Information is highly sensitive and must not be shared beyond the original recipients.

Once completed, your event should look like the following:

docs.title: Integrating and automating MISP
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner misp

MISP is a platform for threat intelligence, not for incident management. Specifically, MISP helps manage Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) in a structured way, and therefore it must be integrated into an existing ecosystem.

Very often, TheHive is used as the incident management platform, but integration requests also commonly involve Splunk, Elastic, Maltego, and detection and prevention systems (antispam, honeypot, firewall, etc.).

A MISP event does not represent a security incident, but rather a threat that is analyzed and evaluated from a threat intelligence perspective. Much of the work (defining IoCs and artifacts) has likely already been carried out on other platforms: we are evaluating the event and its associated IoCs to determine whether they provide added value for us and for the communities we are part of.

docs.title: Automating MISP Tasks
docs.text:
The following activities can be identified for automation:

  • Creating events by ingesting data from external sources (TheHive, honeypot, etc.)
  • Making IoCs available to external platforms (firewalls, EDR, antispam, SIEMs, etc.)
  • Facilitating incident analysis by providing IoCs to external platforms (Maltego, TheHive, etc.)
  • Sending and receiving feedback on events (thumbs up = observed and malicious, thumbs down = observed but not malicious)

docs.title: API
docs.text:
MISP offers APIs in OpenAPI 3.0.0 format that allow programmatic interaction with the platform.

To use the API, an authentication key is required. This key can be generated by navigating to My Profile → Auth keys → Add authentication key:

The key must be included in the Authorization header.

docs.title: PyMISP
docs.text:
Alternatively, the Python library PyMISP is available. PyMISP allows native interaction with MISP using Python.

In my experience, I found PyMISP more challenging to use than the native APIs. This is primarily because the documentation is not always clear, and for some tasks, I had to reverse engineer the code.

docs.title: CIRCL
docs.text: CIRCL is the CERT for the private sector, municipalities, and non-governmental organizations in Luxembourg. CIRCL is a highly active contributor to MISP, and their website is worth visiting for its excellent MISP documentation.

docs.title: Consuming MISP IoCs from a Firewall
Consuming MISP IoCs from a Firewall
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate misp

Once our MISP instance is properly configured, it contains a set of threat intelligence data that can be leveraged by prevention tools such as Firewalls, Email Gateways, and more.

Let’s explore how to extract IoCs from MISP. Specifically, we’ll look at how to create a list of IP addresses to be proactively blocked by perimeter systems.

Modern firewalls are capable of ingesting External Dynamic Lists (EDLs), which are simply text files hosted on web servers containing lists of IP addresses. These lists can then be referenced within security policies to take specific actions.

While the number of IP addresses that can be managed via EDLs might seem substantial, it becomes clear that these limits are relatively low when compared to the global volume of IP-based IoCs.

This underscores the importance of managing IoCs in a structured way, with particular attention to their lifecycle.

docs.title: Native Export
docs.text:
MISP natively supports exporting attributes in multiple formats. By navigating to Event Actions → Export, we can generate IoC lists in various formats:

Further down the page, we can immediately retrieve lists of IoCs for a specific attribute type in plain text format:

For instance, clicking on ip-dst will instantly provide a file containing all ip-dst attributes marked as exportable for IDS purposes.

However, as discussed earlier, the list might exceed the limitations imposed by our firewall. Therefore, we need greater control over the export process.

docs.title: Export via API
docs.text:
By building our own IoC export mechanism, we gain enhanced control over the number, type, date, and format of indicators.

We want to obtain a list of all IP-type IoCs, limiting their number and prioritizing the most recent entries. While the request appears simple, fulfilling it requires a robust lifecycle management system for IoCs, a non-trivial task. Consider, for example, a C2-related IP address:

  • When can it be considered obsolete?
  • How do we define it as obsolete?
  • Is it possible for an obsolete IP to become relevant again? How should this be handled?

For the purposes of this article, we assume the IoC lifecycle is already being properly managed, and we focus solely on the automation process.

Our goal is to generate a list of IP addresses (including both ip-src and ip-dst), limit the total number, and prioritize the most recent entries.

The API we’ll use is restSearch, which provides paginated attribute listings based on specified parameters.

The request is a POST with the following parameters:

data = {
    "controller": "attributes",
    "type": ["ip-src", "ip-dst"],
    "to_ids": True,
    "deleted": False,
    "timestamp": last_days_unix,
    "order": "timestamp desc",
    "limit": config["export"]["last_ioc"],
}
url = f"{config['misp']['url']}/attributes/restSearch"
req = requests.post(url, json=data, **params_post)
req.raise_for_status()

The output can then be parsed into a plain-text list of unique IP addresses:

for item in req.json()["response"]["Attribute"]:
    if item["value"] not in ip_list:
        ip_list.append(item["value"])
ioc_page = "\n".join(ip_list).encode("utf-8")

The full script is available in the GitHub repository. When executed, it provides the IoC list in plain-text format via HTTP:

./get_ioc_to_edl_api.py

Most recent IoC:  Wed May 14 15:38:15 2025
Most old IoC:     Wed Nov 27 09:37:03 2024
Exporting 2549 IP addresses
Webserver started on port 8080
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:31:50] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:31:50] "GET /favicon.ico HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:32:01] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [17/May/2025 10:32:01] "GET /favicon.ico HTTP/1.1" 200 -

Generating the list consumes time and computing resources from the MISP server. In production environments, it is advisable to update the list on an event-driven or scheduled basis, populating a cache file that can then be served to security tools.

docs.title: Export via SDK
docs.text:
Similarly, we can generate our list using PyMISP. The code is very similar to the API-based approach:

res = misp.search(
    controller="attributes",
    type_attribute=["ip-src", "ip-dst"],
    # to_ids=True, # Filter not working
    deleted=False,
    timestamp=last_days_unix,
    order="timestamp desc", # Filter not working asc/desc
    limit=config["export"]["last_ioc"],
    pythonify=False,
)

However, in my tests, I encountered some issues: the to_ids filter does not seem to work correctly, nor does the sorting. The sorting issue directly affects the ability to retrieve the most recent IoCs.

At this time, I personally prefer the API-based approach.

Both scripts are available in the GitHub repository.

docs.title: Network simulators are a must
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

For anyone working in IT, theory alone isn't enough. Practical experience is crucial to fully grasp concepts and develop the skills needed to design, configure, and manage complex environments. In the early 2000s, network administrators often bought second-hand hardware to build labs for studying and experimenting with configurations before deploying them in production.

Then came virtualization, which greatly simplified the process and made the concept of a lab accessible to many without the need for expensive hardware. Initially used by network administrators, simulators have since become foundational for the training of all IT professionals.

Today, it's unimaginable to work without simulated environments. Both professionals and students need them to experiment, study, and stay updated. While simulators were once primarily for network administrators, now they include ready-made scenarios for both defensive and offensive security.

docs.title: The benefits of using network simulators
docs.text:
• Accessibility: From students to professionals, anyone can access complex network environments without the need for expensive equipment.
  • Safety: Tests can be conducted in a secure environment, without the risk of compromising real networks.
  • Flexibility: You can experiment with configurations that would be impractical or too risky to implement on a real network.
  • Certification Preparation: For those preparing for certifications like CCNA, CCNP, and others, these tools provide a practical environment to practice in.
  • Demo and POC: A simulated environment is ideal for realistically showcasing technological solutions.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Using network simulators and emulators is now indispensable in IT training and research. They offer a safe, accessible, and flexible way to experiment and learn, allowing you to acquire practical skills without the constraints of physical hardware. Whether you’re a student aiming for certification or a professional wanting to test new configurations, these tools are an essential addition to your educational and professional toolkit.

docs.title: iou-web the beginning
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

I've been working with network simulators since around 2011 when I decided to pursue my CCIE R&S certification. Around that time, another pivotal event set me on the path of development: Cisco released a binary called IOL (IOS on Linux), which essentially simulated a Cisco IOS router. Unlike other solutions, the resources required to simulate this router were significantly lower.

Back then, GNS3 was the only available option, which used Dynamips to emulate the hardware needed to run official IOS images. However, the emulated platforms were limited, and manual optimization was required to minimize resource usage. I faced two major issues that were deal-breakers for me:

  • I was working with two different computers, and synchronizing the environment between them with GNS3 was complicated.
  • The combination of GNS3 and Dynamips was unstable.

I decided to create my own interface to manage simulators based on IOL. After a few months, iou-web was born: a PHP-based web interface that orchestrated the creation and management of labs for IOL. My requirements were:

  • Portability: Labs must be exportable and importable.
  • Stability: Running labs must be stable, avoiding crashes.
  • Performance: Labs must run on a cheap laptop or VM.

Meanwhile, I discovered that Cisco had developed similar software internally called WebIOL. WebIOL was developed in Perl and was released exclusively for Cisco employees, featuring basic labs from the Cisco 360 program.

After a couple of alpha versions, iou-web was publicly released on January 23rd, 2012.

Unlike GNS3, which supported real IOS images via Dynamips, iou-web supported only IOL. However, because IOL was faster than Dynamips, many users preferred iou-web.

Basically, iou-web, often referred to as webiou, was a web interface for IOU. It allowed users to:

  • Create Network Topologies: Easily build network topologies for IOU through a user-friendly web interface.
  • Manage Devices: Start and stop devices with simple web-based controls.
  • Visualize Topologies: View a graphical L2 diagram of the network topology for better understanding and management.

The old historical iou-web repository is available to the public on GitHub.

docs.title: UNetLab the evolution of iou-web
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

In 2013, I realized that iou-web was too limited. I needed a "unified" approach to emulate a network, including firewalls, load balancers, and more. Additionally, multicasting using IOL was problematic. I had several new prerequisites:

  • Include vendor virtual appliances in labs.
  • Integrate real IOS images in labs.
  • Possibly include emulators from different vendors.
  • Support multi-user environments.

I completely rewrote iou-web to create an extendable network emulator system. The core idea was:

  • Each node (emulated device) must be attached to a common layer.
  • A suitable common layer could be an Ethernet Linux bridge (with OVS support).

On October 6th, 2014, UNetLab, also known as UNL, was released to the public. Developed in PHP using a REST API framework and a single-page application (jQuery), UNetLab quickly gained popularity, with five to six hundred daily users within a few months. Although I wanted to name it UNL, the website URL was unavailable.

Initially, I considered including Huawei eNSP, but since eNSP nodes required a specific string, no one was able to run eNSP nodes outside of eNSP.

UNetLab was used by thousands of people monthly from around the world, providing immense satisfaction and giving me hands-on experience managing widely distributed production software.

In 2015, due to limited spare time, a group of enthusiasts forked UNetLab, leading to the release of EVE-NG on January 5th, 2017. However, I am not part of the EVE-NG team.

In 2014, I had an interesting chat with a member of the Cisco VIRL team during CLEUR 2014 in Milan.

The old historical UNetLab repository is available to the public on GitHub.

Also, refer to these resources that mention UNetLab:

  • Packet Pushers PQ Show 61: The UNetLab Project
  • Approaches and algorithms of virtual telecommunication networks analysis in UNetLab environment (IEEE conference)

docs.title: UNetLab v2 addressing limitations
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

In recent years, my focus has shifted towards network automation. I still need a unified network emulator platform, but the prerequisites have evolved. Before diving into the new requirements, let's highlight the limitations of UNetLab:

  • Per Host Pod Limit: Each host can run up to 256 independent pods due to the console port limit.
  • Per Lab Node Limit: Each pod/lab can run up to 127 nodes due to the console port limit.
  • Per User Pod Limit: Each user can run only one pod/lab at a time due to the console port limit.
  • Single Host: No support for distributed installations of UNetLab (OVS can be used, but many frame types are filtered by default).
  • Config Management: Using expect scripts for getting and putting startup-configs is slow, non-predictive, and cannot cover all node types.
  • No Support for Dynamips Serial Interfaces.
  • No Topology Changes: Topology changes are not allowed while the lab is running, by design.

The console port limit exists because each node console has a fixed port calculated as follows:

ts_port = 32768 + 128 * tenant_id + device_id

Additionally, no more than 512 IOL nodes can run in the same lab because the device_id must be unique for each tenant.

UNetLab v2 must address these issues and meet new requirements:

  • Run a distributed lab (across local or geographically distributed nodes).
  • Support an unlimited number of nodes in a lab.
  • Allow each user to customize a lab without affecting the original copy.
  • Link serial interfaces between IOL and Dynamips.
  • Configure nodes via Ansible/NAPALM/other tools.

I knew how to create a distributed network emulator but needed an easy way to run nodes within a dedicated namespace. The answer came from vrnetlab: using Docker.

Due to the limitations of UNetLab, I decided to rewrite it from scratch. Although EVE-NG, a fork of UNetLab, works to overcome these limitations, I pursued a new path.

docs.title: UNetLab v2 Architecture
docs.text:
The architecture may seem complex, but it was straightforward to implement.

UNetLab v2 was based on:

  • Docker: Controllers, routers, and lab nodes run inside Docker containers.
  • Python: Replaces C, PHP, and Bash with Python 3.
  • Python-Flask + NGINX: Implements and exposes APIs.
  • Memcached: Caches authentication for better user experience.
  • Celery + Redis: Manages asynchronous long tasks in the background.
  • MariaDB: Stores all data, user information, and running labs.
  • Git: Manages version control for original labs.
  • jQuery + Bootstrap: Implements the UI as a single-page application.
  • iptables + Linux bridge: Allows SSH connections to just-started lab nodes.
  • IOL, QEMU, and Dynamips: Runs lab nodes.

A UNetLab v2 cluster must have at least one node, which can be physical or virtual. The first node is the master, containing a controller and a router, while additional nodes contain only routers. Each node also runs multiple lab nodes. Controllers, routers, and lab nodes are Docker instances.

The controller container:

  • Exposes the web UI and APIs to user clients, routers, and lab nodes.
  • Receives registration requests from routers and lab nodes.
  • Manages lab nodes via routers.
  • Contacts lab nodes via Ansible/NAPALM/etc.
  • Provides routing tables to routers.
  • Accessible via SSH using port 2222.

The router containers:

  • Register with the controller.
  • Expose Docker Remote API and lab node API.
  • Obtain routing tables from the controller.
  • Route lab packets between nodes and routers.
  • Ensure connectivity between the controller and remote lab nodes via OpenVPN.

The node containers:

  • Register with the controller.
  • Run emulated nodes (IOL, Dynamips, or QEMU).
  • Bind a management interface of emulated nodes to a local bridge.
  • Route packets between the local router and the emulated node for non-management interfaces.
  • Manage emulated links (up/down).

Since the controller and routers know both inside and outside IP addresses, users can deploy UNetLab v2 nodes anywhere (in the same LAN, AWS, Google Compute Engine, Azure, behind a firewall). Each UNetLab v2 cluster requires the following ports:

  • TCP: 2222: SSH connection to the controller.
  • TCP: 80/443: HTTP/HTTPS requests to the controller.
  • TCP: 5443: HTTPS requests to the router.
  • UDP: 5005: Routed packets between different UNetLab v2 nodes.
  • UDP: 1194: Network reachability between the controller and remote lab nodes.

UNetLab v2 was never completed, but the source code is available on GitHub.

docs.title: UNetLab v3 whishing list
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

The idea behind UNetLab v2 was partly good, but some choices complicated the implementation and negatively impacted system performance. Specifically, managing UNetLab’s network in user space would have caused serious problems, even though it would have made horizontal scalability easier.

Moreover, I had a significant doubt: does it make sense to implement a virtualization system today when several are maintained by companies far better than I could manage? Initially, I considered ESXi, but after the Broadcom acquisition, I leaned towards Proxmox. While ESXi would have required abandoning physical link simulation, Proxmox allows using the same strategy I used with UNetLab.

Using an existing hypervisor significantly simplifies development at the cost of a substantial sacrifice: unsupported systems like IOL and Dynamips would no longer be supported. While this isn't a big issue for Dynamips, IOL has always been my preferred system for creating lightweight labs.

docs.title: UNetLab v3 Wishlist
docs.text:
I should divide the list into functional and non-functional requirements, but for now, let's compile a sort of wishlist together.

In my mind, a hypothetical UNetLab v3 wishlist includes:

  • Free, open-source, community-driven
  • Ability to easily share labs, template repositories, playbooks
  • Support for Ansible, Nornir, NAPALM, Netmiko playbooks
  • Unified but focus on network and security labs
  • Multi-user, multi-tenant, multi-role (e.g., student/teacher)
  • Easy scalability
  • API-first approach, with CLI and web interface

Lab Features:

  • Each lab is isolated by default.
  • Labs can be interconnected.
  • Labs can be shared between users.
  • A management network is deployed per lab.
  • Management network is hidden in topology.
  • Management network is reachable by all nodes.
  • A DHCP server is deployed per lab.
  • An Internet gateway can be deployed per lab.
  • A fake internet gateway can be deployed.
  • Labs are described by a human-readable YAML file.
  • Labs could contain an inventory compatible with Ansible.
  • Imported labs should allow selecting alternative templates if the existing ones are not available.
  • Labs could be signed by users.
  • Live changes (jitter, delay, interface up/down) should immediately reflect in the running lab.
  • Marketplace: A place where users and teachers can share labs and learning paths.
  • Automation: All relevant nodes within a lab should be reachable by automation software by default.
  • Packet capture: Users should be able to capture packets from any specific interface.
  • Scale-out: Labs could be run on multiple computing nodes.

Template Features:

  • Templates are described by a YAML file.
  • The descriptor specifies vendor, OS, version, management interface, credentials.
  • Vendor and OS fields should be defined to facilitate compatibility with external labs.
  • Plugins should be provided for node configuration.
  • Playbooks could be provided for configuring specific node features (interfaces, OSPF, etc.).
  • Templates are preconfigured with DHCP, user, and password.
  • Templates could be signed by users.

Link Features:

  • Links can be L1 or L2.
  • L1 are transparent bridges that forward any frame.
  • Bridges can connect a physical port to a lab to include physical devices (e.g., PLCs).

Node Features:

  • Nodes could be automatically configured via playbooks (e.g., IP addresses, loopbacks, OSPF, CDP, LLDP, etc.).
  • Users can send commands to multiple nodes.
  • Users can send commands via template (Jinja).

Scalability:

  • L1 links are intra-host.
  • L2 links can be inter-host and used to span a lab across multiple hosts.

Teaching Features:

  • Multi-tenancy: Each teacher can manage an independent environment.
  • Classes: Users are divided into classes within each tenant (class-level visibility).
  • Users should be able to start and possibly modify their lab (user-level visibility).
  • Shared access: Users could access the same running lab.
  • Design mode: Changing a lab should not affect running copies; any lab could be converted into a "template."
  • Solo mode: Non-teachers should be able to write and run labs without worrying about classes or students.
  • Content writer: Labs should include additional content (slides, video, etc.).
  • Auto-evaluation: Teachers could include scripts to auto-evaluate users.

Definitions:

  • Host: A system that runs nodes.
  • Lab: A topology that interconnects multiple nodes.
  • Node: A virtualized system, part of a lab, running on a host.
  • Link: A virtual network connection between nodes.
  • Template: The base image from which a node can be executed.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: Developing UNetLab has been one of the most rewarding hobbies I've ever had. I've met many interesting people, most of whom I'm still in touch with. Moreover, it has allowed me to understand how critical it is to maintain software used worldwide without disappointing users due to bugs. But sometimes, I still dream about developing UNetLab again.

docs.title: Proxmox optimizing virtualization
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner proxmox unetlab

During the development of the first version of UNetLab, I dedicated significant time to creating a flexible QEMU/KVM orchestrator. At that time, virtualization-ready images were rare. Choosing a specific QEMU version or parameter could determine the success or failure of virtualizing a particular device.

Years later, the landscape has changed completely: virtualization is almost always an option, as vendors use virtualized environments to create labs. Most vendors now release images for both VMware and QEMU/KVM.

However, IOU remains a topic of interest: a lightweight image simulating a Cisco IOS XE environment. We can think of IOU as a container that doesn’t use standard networking. It could potentially be transformed into a container, but that’s another story.

By foregoing IOU (and Dynamips), we can simplify virtualization management. Specifically, we can rely on an existing hypervisor. For years, I considered ESXi, but after the Broadcom acquisition, I explored other options. After analyzing various environments, including libvirt, I decided on Proxmox for several reasons:

  • It’s a type 2 hypervisor, allowing OS modifications if needed.
  • It provides REST APIs, which we need to verify.
  • It allows kernel modifications to simulate physical links.
  • It’s well-supported and under active development.
  • It’s open source.
  • It scales horizontally and supports VXLAN.
  • It natively supports LXC (though not Docker).

On paper, Proxmox seems the perfect base for UNetLab v3. However, during development, we aim to abstract the UNetLab-Proxmox interaction to allow hypervisor substitution without rewriting code.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
A key factor for UNetLab v3 is scalability. UNetLab v1 was designed for scale-up, i.e., increasing host resources, which is costly and limited.

In UNetLab v2, I considered implementing an MPLS-like network to simulate physical links between nodes on different hosts. This had two issues:

  • Slow performance, as packet handling was in user-space, not kernel-space.
  • Complexity, as writing a new network protocol was required.

For UNetLab v3, I plan to use VXLAN to extend networks between hosts. This has both advantages and disadvantages:

  • VXLAN is natively supported by hypervisors and OS.
  • VXLAN doesn’t allow physical link simulation (some frames are filtered).

The solution is to divide the problem:

  • L1 links, implemented as in UNetLab v1, will be intra-host only.
  • L2 links, implemented via VXLAN, will extend labs across multiple hosts.
  • On lab startup, an algorithm will define node groups within the same host and distribute them across hosts, allowing user modifications.

The complexity lies in the last point, but it’s theoretically feasible. The open question remains whether nodes can be moved between servers and how to manage this.

By following these principles and leveraging modern tools, UNetLab v3 aims to be a powerful, flexible, and scalable network emulator for the next generation of network professionals.

docs.title: Patching the Proxmox kernel
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced proxmox unetlab

Proxmox offers various constructs for building virtual networks. We'll focus on using bridges to emulate physical links, as we did in UNetLab v1.

Linux bridges handle frames differently:

  • Broadcast frames are forwarded to all ports.
  • Multicast frames are forwarded to a subset of ports.
  • Peer-to-peer frames are not forwarded.
  • All other frames are forwarded to all ports.

Key files in the Linux Kernel sources are br_input.c and br_sysfs_br.c.

In br_input.c, the br_handle_frame function decides whether to forward or discard frames based on the destination MAC address. Frames with destination 0x01 are always discarded. A mask called fwd_mask affects the function's outcome in some cases.

We aim to introduce the mask concept for the 0x01 case as well.

In br_sysfs_br.c, the set_group_fwd_mask function sometimes prevents evaluating the group_fwd_mask. We will modify this to always evaluate the mask.

With a modified kernel, you can control the /sys/class/net/vmbr1/bridge/group_fwd_mask mask to enable or disable forwarding any packet. Our modified kernel allows values up to 65535, forwarding any frame, achieving our goal.

Linux bridges handle frames differently:

  • Broadcast frames are forwarded to all ports.
  • Multicast frames are forwarded to a subset of ports.
  • Peer-to-peer frames are not forwarded.
  • All other frames are forwarded to all ports.
