In br_input.c, the br_handle_frame function decides whether to forward or discard frames based on the destination MAC address. Frames with destination 0x01 are always discarded. A mask called fwd_mask affects the function's outcome in some cases.

We aim to introduce the mask concept for the 0x01 case as well.

In br_sysfs_br.c, the set_group_fwd_mask function sometimes prevents evaluating the group_fwd_mask. We will modify this to always evaluate the mask.

With a modified kernel, you can control the /sys/class/net/vmbr1/bridge/group_fwd_mask mask to enable or disable forwarding any packet. Our modified kernel allows values up to 65535, forwarding any frame, achieving our goal.

docs.title: Compiling the Kernel
docs.text:
To compile a kernel for Proxmox, you'll need a system with Proxmox VE installed.

Install dependencies:

apt-get install -y git build-essential dh-make dh-python sphinx-common asciidoc-base bison dwarves flex libdw-dev libelf-dev libiberty-dev libnuma-dev libslang2-dev libssl-dev lintian lz4 python3-dev xmlto zlib1g-dev

Remove conflicting packages:

apt-get purge -y proxmox-headers\*

Check the installed kernel version:

uname -r

Find the commit titled "update ABI file for 6.8.4-2-pve" in the Proxmox Kernel sources. The corresponding commit is 4cab886f26f9c8638593b8c553996c97ca9acc21.

Clone the repository:

git clone git://git.proxmox.com/git/pve-kernel.git /usr/src/pve-kernel
cd /usr/src/pve-kernel

Checkout the specific version:

git checkout 4cab886f26f9c8638593b8c553996c97ca9acc21
make clean
make build-dir-fresh

Modify /usr/src/pve-kernel/Makefile, adding -unl to the EXTRAVERSION variable. Edit br_input.c and br_sysfs_br.c in /usr/src/pve-kernel/submodules/ubuntu-kernel/net/bridge.

Compile the kernel:

make

Install the newly compiled packages on each Proxmox host:

dpkg -i /usr/src/pve-kernel/unl.deb

docs.title: Enabling the Transparent Bridge
docs.text:
Activate the patch by modifying the mask for each bridge:

echo 65535 > /sys/class/net/br1/bridge/group_fwd_mask

docs.title: Updating the Patch
docs.text:
The unetlab-kernel repository contains updated scripts and precompiled packages. To update the patch:

  • Save original br_input.c and br_sysfs_br.c files to a safe location.
  • Modify files according to the latest patch.
  • Create a new patch using diff -Naur.
  • Update the patch.

Precompiled patches and packages are available on GitHub.

docs.title: Creating templates for Proxmox
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate proxmox unetlab

Let's prepare templates to generate nodes for our labs. We'll start with VyOS, an open-source router and firewall. VyOS is available as a rolling release and can be downloaded from GitHub in ISO format. In this example, we'll use the vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso image, downloaded to /usr/src on a Proxmox host.

The official documentation guides us on creating a VyOS node on Proxmox. We'll go through the steps to create a VyOS template and a basic lab with two interconnected VyOS nodes.

On my Proxmox host, I've added an external disk named unetlab for storing ISO images:

pvesh get /nodes/proxmox1/storage

pvesh is the CLI for using Proxmox's REST APIs. Learning to use it now will simplify our future interactions with Proxmox hosts via API.

Referencing the Proxmox documentation, we find the required location for the ISO file. Copy the downloaded file and import it:

cp /usr/src/vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso /var/tmp/pveupload-0001
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/storage/unetlab/upload -content iso -filename vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso -tmpfilename /var/tmp/pveupload-0001

Verify the ISO file is available:

pvesh get /nodes/proxmox1/storage/unetlab/content

Next, create and configure the virtual machine to:

  • Boot from the ISO image
  • Have a dedicated management network interface

Using parameters from the Proxmox documentation and the VyOS documentation:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu -tags unl,template -name template-vyos-vyos-202407171706 -vmid 9001 -cpu host -socket 1 -cores 1 -memory 2048 -scsihw virtio-scsi-single -scsi0 unetlab:2 -net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0 -serial0 socket -ostype other -cdrom unetlab:iso/vyos-1.5-rolling-202407171706-amd64.iso

We have established a naming and tagging standard for our Proxmox templates: each template will have a prefix, and every object will be tagged with unl and a specific tag relevant to the object.

Start the node and configure it via CLI:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/status/start

Access the console via the web interface or CLI:

qm terminal 9001

If the console is occupied, free it with:

killall socat

Default credentials are:

  • Username: vyos
  • Password: vyos

Install the OS on the disk and reboot:

install image
reboot

Configure the device with a management VRF and a DHCP-configured interface:

configure
set vrf name mgmt
set vrf name mgmt table 100
set interfaces ethernet eth0 vrf mgmt
set interfaces ethernet eth0 address dhcp
delete interfaces ethernet eth0 hw-id
commit
save

We configure only one network interface now; additional interfaces will be added when creating nodes from the template. For VyOS, note that each interface is initially assigned a specific MAC address; to use a node as a template, we remove this association with hw-id.

Exit the console and shut down the node:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/status/stop

Remove the no longer needed CD-ROM drive and convert the node to a template:

pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/config -delete cdrom
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/config -boot legacy=c
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/template

By following these steps, you've created a reusable VyOS template for Proxmox.

docs.title: Simulating an L1 link in Proxmox
Simulating an L1 link in Proxmox
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced proxmox unetlab

We now have all the elements needed to simulate an L1 link. Let's create a simple lab with two interconnected VyOS nodes.

docs.title: 1. Create an L1 network bridge
docs.text:
First, create a network bridge that will simulate the L1 link. We will start by defining a naming convention for our network components:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/network -iface unlbr1 -type bridge -autostart 1
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/network

docs.title: 2. Clone VyOS nodes from template
docs.text:
Next, clone two VyOS nodes from the template and connect a second network interface to the newly created bridge:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/clone -newid 10001 -full 0 -name node-vyos1
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/clone -newid 10002 -full 0 -name node-vyos2
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/config -tags unl,root
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10002/config -tags unl,root
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/config -net1 virtio,bridge=unlbr1
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10002/config -net1 virtio,bridge=unlbr1

docs.title: 3. Start the VyOS nodes
docs.text:
Start the two VyOS nodes:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/status/start
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10002/status/start

Wait a few minutes for the nodes to boot up and then configure the new network interfaces:

docs.title: 4. Configure network interfaces and enable LLDP
docs.text:
On each node, configure the new network interface and enable the LLDP protocol to validate the patch:

configure
set service lldp
set service lldp interface all
set interfaces ethernet eth1 address '192.168.0.1/24'
commit
save

docs.title: 5. Enable forwarding of all frames
docs.text:
To enable the forwarding of all frames, run the following commands:

echo 65535 > /sys/class/net/unlbr1/bridge/group_fwd_mask
echo 0 > /sys/devices/virtual/net/unlbr1/bridge/multicast_snooping

Each L1 link requires a manual command to enable the forwarding of all frames. Currently, this operation cannot be performed through the API, but we will revisit this in the future.

docs.title: 6. Verify connectivity
docs.text:
If everything is configured correctly, you should see the adjacent router using the LLDP protocol:

show lldp neighbors

Capability Codes: R - Router, B - Bridge, W - Wlan r - Repeater, S - Station
                  D - Docsis, T - Telephone, O - Other

Device    Local Port    Protocol    Capability    Platform                          Remote
Port
--------  ------------  ----------  ------------  --------------------------------  ------
--------------
vyos      eth1          LLDP        R             VyOS 1.5-rolling-202407171706     eth1

We can confirm that the two nodes see each other via the LLDP protocol, which is typically filtered by bridges.

docs.title: Testing stretched networks with Proxmox
docs.text: 04 August 2024

docs.title: Testing stretched networks with Proxmox
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese advanced proxmox unetlab

Let's explore how Proxmox's SDN functionality works. We'll use the SDN structure to implement extended L2 networks, enabling us to run labs across multiple hosts.

docs.title: Create an SDN Zone
docs.text:
First, create a zone:

pvesh create /cluster/sdn/zones -type=vxlan -zone=unlzone1 -peers=172.25.82.157,172.25.82.158 -ipam=pve
pvesh set /cluster/sdn/zones

In the peers list, add all the IP addresses of the Proxmox hosts.

docs.title: Create a Bridge Associated with the Zone
docs.text:
Next, create a bridge linked to the zone for connecting the nodes:

pvesh create /cluster/sdn/vnets -vnet=unlnet1 -tag=1000004 -zone=unlzone
pvesh set /cluster/sdn/zones

Then, associate the network with the nodes as shown in the previous steps.

If configured correctly, nodes running on different hosts should be able to ping each other, using both native VLAN and tagged VLAN.

docs.title: Design Considerations
docs.text:
From a design perspective, we need to decide how to manage zones and networks within UNetLab: should we create a single zone with all Vnets, or a zone for each Vnet?

According to the official documentation,) a zone defines a virtually separated network. The documentation lacks detail, so we need to understand the constructs created at the OS level.

When creating the zone, we specified the IP addresses of the Proxmox hosts sharing that zone. This configuration is written to /etc/pve/sdn/zones.cfg and generates the /etc/network/interfaces.d/sdn file. No network namespace configurations (ip netns) are present.

We can deduce that the zone is a Proxmox-defined structure that translates into VXLAN interfaces. Since UNetLab won't use L3 networks, we can use a single zone for the entire UNetLab cluster.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
During my initial test, the two VyOS nodes couldn't communicate. By connecting to the two Proxmox servers via SSH, we can see how the SDN configuration translates at the OS level.

Network interfaces of the nodes are associated with a bridge:

brctl show unlnet3

bridge name     bridge id               STP enabled     interfaces
unlnet3         8000.6659fe6b9723       no              tap10001i1
                                                        vxlan_unlnet3

The TAP interface belongs to the node, while the VXLAN interface allows communication with nodes on other hosts.

Check the forwarding table for frames with:

bridge fdb show | grep vxlan

66:59:fe:6b:97:23 dev vxlan_unlnet3 vlan 1 master unlnet3 permanent
66:59:fe:6b:97:23 dev vxlan_unlnet3 master unlnet3 permanent
00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan_unlnet3 dst 172.25.82.158 self permanent
ba:2f:72:71:47:0a dev vxlan_unlnet4 vlan 1 master unlnet4 permanent
ba:2f:72:71:47:0a dev vxlan_unlnet4 master unlnet4 permanent
00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan_unlnet4 dst 172.25.82.158 self permanent

The MAC addresses on the right should match the network interfaces of nodes running on the remote host. In my case, the remote VyOS node had its network interfaces reversed, resulting in an incorrect connection.

Further verification can be done by analyzing the traffic between hosts:

tcpdump -i vmbr0 -nn udp and port 4789

IP 192.168.0.1 > 192.168.0.3: ICMP echo request, id 35144, seq 2, length 64
13:02:10.899649 IP 172.25.82.158.46121 > 172.25.82.157.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000
IP 192.168.0.3 > 192.168.0.1: ICMP echo reply, id 35144, seq 2, length 64
13:02:11.900765 IP 172.25.82.157.35416 > 172.25.82.158.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000
IP 192.168.0.1 > 192.168.0.3: ICMP echo request, id 35144, seq 3, length 64
13:02:11.901642 IP 172.25.82.158.46121 > 172.25.82.157.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000
IP 192.168.0.3 > 192.168.0.1: ICMP echo reply, id 35144, seq 3, length 64
13:02:12.902939 IP 172.25.82.157.35416 > 172.25.82.158.4789: VXLAN, flags [I] (0x08), vni
1000000

docs.title: Lab modeling for UNetLab v3
docs.text: 13 September 2024

docs.title: Lab modeling for UNetLab v3
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

We’ve run a series of field tests to check if the idea we’re working on is feasible and functional. The results are positive, the APIs support most of the key features (but not all).

Our next step is to define and model the data structure of the lab environment.

One of UNetLab’s main issues was that users had to manually build a lab, node by node, setting up interfaces, addresses, and routing before getting a functional environment. We're addressing this by introducing two states:

  • HLL (High Level Lab): A rough outline of the lab in terms of nodes, links, and features.
  • LLL (Low Level Lab): A detailed lab generated from the HLL.

Below, we’ll describe the data structure. Full examples are available in the UNetLab repository.

docs.title: Nodes and Features
docs.text:
Here’s an example with 4 VyOS nodes configured with Loopback and OSPF on all interfaces:

nodes:
  - template: vyos-vyos
    prefix: R
    count: 4
    features:
      - loopback
      - ospf:area=0

Features reference specific Ansible playbooks that configure each node. Variables can be passed with :. The nodes will be named R1, R2, R3, and R4.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
The 4 nodes can be connected in a full-mesh:

topologies:
  - type: full-mesh
    match:
      - R

Or in a custom topology:

topologies:
  - type: defined
    links:
      - R1, R2, R3
      - R1, R4
      - R3, R4

You can also mix and match topologies:

topologies:
  - type: full-mesh
    match:
      - Site1R
  - type: full-mesh
    match:
      - Site2R
  - type: defined
    links:
      - Site1R1, Site2R1
      - Site1R2, Site2R2

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
Addressing is defined like this:

ipv4_addresses:
  - match: Loopback
    address: 192.168.0.1/16
    mask: 32
  - match: Ethernet
    address: 10.0.0.0/8
    mask: auto

Addressing is configured on an interface-by-interface basis, using the first match. The subnet mask can be set either manually or automatically. In the latter case, the interfaces are assigned as follows:

  • Loopback interfaces get a /32 subnet,
  • Tunnel interfaces get a /31 subnet,
  • Ethernet interfaces get the smallest subnet needed to cover all connected hosts.

To keep it simple, network allocation follows a sequential order based on the first available segment.

In the given example:

  • Loopback interfaces get an address starting from the 192.168.0.1/32 network,
  • Ethernet interfaces get an address starting from the 10.0.0.0 network with the smallest mask required for all expected addresses.

Additionally, interfaces not involved in the topology are disabled.

docs.title: From HLL to LLL
docs.text:
Once the user has defined the HLL, they can confirm and generate the detailed topology (or LLL). Any changes made to the HLL will regenerate the LLL, overwriting any customizations. However, it will be possible to modify the LLL, which from this point on becomes the only relevant version.

Here’s an example of what the LLL might look like:

lll:
  groups:
    - name: Nodes R (vyos-vyos)
      template: vyos-vyos
      match: R
      features:
        - loopback
        - ospf:area=0
  nodes:
    - id: 6964F62C-0376-4ECF-8F03-E1FEADB94194
      name: R1
      interfaces:
        Loopback0:
          ipv4_address: 192.168.0.1/32
        Ethernet1:
          ipv4_address: 10.0.0.0/31
        Ethernet2:
          ipv4_address: 10.0.0.2/31
        Ethernet3:
          ipv4_address: 10.0.0.4/31

Links could be generated like this:

links:
  - id: 9E510FC0-B9D6-459E-9EF0-9113607D2502
    name: R1:Ethernet1 - R2:Ethernet1
    interfaces:
      - node_id: 6964F62C-0376-4ECF-8F03-E1FEADB94194
        interface: Ethernet1
      - node_id: 210827C6-9E59-4CCE-80AC-FD294DDC205E
        interface: Ethernet1

docs.title: Customizations
docs.text:
Once the LLD has been generated, the user can customize it without altering the HLD, which is preserved for historical reasons.

Each node can be modified individually or through a group, with node-specific settings taking priority over group settings.

Links can be customized in terms of bandwidth, delay, and packet drop.

docs.title: Management Network
docs.text: The management network is mandatory: management interfaces are reserved and therefore not considered by the LLD.

docs.title: Internet Connectivity
docs.text: In this initial approach, we haven't included Internet connectivity. However, we can imagine a special node that, once connected to the topology, will enable Internet access.

docs.title: Lab Interconnection
docs.text:
In this first version, we haven't considered linking labs together. However, we can envision special shared links that allow multiple labs to interconnect.

Since each link references a virtual network, once a virtual network is defined, it can be attached to all labs using its UUID.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Any metadata describing the lab will be grouped under a specific key:

meta:
  author: Andrea Dainese
  name: Test Lab 1
  description: First test lab

docs.title: Working on a Lab
docs.text:
When a user wants to work on a specific lab (run or modify it), a copy with a unique UUID will be created. Depending on permissions, this copy can be read, modified, or executed. The user always works on the instance copy and never on the original.

Based on permissions, the user can save the copy by either overwriting the original or saving it as a new copy. Users running a copy will not experience any changes unless they reload it from the original.

Closing a lab essentially means deleting the instance copy and all associated files.

To make node names editable, each node is assigned a UUID. Interface names are static and depend on the node type (template).

docs.title: UNetLab v3 architecture
docs.text: 23 October 2024

docs.title: UNetLab v3 architecture
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

UNetLab's architecture involves several components that need to interact with each other and report task progress to the user. We can identify the following components:

  • The web interface allows users to interact with UNetLab, manage users, and labs.
  • Proxmox hosts manage the nodes and networks of the labs according to instructions received from users and notify the status of the nodes.
  • The orchestrator, which is the engine that manages tasks and input received from the user through the web interface and from the hosts via a specific agent.

docs.title: The orchestrator
docs.text:
At first glance, we can imagine a Redis server collecting input from users (via the web interface) and from hosts. The orchestrator receives messages from Redis and forwards them, transforming them, to the web interface or to agents running on the hosts.

In this sense, the orchestrator is a background daemon.

We can imagine two types of data stored in Redis:

  • Actions: for example, starting a specific node.
  • Messages: for example, a notification that a node was successfully started.

docs.title: The web interface
docs.text: The web interface is served through Django and receives user input, transforming it into tasks sent to the orchestrator via Redis. Similarly, it receives messages to notify users via Redis.

docs.title: The agent
docs.text:
On the Proxmox hosts, we can envision an agent running that:

  • Executes requested actions, such as starting a node.
  • Notifies the outcome of the requested actions.
  • Regularly reports the system's status (host, nodes, templates, networks...).
  • Executes actions not natively supported by Proxmox (see the previously mentioned L1 links).

Regarding system status notifications, we can imagine that the agent only reports actual changes to reduce the workload of the orchestrator and the web interface. If you recall, the old version of UNetLab performed continuous polling to check the status of nodes. This significantly burdened both the client-side web interface and the server-side resources.

We could also imagine that at regular intervals, a complete set of information is sent to avoid any discrepancies that might grow over time.

The system status should include:

  • Host status: reachability, resources used.
  • Data store status: available space, user quota usage.
  • Network status: which are available, type (L1, L2).
  • Node status: which are available, whether they are on or off, resource consumption, associated users, associated images.
  • Image status: which are available, their characteristics.

docs.title: Preparing a Proxmox cluster for UNetLab v3
docs.text: 30 September 2024

docs.title: Preparing a Proxmox cluster for UNetLab v3
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate proxmox unetlab

UNetLab requires a cluster with one or more correctly configured PVE hosts. This page contains all the commands needed to configure a PVE host.

docs.title: Install the custom kernel for UNetLab
docs.text:
To enable L1 links, UNetLab needs a kernel with a specific patch. The kernel and patch are released in the unetlab-kernel repository. You can either download the correct release or compile your own using the provided script.

To download the custom kernel, run the following commands:

cd /usr/src
export TAG=6.8.8-3
wget https://github.com/dainok/unetlab-kernel/releases/download/${TAG}/proxmox-headers-${TAG}-pve-unl_${TAG}_amd64.deb
wget https://github.com/dainok/unetlab-kernel/releases/download/${TAG}/proxmox-kernel-${TAG}-pve-unl_${TAG}_amd64.deb

Now, install the custom kernel:

apt-get update
apt-get install -y build-essential
dpkg -i proxmox--${TAG}-pve-unldeb

Once finished, reboot the host:

reboot

docs.title: Add nodes to the cluster
docs.text:
Create a cluster and add the current node:

pvesh create /cluster/config -clustername unetlab -nodeid 1

Retrieve the fingerprint value using the following command:

pvesh get /cluster/config/join -output-format json-pretty | grep pve_fp

Next, add the remaining hosts to the cluster by running the following command on each host:

pvesh create /cluster/config/join -fingerprint < *pve_fp* > -hostname < *primary ip* > -password < *rootpassword* >

Finally, verify that all nodes have been added:

pvesh get /cluster/config/nodes

docs.title: Configure a dedicated datastore
docs.text:
In this specific case, there is a separate disk to be dedicated to UNetLab. Let’s partition, format, and mount it:

echo "start=2048, type=83" | sfdisk /dev/sdb
mkfs -t ext4 /dev/sdb1
mkdir /unetlab
echo "/dev/sdb1 /unetlab ext4 defaults 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
mount /unetlab

Before proceeding, perform the same operation on any other Proxmox hosts.

Next, add the directory so it can be used as a datastore:

pvesh create /storage -storage unetlab -type dir -path /unetlab -shared 0 -nodes proxmox1,proxmox2 -content images,rootdir,iso,vztmpl

docs.title: Preparing VyOS image for UNetLab v3
docs.text: 30 October 2024

docs.title: Preparing VyOS image for UNetLab v3
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese intermediate proxmox unetlab

As our first image, we choose to use VyOS, which is publicly available on GitHub. We will work from a single host, and later we can distribute our image. Let's download the image to the host:

wget -O- https://github.com/vyos/vyos-nightly-build/releases/download/1.5-rolling-202409220007/vyos-1.5-rolling-202409220007-generic-amd64.iso > /var/tmp/pveupload-0000

The image name must strictly follow the regex /var/tmp/pveupload-[0-9a-f]+.

Upload the image to the unetlab datastore with the correct name:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/storage/unetlab/upload -content iso -filename vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.iso -tmpfilename /var/tmp/pveupload-0000

Delete the image from the temporary directory:

rm -f /var/tmp/pveupload*

docs.title: Preparing the Template
docs.text:
Next, let's create a temporary VM to install and configure VyOS:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu -cores 1 -cpu host -cdrom unetlab:iso/vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.iso,media=cdrom -memory 2048 -name template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007 -net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0 -ostype other -scsihw virtio-scsi-single -sockets 1 -tags "unl;template" -virtio0 unetlab:2,format=qcow2,backup=1,iothread=on -vmid 1000 -serial0 socket -vga none

In this case, we have disabled the graphical card and added a serial interface to be used as a terminal.

Start the virtual machine:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/status/start

At this point, access the Proxmox host's web interface. Log in with the user vyos and password vyos, then install the operating system onto the disk with the command:

install image

The installation will guide you through a few questions:

[...]
Would you like to continue? [y/N] y
What would you like to name this image? (Default: 1.5-rolling-202409220007)
Please enter a password for the "vyos" user:
Please confirm password for the "vyos" user:
What console should be used by default? (K: KVM, S: Serial)? (Default: S)
[...]
Which one should be used for installation? (Default: /dev/vda)
Installation will delete all data on the drive. Continue? [y/N] y
[...]
Would you like to use all the free space on the drive? [Y/n]
[...]
Which file would you like as boot config? (Default: 1)
[...]

Once the installation is complete, reboot the node with the reboot command.

As soon as the node is back online, let's configure it to be used by UNetLab. Specifically, we need to set up a management interface, ideally in a dedicated VRF:

configure
set vrf name mgmt
set vrf name mgmt table 100
set interfaces ethernet eth0 vrf mgmt
set interfaces ethernet eth0 address dhcp
set service ssh vrf mgmt
delete interfaces ethernet eth0 hw-id
commit
save

Shut down the node:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/status/shutdown

Remove the CDROM and set the boot order:

pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/config -delete cdrom
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/9001/config -boot legacy=c

Now convert the node into a template:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/template

docs.title: Verifying the Template
docs.text:
Before continuing, let's verify that the template works correctly. Create a node from the template and check that the first interface has an IP configured via DHCP, and that SSH access is possible with the username and password:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/clone -newid 10001 -full 0 -name node-vyos1
pvesh set /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/config -tags "unl;node;user_root" -net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0
pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/status/start

Once finished, shut down the node and delete it:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001/status/stop
pvesh delete /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/10001

If you notice that the template has issues, you can revert it back to a VM and reconfigure it.

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/qemu/1000/config -template 0

docs.title: Backup and export
docs.text:
Finally, create a backup:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox1/vzdump -storage local -vmid 1000 -mode stop

You can retrieve the file /var/lib/vz/dump/vzdump-qemu-1000-*.vma* which is the image of our template. This file can be used to recreate the template on other nodes. For simplicity, rename it to vzdump-qemu-template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.vma.

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
If the unetlab datastore is not shared among all hosts in the cluster, you can copy the backup to the other hosts:

scp /var/lib/vz/dump/template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.vma root@172.25.82.158:/var/lib/vz/dump

Then, import the backup, assigning a new ID to the template:

pvesh create /nodes/proxmox2/qemu -vmid 1001 -archive local:backup/vzdump-qemu-template-vyos-vyos-1.5-202409220007.vma

docs.title: Developing UNetLab v3 with AI (LLM)
docs.text:
Andrea Dainese beginner unetlab

UNetLab v3 is built on Django along with various other frameworks. I am not a professional developer, nor do I consider myself one, yet I’m often told that my prototypes are extremely useful, especially because I can build them in very short timeframes.

However, since software development is not my main job, my coding activities are irregular, and long breaks between projects often cause me to lose familiarity with the syntax. In the past, Google was my primary tool: I constantly searched for code snippets and constructs just to recall the correct syntax. Using official documentation, Googling for suggestions, and searching for examples to solve specific problems was a very time-consuming process.

With the advent of “artificial intelligence”, I experimented with different approaches until I found a more efficient workflow that I am now using successfully.

docs.title: ChatGPT for Code Generation
docs.text:
A couple of years ago, I started using ChatGPT to directly generate the code I needed. My prompts were along the lines of:

Create a Python function using Netmiko to connect to a Cisco device, elevate privileges, retrieve the MAC address table, parse it with TextFSM, and return a dictionary where the keys are interface names and the values are lists of MAC addresses.

At the time, the results were almost always subpar: the generated code often included fictional functions and generally didn’t work.

Adapting the generated code took longer than writing it from scratch.

Moreover, for my needs, describing what I want in detail takes significant time, converting my ideas into descriptive text always leads to incomplete or oversimplified instructions.

docs.title: Copilot in Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
About a year ago, I tried a second approach: following a colleague’s suggestion, I enabled GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code and started using it as a coding assistant. The experience was insightful because it made me reflect on my own workflow.

At first, there was a “WOW” effect: Copilot seemed to understand what I needed and proactively suggested code snippets. I no longer had to write prompts, the interaction felt more natural.

However, I soon realized that Copilot’s constant suggestions were disrupting my mental flow.

When I code, I enter a focused mental state where I translate my ideas into code, following a “red thread” of logic as I go. Copilot’s suggestions would interrupt this state and trigger my critical-thinking mode, since each suggestion needs to be evaluated in context.

Switching back and forth between these two mental modes was exhausting. At some point, I began to subconsciously trust Copilot’s suggestions, losing control over my own code.

There was a specific incident where I had to debug a faulty function. Copilot suggested a fix that looked perfect, and I trusted it. I adapted the rest of the code based on that function, only to discover an hour later that Copilot’s suggestion contained a structural flaw, invalidating all subsequent modifications.

I lost an hour and had to spend another hour dismantling and rewriting everything correctly.

That’s when I understood what was happening, disabled Copilot, and returned to my usual workflow.

I wrote a LinkedIn post about it, expecting a flame war, but instead received valuable feedback, mostly about the way I approach coding.

Still, as mentioned earlier, programming is only a side activity for me, required for building prototypes that will later be industrialised by others. It doesn’t make sense for me to formalise a “proper” development workflow, others will always do it better than I can.

docs.title: Building Complete Apps with Replit
docs.text:
More recently, new generative tools have emerged, promising to build entire applications. Many testimonials claim they were able to create fully functional prototypes in just a few hours. Curious but skeptical, I decided to try Replit.

I asked it to generate a Django app for managing firewall rules. As I mentioned, fully describing a software project is challenging, especially during the prototyping phase, when requirements are incomplete and feasibility is still uncertain.

I wasn’t looking for a finished product, but rather a starting structure, a skeleton with models, views, and templates already set up.

Initially, Replit generated a Flask app. While I appreciate Flask, I prefer Django for larger, more complex projects. I asked Replit to convert the app to Django. It replaced some code and showed me a preview of the requested app, suggesting it was working correctly in the Replit backend.

The reality was different: the code was a hybrid of Flask, Django, and non-existent functions, completely non-functional.

There’s also the infamous case of a similar service, Builder.ai, which turned out to be powered by a team of human developers behind the scenes, essentially a scam to attract millions in funding.

docs.title: ChatGPT as a Tutor
docs.text:
Recently, I received an important piece of advice: use LLMs as mentors, asking for guidance, not code. I greatly respect the person who suggested this, so I gave it a try.

Using an LLM as a tutor means asking how to do something, not to do it. Specifically, I started asking:

  • How to achieve a specific feature in Django.
  • Where a specific function is used in Django.
  • What approaches exist to solve a particular problem.

This approach has proven effective because:

  • I stay focused until I hit a specific issue requiring further analysis.
  • I can ask targeted questions without worrying about edge cases (I handle them myself).
  • I can take only what I need, adapt code and style, and integrate it coherently.
  • Most importantly, I get a single interface for documentation, examples, and community knowledge.

Over the last two months, this method allowed me to resume work on UNetLab v3, stalled for over a year, and make significant progress. I implemented WebSockets, replaced RQ with Celery, and built robust APIs with comprehensive error handling.

docs.title: How LLMs Work
docs.text:
It’s important to understand how an LLM works. I’m not the best person to provide a full technical explanation, but I can share my perspective.

In simple terms, LLMs are statistical models that generate outputs based on input patterns and probabilistic associations. They don’t think or understand. The concept of “thinking” is arguably philosophical, and I believe computers will never truly possess it, as thought is not purely mechanical.

LLMs also don’t “hallucinate”, they simply produce text without any concept of reality. Reality cannot be derived from statistical affinity.

Using LLMs (even as tutors) requires keeping this in mind:

  • The output must always be verified.
  • The output style can vary (lack of consistency).

I’ve noticed that LLM-generated code may alternate between single and double quotes, may or may not include comments, may mix snake_case with camelCase, and sometimes uses outdated or imaginary functions.

docs.title: Reverse Engineering
docs.text:
On rare occasions, I’ve had to read the source code of a framework to understand its behavior or fix specific bugs. Reverse engineering is extremely time-consuming, especially when the code is highly optimized.

Sometimes I’ve used LLMs to explain the purpose of a particular function. Occasionally I’ve found useful insights, but often I haven’t.
